stories.Headline: Meta's reported humanoid robot tie-up with Fourier spotlights China-US robotics complementarity: expert
stories.Summary:
Meta built a humanoid robot prototype with the Chinese company Fourier in about three months, according to a report by The Information that other outlets picked up on Sunday. The robot is code named Max, stands about 1.5 meters tall and runs on Nvidia's Jetson Thor chip. It has a screen that mimics facial expressions, built-in speakers and five-fingered hands for picking up small objects. Meta's robotics team traveled to China for the work, and Li-Chen Miller, Meta's vice president of product for robotics, spent almost two months at Fourier's factory in Shanghai. Fourier told the Global Times on Monday that any further updates would be shared through official channels, and the partnership has not been formally confirmed by the Chinese company.

Work on a second version, Max 2, began in September, and it is due to get a new torso, better hands, a projector and extra sensors to help it handle stairs. Meta has no plans to sell either version, according to Tech Times. Meta recruited a robotics supplier development engineer in Shanghai in September and a product design engineer for its Robotics Studio in Shenzhen in October, public job postings showed. Fourier was founded in Shanghai in 2015, began with rehabilitation robots and unveiled its third-generation humanoid, the GR-3, in August 2025. Tech Times reported that Meta acquired the San Diego startup Assured Robot Intelligence in May 2026.

Chen Jing, a vice president of the Technology and Strategy Research Institute, told the Global Times that Meta has strong AI research through models such as Llama and Muse but hardware manufacturing remains a relative weakness. He said Fourier has proven mass-production engineering expertise and much lower product costs than US counterparts, which would explain why Meta turned to it. He said China has the world's most complete robotics industrial chain and that mass-production ramp-up there is significantly faster. He also said US companies hold clear advantages in AI and large-language models, that collaboration letting each side use its strengths is a natural progression, and that so-called decoupling is unrealistic.

Tech Times reported that the US government has formally determined that Chinese-made humanoid robots pose unacceptable national security risks, and it said Fourier operates under Chinese law. The same article said Meta's CTO Andrew Bosworth announced a dedicated humanoid team in a February 2025 internal memo, and that the team is led by Marc Whitten. It also said Chinese manufacturers held 97 percent of humanoid shipments in the first half of 2026, with AGIBOT at roughly 44 percent and Unitree at about 31 percent. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported work on Max 2.

stories.Headline: Clark Launches Clerks—Autonomous AI Audit Employees That Join a CPA Firm’s Team
stories.Summary:
Clark launched Clerks on Nov. 2, 2026, according to the articles. Clerks are autonomous AI employees that perform audit work for CPA firms, and each one is assigned to an engagement the way a staff auditor would be. They review documents, perform tests and prepare workpapers. When something is missing, a Clerk requests it from the client, tracks the response and picks the work back up when the information arrives, without anyone prompting it again. Clark is based in New York City and was formerly known as uiAgent.

Clark also announced an $11 million seed round on Nov. 2, led by Touring Capital, with participation from returning investors Marathon Management Partners, Rerail and Sofeon Ventures. Including the $5 million round Marathon Management Partners led in September 2025, the financing brings Clark's total funding to $16 million. Clerks run on Material Intelligence, Clark's AI operating system, which combines an agent harness, document processing and a multi-layered memory system modeled on human memory. Licensed CPAs make the professional judgments, review the work and sign the opinion. Clark says it offers a 100% accuracy guarantee and a peer review guarantee.

Enes Witwit, founder and CEO of Clark, said that for as long as people have kept accounts, someone has had to check them, and that today that checking happens once a year, long after the decisions it was meant to inform. He said the Clerks do not sleep, stay on the engagement, chase what is missing and keep the work moving between the moments an auditor looks at it. He said they work alongside auditors today, and that Clark is building toward fully autonomous audit employees and toward an economy whose claims are verified as they happen, so fraud and waste are caught while the money is still there. Priya Saiprasad, co-founder and general partner at Touring Capital, said assurance is fundamentally a trust business, and that AI creates an opportunity to expand what CPA firms can accomplish without compromising that trust.

Clark says it measures success not by how many alerts its AI produces, but by how much time auditors no longer spend chasing documents and how much more they spend on questions that deserve their judgment. The company says it will use the funding to expand its senior team across product, engineering and sales, bring Clerks to more firms and more types of engagements, help CPA firms extend their audit services into government, and build toward fully autonomous audit employees. Clark is also working toward continuous monitoring that keeps findings current between audits, with each finding stating what it covers and when it was last checked. The company said the goal is for a firm to tell its client, a regulator or the public not just what was true at year-end, but what is true now.

stories.Headline: Students walk out to protest AI, Sen. Heinrich’s bill over environmental concerns
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 27, University of New Mexico students held a walkout outside Scholes Hall to protest artificial intelligence data center development and to demand transparency and inclusion in the university's AI governance, then marched two miles to Sen. Martin Heinrich's office, according to the Daily Lobo. The walkout was one of several in the state that day, with students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe and community members in Las Cruces protesting at the same time. Organizers from Youth United for Climate Crisis Action criticized Heinrich's newly introduced Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which they said could loosen environmental protections and fast-track data center development. Protesters chanted against Project Jupiter, the hyperscale AI data center, and against Heinrich. Students from UNM Leaders for Environmental Action and Foresight wrote a letter to UNM leadership about the rise of AI on campus.

The letter demands public disclosure of all financial and institutional relationships with Big Tech, guaranteed meaningful student and community participation in AI governance, protection of students' right to refuse generative AI in their education, and investment in education about the political economy of AI. According to the bill summary, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act aims to reform certain federal environmental review and permitting processes to expedite a wide range of project types, with an emphasis on energy-related projects, including data center development. Acoma Pueblo Gov. Charles Riley said the bill rewrites laws that protect cultural resources, water and communities, and that it threatens the National Historic Preservation Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar Jr. said Heinrich, when asked whether he was amenable to any amendments, answered no and would continue to push the bill forward, and that Heinrich walked out in the middle of prayers at a meeting with Pueblo governors.

UNM Director of Communication Steve Carr confirmed the university received the letter and said UNM's AI Steering Committee is conducting listening sessions with students, faculty and staff to inform recommendations for AI governance and institutional practices. YUCCA organizer Zephyr Jaramillo said the bill would strip environmental protections that communities across the state depend on. YUCCA organizer Jonathan Juarez called it one of the most dangerous attacks on environmental protections and community power in generations and said it guts environmental review and weakens protections for water, relatives and sacred sites. The Daily Lobo reached out to Heinrich's office multiple times but did not hear back in time for publication. Aguilar said the Pueblo governors are going on offense to stop the bill and urged the audience to reach out to Congress to stop it.

At the University of Missouri, students and professors have raised concerns about AI's growing role on campus through the introduction of the AI Use Scale and Show-Me AI, according to KOMU. Nicole Monnier, a teaching professor of Russian on the Academic Affairs Committee and the General Education Task Force, said she worries about suspicion that faculty use AI to generate assignments, students use it to complete them and faculty use it again to assess them. Drew Bufalo, a biology undergraduate and tutor, helped found Students for Human Intelligence at the start of the 2026 spring semester to give students a platform to voice their opinions. Bufalo said the group has two main goals, educating students and faculty on the dangers and uses of AI and working with administration to push for more restrictive AI policies. Logan Gee, the group's social media manager, said it is all about finding a balance and there should never be a world where AI outweighs the human elements of a classroom or school.

stories.Headline: Smugglers Reportedly Pair Top-Tier HBM With Throwaway Server Chips To Dodge U.S. Export Controls, Then Melt Them Apart In China
stories.Summary:
A report from The Information, summarized by Wccftech and TechRadar on November 3, 2026, describes how smugglers are moving high-bandwidth memory (HBM) made by Samsung and SK hynix into China despite U.S. export controls. The scheme is run by a man in his 40s who is fluent in Chinese and Korean and has experience in the Korean semiconductor industry. His company is on paper an ordinary chip design firm, but it deliberately designs processors so cheap and weak that no data center would buy them, which gives it a reason to order top-tier HBM. Packaging firms in Taiwan, South Korea and Southeast Asia bond the memory to the processors, and the packages are declared under the processor's classification code and shipped to Hong Kong.

The trick exploits a gap in the December 2024 U.S. rules, which exempted HBM already integrated into logic chip products. Because the package's computing capability is judged by the processor rather than the memory, it falls below the restricted threshold. From Hong Kong the packages are reportedly carried into mainland China in luggage, car trunks, and the bags of toll couriers and daily commuters. Once in China, workshops run by accomplices heat the packages until the solder melts, detach the memory stacks, and discard the processors. The process is delicate, since heating too quickly or too slowly can warp or crack the stacks, but smugglers accept the failure rate because of the profits.

The separated memory goes to a chip broker in Shenzhen who is in his early 20s and has three years in the trade. He reportedly got his start at a chip company, where he built contacts who know how to extract memory from legitimate Samsung and SK hynix supply chains. He said HBM3E that sold for a few hundred dollars a year ago now costs about $4,000 a stack. Since one AI chip package needs six to eight stacks, the memory alone would cost $24,000 to $32,000 before the chip, server and power are added. He does not accept that he is a smuggler and believes he is contributing to his country.

The report says China's own HBM development is progressing slowly, so smuggled memory is currently the best alternative. It also notes that NVIDIA's top-tier B300, which is on the U.S. export control list, has somehow ended up in China. Chinese tech commentator AB Kuai.Dong summarized the report for his followers on X, describing the decoy chips as clunky processors and calling the arrangement a compliant export. Wccftech rated the report 55% plausible, citing strong sourcing but limited corroboration.

stories.Headline: Copyright Infringement Lawsuit Against OpenAI Draws More than 50 (Very Illuminating) Amicus Briefs
stories.Summary:
In re OpenAI Copyright Infringement Litigation is a consolidated case that combines more than a dozen major AI lawsuits, including cases filed by the Authors Guild and news organizations such as the New York Times. By the October 30 deadline, the court overseeing the case received 51 amicus briefs from publisher and author associations, individual creators and journalists, copyright scholars, tech groups, and some U.S. legislators. Amicus briefs let parties who are not part of a case, with the court's permission, weigh in on the litigation. In cross-motions for summary judgment filed last month, the plaintiffs argued that OpenAI committed copyright infringement by copying works, including from pirated sources, to train its models, and that its outputs can also be infringing. OpenAI's attorneys countered that its copying for training qualifies as fair use and that its outputs are not infringing.

Of the 51 briefs, 26 support the plaintiffs, 18 support the defendants, and eight are neutral. A final round of briefs is due on November 6, after which oral arguments will be set before judge Sidney H. Stein. On September 4, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a Statement of Interest urging the court to find that using copyrighted works for AI training is fair use. In October, judge Stein struck from the evidence a study suggesting AI books were displacing human-written works, after OpenAI attorneys argued the author failed to disclose a conflict over funding; the author denies the conflict, and the plaintiffs did not oppose the motion to strike.

The Association of American Publishers, CCC, IBPA, and STM Publishers said in their brief that copyright goals are undermined when fair use authorizes uncompensated appropriation of creative labor where licensing is practical and commercially reasonable. Ken Burns said large language models copied transcripts of his films and perhaps companion books without his permission, and that copycat filmmakers use the outputs to make competing films at far lower cost. WME said it comes not as an opponent of AI but as a participant in the licensing market, and that its position is that AI use of creative materials should be licensed, not stopped. Members of Congress responding to the DOJ's Statement of Interest called it breathtaking in scope and said it proposes what is in effect a blanket exemption that would preclude every copyright claim within the ambit of training LLMs.

On the defendants' side, Authors Alliance addressed only whether so-called market dilution is a cognizable form of harm under the Copyright Act, calling the theory a radical departure from settled copyright law. Kevin Kelly said a ruling for the plaintiffs on fair use would grant them far more than the limited monopoly Congress intended and would hinder new technologies and new works. EFF said the Constitution gives Congress the role of adjusting copyright law for new technologies, and that the court should apply well-established precedents that favor fair use here. Tim Hwang and Samuel Roland of the Foundation for American Innovation filed a proposed amicus brief supporting OpenAI, arguing that under Google LLC v. Oracle, courts may consider public benefits that copying enables, including the national-security value of capabilities that enable new analysis and software.

stories.Headline: China invests heavily in embodied AI for robotics
stories.Summary:
Chinese companies are moving resources away from building humanoid robot hardware and toward software that lets robots understand their surroundings and learn tasks without being programmed for each job. This field is called embodied AI, and it has set off an investment boom. In the first half of 2026, Chinese embodied AI companies raised 93.5 billion yuan, or $13 billion, across 322 deals, according to the research firm ITjuzi. That was five times the amount raised a year earlier.

The money is increasingly going to specialist developers of robot intelligence as well as to manufacturers. Dermot McGrath, founder of the Shanghai consultancy ZenGen Labs, said robot makers have concluded that margins will come from the brain rather than the hardware as competition pushes hardware prices down. Spirit AI co-founder Gao Yang said the brain is indeed the weakest link in the complete robotics stack. The sector has opened a new front in US-China tech rivalry, with American companies leading in some advanced robot AI systems.

Chinese developers hope their manufacturing strength and access to real-world training data will help them challenge US competitors, according to Reuters interviews with founders and executives at five Chinese robotics firms and with analysts. Specialist startups X Square, Galaxea and Spirit AI have each reached valuations of roughly $3 billion, according to company disclosures. X Square co-founder and COO Yang Qian said the aim is for robots to shift from being driven by code to being driven by common sense. Hong Kong-listed UBTech advertised a chief scientist position with compensation of up to 124 million yuan, or $18 million, including equity and benefits.

Companies are collecting training data in different ways. Spirit AI has hired around 1,000 people to record everyday and industrial activities, ACE Robotics uses wearable sensors to capture workers' movements, and Ant Group's Robbyant trained a model on 160,000 hours of material. DexForce uses computer-generated environments and says it can prepare some industrial tasks within 6 to 8 hours. Chinese firms also face shortages of advanced Nvidia chips due to US export controls, and Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said GPT-7, if released next year, could bring robotics its own ChatGPT moment.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act: New Disclosure Requirements for AI-Generated Advertising
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania enacted the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act after Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806 on October 22, 2026. The bill became Act 99 of 2026 and sets a disclosure requirement for advertisers who use synthetic content in ways that create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of advertised goods or services. The law defines synthetic content as images, video, audio clips, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated, and its definition of AI includes generative AI. It does not require disclosure every time an advertiser uses AI, because the duty is tied to content that creates a false impression.

The law takes effect 60 days after enactment, which is December 21, 2026. A disclosure must be clear and conspicuous, appearing in a size, color, contrast, location, duration, and volume that make it noticeable, readable, understandable, and audible. It must be in the language the consumer uses, must not contradict nearby information, and must appear the first time the synthetic content is shown, in the same medium, and, where technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or very hard to remove. The law excludes content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, or criticism, and content limited to text.

The Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney can seek an injunction when a prohibited practice is occurring or about to occur and proceedings would serve the public interest. They can also bring a civil action, and a court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus actual attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not expressly create a private right of action, and it says disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. The articles say businesses should review consumer-facing ads that use AI-generated or significantly AI-modified images, videos, and audio, and should check the controls used by advertising agencies and third-party marketing vendors.

The articles describe the law as narrower than a general AI transparency mandate and as another state-level requirement in the evolving legal framework for generative AI in commercial communications. They say the most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, or endorsement. Businesses should not assume that a disclosure buried in fine print or added after the content has already been presented will suffice. The articles say reviewing advertising practices and putting disclosure controls in place before the December 21 effective date would be a prudent compliance measure.

stories.Headline: Ex-Legorans Bag $2.4m For Real Estate AI Native
stories.Summary:
Cem Ucan and Kieran John Keenan, former employees of Legora, raised a pre-seed round for their new AI-native law firm Athena, which focuses on commercial real estate. The round was led by a16z Speedrun and was announced on November 3, 2026. One article reports the amount as $2.4 million, while the other gives $2.5 million. Athena launched two months before the announcement and had already signed 22 clients.

Athena's proprietary AI agents work alongside experienced transactional attorneys at its affiliated law firm, Athena Circle, to produce complex deal documents in hours at a fraction of traditional cost. The firm advises on commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing, covering purchase agreements, due diligence, loan documents and closings. It charges a fixed fee per transaction, typically 30 to 50 percent less than clients paid on recent deals. On an early transaction, the team turned around a purchase agreement in under 48 hours, which the client called its fastest turnaround. In its first six weeks, Athena cut attorney review time by more than 70 percent.

Ucan said the AI works hand in hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that move deals forward. Keenan said he measures progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent's work and confidently stand behind it, noting that a draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Troy Kirwin, partner at a16z Speedrun, said clients will still want experienced professionals who take responsibility for the work as AI becomes more capable. L. Miguel Arce, CEO at Mox, a Texas-based multifamily real estate company, said the system learns from every deal and that speed only matters if the work is quality.

The founders met at Legora, where they saw the potential of AI and the limitations of selling it to traditional law firms. Ucan had spent years in Big Law, at one point billing 3,000 hours annually, before moving into legal innovation at Baker McKenzie and Legora. Keenan studied law before building an automated legal reasoning system at his own startup, and José Braz, who developed Legora's legal research agent, joined as founding engineer. The founders expect refinancing pressure from commercial properties acquired in 2021 and 2022, whose three-to-five-year loans are now approaching maturity, to drive a new wave of transactions. Athena plans to expand across property types, geographies and eventually other areas of transactional law.

stories.Headline: ​The Case For Analog Work Verification In An AI World
stories.Summary:
Mark Giordono, the CEO of Destination Imagination, wrote a Forbes Business Council post published on November 3, 2026, arguing that analog verification of work matters more in the age of AI. He pointed to a white paper by a former executive dean for administration at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and a former deputy dean of the Yale School of Engineering and Applied Science, which argued that AI makes it harder for universities to verify whether students have genuinely acquired the skills their degrees certify. Giordono said it is necessary to know whether a business partner or employee can actually do a certain thing or whether AI tools are doing the work for them, and he compared the latter to a modern workplace version of Cyrano de Bergerac. He also cited a 2025 preprint posted to arXiv, in which researchers examined the effects of using an LLM to write essays and noted that excessive reliance on AI-driven solutions may contribute to cognitive atrophy.

Giordono described several human-centered, interactive methods for verifying work. The first is live meetings with Socratic back-and-forth, held virtually or in person and one-on-one with a manager, to surface the assumptions, thought processes and reasoning behind employees' proposals, decisions and deliverables. A similar method is a thesis defense strategy, in which every deliverable comes with a live explanation of the thought process behind it. He also suggested roleplay and practice tasks, especially during hiring, orientation and promotion preparation, and a live-task method in which candidates complete sample tasks on the spot. He cited a Wall Street Journal report from September 2026 that corporate restructurings and AI use have automated away many repetitive tasks junior staffers used to do, and that some companies, including EY, have designed simulations to let junior staff practice asking clients for information or confronting a co-worker about a missed deadline.

Giordono said he still sees value in digital assessments such as AI-powered evaluations and online aptitude tests, which can be easier to administer at scale and can promote consistency. But he warned that relying on them exclusively risks overlooking qualities such as creative thinking, and he cited research published in 2026 by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence that found substantial evidence of racial disparities in AI-based candidate screening. He said analog assessments can give a more holistic view and facilitate connection, but without clear evaluation criteria they can leave room for appearance-based judgments and bias and can disadvantage people with different communication styles. He recommended steps such as auditing algorithms, establishing clear evaluation criteria and holding regular one-on-one meetings instead of high-stakes group meetings, and he said the biggest risk mitigation step is balance, using both approaches thoughtfully to assess not just the work people produce but also their understanding of it, their skills and the reasoning behind their decisions.

He said firm-defined policies and playbooks guide the AI, a unified audit log tracks every action, and the accountant makes the final call. Diana Williams, vice president of Product for Accountants, demonstrated the latest additions to Intuit Accountant Suite. Wyatt Jenkins, senior vice president of Mid-Market Product, outlined four industry editions for Intuit Enterprise Suite, with Construction and Manufacturing in beta and Nonprofit and Franchise in pilot.

stories.Headline: Is Training an AI Model Infringing? Tulane Law Professor Brian Frye Breaks Down AI's Legal Battles
stories.Summary:
More than 100 copyright infringement lawsuits are pending against AI companies, and more are expected. Most of them claim that training an AI model on copyrighted works is infringing. Tulane Law Professor Brian L. Frye, an intellectual property and copyright law scholar, recently filed an amicus brief in the consolidated OpenAI copyright infringement litigation, New York Times v. OpenAI. He explained the legal issues at stake and how they could shape the future of artificial intelligence.

AI companies train their generative models on datasets that may include billions or even trillions of works, many protected by copyright. Copyright owners say training is infringing because AI companies must make copies to train their models, which then generate competing works. AI companies respond that training is a fair use, because it uses the works for the transformative purpose of creating models that generate new works. Frye said both sides see the dispute as existential, which is why so many lawsuits have been filed, defended vigorously, and joined by third parties filing amicus briefs.

Frye wrote the brief with Ron Suskind, a Pulitzer-prize winning journalist and filmmaker, and the CEO of a small AI company that created a model intended for journalists. The brief argues that training an AI model on copyrighted newspaper articles does not harm the market for or value of those articles, because their primary value lies in attribution, not reproduction. It says newspapers are really selling their brand, not individual articles, so AI companies can mitigate harm by attributing output to its sources, which would drive new readers and revenue to newspapers. Frye said neither party can admit that compromise is possible, for fear of compromising its litigation position, and that the court should focus on the public interest by requiring a compromise that benefits the parties and the public.

Frye said the law is all in a muddle, with only a few courts having ruled on the merits, disagreeing among themselves. Two district courts held that training an AI model is a transformative use of its training data, but both held it might harm the market for or value of the copyrighted works, in different ways and for different reasons. The Third Circuit held that training a non-generative AI model on legal headnotes to create a competing legal research tool is not fair use at all, but its reasoning is widely criticized. Frye said it is inevitable that courts will eventually hold that training an AI model is non-infringing, probably as fair use, but likely not until a case reaches the Supreme Court, and he is confident the Supreme Court will eventually agree, noting the Department of Justice already sent a letter to the district court in the OpenAI case essentially arguing it would be in the national interest to find training is fair use.

stories.Headline: Humans Matter, too: Amazon Robotics, Anthropic and Duckbill Leaders on the Future of AI
stories.Summary:
A panel of industry experts gathered at WBUR CitySpace in Boston on October 29 to discuss findings from the latest Bentley-Gallup Business in Society Report, including Americans' lack of trust in businesses to use AI responsibly. The event, titled The Business of AI: Opportunity, Trust and What Comes Next, was moderated by Shirley Leung, a columnist and associate editor at The Boston Globe. The panelists were Tye Brady, chief technologist at Amazon Robotics; Meghan Verena Joyce, co-founder and CEO at Duckbill; and Richard Tibbetts, former engineering manager at Anthropic. The report found that young Americans ages 18 to 29 are the biggest skeptics, with most in that group not trusting businesses to use AI responsibly, the highest share of any age group. The event drew about 60 attendees, including Bentley students, and included networking, a panel discussion and a Q&A session.

The panelists agreed that humans will continue to play a big role in AI. Tibbetts said the job should be broken down to identify which parts can be improved with AI, and that successful projects come from a specific understanding of the job and a willingness to reshape it as a hybrid between human experts and AI that automates some of the toil. Brady said technology succeeds when it solves a problem that helps people do their jobs safer and more productively, and that there is no substitute for humans and natural intelligence. Joyce said putting technology into the world without a human in the loop is a technology in search of a purpose, and that it is the company's job to evaluate that on behalf of consumers and deliver genuine value. The report also found that the lack of trust Americans have in businesses to use AI responsibly decreased from last year.

The day opened with remarks from Bentley President E. LaBrent Chrite, who said that as businesses race to take advantage of AI, leaders must address concerns about how the technology is created and deployed. Gallup Senior Partner Stephanie Marken followed with an overview of the survey findings, emphasizing the need to consider the various applications of AI when it comes to trust, such as driving a car or helping with learning versus recommending individuals for an employer to hire. Joyce said the biggest gift to give children and students is a fearlessness for change, and that the ability to lean into change and be an optimistic leader is the most important thing. The article does not say what happens next beyond the event itself.

The hackathon ended with teams presenting solutions to a panel of judges.

stories.Headline: White House: AI Vetting Framework Still a Secret
stories.Summary:
The White House is withholding its full frontier artificial intelligence review framework after a nonprofit group sued for its release. The Office of the National Cyber Director told Protect Democracy in a letter on Friday that it would withhold all 60 pages of records it found in response to the group's Freedom of Information Act request, including the seven-page framework itself. The office cited exemptions covering national security and confidential commercial information. The letter arrived on the Oct. 30 deadline that federal attorneys accepted as part of an open records lawsuit filed by Protect Democracy in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

The nonprofit had withdrawn a motion for a preliminary injunction and agreed to seek only four categories of records. These were substantively unredacted copies of the framework, the participation terms given to companies joining the Gold Eagle AI vulnerability clearinghouse, the list of individuals and entities deemed trusted partners, and records showing what legal authority the government relied on for both programs. The government also committed to producing a Vaughn index, a document-by-document accounting of what it held back and why, by the same date. A separate nonprofit, Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, said Monday that the government told it late Friday the full document would stay secret on national security and other grounds.

Protect Democracy argued in its September complaint that the White House declined to disclose the framework's contents, participants or legal basis even while acknowledging that the framework is not classified. The complaint also cited the July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing sandbox and breached Hugging Face, arguing that outside testers cannot evaluate whether federal reviews account for that kind of failure. LASST wrote that the public should not have to sue to find out how the government reviews powerful AI models before they are released. The group said the government had told a court on Oct. 23 that it had found the framework and would turn over whatever was not exempt by Oct. 30.

President Donald Trump created the review process through a June 2 executive order that lets developers voluntarily give the government access to covered frontier models for up to 30 days before releasing them to other trusted partners. The National Security Agency holds primary responsibility for deciding which models qualify, using classified benchmarks for advanced cyber capabilities, and the order explicitly rules out mandatory licensing or preclearance. The White House has said it completed the framework by the order's Aug. 1 deadline and discussed it with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and other developers, but it declined to make the document public. The administration also has not identified the companies participating in Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse launched in July to coordinate patches for vulnerabilities uncovered by AI models.

stories.Headline: Researchers say LLMs can be good at natively reading and writing neural network weights; GPT-6 Astra edited Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights to make it better at math (Rikiya Takehi)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at MIT CSAIL, including Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, published findings on November 2, 2026, showing that frontier large language models can natively read and write neural network weights. In one experiment, GPT-6 Astra was given the raw weights of small networks trained to play four games and correctly named the game for all four, without being told the options. In another, Astra identified which shape each of three diffusion models was trained to generate from the weights alone, with no forward passes allowed. The team calls this approach Weight-Space Programming.

The results include several specific numbers. Astra read 17,253 weights to identify the Breakout network with 99% confidence, and it edited 3.5% of a policy's weights in one shot to raise a control task from 0% to 100% success. Asked to improve Qwen3.5-0.8B on math without gradients, Astra found a cause of reasoning loops that Qwen's own model card warns about and edited 0.016% of the weights. Under the same sampling settings, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1%, and IFEval tripled. In a language-model test, Astra named the correct training language for all three 7.2M-parameter models and found every copying head, matching the measured ones.

The authors say the work could matter for both optimization and interpretability. They describe the method as reasoning-driven optimization, in which the model figures out what each part of a network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly, without writing training loops or using gradient descent. They note that Astra found a technique previously presented by Elhage et al. without being told about it. The post argues that weights, long written by optimizers, may soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about them.

The article frames this as an early result. It says deep learning has long relied on small symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon to encode simple biases, and that this is changing. The experiments cover small networks and one real language model, and the authors call the findings early and exciting. The post does not say what happens next beyond suggesting that LLM-based weight optimization is coming.

stories.Headline: US stocks: Nasdaq ends higher as AI heavyweights rebound ahead of midterm results
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq ended higher on Tuesday, Nov 3, 2026, as AI heavyweights rebounded ahead of US midterm election results. Apple fell 1.9 per cent after it warned that the cost of memory chips would continue to rise, pressuring its holiday-quarter gross margin. Memory-chip maker Micron Technology gained 2.6 per cent, while Nvidia rose 2.3 per cent after falling in the last four sessions. The broader Philadelphia chips index jumped, while AMD rose ahead of its quarterly report due after the bell, and Microsoft and Amazon each moved more than 2 per cent higher.

The S&P 500 climbed 0.36 per cent to end the session at 7,568.92 points, while the Nasdaq gained 0.83 per cent to 25,372.01 points. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.38 per cent to 51,787.04 points, and six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by consumer staples, down 1.76 per cent, followed by a 1.75 per cent loss in materials. The Nasdaq 100 on Monday ended more than 10 per cent below its Oct 6 record-high close, confirming that the tech-heavy index has entered a correction. The S&P 500 is down about 3 per cent from its record-high close on Oct 6, and it remains up over 10 per cent in 2026.

Jay Hatfield, chief executive officer at Infrastructure Capital Management, described the move as a rotation from safe tech like Apple into riskier tech like chipmakers. He said it was clear dip-buying in a higher-risk, Nasdaq-driven market. Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management, said markets will assess potential implications for fiscal policy, regulation, taxation and government spending. He said it will be good to put the elections behind, as they have been an anticipated volatility event for quite some time.

American voters will deliver a verdict on the first two years of President Donald Trump's second term in Tuesday's midterm elections. Polls and nonpartisan analysts favour Democrats to wrest the House from Republicans, while control of the Senate remains uncertain. Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note earlier this week that the elections should help remove a major market overhang. They believe a US market correction that began in June is in its final innings.

stories.Headline: Explainer: How AI muddies the waters ahead of U.S. midterm elections? - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, AI-driven disinformation is flooding voters' feeds, according to Xinhua. The Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks AI-generated political advertising, said AI was making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way. Earlier in October, the project said it had identified 220 such advertisements worth more than 137 million U.S. dollars, up from 50,000 dollars during the 2024 election cycle, and called that an almost certainly low estimate because AI use is hard to detect. Much of the content carried no disclosure that AI had been used, and analysts warned it could mislead voters and undermine the integrity of elections.

Some ads were provocative, such as one showing a Republican candidate for governor embracing Hillary Clinton beneath a slogan calling him a Clinton lover and Trump hater. Another depicted Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed laughing at cards reading "Death to America" and "Celebrate 9/11," and one showed James Fishback, a Republican primary candidate for Florida governor, hosting a party with Iranian leaders who used scimitars to attack the Star of David. Frances Haugen, a former Facebook data engineer turned whistleblower, said an information operation can now be run with quality that was impossible in 2016 for very little money, and that tweaking posts lets some get past content moderation. A survey by the American Association of Political Consultants Foundation found only 1 percent of respondents considered AI their most credible source of election information, while one in five voters plans to use AI to look into a race on their ballot, and twice that proportion has already received election details through an AI search summary.

A cottage industry has emerged to advise candidates on shaping what AI says about them. The left-wing group Run for Something launched CampSight, which tracks what large language models say about issues or candidates and recommends ways to shape those narratives, while the Center for Campaign Innovation has published research on how AI models answer questions about candidates and which sources they cite most. Eric Wilson, the center's executive director, told The Atlantic that they were campaigning for the AI vote now. The Wall Street Journal reported last year that Silicon Valley was channeling more than 100 million dollars into political-action committees and advocacy groups to fend off stringent AI regulation, including Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz that reportedly spent 8 million dollars seeking to unseat Democratic New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores over his sponsorship of the RAISE Act, an AI safety bill signed into law last December.

In 2025 a group of Republican senators proposed a moratorium on state AI laws as part of budget reconciliation after a lobbying push by tech groups, and though the Senate rejected it, related preemption efforts continued. In December, President Donald Trump issued an executive order establishing an AI litigation task force to challenge state laws deemed more than minimally burdensome and directing the Commerce Department to consider withholding federal broadband funds from states with onerous AI regulations. Susan Hyde, a professor of political science at UC Berkeley, said the deeper concern is whether voters can make informed decisions when they can no longer trust the information they receive. The Brennan Center for Justice said transparency and human oversight are lagging behind AI's rapid development, and that chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok failed to decline requests to generate images playing on election conspiracies such as ballot box stuffing or non-U.S. citizens voting, adding that policymakers need to act quickly to curb the bots' tendency to create or ignore election disinformation.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence, Plans for the Future Discussed at 2026 State of the Valley
stories.Summary:
The 2026 State of the Valley luncheon was held on a Wednesday, with local city and county government members, schools and citizen ballot issue committees taking part, according to the Rural Radio Network. Artificial intelligence was one of the topics discussed, along with the November ballot measures and races, keeping young people in the valley and future projects for Gering and Scottsbluff. Scottsbluff Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Andrew Dick said AI is a hot topic in education and can help both staff and students. The event was sponsored by the Government Affairs Committee of the Scottsbluff-Gering Chamber of Commerce.

Under the district's board policy, students may not use an AI tool unless their teacher gives permission, Dr. Dick said. He said one of his fears is that AI takes away students' chance to develop critical thinking and writing skills. As one example, he said teachers may assign more in-class writing instead of a five-page research paper done at home, so students have to show those skills. Gering City Council member Susan Wiedeman pointed to the city's electric system upgrade, saying three new substations have been built and much of the city has been converted to higher voltage. She said the last substation, on 21st Street, would cover most of the west side from 10th Street west, and she hoped it would be built and online by the end of 2027, asking Electric Utilities Superintendent Domingo Palomo.

A separate report from Menlo Ventures said enterprise AI deployment spending reached $177 billion by September 2026, up from $33 billion a year earlier, a 5.4x rise compared with 3.9x the year before. It said every dollar put into developing models this year is generating $1.70 of revenue, and that agents now account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, about 7x human-driven usage. Frontier labs took 69% of deployment dollars, up from 50%, with Anthropic's share of enterprise API spend rising from 40% to 55% and OpenAI's from 27% to 31%, while Google's fell from 21% to 9%. Coding, at $34.0 billion, and chatbots, at $25.0 billion, made up 76% of the $77.3 billion app market, and 55% of AI dollars came from net new spend.

The report said AI spending grew from $1.7 billion in 2023 to $8.5 billion in 2024 and $33 billion in 2025, reaching $176.8 billion by September 2026. It said the launch of Anthropic's Opus 4.5 in November 2025 was an inflection point, as the model let AI carry out complex, multi-step tasks with limited human oversight. Agent traffic tripled the week after that launch and overtook human traffic in early February following the launches of Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.3-Codex, growing 37x since then against 5x for human usage. The report said fears of a "SaaSpocalypse" selloff earlier this year did not match its data, which it said shows AI expanding markets rather than displacing revenue, and that open-source models' share of usage rose from 11% to 19%.

stories.Headline: Cadence Joins Genesis Mission to Advance AI-Driven Science and Microelectronics - I-Connect007
stories.Summary:
Cadence announced that it has joined the Genesis Mission Consortium, a public-private partnership run by the U.S. Department of Energy that uses artificial intelligence to speed up scientific discovery, strengthen national security and advance energy innovation. Cadence will contribute AI-enabled design and simulation technology and technical expertise, working with DOE National Laboratories on priorities in advanced microelectronics, quantum and superconducting systems, data center energy efficiency and AI-driven scientific workflows. The consortium was launched by Executive Order in November 2025 and is led by DOE Under Secretary for Science Dr. Darío Gil. It aims to double the productivity and impact of American science and engineering within a decade by connecting the nation's leading supercomputers, AI systems, experimental facilities and unique datasets across the 17 DOE National Laboratories.

Cadence's role builds on longstanding work with DOE and DOE/NNSA National Laboratories, including Sandia National Laboratories, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, NASA Ames Research Center, Argonne National Laboratory and Brookhaven National Laboratory. The company plans to support the mission through subject-matter expertise, taking part in scoping and piloting AI model development and validation, data standards and high-performance computing. It will also provide targeted access to its capabilities, including AI-enabled electronic design automation, system design and analysis, multiphysics simulation, digital twin, advanced packaging and 3D-IC workflows for pilots and demonstrations. In addition, Cadence will support integrating its workflows with DOE laboratory high-performance computing environments, including reproducible packaging and AI performance benchmarking, and will work with National Laboratories and academic partners on training and curriculum for AI-enabled engineering.

Tom Beckley, senior vice president for Strategic Technology Programs at Cadence, said the company has long believed that AI-driven design and physics-based simulation will reshape how critical systems are built, from advanced semiconductors to AI factories and next-generation physical AI and scientific applications. He said joining the consortium reflects a commitment to put Cadence's AI-enabled EDA and SDA technologies and engineering expertise in the service of America's scientific leadership. He added that Cadence is honored to work with DOE National Laboratories, consortium partners and the research community to help accelerate discoveries that strengthen U.S. competitiveness, energy security and innovation. Dr. Jeffrey S. Vetter, corporate fellow and section head of Advanced Computing Systems Research at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, said the mission represents an extraordinary opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery through simulation, high-performance computing and advanced design tools, and that the collaboration will help deliver advanced engineering capabilities into research workflows.

The consortium brings together DOE, National Laboratories, other federal agencies, industry and academia to address national science and technology challenges in advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, materials science, nuclear energy, quantum information science and semiconductors. Cadence said its participation advances its strategy of combining agentic AI, physics-based simulation, digital twin technology and high-performance computing to accelerate innovation across semiconductor design, physical AI systems and AI factories. The company aims to extend these capabilities to the DOE research community. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Cadence's plans to support the mission's priorities.

stories.Headline: AI-generated political ads raise concerns in Alabama elections
stories.Summary:
AI-generated political ads have raised concerns in Alabama as election day approached in November 2026. Critics questioned the legality and impact of the ads despite state laws requiring disclaimers. The ads must include a disclaimer stating that the media has been manipulated by technical means and depicts speech or conduct that did not occur. This requirement stems from legislation passed in 2024 to regulate materially deceptive media in elections. A flyer with AI-generated content urged people to vote against Doug Jones for Alabama Governor.

The flyer was distributed by ProgressPAC, the political action committee for the Business Council of Alabama. Podcast host Chad DuBois said hundreds of people messaged him about the flyer, and not one knew about the small fine print stating the content was fake. Doug Jones criticized the tactic at a rally last week, calling it dirty and saying it had stooped to lies and misinformation. Nationally, more than $80 million was spent on 164 AI-generated or enhanced ads as of Sept. 4, according to the Wesleyan Media Project. A separate report found 220 ads partly made with AI in federal campaigns, with more than $137 million spent and only 27% including a disclaimer.

DuBois urged lawmakers to address loopholes and implement stricter regulations on AI-generated ads. He said the loopholes would continue to be found and the problem would get more realistic until lawmakers decide enough is enough. Saurav Ghosh of the Campaign Legal Center said AI is incredibly convincing and threatens to mislead voters about information such as voting eligibility and timing. Cayce Myers, a public relations professor at Virginia Tech, said whether AI use affects a politician's credibility depends on the viewer. Bruce Schneier of Harvard said AI is a tool that can help good or evil things.

There is no federal regulation for the use of AI in campaign ads ahead of November's general election. Federal bills such as the AI Ads Act and the REAL Political Advertisements Act would require disclaimers on ads using AI-generated content. WVTM 13 reached out to the Business Council of Alabama multiple times about ProgressPAC's flyers but received no response. In Massachusetts, Brian Shortsleeve posted an ad with an AI-generated clone of Governor Maura Healey's voice, and he did not respond to requests for comment. Steven Leibowitz told The Boston Globe he used ChatGPT to remove a background from an image, which altered appearances.

stories.Headline: Anthropic posts $17B third-quarter revenue as landmark AI debut nears
stories.Summary:
Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of about $17.0 billion, more than twelve times the year-ago figure, in an amended Form S-1 filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, November 2, 2026. The San Francisco-based company posted a net loss of $23.3 billion for the three months ended September 30, wider than the $12.1 billion operating deficit a year earlier. Quarterly operating expenses rose 292% year over year to $17.5 billion, driven by surging compute costs. For the nine months ended September 30, 2026, revenue was $33.2 billion, a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%, and adjusted operating income was $4.08 billion on revenue of $33.24 billion.

The filing disclosed committed spending of about $895.4 billion, mostly tied to compute capacity and data center partnerships with cloud providers. About $447.5 billion is scheduled through 2030, and roughly $69.8 billion is due within the next twelve months, with nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations due by September 2027. The company said about $320 billion of the commitments are existing contractual obligations and about $451 billion covers signed leases that have not yet begun, expected to start between 2026 and 2028. Anthropic put the value of its blank-check compute arrangements at $150 billion to $175 billion, which could push the total past $1 trillion, and it said deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Broadcom totaling $437 billion are non-cancellable.

The prospectus warned that revenue will not keep growing at comparable rates and may not keep growing at all, and it said meeting the compute obligations depends on generating significant revenue growth. It said the company could use debt and equity financing, which over time could dilute existing shareholders or force borrowing on unfavorable terms. The filing also said cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44% of revenue in the nine months, that no customer accounts for more than 10% of revenue, and that reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they develop competing products or offer rivals' models. Anthropic also reported a net revenue retention rate of roughly 900% and 250 enterprise customers spending more than $10 million a year.

Revenue growth is already slowing, with third-quarter revenue up 46% from the second quarter, when revenues grew nearly 2.5 times from the first quarter, while compute and infrastructure costs grew 77% in the same period. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering with 20 co-managers, and the company aims to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker "ANT" before the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday. Bloomberg reported that bankers are assessing fair valuation targets between $1.4 trillion and $1.75 trillion. The debut is positioned as the first pure-play frontier AI laboratory to test public equity markets, and the prospectus claims AI will reshape the economy in ways greater than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet.

stories.Headline: St. Louis County, Mo., Council Turns to AI for Budget Cuts
stories.Summary:
The St. Louis County Council in Missouri approved a yearlong contract in September 2026 for an AI budget tool from Plano, Texas-based Tyler Technologies. The council is paying $273,300 for the company's Priority Based Budgeting solution, according to St. Louis Magazine, while the Post-Dispatch reported the cost as $273,000. The tool has already produced reports with ideas such as trimming jail overtime, charging vendors at events and cutting some holiday programming. The county is facing a $53 million deficit this year.

The software works by taking a government's line-item budget data and searching a database Tyler built from budget information from governments across the country. It then produces reports with ideas and case studies, including brief seven-page reports a council member could use in a department budget hearing. One parks report suggested charging separate fees for commercial vendors and private rentals during seasonal and holiday programming, which it said could raise $14,000 to $29,000 a year. Another idea, using building-energy monitoring to find after-hours waste as Boise did, could save $19,000 to $29,000 a year. Tyler's Chris Fabian said the tool uses traditional machine learning rather than generative AI.

The council's budget director, Chris Grahn-Howard, said he is hopeful the tool will brainstorm directions nobody else has thought of. He said the real outcome will come when the council digs into the details next year, and that the annual cost will drop to roughly $250,000 in Year 2. A spokesperson for County Executive Sam Page, Elizabeth Eisele, said the county is already doing most of the suggested things, citing LED lighting, online permitting and an online reservation system as examples. She said filling corrections jobs is hard because St. Charles County and St. Louis city raise pay too. Doug Linkhart of the National Civic League said AI could be part of the mix but should not be relied on, and that asking people for ideas would be better.

The council and Page have been locked in a bitter budget fight for years, and the lone no vote on the purchase was Councilwoman Lisa Clancy, Page's only council ally. Eisele noted that the AI has suggested some of the same ideas Page previously offered, including updated fees and bringing in sponsors to share costs, and that legislation for the Parks Department has been prepared but not acted on. Grahn-Howard said conversations with Tyler began nearly a year ago and the mid-September signing came too late to help much with this year's process. Some ideas could be incorporated into this year's budget, but the council will look at the reports in more detail next year. Tyler has drawn bad headlines elsewhere, including in Kansas City over property assessments and in Kirkwood over a $15 million deficit, though Grahn-Howard said those are different products.

stories.Headline: Meta Stock Slips as S&P Delivers Stark Warning Over AI Spending
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms shares slipped 0.5% in morning trading on November 2, 2026, after S&P Global Ratings shifted its outlook on the company to negative from stable. S&P cited uncertainty around Meta's AI spending plans and future cash generation. The agency said the spending program has made it harder to judge when investment levels may ease and how much free operating cash flow the company can preserve. S&P also flagged a rise in Meta's financial leverage, which climbed from about 0.1 times in 2025, with much of the increase tied to leasing data center capacity rather than new debt.

The leases cover infrastructure tied to projects named Beignet and Sopaipilla, which indicates contractual commitments rather than traditional borrowing drove the leverage increase. Separately, Meta shares fell 0.13% to $614.22 at 9:45 a.m. ET on November 2. The UK Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation on October 30 into Meta's access to business content. The proposed rules could let Meta collect and reuse material from publishers' and businesses' websites without giving them control over that use.

The CMA will examine whether Meta holds a dominant position in a relevant UK market and whether the conditions abuse that position. Implementation shifted from October 30 to November 20 before Meta announced an October 28 pause pending industry consultation. The regulator has made no finding that Meta broke competition law, and evidence gathering comes next. Meta has paused its proposed content terms, but the UK investigation is moving ahead.

S&P's outlook change brings more attention to the financial demands of Meta's AI expansion and the company's ability to balance infrastructure commitments with cash generation and financial flexibility. Revised terms could affect Meta's flexibility in using third-party content, although no financial impact has been quantified in the material provided. GuruFocus assigns Meta a GF Score of 99/100, with profitability, growth and momentum leading the profile, and a price-to-earnings ratio of 20.94. stories.Headline: Hail, no: CSU taps AI to stretch ice storm forecasts by hours and days
stories.Summary:
Colorado State University researchers are developing an artificial intelligence-powered forecasting system that could extend warnings of destructive hailstorms by hours or possibly days. The project is led by Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor of atmospheric science, and draws on work with the chipmaker NVIDIA. It is funded in part by the National Science Foundation, and the forecasts are set to be deployed in 2027. The effort brings together climatologists, electrical engineers and other specialists, including cross-border work with the University of Wyoming.

Traditional hail forecasting often gives only 30 to 60 minutes of warning. One system developed with NVIDIA, called Hail-StormScope, predicts how storms will develop over the next two to three hours, while a CSU machine-learning model estimates severe weather risks up to eight days ahead. The project uses nine years of historic weather observations from across the whole United States, along with high-resolution radar data. It also relies on CSU climatologist Russ Schumacher's statewide network of amateur weather observers, whose home stations include a foil-covered styrofoam platform that records hailstone sizes before they melt. Drones will be sent out after storms to get a birds-eye view of the hail's destructive path.

Rasmussen said hail is a growing challenge in the state, and that understanding it and its risks in the current climate, and how it may change in future climates, means there is something that can be done about it. She said the time when hail is actually seen in the Denver metro region is expanding earlier into the spring and later into the fall. She recalled the June 2023 storm at Red Rocks Amphitheater near Morrison, where golf-ball sized hail injured nearly 100 people, and said things moved too quickly for security personnel to respond. Schumacher said the existing system largely tries to assess the chance that severe hail will occur, which is a yes or no decision, whereas the NVIDIA model tries to predict the full evolution of the storms.

Colorado is among the nation's most hail-prone states, and hail damage has become a major contributor to rising homeowners insurance premiums statewide. Researchers say the timing and intensity of damaging storms are changing, creating additional challenges for forecasters and insurers. With days' notice instead of hours, farms could rush to harvest crops or protect animals, and building codes could be changed to add hail protections, as Fort Collins has already done with requirements for resistant roof tiling. Insurance companies and regulators could more precisely assess risk and damages. Researchers are still evaluating whether to integrate the two models into a single forecasting system or provide their predictions together to help meteorologists make better decisions.

stories.Headline: Smugglers Melt Solder to Strip Korean HBM for Huawei
stories.Summary:
Smugglers are diverting high-bandwidth memory made by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix into China by packaging it with low-end server processors, The Information reported on November 2, 2026. The combined package is classified as a low-end server processor rather than a standalone HBM product, so it slips past U.S. export limits. Once the packages reach China, technicians heat them to melt the solder, pry off the HBM and discard the server processors. The work needs precision and failure rates are high, because too much heat warps or cracks the memory stacks. Smugglers accept the risk because the profit is large even after ruined units are counted.

The HBM obtained this way flows mainly to Huawei's customers, and Huawei has told some customers that its next-generation Ascend 960DT AI chip will contain substantial amounts of Samsung and SK hynix memory. Huawei has said the chip will deliver twice the performance of its existing products. Unable to buy memory directly from the Korean suppliers, Huawei has told some customers ordering its AI chips to source the memory themselves. Samsung and SK hynix together control more than 80% of the HBM market, and Chinese domestic output is minimal. A broker in their 20s who arranges smuggled memory deals in China told The Information the work is about contributing to the motherland.

According to that broker, the price of a single HBM3E unit has jumped to about $4,000 from several hundred dollars a year ago. Because one AI chip package requires six to eight memory units, the memory alone adds $24,000 to $32,000 on top of the cost of the AI chip, servers and power. SK hynix said it strictly complies with all applicable laws and regulations, including U.S. and Korean export controls, and has not supplied products to Huawei since Washington imposed export restrictions in 2020. One smuggler who has been ordering memory chips from Korea said the routes are now being used by other dealers, and that crackdowns in Korea and the U.S. will only get tougher.

That smuggler said they plan to sell most of their stake in the company next year. The situation is awkward for the two Korean suppliers, which could come under U.S. government scrutiny if their memory is found inside Chinese-made AI chips. Taiwan's TSMC faced a U.S. investigation in 2024 after one of its chips turned up in a Huawei product, and was later ordered to halt all AI chip exports to China. HBM is a critical component that lifts AI chip performance by moving data at very high speed, and the shortage limits the ability of Chinese firms such as DeepSeek and Moonshot to keep training and deploying large models.

stories.Headline: Revolut says it cut AI coding inference costs by ~90% in less than a year by making self-hosted GLM models its default over commercial tools like Claude Code (Tobias Mann/The Register)
stories.Summary:
Revolut, a British fintech, cut its AI coding inference costs by about 90 percent in less than a year by making self-hosted GLM models its default instead of commercial services like Claude. David Abitbol, the company's ops and infrastructure lead, described the change at the AI Engineer conference in New York last month. Revolut first adopted GLM-5.1 and then moved to GLM-5.3, which it now serves using 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs. Before the switch, Revolut had deployed Gemini in early 2025 and Claude Code in early 2026. After rolling out AI coding tools to roughly 2,000 engineers, the company saw a 60 percent improvement in coding time and a 70 percent improvement in lead time.

Self-hosting GLM-5.1 cost about $0.30 per million input and output tokens, roughly a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. GLM-5.1, made by Chinese developer Z.ai, has about 754 billion total parameters, with 40 billion activated for each token generated, and needs roughly 380 GB of GPU memory for its weights plus 6 to 26 GB per user for context. To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, the same GPU count as seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. Abitbol said the biggest gains came from tuning hyperparameters, switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths, not from adding GPUs. With these changes, Revolut reached under 3 seconds to first token at context windows of around 256,000 tokens and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second.

Abitbol said Revolut had been highly skeptical about AI costs, with engineers spending $1,000 to $10,000 a month for not much return, so it launched with strict budget limits. He said cheap tokens let engineers stop saving them for the end of the quarter or the hardest tasks, and the biggest gains came from using the models for debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. He called long context a scam and said 256,000 tokens is really what is needed, adding that once time to first token exceeds 5 seconds his Slack inbox fills up. He said open source is now a priority at Revolut, billing is flat with no bill shock, and the frontier is the exception. He acknowledged that Chinese open weights models may raise privacy and security concerns, but said the main worry is accessing them through APIs running out of China, and that running them on-prem or on regional cloud resources leaves nothing to worry about.

GLM has not fully replaced GPT or Claude, because the Chinese model is text only and not ideal for things like UI work. Revolut uses a model router to send vision queries to models like Gemini or GPT Luna while keeping code generation on GLM. Abitbol also said engineers who sign in after 5 pm get closer to 800 tokens a second. Separately, Anthropic introduced message threads as part of Claude's Messages API, and the feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. Anthropic reports that message threads cut median time to first token by about 35 percent for requests of 500,000 to 1 million tokens, though token consumption and costs stay the same.

stories.Headline: Florida Learjet crash victims identified: 20-year-old copilot, tech entrepreneur and his family among those killed
stories.Summary:
A private Learjet flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas crashed and exploded near West Palm Beach, Florida, on Sunday. The victims were identified as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, and caregiver Anita Maria Cetina. Passengers Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr also died, along with copilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. The identity of the pilot, who was also killed, has not been made public. Robinson, 45, was the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com and the CEO of Moltsets, and he previously worked at Lehman Brothers and Barclays.

He told the ProfitLed podcast that he and his family lived in Aspen, Colorado, and that he felt like he was living the dream. Filgueiras was 20 years old and had held a pilot's license since 2023, when she was a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School. Her license showed she had the rating to fly the jet but not to be in command of the flight, and the Palm Beach County School District paid for her license through the school's aviation academy. A statement from the families of the seven passengers identified the victims. The family of Reed and Fehr said the couple was full of joy and adventure, loved each other fiercely and were building a life together.

It was not immediately clear what their relationship was with Robinson and Sharp. Thom Singer, CEO of the Austin Technology Council, told the AP that Robinson was part of the entrepreneurial fabric of Austin. stories.Headline: Incheon Port Authority Sets AI Rules for Port Operations
stories.Summary:
The Incheon Port Authority drew up and distributed the Incheon Port Authority AI Guidelines on the 3rd, according to a report by Seoul Economic Daily. The authority said the guidelines are meant to control the risk of malfunctions in AI used in port administration, operations and safety management. They respond to two laws that took effect this year, the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Establishment of a Foundation for Trust in January and the Act on Promoting AI- and Data-Based Administration in August. The authority said it has institutionalized detailed controls tailored to port worksites such as berth allocation, hazardous materials management and facility inspections.

The guidelines rest on four basic principles, safety, reliability, accountability and public interest, and eight detailed provisions. A human oversight framework is mandatory even for autonomous control systems, so a person can verify, correct or halt the final outcome. For high-risk AI that directly controls equipment in areas needing special caution, two or more supervisors must be stationed, and a switch to manual control is required as a rule within 30 seconds of a malfunction. Uses are sorted into three tiers, statutory high-impact, priority-managed and general, based on how much AI is involved in decisions and the scale of potential damage. Automated lock gate control and automatic berthing and mooring equipment are classified as statutory high-impact and must undergo a prior impact assessment.

Berth allocation recommendations and recommendations on where to store hazardous materials fall under the priority-managed tier, requiring final approval by the responsible official and periodic revalidation. Simple tasks such as responding to public inquiries or summarizing documents are classified as general to improve work efficiency. AI involved in distribution and allocation must undergo a fairness audit at least once every six months, with the results disclosed. The authority is also providing a separate checklist that outside partners including shipping lines, cargo owners and terminal operators can use voluntarily.

Kim Young-guk, head of the authority's planning and management division, said the guidelines establish standards for the responsible use of AI as a public institution. He said the authority will lead a trust-based AI transition that guarantees the continuity of logistics flows and safety at port worksites. The authority plans to complete company-wide governance by appointing a chief AI officer and establishing an AI ethics committee. It also plans to conduct training to embed the rules in the field.

stories.Headline: Europe's Biggest Tech Startup Cuts AI Coding Costs by 90% Using Chinese Model
stories.Summary:
Revolut, the British fintech company, cut its costs for AI coding tasks to about one-tenth of what it had been spending on Anthropic and OpenAI by self-hosting the open-weight GLM model from the Chinese AI lab Z.ai on dedicated NVIDIA GPUs. David Abitbol, who leads AI operations at Revolut, revealed this at a technical session at the AI Engineering conference. The company began experimenting with AI tools in January 2025, first introducing Gemini for internal data access and then testing Anthropic's Claude Code. Concerned about commercial AI costs, with some engineers spending $1,000 to $10,000 monthly without clear returns, Revolut imposed strict usage budgets before it began self-hosting open-source models in April 2026 and settled on the GLM family for coding work.

The deployment improved engineering lead times by 70% and coding time by 60% across a sample of 2,000 engineers. Abitbol said self-hosting GLM brings the blended cost of tokens to 30 cents per million. The infrastructure consists of 56 NVIDIA B200 GPUs serving about 2,000 engineers running GLM-5.3, with a target time to first token below three seconds and interactive workloads served at around 200 tokens per second, rising to 800 tokens per second after 5 pm when GPU demand is lower. Between April and August, requests per second rose from about three to more than seven while time to first token fell from over 10 seconds to around 1.6 seconds, an 88% performance improvement despite a 76% increase in demand. Revolut still uses frontier tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini for specialised workloads including image recognition, while its internally hosted GLM models handle most coding tasks.

Abitbol said Revolut downloads model weights and runs inference on US-based infrastructure rather than sending requests to Chinese-hosted endpoints. He said open source is now a priority at Revolut, the economics are favourable, the billing is flat and there is no bill shock at the end of the month. He attributed the performance gains to inference optimisation rather than simply adding computing capacity. In October, CEO Nik Storonsky said Revolut was developing proprietary AI models trained on customer transaction data, citing the company's 30 million to 40 million daily transactions as a source of training data.

Revolut was valued at $115 billion in a secondary share sale in July, up from $75 billion last November and $45 billion in 2024, reinforcing its position as Europe's most valuable private technology company. Chinese open-weight models from labs including DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.AI, Alibaba and Tencent have won over users with lower costs and strong capabilities, and the top Chinese models lag the leading closed US systems by just 3% on benchmark scores. Some Western enterprises fear the models are too aligned with the Chinese Communist Party, and startups such as Hirundo and Lazarus AI edit the models to realign their values and remove censorship for Western markets. In October, the Trump administration barred civilian government agencies from using products or services from DeepSeek, citing a potential threat to national security. Graham Webster of Stanford's DigiChina Project said most users of Chinese models do not care about their alignment, and Stu Clott, a developer in San Diego, said he has not had a single situation where censorship got in his way.
