stories.Headline: Parents Angry After School's AI Move With 6-Year-Olds
stories.Summary:
A South Carolina elementary school put a photo of a 6-year-old student named Harper into an AI tool, and the tool produced an image of her as a 25-year-old nurse. The girl's mother, Nikki Anderson, found out and was not happy, though Harper was thrilled. Anderson raised concerns about data privacy and the lack of parental consent. She was also alarmed that Harper became focused on looking like a conventionally beautiful woman in the photo rather than on a future career. Anderson's Instagram post about the episode went viral.

District officials said the teacher used a personal ChatGPT Plus account in a way that was not consistent with expectations, and they said the images have been deleted. The case was reported by Caitlin Gibson in the Washington Post. AI and child-development experts warned that schools are improvising with powerful tools before guardrails are in place. One AI literacy educator described the situation as everyone drinking out of a firehose. The episode raised questions about privacy, policy and how children imagine their futures.

A September survey by the National Parents Union found that 77% of parents want K-12 public schools to teach students how to use AI tools effectively. The survey of 1,528 parents also found that 85% support schools teaching students about AI safety. Less than half of parents, 46%, believe their state is handling technology use in schools well enough. The survey was conducted Sept. 7-11, and the National Parents Union includes more than 1,800 affiliated parent organizations across the U.S. and Puerto Rico.

The survey also found that 81% of parents want to prohibit public schools from buying technology not proven to be safe and effective for learning. A similar majority, 79%, support requiring all public school teachers to be trained in digital and AI literacy and responsible technology use. In a 2026 Educators for Excellence survey, less than a quarter of teachers said they had received adequate training to help students use AI tools effectively, and 43% said they had received no training at all. States and districts are operating without federal guidelines on K-12 AI integration, and in most schools decisions are left up to individual teachers. New York City and Los Angeles public school systems restricted students' use of AI for at least a year.

stories.Headline: Uber builds MCP gateway for AI agent access to 800+ servers
stories.Summary:
Uber has built an MCP Gateway to standardise how its AI agents discover and invoke internal services, the company said. The platform supports more than 800 MCP servers and over 5,000 tools. It provides a common layer for discovery, protocol translation, authorisation, and execution. Uber engineers describe it as a microservice architecture that exposes existing APIs as MCP tools without requiring changes to the underlying services.

The architecture separates the MCP Registry, which acts as the control plane, from the Proxy Gateway, which handles runtime execution. The registry keeps tool definitions, schemas, ownership, and enablement settings, while the proxy translates MCP requests into HTTP, gRPC, or TChannel calls and converts responses back into MCP-compatible results. Uber's AutoCrawler automates tool discovery using Cadence, scanning internal interface definition language registries and extracting API definitions from Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas. It generates MCP-compatible schemas and uses a large language model to produce tool descriptions, and newly discovered tools stay disabled until their owning teams review and explicitly enable them.

The gateway enforces authorisation at both server and tool levels through Uber's internal access control system, and it supports redaction of personally identifiable information and other sensitive data in tool responses. For third-party integrations, including Jira and Google, a separate service exchanges internal user tokens for the corresponding third-party authentication tokens. Uber developed Omni MCP to support incremental discovery, letting agents search for servers, discover relevant tools, retrieve individual schemas, and invoke selected tools as needed. Response Projection lets agents request specific response fields instead of receiving complete payloads, and Uber's aifx command-line interface lets coding agents discover and invoke tools, writing results to files for selective inspection.

Ajay Sharma, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft CoreAI, wrote in a LinkedIn post that Azure API Gateways has been doing this for a while and called it a recipe for order to the chaos that LLMs come with. Kelly Goetsch, President at Pipe17, observed in a LinkedIn post that Uber's new MCP gateway looks identical to gateways built over the decades for APIs and later GraphQL. Tamir Dresher highlighted in a LinkedIn post the continuing relevance of established distributed systems concerns, including security, discovery, observability, and governance. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: As 2027 housing forecasts darken, here's the data brokers are keeping an eye on
stories.Summary:
Fannie Mae and Goldman Sachs cut their 2027 housing outlooks, according to a Mortgage Professional report published on November 3, 2026. Fannie Mae's Economic and Strategic Research Group now expects the 30-year average fixed mortgage rate to hold steady at 7.5% through all four quarters of next year. Goldman Sachs projects existing-home sales to total 3.9 million in 2027, down from an estimated 4 million in 2026 and 26% below 2019 levels. The report said inflation fears and economic jitters drove the revisions.

The report said the Labor Department's fresh data released Tuesday showed September job openings climbed to 7.52 million, beating forecasts by 420,000. It said the consumer price index came in at 3.7% in September, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, and that the war in Iran continues to pressure oil prices. Sonoran Lending president and senior loan officer Jay Lessard said inflation remains the number one data point to watch, with fiscal policy, government borrowing, geopolitical risk, tariffs and energy prices also on his radar. He told Mortgage Professional America that mortgage rates are not determined by one Fed meeting but are influenced every day by what investors believe inflation, economic growth and Fed policy will look like six or 12 months out.

Lessard said his longer-term outlook is cautiously optimistic but his near-term view has become more guarded, mainly because rates rose sharply after early September as inflation concerns returned and Treasury yields climbed. He said the path to lower mortgage rates will not be a straight line, and that he still sees an opportunity for rates to improve if inflation moderates and growth and the labor market cool, but he does not expect a dramatic move lower overnight. The report said the next big release to watch is the Bureau of Labor Statistics nonfarm payrolls report, due at 8:30 a.m. ET on Friday, November 6.

A separate Medscape article by Michael Scaturro, published November 2, 2026, reported that data brokers track people's locations through smartphone data and sell inferences about their health. It said Chris McQueen, who finished leukemia treatment a year and a half ago, kept seeing ads for fake cures during oncologist visits and bloodwork. The article said more than 92% of patients in a 2022 American Medical Association survey said their health data should not be available for purchase, and that location data from phones is not covered by HIPAA. It said California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill on September 27 that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data, saying it went a step too far, and that a Stanford University study showed only 9% of data brokers are adhering to an existing California privacy law.

stories.Headline: Shanghai AI startup StartLux explores opportunities in decision models and local AI
stories.Summary:
Shanghai-based AI startup StartLux is exploring decision models and locally deployed AI, according to China Daily. Its model StartLux-Decision v1.1 27B Instant recently ranked first among 174 entries on Hugging Face's Decision Index 0.3.2 leaderboard with a score of 69.12, based on company-published results. Chuan-Wei Kuo, co-founder and chief technology officer of StartLux, said decision models could cut computing costs and improve efficiency. Unlike general-purpose large language models that mainly generate text, decision models choose from predefined options and return probabilities, which suits customer service routing, web operations and AI agent execution.

Kuo expects more than 80 percent of AI demand to be handled locally within the next one to two years. StartLux plans to launch a consumer-facing local AI agent, followed by enterprise solutions next year, with products designed to process data locally rather than send it to third-party servers. Gao Chengyuan, head of Influence Academy, said decision quality and speed are becoming more important as AI moves from talking to doing, and that local deployment could suit government, financial and industrial customers needing data security, low latency and cost control. Kuo said the decision model field remains exploratory, with progress depending on technological breakthroughs and practical applications, and that StartLux will continue developing its recursive self-improvement framework, whose Auto Research approach uses AI to generate hypotheses, conduct experiments and evaluate results.

Inc42 reports that decision models are gaining attention as companies move from chatbots to AI agents. TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida, released Jev in September, focusing on scores and yes-or-no probabilities rather than text. Cloudflare introduced Clef and Clef-flash, Microsoft released Decision-1 based on Alibaba's Qwen family, AWS introduced Strands Decider 2B, OpenAI launched a Decisions API, and Perplexity has explored decision-oriented APIs. Articul8 AI, spun out of Intel in 2024, has developed around 28 domain models and says its approach can reduce token usage by more than 50% in relevant workflows, and in October it announced Bivia, a multimodal decision model. Ananthanarayanan S, Articul8's managing director for India, said enterprises need a system connecting their data and domain knowledge with models suited to specific workflows.

PurpleTalk's applied AI research lab Sthānika developed the Sieve family, and Sieve-31Bv3 returns a defined answer with a confidence score. The company said Sieve-31Bv3 scored 71.1 on the full Jev Decision Index and 71.7 on the public test, where it ranked third. Sridhar Muppidi, cofounder of PurpleTalk, said the private tests matter most because they come from domains outside the public suite, and Bharat Lingam, CEO of PurpleTalk, said decision models will open a new category of agentic systems that are more reliable, more controllable and fast enough for voice, customer experience and robotics. Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations has developed Laya, an open-weight decision model meant to run locally on laptops and mobile phones, and founder Nandakishore Mukkunnoth said the initial focus was small, fast models that did not always require cloud access. Shubham Gupta, founding general partner at Together Fund, said what cannot be copied is a company's own record of decisions and outcomes, and that the real test for startups is how fast a model improves on a specific, high-volume workflow.

stories.Headline: Renewable Innovations joins federal hydrogen fuel-cell push for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Renewable Innovations has joined a federal collaboration to advance fuel cell power for AI data centers, according to a company press release reported by Energies Media on November 2, 2026. The project is a three-year research and development effort led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratory of the Rockies. It is called "FC-DC: Fuel Cell Solutions for Brownfield and Greenfield Data Centers" and was selected through the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office initiative on using fuel cells to meet the demands of the AI revolution. The partnership aims to develop and validate fuel cell systems for the rapidly growing power needs of AI infrastructure.

As part of the project, Renewable Innovations will design, develop, build and validate a fuel cell rack system meant to power and cool a high-power compute rack directly on the data center floor. The work will look at how tightly coupled fuel cell and compute-rack architectures can handle the demanding, dynamic power profiles of AI workloads while improving efficiency, reliability and simplicity. The company says that more than seven years ago it showed hydrogen fuel cells could provide reliable power for data centers, and it is now building on that foundation for the AI era. The National Laboratory of the Rockies leads the project with Renewable Innovations and a group of technology and industry partners.

Separately, the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management is pursuing AI data centers on remediated land at federal nuclear sites, ExchangeMonitor reported on October 30, 2026. Robert Seifert, the office's director of infrastructure disposition and regulatory policy, spoke at the Energy Technology and Environmental Business Association's annual conference in Knoxville, Tennessee. He said the effort is a priority under President Donald Trump's administration and that Assistant Secretary Tim Walsh has pushed for the office to focus on AI in nuclear cleanup and future land reindustrialization. The department issued a request for information last year identifying 16 nuclear complex sites as candidates, and in July 2025 it selected four: Idaho National Laboratory, the Oak Ridge Site in Tennessee, the Paducah Site in Kentucky and the Savannah River Site in South Carolina.

Seifert said Idaho, Paducah and Savannah River are under development and moving forward in the leasing process, while Oak Ridge will take a different approach, with the department considering working with nuclear developers in the area on a potential campus. The department is also developing a data center and energy project at its Portsmouth Site in Ohio. Seifert said the department wants companies bringing data center compute to its lands or facilities to bring the associated power as well, without significantly raising customers' electricity rates, and he pointed to the administration's Ratepayer Protection Pledge released in March. He also said cleanup dollars do not go to these efforts and are appropriated for the cleanup mission.

stories.Headline: Qualcomm HBC Compared to HBM
stories.Summary:
Qualcomm announced on November 2, 2026, that it has validated first-generation silicon for its high-bandwidth computing (HBC) architecture in the lab. The company said its engineers used industry-standard automated test equipment to confirm the complete memory read-write path and near-memory computations at production levels. Qualcomm first introduced the HBC architecture in July 2026 as a way to address the memory wall in AI inference. The validation comes ahead of sampling for the Dragonfly AI250, which Qualcomm says is due for release next year.

The testing found that HBC can deliver as much as 18 times the memory bandwidth of LPDDR and an energy-efficiency measurement of five times the terabit-per-second-per-watt compared to HBM4, the sixth generation of high-bandwidth memory. In HBC, a stack of LPDDR-based memory sits in the package with a compute die underneath it, so data moves across micrometers rather than millimeters. Qualcomm says this gives the AI model faster access to data and reduces the time, energy and cost of moving it. The AI250 is expected to start sampling in the first half of 2027, with Dragonfly C1000 CPUs also set for next year and Dragonfly AI300 samples coming in 2028.

Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, said traditional architectures have plenty of DDR capacity but a narrow link that moves data slowly, while HBM increases lanes and speed at a premium in cost, power and complex packaging. He described HBC as a co-processor where most decode operations happen inside the package, so the slower link to the AI250 does not affect end-to-end performance because only results are sent back. He said the solution gives the bandwidth needed at the lowest energy, with at least an order of magnitude less energy spent moving data. He also said the validation is important because HBC is a clear differentiator, since the compute sits under the memory stack, and that it should erase doubts about high-yield manufacturing of the AI250 next year.

Qualcomm has for more than a year been working to become a larger player in the AI datacenter space and an alternative to Nvidia. HBC will be integrated into the Dragonfly AI250 to create what executives call a full AI inference accelerator platform, which will be foundational to the Qualcomm Dragonfly Rack for inference workloads. Giaretta said Qualcomm is working with various partners on different ways HBC can be used and that the AI250 is not the only product where it will appear. He said the company usually does not do a blog or pre-briefing for a chip bring-up, but did so because the technology is completely new.

stories.Headline: Africa's AI ambitions depend on stronger digital public infrastructure, expert says
stories.Summary:
Remy Takang, a Belgium-based Cameroonian lawyer and certified AI governance specialist, gave a caution in an interview with Biometric Update published on November 3, 2026. He warned that African countries must not rush to unveil or draft national AI strategies without first building reliable digital public infrastructure. As of April, 22 African countries had published national AI strategies, while a further 21 were drafting one, according to the African AI Governance Index tracker. Takang advises on AI assurance and data protection through his own practice at RTivara Advisory and also works with A-Law International Law Firm.

Takang described digital public infrastructure as a shared set of digital systems and rules on which a country operates, with three commonly recognized pillars: digital identity, digital payments and data exchange systems. He said AI cannot deliver meaningful public value without these foundations, comparing the infrastructure to a road and AI to a vehicle. He cited the need for dependable electricity, stable internet connectivity and adequate computing capacity, and said governments have to make the necessary financial sacrifices. He pointed to Cameroon, where citizens sometimes struggle to access digital services because of unstable electricity and internet connectivity, and mentioned an announced data center to be financed by Cybastion. He also cited a policy brief he wrote in September 2026 reviewing Cameroon's national AI strategy, which found limited progress, with a proposed AI authority, presidential council, regulatory sandboxes and national computing infrastructure not in place at the time of his research.

Takang recommended a rights-based legal framework for high-impact AI systems, with particular emphasis on the right to redress, and said people harmed by AI applications must be able to seek remedies easily. He argued that African countries do not necessarily need a single, comprehensive AI law, and that existing sector-specific laws could be amended to accommodate AI. He cautioned against copying the European Union's AI Act and called on governments to build on the African Union's continental AI strategy, launched in 2024, which sets a target for member states to develop national AI strategies by 2030. He also highlighted the need for cross-border collaboration, continent-wide data classification standards and harmonized rules on data flows.

Takang said integrating AI with digital public infrastructure could help a farmer in Cameroon with a trusted digital ID, a mobile payment account and shared agricultural data receive advice in their own language, warnings about pest outbreaks and access to credit or subsidies. He said AI could help identify diseases early and detect outbreaks in healthcare, and assist social protection schemes by analyzing data and helping prevent fraud. He noted that recent research found grievance redress mechanisms for 15 interoperable digital public infrastructure systems remain fragmented, and recommended that redress mechanisms be as interoperable as the services they support. He stressed inclusivity, asking whether rural areas have constant electricity and strong internet connections.

stories.Headline: China plans AI safety rules spanning development and deployment
stories.Summary:
China plans to introduce wide-ranging artificial intelligence safety standards that would cover both the development and deployment of AI models, Bloomberg reported. Wang Ruomeng, a senior official with the National Development and Reform Commission, announced the plan at a briefing in Beijing on Tuesday. The framework would cover the entire life cycle of AI systems, including data, computing resources and algorithms. The measures would affect developers such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba, whose models are central to China's efforts to compete with American companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Authorities would speed up legislation on the foundations of AI and its use in important sectors, and would introduce ethical guidelines and safety standards. Officials would regularly assess how the rules are implemented and revise those that no longer reflect technological developments. Beijing also plans a transition period, whose length was not specified, and guidance meant to reduce the burden of compliance. Sector-specific regulatory sandboxes would let developers test applications and learn from failures under supervision. Developers and operators would be expected to strengthen their own risk management and to disclose safety threats, incidents and vulnerabilities.

Wang said AI safety is not a problem one company, industry or country can tackle alone and called it a global challenge requiring international cooperation. He urged governments to strengthen cooperation on safety governance, coordinate the disclosure of vulnerabilities and responses to risks, and build greater confidence in one another's systems. The proposals also address employment: authorities will monitor how AI changes the labor market and displaces workers, and will provide broad protections for those affected. The initiative reflects Beijing's attempt to balance technological ambition with concerns that increasingly capable systems could escape human control or make cyberattacks more damaging.

The announcement comes amid discussions between Washington and Beijing about managing the technology's risks. China and the United States agreed in September to pursue a shared understanding of AI's benefits and threats, ahead of a Washington summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at which AI featured prominently. Despite the planned safeguards, China will continue encouraging open AI development during its 15th five-year plan, which runs through 2030. That commitment preserves an approach that has helped Chinese models gain users internationally, Bloomberg reported.

stories.Headline: Call for proposals: EU AI Media Platform – Modular multilingual public-interest infrastructure for European news and audiovisual media (IA) - Apply AI
stories.Summary:
Fraunhofer researchers and partners are developing an AI-driven civil protection dashboard in the RegioGuard-PRO project, which runs from March 2026 through March 2028. The platform aggregates data from many sources, detects developing situations early and gives municipalities and emergency responders recommendations for action. It builds on two earlier projects funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, AKRIMA and HERAKLION. A ready-to-use demonstrator is planned within two years, and demonstration centers are being set up in Trier, Mainz and Wildau.

The project partners include fuseki GmbH, which leads and coordinates the work, Fraunhofer EMI, the Technical University of Applied Sciences Wildau, the University of Freiburg, the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, the German Red Cross Rhineland-Palatinate Regional Association and the City of Trier. The platform combines social, infrastructure, transportation, population, environmental, building, asset and weather data into an integrated situational awareness picture. For one use case, partners are studying a 100-year flood event using flood hazard maps from the Federal Institute of Hydrology, road network data from OpenRouteService and OpenStreetMap, and data from the German Federal Agency for Cartography and Geodesy. The analysis accounts for factors such as the availability of critical infrastructure and the potential scale of damage.

Fraunhofer EMI research scientist Kai Fischer said municipalities often have vast amounts of data during crises, but it is scattered across sources and not interconnected. He said the platform consolidates and analyzes large data sets, which enables early detection of hazards and faster action. He described the integrated AI model as working much like a chatbot that gives users access to the data analyses. He also said what-if analysis reveals a municipality's vulnerabilities and calculates expected water quantities, allowing officials to take targeted precautions.

The project is funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space under the Practical Lighthouses of Civil Security grant guideline. The demonstration centers will also serve as knowledge-sharing hubs, passing findings to other municipalities and civil protection organizations. With the Lörrach district, researchers are exploring extreme weather applications, including where people can cool off or seek shelter during heat waves. The aim is to bring all data and analysis results together on a single platform to create a real-time warning system.

stories.Headline: Klook launches K.ai, an AI agent that manages merchants' back-office operations
stories.Summary:
Klook launched K.ai, an AI agent for experiences merchants, on Nov 3, 2026, according to an announcement carried by The Straits Times and PR Newswire. The agent works inside Klook's merchant portal and goes beyond answering questions to carrying out tasks such as checking bookings and availability and updating inventory and pricing. Klook is introducing it to merchants through a phased global rollout ahead of the year-end travel season. The company described K.ai as helping merchants manage their businesses by executing everyday tasks in the portal.

The articles give several figures on the sector and on early results. Euromonitor data cited by Klook says only about 34% of experiences bookings are made online, compared with 66% for accommodations and 81% for flights. Small and medium-sized operators make up around 95% of the experiences sector, and many lack the digital reach to sell beyond walk-ins and offline channels. Klook says tasks can now be completed 95% faster for individual inventory and pricing updates and 97% faster for batch checks of products, inventory and orders. Merchants using K.ai recorded 3.4 times as many monthly bookings as those not using it, according to the company.

Bernie Xiong, Co-founder and CTO of Klook, said many experiences merchants do not have dedicated teams for technology or back-office operations. He said K.ai brings practical agentic AI capabilities into their day-to-day operations and removes much of the manual work of running their businesses. He said this lets merchants spend more time delivering meaningful experiences for travelers. Erica Yu, Co-founder of MyProGuide in Taiwan, said she used to block out an hour every morning to update prices and availability across her tours. She said she now tells K.ai what she wants and it is done quickly, and that she is catching last-minute demand she used to miss.

Klook says experiences remain one of travel's least digitized categories, and it links this to fragmentation, since many SME operators lack the digital reach to sell online. By bringing these merchants online, Klook says it makes them discoverable and bookable to travelers worldwide, and by embedding AI into its existing tech infrastructure it helps them move from manual processes to AI-powered business management. K.ai also offers one-click product listing, which generates structured listings from uploaded materials for merchants to review and edit. It also turns customer reviews and performance data into insights through its Reviews and Dashboard pages, highlighting changes in business performance and possible reasons behind them.

stories.Headline: Posters: AI for vaccine education, homelessness research, diabetes care
stories.Summary:
At APHA 2026, poster sessions ran Sunday through Tuesday and covered a wide range of public health topics. Arnav Goel, a fourth-year medical student at Cooper Medical School of Rowan University in Camden, New Jersey, presented a poster combining measles and artificial intelligence. Pennsylvania was experiencing a record-breaking measles outbreak with more than 1,400 cases and five deaths, which led him to think about improving vaccination rates. He outlined a conceptual framework for an AI chatbot that could nudge parents to vaccinate their children by educating them and dispelling misinformation.

Goel said AI is an incredibly persuasive tool and noted that recent studies argue AI can persuade better than people or pamphlets made by people. He raised ethical questions about using a chatbot this way, including the risk of hyper-nudging and subverting autonomy. His framework says the AI tool should not store data for training the program, and people should analyze the data to make sure the AI works as intended. He said AI tools are still in their infancy but are not fading away, and he thinks it is better to be at the table and help regulate them than to ignore them.

Shannon Smith, who works with her PhD adviser at UNT Health Fort Worth, combined her interests in substance use, sleep and healthcare for unhoused people in her research. She noted that 771,000 people in the U.S. experienced homelessness on a single night in 2024, and that sleep disruption is common. She recruited English-speaking adults from a homeless shelter in Dallas to complete a self-reported survey about alcohol use, sleep disruption and depressive symptoms over the past 30 days. Her data did not show a clear connection between sleep and alcohol use in this population, which she said could be due to self-reporting over 30 days or because shelter residents cannot drink alcohol there.

Chunfu Liu, chief epidemiologist for the Montgomery County, Maryland health department, presented a poster on type II diabetes, one of the top five causes of death and hospitalization in that county. The department conducted a case-control analysis of emergency room visits to inform the county council, which allocates funding and resources. Researchers identified 9,778 patients with type II diabetes and 2,338 with uncontrolled type II diabetes, and used 77,095 patients with injury-related ER visits unrelated to diabetes as the control group. Liu said food insecurity was highly associated with diabetes and even more with uncontrolled diabetes, with a clear gradient effect, and the county now has data to show its council.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Adds Ability To Hide Private Chats Using A PIN
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began rolling out a new ChatGPT feature called Locked Chats, which lets users protect private conversations with a four-digit PIN. The feature was reported by iHeartRadio on November 2, 2026. It is meant to add an extra layer of privacy for people who share their device with others. Once a chat is locked, it moves to a separate Locked Chats section and disappears from regular chat history, pinned chats, and standard search results.

Users can open locked chats by entering the PIN, or on supported devices with Face ID, Touch ID, or the phone's unlock method. The same PIN works across all devices linked to the user's OpenAI account. Locked Chats are available on the Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans, on web browsers, iPhone and Android apps, and the Mac and Windows desktop apps, but not on ChatGPT for Healthcare. Temporary Chats, archived chats, group chats, and some other types cannot be locked. Users select "Lock chat" from a conversation's menu, and OpenAI is releasing the feature gradually, so the option may not appear for everyone at first.

OpenAI said Locked Chats make it harder for others to casually view private conversations, but they do not provide end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault. Locking a chat does not change how long OpenAI keeps the information or the "Improve the model for everyone" setting unless users turn it off themselves. If a user resets a forgotten PIN, all locked chats, related files, and memories are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered, even by OpenAI's support team. Previously shared links are not revoked by locking and must be deleted manually. For workplace accounts, organizational policies still apply, and authorized compliance systems may access locked chats, though workspace administrators cannot unlock chats or reset a user's PIN.

OpenAI described the feature as giving users more control over their privacy, while recommending caution for highly sensitive information. The company said Locked Chats are mainly for convenience and access control, not absolute confidentiality. Memory created before a chat is locked can remain accessible in regular Memory, while new information from locked chats is stored separately in the Locked Chats memory area. Biometric authentication applies only to the specific device where it is set up.

stories.Headline: AI didn't sink Weil. It could prevent the next Big Law failure.
stories.Summary:
Weil Gotshal, a 95-year-old law firm known for handling some of the biggest bankruptcies in American history, announced plans to wind down after an exodus of high-profile partners, according to a story published on November 2, 2026. The announcement came hours before a private lunch of lawyers hosted by Business Insider at its The Long Play event, which LexisNexis sponsored. The lunch was led by reporter Melia Robinson, who curated the guest list and tried to seat lawyers who had left one firm away from their old bosses. A spokesperson for Weil did not respond to a request for comment. The lunch guests agreed that AI did not kill Weil, but the firm's collapse exposed weaknesses that large law firms have always faced.

The discussion focused on whether AI could make those weaknesses worse or help firms become less fragile. Eric Greenberg, general counsel of Cox Media Group, said law firms have always been vulnerable, but the hot lateral hiring market is making them especially so, and he described Weil as a case of a run on the bank where people did not want to be left at the firm. David Wang, chief innovation officer of Cooley, said Big Law remains a business built on relationships, and when a star partner leaves, a firm can lose clients, revenue and years of knowledge. Avi Gesser, a partner at Debevoise & Plimpton who leads its artificial intelligence practice, suggested the technology could act as a tourniquet, and his firm is building tools to capture the expertise of its litigators so that knowledge becomes an asset of the firm. Greenberg said client loyalty could shift from sticking with a person who knows their stuff to a firm that knows their stuff.

Sharon Crane, president of the Practising Law Institute, raised a concern about why a lawyer would give away what makes them valuable, asking what they would take with them if they left. Gesser said partners are not necessarily compensated for time spent teaching the firm's systems what they know, so firms will have to rethink how they reward that work. Oz Benamram, chief AI officer at Pillsbury, said partner agreements may need a rewrite, because departing partners might want to take playbooks built from their expertise, and clients could also claim that knowledge. Michael Gerstenzang, senior partner at Cleary Gottlieb, said AI might make firms less dependent on individual lawyers, but it could also make those lawyers less dependent on the firms. He described legal work as a team sport, where a top M&A partner needs tax specialists, antitrust experts and employment lawyers, but he imagines a future where AI handles some of that specialized work, leaving Big Law with a paradox: the same technology that could make firms harder to leave might make it easier for their most valuable lawyers to walk away.

stories.Headline: People Are Using AI for Divorce Advice and It’s Driving Their Lawyers Crazy
stories.Summary:
Family lawyers say many divorcing clients are now bringing them legal advice, draft documents and strategy suggestions that appear to have been generated by AI chatbots such as ChatGPT. In a spring survey of 133 lawyers at the national family-law firm Cordell & Cordell, 80% said clients had sent them correspondence, draft pleadings or strategy ideas they believed came from AI. Steven Benmor, a Toronto family lawyer, recently drafted a prenuptial agreement as his client asked, then received a 13-part list of revisions nearly as long as the prenup, some so detailed he said no human could have written them. Logan Burns, a 35-year-old pastor and roofing salesman in LaGrange, Georgia, paid $19.99 a month for a chatbot instead of a $7,000 lawyer in a custody fight and wrote a judge a letter arguing the court lacked jurisdiction, and the judge sternly told him that was not how it worked. Damien Charlotin, an adjunct professor at UC Law San Francisco who tracks AI errors in court cases, has counted 148 family-law rulings in which judges flagged fake citations or other apparent AI mistakes, more than 100 of them this year.

Lawyers say the chatbots tend to accept one side's account of the facts, even though the two sides in a family case often disagree. Hossein Berenji, a Los Angeles family lawyer, said a client's chatbot simply accepted his story about his finances and told him he had an easy win on cutting spousal support, without asking to see financial statements or spending. The man persuaded his first lawyer to follow that strategy, and the other side used the same company records to argue his income had not really fallen, and about a year later the judge agreed. Berenji's firm brought in a forensic accountant who found much of the company's product had spoiled while the business still paid overhead, and at a recent hearing a judge tentatively agreed the man's finances had changed and put his support payments on hold. Berenji said the man blamed his lawyer rather than the chatbot, and the firm spent time convincing him to move away from the AI advice.

Maha Kamal, a Denver family lawyer, joined a custody case for a mother after the children's father, mostly representing himself, sent the court a series of filings that appeared to be written by AI and accused the mother of breaking the judge's orders. By the time Kamal asked the judge to call both parents in, there were nine filings, and she pointed out that one cited a legal principle that did not exist. Kamal said the judge warned the father he could be ordered to pay the mother's legal fees and other penalties if it happened again, and the father denied using AI and argued nothing prohibited it. He kept filing, the judge kept turning him down and said the court would not consider more filings before the final hearing, and the parents eventually settled. Kamal said it could be used as a form of litigation abuse.

Judges are losing patience too. A Florida husband representing himself in his divorce used AI to file at least 145 motions, then sent an appeals court 45 AI-generated pages and an 863-page appendix explaining himself, according to court records. In May, the court ordered its clerk to reject his future filings unless a lawyer signs them. Benmor's advice to clients is not to spend money unduly by asking a human expert to debate a robot expert.

stories.Headline: New Graduate Degree Program Supports Career Advancement in AI-Driven Economy
stories.Summary:
The University of Toledo has created a new online master's degree in data science and AI, the university announced on November 3, 2026. The program is run through UToledo's School of Interdisciplinary Data Science, which the College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics launched last year. It is the latest addition to that school, which also offers an existing Bachelor of Science in Data Science. The new degree is expected to enroll its first cohort in spring 2027.

The program focuses on combining artificial intelligence tools with data science work. Students will take courses in machine learning and AI, cloud computing and big data systems, statistics, data analysis and visual presentation, and programming languages including Python, SQL and R. Courses also cover the ethical and responsible use of AI, and the program ends with a capstone project on a real-world data problem. Students can also pursue certifications through the Amazon Web Services Academy, and UToledo is the only AWS Academy member institution in Northwest Ohio and one of only four four-year public universities in Ohio. The program recently received state approval and expands UToledo's roster of more than 50 online degree and certificate programs.

Dr. Bill Kalies, a professor in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics and director of the School of Interdisciplinary Data Science, said data science and AI are priority areas for workforce development. He said the program aligns with industry trends so graduates can meet current workforce needs and adapt as AI and big data technologies evolve. Dr. Mitchell S. McKinney, provost and executive vice president for academic affairs, said UToledo constantly evaluates its programs to meet the needs of students and employers. He said the university is well positioned to meet growing demand for data scientists as AI transforms work across industries. Dr. Nikolas Podraza, interim dean of the College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics, said employers are creating new data science roles and often want employees with advanced degrees, and that the program focuses on skills for career advancement.

The university says graduates will be positioned for roles such as data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI engineers and data analysts. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics expects data scientist employment to increase by more than a third between 2024 and 2034, and it calculates that data scientists earned a median salary of $112,000 in 2024. The program is designed for working professionals and recent graduates, with asynchronous courses that the university says bring campus resources and faculty to a wider variety of students. UToledo is a headlining sponsor and co-host of Great Lakes AI Week, which runs from Tuesday, November 10, to Thursday, November 12, and brings together business, technology and community leaders from across the region.

Articles.Title: New Graduate Degree Program Supports Career Advancement in AI-Driven Economy

stories.Headline: SBU Study: AI May Improve Patient Discharge Summaries
stories.Summary:
A Stony Brook University study published online in Digital Medicine, a Nature partner journal, found that artificial intelligence could help physicians prepare hospital patient discharge summaries more efficiently and with greater accuracy and completeness. The research team compared AI-generated and human-authored discharge summaries for 60 internal medicine hospitalizations at Stony Brook University Hospital lasting 7 to 21 days. The summaries were assessed in pairs by hospitalists and primary care physicians. The method used a large language model, a form of AI that can process and generate text, to develop summaries for complex patient cases, and clinicians helped design the approach based on the information physicians need after discharge.

Physician reviewers preferred the AI-generated discharge summaries in 95 percent of the evaluated hospitalizations. They gave the AI summaries higher scores for overall quality, readability, accuracy and completeness, and they identified fewer missing clinical details than in the human-authored summaries. Primary care physicians also found the AI summaries easier to understand, easier to explain to patients and caregivers, and more useful for follow-up care. Both types of summaries contained errors, but reviewers found no statistically significant difference in the estimated severity or likelihood of harm associated with those errors.

Rachel Wong, MD, co-corresponding author and clinical associate professor in the Departments of Internal Medicine and Biomedical Informatics in the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, said the results provide evidence that artificial intelligence can support discharge documentation for complex hospital stays. The authors stress that physician review and verification remain essential before any AI-generated discharge draft is used for a patient record. Fusheng Wang, co-corresponding author and professor in the Department of Biomedical Informatics and Department of Computer Science, said the next steps are to continue developing the tool with emphasis on assessing accuracy, safety, actual time savings for physicians and how it would fit into clinical workflows. He also said a pilot study to evaluate the tool in everyday clinical practice at Stony Brook Medicine is being considered.

Discharge summaries give patients essential information when they leave a hospital, including their treatment, medication needs, changes in medication, unresolved medical issues and follow-up needs as an outpatient. Primary care physicians rely on them to continue care and they serve as a roadmap going forward. The study focused on longer, complex hospital stays, where a larger volume of medical information must be summarized and where discharge documentation can be a significant burden for providers. The project involved an interdisciplinary team of researchers including computer scientists, biomedical informaticists, physicians and a communications expert, with lead author Tyler Osborne, a PhD candidate in the Department of Computer Science, and assistance from the Research Services and Innovation Team from Stony Brook Medicine Information Technology.

Articles.Title: SBU Study: AI May Improve Patient Discharge Summaries

stories.Headline: UC San Diego Launches AI-Driven Chip Design Research Initiative Supported By Qualcomm Technologies
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego announced on November 2, 2026, that Qualcomm Technologies gave a $500,000 gift to its Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing. The gift launches the AI in Microelectronic Systems initiative, known as AIMS, a collaboration between Qualcomm researchers and UC San Diego faculty. The initiative will study ways to improve the design of systems-on-chips, which combine multiple computing components into a single device. It will also look at hyperscale computing architectures used in mobile devices, autonomous systems, cloud computing and large-scale AI.

The Halıcıoğlu School is adding $250,000 in matching funds to the gift. The money will support work by faculty including Yusu Wang, Jinendra Ranka, Lily Weng, Mahidhar Tatineni, Martin Kandes, Zhijian Liu and Arya Mazumdar. The research will cover processor design, hardware accelerators, memory systems, interconnects, workload characterization and performance optimization, with attention to energy efficiency. The gift carries no requirements for research deliverables, services or reporting.

Rajesh K. Gupta, dean of the Halıcıoğlu School, said AI is placing great demands on computing infrastructure while also offering powerful tools to design it. He said the collaboration allows the school to bring together expertise in AI, computing systems and microelectronics and to prepare the next generation of researchers and engineers. Hemanth Sampath, vice president of engineering for Qualcomm Technologies, said UC San Diego has been one of Qualcomm's most valued academic partners. He said the company is proud to support AIMS and to work with UC San Diego researchers on AI-enabled system and semiconductor design.

The initiative builds on existing ties between Qualcomm and UC San Diego, including Wang's work on AI-assisted chip design. Researchers led by Ranka have also set up an independent benchmarking infrastructure for AI processors, which has already given the Qualcomm team targeted feedback. The article describes the collaboration as continuing a relationship that helped shape San Diego as a center for wireless communications, computing and innovation. It does not say what specific results are expected or when.

Articles.Title: UC San Diego Launches AI-Driven Chip Design Research Initiative Supported By Qualcomm Technologies

stories.Headline: Jennifer Miller to Serve on Connie's Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Committee (AIEC)
stories.Summary:
Jennifer E. Miller, PhD, an associate professor of medicine in general medicine and co-director of the Program for Biomedical Ethics at Yale School of Medicine, has been invited to serve on the Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Committee for Connie, Connecticut's Health Information Exchange. The article was published on November 2, 2026. Connie was established in 2019 and oversees and advances services that support the secure exchange of health information across Connecticut. It is authorized by state statute and provides infrastructure intended to improve healthcare delivery, quality, safety, and value for healthcare organizations, providers, and residents throughout the state.

The committee is a key part of Connie's AI governance framework and will guide the safe and responsible evaluation and application of AI technologies. The article says AI offers significant opportunities to enhance Connie's services in clinical care, operational efficiency, and consumer empowerment. It also says AI introduces risks that must be carefully evaluated, managed, and monitored to ensure responsible and trustworthy use. The committee will be chaired by Dr. Allen Hsiao, chief health information officer for Yale New Haven Health and Yale School of Medicine.

Miller is the person named as joining the committee, and the article identifies her by her Yale roles in medicine and biomedical ethics. The article does not include any statement from Miller about the appointment. It also gives no comment from Hsiao beyond naming him as chair. The article does not say when the committee will meet or what specific work it will take up first.

The context is Connie's role as Connecticut's health information exchange and its effort to govern the use of AI in its services. The article describes the committee as playing a critical role in guiding evaluation and application of AI technologies. It does not say what happens next beyond the committee's expected work. No start date, meeting schedule, or further steps are given.

stories.Headline: Q&A: How are AI and religion connected?
stories.Summary:
Wes E. King, an assistant teaching professor at the University of Washington, developed a special topics class on AI, robots and religion in 2019 while finishing a seminary degree and studying for a doctorate in the Information School. King has taught the class ever since and received a Distinguished Teaching Award this year. In the class, students analyze whether transhumanism, a movement to use technology to transcend human limits, is a religion. King spoke with UW News about the class, the pope's view of AI and finding hope.

The article cites several recent events that brought the question of AI and religion forward. In May, Pope Leo XIV issued an encyclical on the church's mission in the time of AI, writing that humanity must never be replaced or surpassed. Anthropic has met with religious leaders on how to make moral AI, and people held a funeral for an AI model. King said the idea that AI is our only hope for salvation goes back to Edward Fredkin, an early AI developer in the 1950s.

King said characterizations of AI companies as cults or techno-religions are not far off, pointing to ideologies such as transhumanism, effective altruism and rationalism that motivate development communities. King warned that faith in techno-power could lead to treating AI as infallible and outsourcing moral dilemmas. King also said the pope got some things right, including problems with labor and power, but was wrong to center humanity and to classify queer and trans people as less than human. King said seeking moral guidance from dominant religious traditions is a dead end unless tech leaders acknowledge their existing beliefs and disrupt their own business models.

King said religion and technology are deeply connected, contrary to a common trope, and described a firehose of information and a firestorm of questions about these connections. King pointed to feminist and queer theologians who interpret religious texts through stewardship and symbiotic relationships rather than human dominance. King said technologies should be developed for flourishing, not only for human flourishing. King ended by saying hope lies with voices that have been silenced, including women, queer folks, Indigenous leaders, mystics and the Global South.

Articles.Title: Q&A: How are AI and religion connected?

stories.Headline: UH Launches Free ‘AI for Hawai i’ Course for Everyone
stories.Summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi launched a free online course called Artificial Intelligence for Hawaiʻi on November 2, 2026, according to the office of Governor Josh Green. The course is open to everyone and requires no UH affiliation or login. It is self-paced and hosted on the UH OneAI Hub. It uses instructional videos, Hawaiʻi-based examples and hands-on activities. The course teaches foundational AI knowledge and practical skills and addresses responsible and ethical use through a Hawaiʻi lens.

It is designed for UH students and employees, educators, government employees, small business owners, nonprofit staff and other community members. The articles cite CNBC as saying 80 percent of hiring managers consider AI skills a priority when evaluating candidates. They also cite the National Association of Colleges and Employers as saying 60 percent of employers already assign interns projects involving AI tools. UH President Wendy Hensel said AI is changing how people work, learn and live and that Hawaiʻi cannot afford to sit on the sidelines. She said UH has both an opportunity and a responsibility to help the state lead through this change.

She said that means making AI education accessible to everyone and giving people practical skills to use these tools effectively, responsibly and in ways that reflect Hawaiʻi’s values. The course was informed by UH experts in Hawaiian values, culture, language and ʻike Hawaiʻi. The course is part of UH’s broader effort to provide AI education and resources statewide as the technology reshapes education, business, government and the workforce. A UH Task Force on Hawaiian Values and Culture examined issues unique to AI in Hawaiʻi, including protocols for how ʻike and ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi resources should be used and what information should and should not be contributed to AI systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the course being available.

Articles.Title: UH Launches Free ‘AI for Hawaiʻi’ Course for Everyone

stories.Headline: ‘What Are We Building?’ AI lecture series continues Nov. 16
stories.Summary:
Marquette University's "What Are We Building?" series, a year-long communal exercise about artificial intelligence, will continue with two lectures on Monday, Nov. 16, in the Eisenberg Room in Sensenbrenner Hall. The university-wide initiative invites the Marquette community to consider questions surrounding AI and the role of a Catholic university as a place for moral and spiritual discernment about emerging technologies. Dr. Taylor Nutter, assistant professor of theology at Mount St. Mary's University, will present both lectures.

The first is an academic lecture and panel titled "Magnifica Humanitas and the Structural Critique of Technocracy: Exploring the Longue Durée of AI" at 3:30 p.m., intended for an academic audience though all are welcome. The second is a public lecture titled "'AI Is Not Morally Neutral': Pope Leo XIV, Technology, and Social Justice" at 7 p.m., open to Marquette faculty, staff and students as well as the public. The series is described as a year-long communal discernment exercise about AI. It is a university-wide initiative, and it frames the role of a Catholic university as a place for moral and spiritual discernment about emerging technologies.

Both events take place on the same day, Monday, Nov. 16, and both are held in the Eisenberg Room in Sensenbrenner Hall. The academic lecture and panel begins at 3:30 p.m., and the public lecture begins at 7 p.m. Dr. Taylor Nutter is the assistant professor of theology at Mount St. Mary's University who will give both lectures. The academic session is described as intended for an academic audience, though all are welcome.

The evening session is described as open to Marquette faculty, staff and students, as well as the public. The article does not quote Nutter directly. More information and additional events are available on the AI at Marquette website. The article does not say what happens after the Nov. 16 lectures.

stories.Headline: Professor Creates AI Tool Connecting Newsroom With Readers
stories.Summary:
Vania André, an assistant professor of public relations at Hofstra University and publisher of The Haitian Times, created an app that helps journalists better understand their audiences. She was featured by Generative AI in the Newsroom, or GAIN, for the work. The article about the app was titled “How The Haitian Times Vibe-Coded Its Own Audience Research App.” André used Lovable, an artificial intelligence platform, to turn extensive audience research into an interactive newsroom tool.

The app draws on focus groups in nine cities and nearly 500 survey responses. It helps staff explore how different readers might respond to story ideas, language, and coverage. The tool also flags potential cultural sensitivities, so journalists can consider the varied perspectives of readers in Haiti and the Haitian diaspora. Its simulated responses offer ideas to test through further audience engagement.

André is the person behind the tool, and the GAIN project featured her for it. GAIN is an effort to collaboratively explore the responsible use of generative AI in news production. The Hofstra news item was posted on November 3, 2026, and was credited to Ginny Greenberg. The articles do not say what happens next with the app or the project.

Articles.Title: Professor Creates AI Tool Connecting Newsroom With Readers

stories.Headline: From 2G to 6G: Jin Yang Brings Wireless and AI Expertise as Adjunct Professor
stories.Summary:
Jin Yang has joined the University of California, Davis as a new adjunct professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, the college announced on November 3, 2026. She brings three decades of industry experience in wireless communications at NVIDIA, Verizon and AirTouch. Over her career she helped guide the evolution of wireless technology from 2G to 5G, and she is now focused on 6G and beyond. She also taught mobile wireless communications at Portland State University early in her career.

Yang is mentoring graduate students and consulting on their research at UC Davis. She is developing a course on AI-native wireless communication that explores how sensing, computing and wireless networks can work together to support intelligent, autonomous systems. She is also working with the department on a master's student project course where students experience the entire lifecycle of designing an AI product. The course will use a digital twin to simulate a wireless network in a small area of San Francisco, and students will study algorithms and adjust parameters such as transmission power.

Yang said the industry and research are at an inflection point with AI and automation, with tasks once done manually becoming autonomous. She said her industry work involved continuous trade-offs between performance, economics and scale, and that translating theory and practice is what she can contribute. She said she wants to help students understand industry career paths and connect them with her professional network. She also said projects will include writing and oral presentations because communication is equally important.

Yang has known UC Davis professors for decades, including Distinguished Professor Zhi Ding, and has mentored interns from the university. She was previously involved in the Industrial Affiliates Program and spoke at the UC Davis Industrial Affiliates Symposium. She said she is eager to work alongside Ding and assistant professor Yubei Chen and to support the next generation of researchers. She said she looks forward to building lasting partnerships with colleagues across academia and industry.

Articles.Title: From 2G to 6G: Jin Yang Brings Wireless and AI Expertise as Adjunct Professor

stories.Headline: Meet the AI Expert Helping Guide Colby through a Technological Revolution
stories.Summary:
Vijayanta Jain, a computer scientist, joined Colby College's Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence last year as a postdoctoral associate. In May, the institute brought him on board to work directly with faculty across disciplines. He helps them identify where AI tools might advance teaching and research, and then develop the tools to make it happen. The Davis Institute is the nation's first cross-disciplinary AI institute at a liberal arts college.

Jain earned his Ph.D. in computer science from the University of Maine, where his research focused on privacy, software engineering, and AI. Before that, he graduated summa cum laude from Texas Tech University. His work at Colby includes helping make AI models available on the College's own servers, a secure alternative to commercial systems. He also teaches AI Lab with David Watts, an experimental research seminar that brings together students from all four academic divisions.

David Watts, director of the Davis Institute, said the College is lucky to have Jain join during a pivotal moment. He said Jain's deep technical expertise, broader knowledge about privacy, and outstanding teaching skills made him stand out as an ideal candidate. Jain said that as new models come out, understanding their capabilities and risks is becoming a bit of a challenge. He also said a lot of people think AI means generative AI, which is not true, and that AI encompasses many different kinds of technologies.

Jain has worked with Elizabeth McGrath, an associate professor of physics and astronomy, who had thousands of Hubble Space Telescope images of galaxies on a hard drive. He suggested using convolutional neural networks to automate classification of their structures and shapes, and his model has helped accelerate her work. He is also working with Professor of Psychology Chris Soto to explore how locally hosted language models can streamline scientific-literature reviews. Jain said that when you are doing a lot of interviews and want to understand sentiments at a large scale, AI is a really good solution.

Articles.Title: Meet the AI Expert Helping Guide Colby through a Technological Revolution

stories.Headline: Janet Yellen says college still matters in an AI-driven economy
stories.Summary:
Janet Yellen, the former Treasury secretary and former Federal Reserve chair, spoke at Metropolitan State University of Denver on Oct. 29, 2026, in a conversation with university President Janine Davidson as part of the President's Speaker Series. She said she had no real career plan when she arrived at college and took an introductory economics course that she called love at first sight. According to the article, she is the only person in U.S. history to lead the White House Council of Economic Advisers, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department, and the first woman to hold the last two positions. She became Treasury secretary in 2021. Yellen said college graduates earn about $1,700 a week on average compared with less than $1,000 for workers without a college education, a gap that adds up over a 40-year career.

She acknowledged that rising tuition and student debt have made the investment harder for many Americans, but said college also enriches life and builds a love of learning and the ability to adapt. She said artificial intelligence is affecting entry-level jobs, particularly work in research and analysis that has traditionally helped young professionals gain experience. She said AI could raise productivity and living standards, as earlier technological advances did, but that public policy must make sure the benefits are widely shared and that people harmed get retraining and support. Yellen said she was struck, when she became Treasury secretary, that no portrait of a woman hung among those of her predecessors going back to Alexander Hamilton, and that she was stepping into something no woman had done for 232 years. She said she grew up in Brooklyn listening to her father, a physician whose patients included dockworkers and manufacturing employees, talk about the effects of unemployment.

She said economics is really about people and their lives and what can make their lives better. She said she learned that hardships were not inevitable and that good government policy could make a huge difference. Yellen praised MSU Denver's emphasis on career-connected education, including employer partnerships and hands-on experience, as an advantage for graduates entering an AI-driven workforce. She stressed the importance of skills AI cannot easily replicate, including judgment, compassion, communication and understanding other people's needs. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Janet Yellen says college still matters in an AI-driven economy

stories.Headline: AI Constitutions: - Berkman Klein Center
stories.Summary:
The Berkman Klein Center hosted an event titled “AI Constitutions: How to Tell an AI What to Do, Rules, Cases, and Interpretation” on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The start time was changed to 5:00 pm, and the session ran from 5:00 PM to 6:00 PM ET. It took place at 1557 Massachusetts Ave., 5th Floor, Cambridge, MA 02138. The speakers were Nick Caputo of the Johns Hopkins School of Government and Policy and the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, and Jordi Weinstock of Harvard Law School and the Berkman Klein Center.

The event examined what the law can teach about where AI systems should exercise judgment when their instructions leave room for interpretation. AI developers now govern their most capable models through written constitutions, which set out a model’s values, priorities and character and are used directly in training. Anthropic’s constitution for Claude is the most prominent example. The discussion raised questions law has dealt with for centuries, including who has the authority to write these documents, how vague principles should be interpreted when they conflict, whether a model can meaningfully consent to the values it is trained on, and what role governments should play.

Caputo’s research treats AI alignment as a problem of jurisprudence, and his work in progress asks whether Claude can consent to its own constitution. Weinstock teaches at Harvard Law School about the confluence of AI and traditional law and served as an external reviewer of Claude’s constitution. The two discussed what legal theory can and cannot tell us about AI constitutions. The event page was last updated on November 3, 2026.

Articles.Title: AI Constitutions: - Berkman Klein Center

stories.Headline: Elise Penn, S.M. '24, Ph.D. '25: Atmospheric chemistry meets artificial intelligence - Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
stories.Summary:
Elise Penn, S.M. '24, Ph.D. '25, joined Zeus AI in 2025 as a research scientist, according to a Harvard SEAS alumni profile published November 3, 2026. Zeus AI is a Cambridge-based start-up that uses artificial intelligence to create weather modeling data from observable conditions and satellite data. Penn earned her master's in environmental science and engineering and her Ph.D. in atmospheric chemistry at SEAS, where she worked in the Atmospheric Chemistry Modeling Group led by Daniel Jacob, the Vasco McCoy Family Professor of Atmospheric Chemistry and Environmental Engineering. Before Harvard she received a bachelor's in geological engineering and applied math at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where she worked with Professor Tracey Holloway on research preparing for the TEMPO satellite project.

At Zeus AI, Penn works on modeling based purely on observations rather than numerical weather prediction, which relies on mathematical equations and physics models. She said the company is trying to see how far it can push pure observation modeling, turning federal technology such as satellite data into products for commercial use, and also developing technologies the federal government can use to inform policy decisions. She said she was attracted to Zeus because its two co-founders started at NASA and are serious weather modeling researchers with a lot of AI experience. At SEAS her dissertation used satellite observations of methane as a proxy to estimate concentrations of the hydroxyl radical, known as the detergent of the atmosphere because it breaks down methane and other pollutants. She also worked as a research assistant at the non-profit Carbon Mapper, studying whether emissions from coal mines across the country could be estimated from a few individual methane plumes, and found it worked pretty well.

Penn said she liked math and science and was drawn to atmospheric chemistry because she could use applied math skills on a very applied problem that could help people. She said the weather modeling field has been very successful in creating AI models that are just faster, and that she gets to pull in that expertise and combine it with the atmospheric chemistry work she is interested in. She said she likes working at a small start-up because she has more control over the outcome, it is faster paced, and it has more resources than academia, and that getting to work on AI models, learn new things and do research is pretty perfect. The article gives no further details on Zeus AI's products or on what happens next.
