stories.Headline: Short Takes from the AI at 70 Conference
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth held a three-day conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? from late October into early November 2026, with more than two dozen panel discussions, keynote speeches and other presentations. The talks featured pioneering researchers, AI leaders and scholars who study the technology's effects on society. On Oct. 29, a session on AI in International Security and Conflict was co-sponsored by the Davidson Institute for Global Security. On Oct. 30, separate sessions covered teaching and learning in the age of AI, held at the Hanover Inn, and the history of AI and the future of human knowing, held in Moore Theater.

At the security session, Sasha Baker, OpenAI's head of national security policy and a former acting undersecretary of defense for policy, said AI models are increasing the rate of change and the ability to scale, and that most militaries and governments are still grappling with what that means. James Patton Rogers, a lecturer in security and technology at King's College London, said the proliferation of drones and increasingly autonomous weapons points to a global shift in power. He cited Iran's high-tech response to the United States' Operation Epic Fury, using drones and precision missiles over greater distances, as making the U.S. and its allies reconsider their footprint in those regions. Baker cited a U.S. Department of Defense directive requiring appropriate human judgment in autonomous weapon use, and said there is always a commander who is accountable. Patton Rogers noted that the United Nations has discussed lethal autonomous weapons for a decade with limited progress on regulation.

On teaching, James Dobson, associate professor of English and creative writing, said AI has drained much of the color from learning, made assessing student learning difficult and taken an emotional toll, while also enabling research and teaching across fields. Roopika Risam, a Dartmouth AI Fellow and chair of the Department of Film and Media Studies, described a faculty effort that defined four core competencies, with AI literacy as a subset, and said open and honest conversations about generative AI are needed. Molly Crockett, a professor at Princeton University, warned that claims about AI simulating human cognition rest on an illusion of generalizability, and said the future of human knowing might depend on asking less of machines and more of each other. Hany Farid, a professor of computer science, said technical solutions can be developed but trust is a very human thing, and that eroded trust in institutions is a problem society must resolve. An Oct. 29 panel on Arts, Ethics and AI opened with audience members creating a song with Nona Hendryx's AI-powered avatar, and featured Hendryx, Paul D. Miller, who performs as DJ Spooky, and professor Jacqueline Wernimont, moderated by Risam.

Articles.Title: Short Takes from the AI at 70 Conference

stories.Headline: New $15M Department of Energy Genesis Award Will Use AI to Decode the Shape of RNA
stories.Summary:
The Department of Energy announced on October 8 a set of 12 Phase II Genesis Mission awards totaling $159 million. One of them is a three-year, $15 million award to UC San Diego Professor of Biochemistry and Molecular Biophysics Navtej Toor. His project is titled “Decoding the RNA Structurome to Secure AI Advantage for the Bioeconomy.” It aims to expand the library of known RNA structures and use that data to train artificial intelligence models that predict the three-dimensional shape of RNA from its sequence alone. The project will determine RNA structures from select DOE model organisms, including two photosynthetic microbes that make fuels and chemicals from carbon dioxide, and the bioenergy crops sorghum and poplar.

Toor's lab has reduced the time to determine an RNA structure to two weeks using a scaffold technology, compared with the years crystallography can require. In the past year alone the lab determined 60 protein-free RNA structures, nearly a third of the field's 50-year total of fewer than 200. Toor's goal is 1,000 protein-free RNA structures by the end of the project, five times as many as the entire field has produced in the past 50 years. Toor said a data shortage, not computing power, blocks accurate AI prediction of RNA shapes and limits the design of organisms for energy and biomanufacturing. He said the project closes the RNA data gap through paired advances in experimental measurement and in AI algorithm design.

He described algorithm development as running in a closed loop with the experiments, with models flagging the RNA molecules they predict least confidently, those molecules imaged next, and retraining on the results advancing the AI. Chancellor Pradeep K. Khosla said the research will expand understanding of how RNA functions within living cells and drive advances in biofuels, health care and biochemistry. UC San Diego leads the project with co-investigators Rhiju Das of Stanford University, Wah Chiu of SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory and Daniel Haack of A-Form Solutions, Inc. Additional partners are the University of Washington, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus, Google and NVIDIA. Toor is a co-founder of A-Form Solutions, Inc., which may potentially benefit financially from the research results. Toor said the goal is an online program that accepts any RNA sequence and returns an accurate three-dimensional structure, which could eventually be applied to human RNA.

Articles.Title: New $15M Department of Energy Genesis Award Will Use AI to Decode the Shape of RNA - UC San Diego Today

stories.Headline: Guru Madhavan on Engineering AI for the Public Good
stories.Summary:
Guru Madhavan, a Stony Brook University alumnus who earned an MS in 2002 and a PhD, spoke with the Stony Brook AI Innovation Institute in an interview published on November 3, 2026. He is the Norman R. Augustine Senior Scholar and Senior Director of Programs at the National Academy of Engineering. The interview covered his views on the current societal shift into artificial intelligence. Madhavan described AI as far more than an instantaneous answer generator, calling it a new, invisible layer of civic infrastructure.

Madhavan is a systems scholar whose career spans engineering design, public health, technical advising and civic responsibility. He has written foundational texts including Applied Minds and Wicked Problems. At the National Academy of Engineering, he leads a multi-stakeholder initiative to advance understanding of complex technical and social systems and to identify unifiable approaches to manage them better. He said he is interested in large engineering systems with large consequences, and even small engineering systems with extra-large consequences.

He pointed to aviation, power grids, health infrastructure and digital commerce as examples. He said these all operate through a large network of invisible coordination, standards and maintenance regimes often put together by people of diverse backgrounds. The full interview with Madhavan was conducted by Ankita Nagpal and is available at the AI Innovation Institute website. The article does not say what the initiative will do next or when any further work is expected.

Articles.Title: Guru Madhavan on Engineering AI for the Public Good

stories.Headline: When AI Makes Unacceptable Decisions Feel Normal
stories.Summary:
A Wharton article published on November 3, 2026, warns that repeated use of AI can quietly reshape human judgment. It was written by Cornelia Walther, a visiting scholar at Wharton and director of the global alliance POZE, who spent over 20 years at the United Nations. She describes a manager who first uses an AI assistant to sharpen notes for a performance conversation, then to compare employees and suggest promotions, and finally to surface positions for elimination during a restructuring. Each step is easy to justify because the system is fast and apparently helpful, yet the tool moves from improving the language of a decision to taking part in making it.

The article says the central risk is a slide from assistance to substitution, since asking AI to articulate a view differs from asking it what view to hold. It cites a 2025 study of knowledge workers that found greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical-thinking effort, with cognitive work shifting toward checking what the system produced. It also cites a 2026 study on cognitive agency transfer that distinguishes autonomous offloading, where AI supports a person's own thinking, from dependent offloading, where the system structures the problem and supplies the conclusion. Dependent use was associated with weaker perceived independent judgment, deep processing, and autonomous capability, though the study does not establish long-term cognitive decline.

Walther describes four stages of agency decay: experimentation, integration, reliance, and addiction. She cites a 2025 study, "Accepting the Unacceptable in the AI Era," in which AI recommendations reduced moral awareness among managers handling multiple organizational decisions, making unethical recommendations easier to accept. She also cites a 2026 experiment finding that ChatGPT advice influenced judgments in a moral dilemma even when the advice contained no supporting moral argument. She writes that organizations keep the liability while gradually outsourcing parts of the capacity that make responsibility meaningful, and she proposes four questions to preserve human authorship before a consequential use, including what part of judgment is being delegated and what one thought before the AI answered.

The article says business leaders already worry about privacy, cybersecurity, hallucinations, intellectual property, discrimination, and compliance, and that another worry sits beside them: what repeated AI use is doing to the quality of human judgment inside the organization. It argues that a person can remain formally in the loop while moving substantively downstream of the machine, since the framing, shortlist of options, and first recommendation may all be generated elsewhere. Walther writes that vigilance means noticing the transition while the boundary is still visible. Otherwise, she says, outsourcing judgment will eventually feel entirely ordinary, and people may fail to remember why keeping hold of it once seemed important.

Articles.Title: When AI Makes Unacceptable Decisions Feel Normal

stories.Headline: Brown archaeologist to co-lead AI project to advance understanding of ancient Andean empires
stories.Summary:
Parker VanValkenburgh, an associate professor of anthropology and of archaeology and the ancient world at Brown University, is co-director of a new study supported by Schmidt Sciences. He and Vanderbilt University researchers Steven Wernke and Yuankai Huo were awarded $732,574 for a project called “Scaling Archaeological Vision: Imperial Landscapes of the Andes through AI-Assisted Survey.” The work builds on more than a decade of previous research. The team previously developed the Geospatial Platform for Andean Culture, History and Archaeology, or GeoPACHA, which uses satellite imagery and AI to map and study archaeological sites across the Andes.

The researchers will develop DeepAndes Workbench, an AI platform through which archaeologists and other scholars can query an agent with images and verbal prompts to distinguish specific types of archaeological features. They say the tool will advance understanding of how three ancient Andean empires, the Wari, Inka and Spanish, adapted to local conditions and successively influenced one another. The result is expected to be the first set of continental-scale maps of how empires standardized, adapted and layered their built environments. Researchers will be able to use the tool to detect specific features of, for example, Wari ceremonial buildings from the eighth century or Inka imperial buildings from the 15th century.

VanValkenburgh described DeepAndes Workbench as an image search engine for archaeological sites, a tool that will let colleagues look for distinctive kinds of buildings and features, many of them built by the Wari, the Inka and the Spanish. He said expert users will provide feedback on the results they get back, which will in turn help improve the models. He also said the tool is not an all-seeing eye that knows everything about Andean archaeology, but a tool researchers can use to extend their vision. He said this in turn models the kind of disaggregated, diverse and question-driven scholarly community that tends to exist in the humanities.

VanValkenburgh, Wernke and Huo are partnering with a team of approximately 15 collaborators across the United States, Peru, Chile and Australia. They are also working with researchers at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, which is part of the U.S. Department of Energy and conducts research in areas including supercomputing. Schmidt Sciences is also providing in-kind supercomputing resources. The new grant supports continued activities of GeoPACHA toward the development of DeepAndes Workbench.

Articles.Title: Brown archaeologist to co-lead AI project to advance understanding of ancient Andean empires

stories.Headline: UC San Diego’s Halıcıoğlu School Expands AI Computing Infrastructure to Address Critical Shortages
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego's Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing announced on November 3, 2026, that it is expanding its shared AI computing platform. The school launched PARASOL, the next generation of its longstanding Data Science and Machine Learning Platform. The expansion is enabled by the founding gift from computer scientist and philanthropist Taner Halıcıoğlu. The new investment nearly triples the campus GPU capacity.

Beginning in Winter quarter 2027, four new high-performance GPU servers with a total of 32 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs will nearly triple PARASOL's overall GPU capacity. They will nearly quadruple the peak-period capacity available to Halıcıoğlu School courses. Each year they will provide about 66,800 GPU-hours during peak instructional periods and more than 213,000 off-peak GPU-hours for research and other work. Demand from Halıcıoğlu School programs alone is projected to more than triple, from about 43,000 hours a year in 2026 to more than 140,000 by 2030. A new reservation system gives School students and faculty first priority while PARASOL keeps serving coursework and student research campuswide.

Chancellor Pradeep K. Khosla said transformational gifts let the university promote its academic mission through new offerings and services. Dean Rajesh Gupta said the real transformation is the bridge between coursework and research for students. Adam Tilghman, lead architect of PARASOL at IT Services, said planning for growth led the team to rethink how it delivers the platform. Kevin Chou, Interim Chief Information Officer at IT Services, said PARASOL expands capacity while helping build infrastructure that can grow with student and faculty needs.

Students have turned to commercial cloud GPU services for coursework and independent projects, which the article says underscores the need for university-supported infrastructure. Halıcıoğlu School students will be the first to receive automatic access to Open Learning workspaces for exploring large language models and other AI tools. The deployment will let university leaders monitor demand and plan further investments. Instructors can request PARASOL access through the IT Services & Support Portal, and current DSMLP, Datahub and Research Cluster users keep their existing accounts.

Articles.Title: UC San Diego’s Halıcıoğlu School Expands AI Computing Infrastructure to Address Critical Shortages

stories.Headline: U of A's AI chief: Tech should help, not replace, workers
stories.Summary:
The University of Arizona launched an “AI in a Domain” leadership cohort earlier this year, and 49 faculty and staff members are taking part in the three-tiered program, according to the Arizona Daily Star. The group is working on a roadmap for how to use artificial intelligence responsibly and effectively in education, research and university operations. David Ebert, the university’s chief AI officer and chief data science officer, leads the effort and spoke to the paper in an interview. He said the goal is not to replace jobs but to help people become more effective so they can do more.

The roadmap will guide the university for six months at a time and will change every semester, Ebert said, and it will be opened to the broader university community for feedback. The university has had AI guidelines for over a year and uses a three-phase approach to courses: free use of AI as long as it is documented, use in certain tasks or assignments with documentation, and no use of AI at all. The university holds two town halls a semester, one a listening session and one to update resources, plus weekly and biweekly sessions where three people each talk about a new way they have used AI. About 250 people applied across the three programs, the AI Campus Champions, AI Fellows and AI Associate Directors, and 49 were selected. Ebert’s office also runs AI innovation pilots, with a staff of 25 people who can work with applicants for six months to help build a prototype.

Ebert said his office does not see AI replacing jobs, and he does not think it can replace the academic instruction faculty offer. He described AI as another learning aid, like a tutor or an introductory lab assistant, and said people should understand it and use it as a resource rather than rely on it. He said the university wants to find best practices and look long-term at how education needs to change, so graduates have skills that last 30 to 50 years in their careers. He said employers he has talked to want fundamental knowledge about AI, including the right values and how to judge whether something is correct. He also said privacy and data security must be considered alongside AI exploration.

The cohort was created to get people in different disciplines talking about how AI should be assimilated into university functions, and it looks at what the university has done before and what other universities are doing. The first cohort includes only faculty and staff, but Ebert said they would like to bring in students and their ideas as the program develops in spring 2027 and the following year, and his office already reaches out to student government associations and graduate student associations for input. His office is also working with Provost Patricia Prelock’s office on an education task force that will hold conversations across the university to develop guiding principles for AI in education. Ebert said decisions about AI in a given class, course or degree will be made individually by department and by college. Separately, Law360 reported that Southern Co., an Atlanta-based energy provider, expanded its chief legal officer’s duties to include oversight of technology efforts such as its artificial intelligence strategy and emerging technology governance.

stories.Headline: Your Next Client May Ask AI Who to Hire. Will It Recommend Your Firm?
stories.Summary:
A recent article in CPA Practice Advisor described how prospective clients may soon ask artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT which accounting firm to hire, instead of searching Google or asking a colleague for a referral. The article, published on November 2, 2026 and written by Heather Robinson, said a business owner expanding into multiple states might ask an AI platform for firms that specialize in mergers and acquisitions, tax strategy and multistate expansion. The article said AI tools pull information from multiple sources, compare options and generate recommendations within seconds. It added that AI recommendations are not always accurate or consistent, and that different platforms can give different answers.

The article said firms should test what AI platforms say about them by asking questions such as which industries they specialize in and what differentiates them from competitors. It said firms should check whether the information is accurate, reflects current capabilities and describes the firm they are trying to become. It recommended that marketing, business development and subject matter experts work together to answer the questions prospective clients ask. It also said firms should back their claims with client success stories, clearly defined specializations, professional credentials and original insights, and it listed five questions for leadership meetings, including how progress will be measured.

A separate article in The Seattle Times, published on November 1, 2026 and written by Sarah Kessler of The New York Times, reported that top law firms are promoting their use of AI but clients are asking when the efficiency will lead to lower bills. It said Sullivan & Cromwell introduced a tool called Agreement Analyzer, Cooley brought out Go Public for the S-1 drafting process and Ropes & Gray said it was developing a tool that could produce a detailed diligence report in hours rather than weeks. Neill Jakobe, vice chair of Ropes & Gray, said clients accept that AI makes firms faster but want to know what that means for them. Jennifer Leonard of Creative Lawyers said some clients have used AI agents to find billable line items where AI could have saved hours and have asked for discounts on that work.

The Seattle Times article said in-house legal teams often ask firms to cut bills by 20% to 30%, while firms push back by saying AI does not yet save that much time and is changing the mix of hours toward more substantive analysis. It said law firms also face competition from so-called AI native firms, and that Norm AI, a technology company with an affiliated law firm, raised $260 million at a $1.2 billion valuation in July from Khosla Ventures, Blackstone and Bain Capital. It said 35% of the 55 large law firms surveyed by Citi last year expected to change their billable hour models in the next year because of AI, while 65% expected changes by 2035. It added that revenue at large firms grew more than 12% on average in the first six months of the year, while average standard billing rates rose by double digits, according to Wells Fargo.

Articles.Title: Your Next Client May Ask AI Who to Hire. Will It Recommend Your Firm? - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: Dickenson schools earn distinguished status; board approves AI policy, announces $740,974 grant
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 28, Superintendent Haley Robinson told the Dickenson County School Board that all schools in the division had earned full accreditation and distinguished performance ratings from the Virginia Department of Education. She said the division was one of just three of 19 school divisions in the region to receive the distinguished designation for every school. Robinson credited employees across the system, including teachers, administrators, custodians, cafeteria workers and support staff. The board also heard presentations on bullying prevention activities tied to National Bullying Prevention Month from Ridgeview Elementary, Ridgeview Middle and Ridgeview High schools.

The board unanimously approved a new artificial intelligence policy at the same meeting. The policy requires AI systems used in the division to undergo a review of their privacy and security protections. Employees may not enter student information into AI applications without completing the division's formal approval and security procedures. Teachers may use AI for lesson planning, but they remain responsible for checking the accuracy of AI-generated materials before using them. Ryan Wallace was named the division's AI coordinator and will oversee the policy, including review and approval of AI tools and a list of authorized applications.

The division also announced a $740,974 grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Distance Learning and Telemedicine Program, obtained with Scott County Public Schools. The money will support educational technology and access to health-related services in rural communities. The articles did not detail specific equipment purchases, implementation schedules or how the funding would be split between the two divisions. The meeting highlighted student achievement, school safety and expanded educational opportunities.

Separately, an op-ed in SFGATE by Tara Chklovski said the San Francisco Unified School District still has no AI policy beyond a resource page. She wrote that the district has made Amira, an AI reading tutor, central to early literacy work, and that the Board of Education plans to vote on a technology policy in March. Three of the board's seven seats were on the Nov. 3 ballot. Chklovski argued that students should define a problem, learn how AI works and then build with it, documenting their AI use along the way.

stories.Headline: Argentina's Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven at the end of the world
stories.Summary:
President Javier Milei of Argentina is pitching Patagonia as a haven for artificial intelligence data centers, promising a hands-off approach to attract foreign investment. He told the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington last month that Argentina will not regulate artificial intelligence and will leave it free. Visitor logs obtained by The Associated Press show a steady stream of tech figures meeting with Milei and his aides in recent months, from venture capitalist Peter Thiel to representatives of OpenAI, Amazon, Google, Oracle and data center companies. Milei has also proposed creating "nonhuman corporations" run entirely by AI agents, and he frequently posts AI-generated images on social media.

The biggest test is near Trelew, where a Polish developer, Green Capital, plans a $3 billion campus that at full capacity could use nearly three times as much electricity as Buenos Aires. Construction is not expected to begin until around 2028, and if operated continuously at its projected peak, the finished campus would use about 2.7 times as much electricity in a year as the entire city of Buenos Aires consumed in 2025, according to an AP calculation. To win over companies wary of Argentina's chronic economic instability, Milei is pushing an incentive scheme that would cut the corporate income tax rate to 15% from 25% for projects of at least $1 billion in AI and other emerging industries, a measure awaiting Senate approval. The proposed incentives do not require companies to reserve computing capacity for local consumption or to disclose their energy and water use.

Green Capital promises to generate all its own electricity from wind turbines, solar farms and gas-fired generators rather than strain Argentina's congested grid. Marta Zlotnick of Green Capital said the company compared potential locations around the world and Patagonia came out on top in every category. Provincial officials are counting on the project to deliver billions of dollars in investment; Andrés Arbeletche, cabinet coordination secretary for Chubut, said that for them it is all a benefit and they give nothing up. But some residents of Trelew say they have no way to judge those assurances, since environmental studies are still underway, permits are pending and the company has not specified how much water the project would need or how much of its power would come from gas. Cristina Gibón, 46, who fears the environmental toll, said there is just so little information.

Francisco Sáenz, an agricultural engineer and fourth-generation sheep farmer whose family is among 14 landowners who have leased a combined 130,000 hectares, about 321,000 acres, to Green Capital, said sheep farmers are looking for more income. Critics warn Milei is pushing to deploy AI in Argentina without safeguards against risks such as mass surveillance and cyberattacks. Nicolás Wolovick, a computer science professor at the National University of Córdoba, said that without rules Argentina will become a laboratory, likening it to companies going to developing countries to test strange drugs they cannot test in major developed countries. Milei may hear similar concerns next week when French President Emmanuel Macron visits Argentina on his Latin American tour. Some investors are holding back until the election next year could unravel Milei's free-market reforms, and even some in his own government acknowledge efforts to build a clear legal framework, with companies waiting for Argentina to settle rules on training AI with copyrighted works.

Articles.Title: Argentina's Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven at the end of the world - San Mateo Daily Journal

stories.Headline: China to Fast-Track AI Law, Calls on Developers to Disclose Incidents
stories.Summary:
On November 3, China's National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic planner, promised to speed up work on a single artificial intelligence law. Wang Zhomeng, deputy director of the commission's Department of Innovation and High Technology, announced the plan at a briefing in Beijing. The rules would cover the whole AI lifecycle, from development to deployment. The changes would affect startups DeepSeek and Moonshot AI with their Kimi models, as well as Alibaba's Qwen family, according to Bloomberg.

The law will pull together lessons from existing rules to form a basic comprehensive law behind all other regulation in the field. Officials will also speed up rules on data, computing power and algorithms, plus key application areas. Safety and ethics standards will apply at every stage, from training through operation. Compliance will be checked periodically and outdated provisions revised, and there will be a transition period, though no length was given. Agencies will offer guidance and expand assessment, advisory and certification services to cut compliance costs, and regulatory sandboxes will test innovations under government oversight with temporary waivers.

Developers and operators must disclose security threats promptly and report incidents and found vulnerabilities to authorities. The government will watch job shifts and warn about worker displacement, and it plans to add model trainers and data annotators to the national occupational list. Tools will target deepfakes, algorithmic discrimination and personal data leaks, with special protection for older adults and minors, and the agenda includes fighting addiction and emotional attachment to AI. Wang said support for open development will continue, and he called on countries to build trust, coordinate disclosure of flaws and respond to risks together, saying AI safety cannot be solved by one company, industry or government alone.

China currently regulates the sector through ministerial rules, with interim measures for generative AI services in force since August 2023 and mandatory labeling of generated content since September 2025. From July 15, 2026, an advance level of control is set for each step of an AI agent, from human-only decisions to full autonomy. On May 11, the State Council's 2026 legislative work plan first included language about a comprehensive AI law, and the National People's Congress Standing Committee added AI initiatives to its list of documents to consider once texts are ready. No adoption timeline has been announced.
