stories.Headline: How to Get Breached, Step 5: Paste Client Data Into Any AI
stories.Summary:
A November 2, 2026 article by Scott Carr in CPA Practice Advisor describes how accounting firm staff may paste client tax returns, bank statements and Social Security numbers into free AI chatbots, a practice the article calls shadow AI. The piece is Step 5 in a series that offers bad advice so readers do the opposite. It gives a hypothetical example of a junior preparer who uploads a client's full return PDF into a free chatbot from her personal account and repeats it the next day with another client, while no one reviews the tool's data terms. The firm keeps no record of what was uploaded and cannot confirm whether it was retained.

The article says firms should classify data so tax returns, Social Security numbers, bank records and client financials are off limits for unapproved tools, and should add an acceptable use policy to their written security program. It recommends choosing approved tools with admin controls, multifactor authentication, activity logging and written terms on data retention and training use, and reviewing the vendor like any service provider. It advises taking inventory before the next filing deadline, requiring admin approval before AI apps connect to email, document storage or practice management software, and using DNS filtering to block or flag unapproved AI services. It also calls for log monitoring, staff training before busy season, offboarding that removes access to every tool tied to client data, and written records.

The article says many accounting and tax firms fall under the FTC Safeguards Rule, which expects a written information security program, a risk assessment and oversight of service providers that touch customer information, and that an AI vendor handling client data can be one of those providers. It notes the IRS offers guidance in Publication 4557, Safeguarding Taxpayer Data, and that Section 7216 limits how preparers may use and disclose tax return information, advising firms to confirm with their advisors how these apply. Carr, owner of Farmhouse Networking in Grants Pass, Oregon, writes that clients do not need a firm that avoids AI but one that can explain how it uses AI and why their data stays protected. The article says a short policy, a short list of approved tools and basic monitoring let firms answer client questions with confidence.

Articles.Title: How to Get Breached, Step 5: Paste Client Data Into Any AI - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: South Korea's Parliament Weighs New Local-Government Permits Ahead of AI Data Center Law, Industry Warns of "Double Regulation"
stories.Summary:
South Korea's National Assembly is considering amendments to the Special Act on AI Data Centers, which takes effect on March 10. Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Chae Hyun-il introduced a bill requiring a permit from a provincial governor or city, county or district mayor for new or expanded AI data centers above a size set by presidential decree. A separate amendment by lawmaker Han Jeong-ae would bar the law's one-stop licensing exception from applying to certain building permits tied to protecting residential and educational environments. The government is reportedly considering lowering the threshold for qualifying as an AI data center to 5MW from 10MW.

Chae's bill would require the new permit in addition to the existing building permit, along with mandatory public consultation with nearby residents. The permitting authority would have to consult with the Minister of Science and ICT, disclose the business plan in advance and gather residents' opinions. Han's bill would also require consideration of a region's power self-sufficiency rate and the share of electricity-use facilities that follow a local-production, local-consumption model when designating AIDC special zones. The current law focuses on one-stop licensing through the Ministry of Science and ICT to speed up construction.

A Ministry of Science and ICT official said the law requires data centers to obtain an existing building permit because they involve constructing buildings, but the bill creates a new permitting right separate from that. An aide to Chae said the legislation responds to the concentration of data centers and resident complaints in areas such as Seoul's Yeongdeungpo district, where four data centers operate and nine more are planned, including some next to schools. A cloud industry official said a new permitting procedure needs clarity on the size of facilities covered, screening criteria, how resident opinions are gathered and processing deadlines. Another industry official said there is concern over whether the new permitting system will preserve the special law's intent of speeding up licensing.

Just over four months remain before the special law takes effect. President Lee Jae Myung said in his budget address that South Korea will invest 21.3 trillion won, nearly twice this year's amount, in AI and the three megaprojects of semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers. The government's work on subordinate legislation is another variable, and the final criteria for qualifying as an AI data center have not been set. How the National Assembly reconciles community acceptance and investment speed is expected to affect South Korea's AI infrastructure buildout schedule and private investment plans.

Articles.Title: South Korea's Parliament Weighs New Local-Government Permits Ahead of AI Data Center Law, Industry Warns of "Double Regulation" - finance.biggo.com

stories.Headline: AI-Native Firms and Big Law Will Follow Medical Centers’ Model
stories.Summary:
A Bloomberg Law column published on November 2, 2026, argues that Big Law firms and AI-native legal startups will converge on a model like the Mayo Clinic. The columnist, Eric Dodson Greenberg, chief legal officer of Cox Media Group, says each side has half of what clients need. AI-native firms are hiring partners from elite firms, and Norm Law brought in former Sidley Austin global chair Mike Schmidtberger. Legacy firms are adding technology, including Kirkland's announced $500 million AI investment and Debevoise's client subscriptions to its AI tools.

The column says the medical-center model combines top experts with the best technology, and that the combination is the brand. It points to Mayo Clinic paying physicians fixed salaries rather than pay tied to volume, which makes team-based care work. It also cites MD Anderson Cancer Center, which spent tens of millions of dollars on an AI project that was abandoned. Greenberg says prestige does not guarantee quality and that technology without governance is a risk.

A separate Artificial Lawyer article, also dated November 2, 2026, reports on a ClioCon talk by writer and philosopher Malcolm Gladwell. Gladwell described a less invasive, team-based heart bypass technique and a data-led, community-based policing approach that cut murders in Boston. He concluded that both ideas were largely ignored because they would change the professional identity of surgeons and senior police officers. The article applies this to law firm partners, saying AI makes the partner less of an absolute authority and more of a planner and project manager.

The Bloomberg column says the outcome is not certain and that some firms will keep their original models and do well. It says general counsel will ask who the lead partner is, what technology supports the work, and what the institution integrating them looks like. The Artificial Lawyer piece says partners still need to win and keep clients, but clients using AI may rely on them less. It says partners must scope work within billable limits and use AI to get the work done.

Articles.Title: AI-Native Firms and Big Law Will Follow Medical Centers’ Model

stories.Headline: Corporate America's AI bill is ballooning. This startup raised $30 million to make sense of where the money is going.
stories.Summary:
Larridin, a San Francisco startup, raised $30 million in Series A funding, Business Insider reported on November 2, 2026. The round was led by Pelion Ventures, with Andreessen Horowitz, Gradient Ventures, GFT Ventures, W23, Thayer Investment Partners, DG Daiwa Ventures, Alumni Ventures, and Cougar Capital also taking part. A16z and Gradient Ventures had earlier backed the company's $17 million seed round. The company was founded by CEO Russell Fradin, CTO Ameya Kanitkar, and Jim Larrison, and Fradin and Larrison previously worked together at Comscore.

Larridin's platform measures how much AI improves employee productivity and where adoption could be better. It connects to companies' internal systems and analyzes employees' prompts to different AI tools to see who uses AI effectively, who needs more training, and how much time is saved. Kanitkar said the platform protects privacy by analyzing AI interactions without storing their contents, producing scores and high-level insights instead. Fradin said business picked up around the second quarter of this year as more companies worried about AI costs, and the company grew from one enterprise customer in December last year to 50 now. After the round, Fradin said he wants to double Larridin's 20-person head count by adding sales, engineering, and marketing staff.

Jeff Kearl, a general partner at Pelion Ventures, said AI has gone from a small or nonexistent expense to one of the top five to 10 most expensive items on company ledgers. He described companies asking where the money goes, who uses the tools, and how to make sense of it. Alex Rampell, a general partner at A16z, said Larridin addresses a need in enterprise AI for a sort of AI boss who can tell staff what they should and shouldn't do with AI. He said the underlying idea is whether people using AI tools are doing the right thing and whether the outcome is appreciably different.

The funding comes after months of change in how companies spend on AI. Early in the year, companies urged employees to use AI as much as possible, and some, like Duolingo, added AI use as a performance metric. Uber CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga went viral in April when he said Uber had burned through its entire Claude Code budget for the year. At least 17 companies, from Salesforce to Oracle, announced AI-related layoffs, and Oracle said in June that AI deployment and adoption had reduced its workforce. Sentiment shifted around the middle of the year as large AI bills appeared, and companies began focusing on return on investment, with tactics like modelmaxxing and cheaper open-source models from Chinese labs such as Moonshot AI and Z.ai.

Articles.Title: Corporate America's AI bill is ballooning. This startup raised $30 million to make sense of where the money is going.

stories.Headline: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)
stories.Summary:
Scott Alexander published an article on LessWrong on October 31, 2026, arguing against a set of ideas he groups under the name SURA, which stands for Stop Unilaterally and Raise Awareness. He describes SURA as the view that alignment-focused AI companies, their employees, and alignment-friendly countries should all halt or restrict AI work on their own, even if rivals keep racing. He says this idea has become popular among newer members of the AI safety community, who often do not know that a backup plan was ever considered. He also says older members now treat that backup plan with scorn, as if it had been debunked.

The article lays out two broad plans for handling the AI transition. Plan A is a global pause on AI development, ideally lasting decades, during which people research alignment or work to make the pause permanent. Plan C applies when no global pause happens, and it calls for alignment-focused labs to coordinate a mutual pause for as long as their joint lead lasts, then use that time to research alignment and release carefully aligned superintelligence at the last moment. Alexander cites forecasts from the AI Futures Project, where team members put survival chances under Plan C scenarios mostly in the 25 to 50 percent range, with FutureSearch at 44 percent.

He says the average gain from moving from a poorly thought out default race to a consciously managed Plan C effort is about 20 percentage points. Alexander argues that each plank of SURA would hurt the chances of Plan C working. If leading alignment-focused companies quit the race, less careful companies end up ahead, and if their employees quit, those companies become less prepared to do alignment research. He adds that a unilateral US stop would either hand superintelligence to China first or force the US to restart with no lead.

He traces SURA's popularity to assumptions he questions, including the belief that alignment is doomed and that racing is simply evil. He also says the current consensus comes from people fitting themselves into a mass-politics shape that forbids subtlety and demands clear villains. The article says that from the start of the AI safety community until about 2023, the common view was that a global pause was unlikely and people should prepare for Plan C. From 2023 onward, as the public woke up to ChatGPT, the community decided a pause was more likely than expected and put more resources into it. Alexander says the pendulum has now swung too far, and he plans to challenge SURA's assumptions and argue that SURA hurts even the chances of getting Plan A. He also cites Buck Shlegeris saying AI takeover risk does not feel like by far the largest concern, and Paul Christiano's older estimate of around 20 percent.

Articles.Title: A look at AI safety debates and the rising popularity of "Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness", or SURA; safety-focused AI labs shouldn't abandon the AI race (Scott Alexander/LessWrong)

stories.Headline: Open source and practical AI take center stage at Wuzhen Summit
stories.Summary:
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit opened on Monday in Wuzhen, East China's Zhejiang Province, and runs from November 2 to 5. Its flagship "Light of the Internet" Expo features 671 companies and institutions from 54 countries and regions, showing over 1,000 new technological achievements. Displays include robots filling prescriptions at smart pharmacies, automated garment sewing and precision assembly, and 6G communications enabling remote operation of construction machinery. The summit's theme is "Open Source and Openness, Joint Contribution and Shared Benefits - Jointly Building a Community with a Shared Future in Cyberspace."

The expo has six themed areas covering communications infrastructure, computing capabilities, manufacturing, everyday services and cybersecurity. For the first time, the WIC invited developers under 40 to debate how open models can address real industrial needs. The summit holds 27 sub-forums on topics from agent interoperability to embodied intelligence and green, low-carbon transitions. Exhibitors include Alibaba, Huawei, ZTE, Sugon, Intel, Qualcomm, Microsoft, Schneider Electric and Kaspersky.

Xiang Ligang of the Beijing Institute of Intelligent Era Industry said global AI development is forming two paths, with the US tending toward closed-source approaches that create silos. He said AI must become a service system integrating cloud infrastructure, data centers, talent and communications, and no single company can do this alone. Liu Dingding, a technology industry analyst, said the WIC's focus is shifting from demonstrating technological capabilities to showing how AI serves real production and everyday needs. He Weiwen of the Center for China and Globalization said global AI cooperation should be built under a multilateral framework for shared benefits, warning that exclusive groupings would bring economic costs and weaken cooperation.

The article says the WIC comes as some countries try to erect protectionist walls and form exclusive circles. It says the Quad foreign ministers' meeting expressed intent to provide more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance for trusted AI technologies across the so-called "Indo-Pacific." Wuzhen itself had only 12 internet-related enterprises before the first summit, and by 2024 the number had surpassed 1,200. Wuzhen's GDP grew from 2.84 billion yuan to 10.89 billion yuan, which the article describes as effectively "rebuilding three Wuzhens."

Articles.Title: Open source and practical AI take center stage at Wuzhen Summit - Global Times

stories.Headline: Gemini opens the door to digital twins... Transform your face and voice into a virtual character using artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Google has added a feature to its Gemini app that lets users create a digital avatar copying their face and voice, according to a report from Voice of Emirates dated November 3, 2026. The tool turns recorded facial and voice data into a virtual character tied to the user's account. Users can then make photos and videos with the avatar without appearing on camera each time. The report says the feature is part of Google's wider push into artificial intelligence for personal content creation.

To set it up, users open the Gemini app or website, choose Add Files and then the Avatar section, and scan a QR code with their phone. They must allow camera and microphone access, record their face in good light with the phone at eye level, and speak clearly in a quiet room. The avatar can then be picked inside Gemini and used to generate images and videos. Users can also share the avatar with chosen people and control or revoke their access later.

The service requires users to be at least 18 and to have a personal Google account, and some video features need a subscription to eligible Google AI plans. Availability is limited by geography and language. Google provides settings to review, control and delete recordings, and the report says privacy settings should be checked before an avatar is made or shared. The report describes the technology as a shift, with AI now able to produce virtual versions of real people rather than only fictional characters.

Articles.Title: Gemini opens the door to digital twins... Transform your face and voice into a virtual character using artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: OpenAI Lobbyist: AI Could Define 2028 White House Race
stories.Summary:
Chris Lehane, OpenAI's chief global affairs officer and a veteran Democrat strategist, warned in a private memo that artificial intelligence could decide the 2028 White House race, Politico reported. The memo was sent to roughly half a dozen prospective presidential candidates, along with lawmakers and political operatives, according to a person familiar with the discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity. Lehane urged White House hopefuls to back AI development or risk putting the United States at a disadvantage against Beijing. He warned Democrats in particular against opposing data centers and other infrastructure critical to maintaining America's technological edge. Lehane wrote that if the United States falls behind China, this could well be the 2028 version of the 2002 vote to go to war in Iraq.

He argued that candidates must find a middle ground between allowing AI to advance unchecked and concentrating control of the technology among powerful interests. He said the candidate who can articulate a compelling third path will have an opportunity to define a new contract for this new era. Lehane compared the political stakes to former President Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal in 1932, arguing that the next president could redefine the relationship between people and a transformative new force in their lives. Lehane, a former press secretary to then Vice President Al Gore, predicted that by 2028 AI will become an even bigger political issue as its capabilities expand and Americans grow more familiar with the technology. His memo urged candidates to address protecting children, keeping humans in control of major decisions, overhauling taxes, and ensuring AI makes life more affordable.

He also warned against allowing the Chinese Communist Party to dictate the future of AI. Lehane wrote that policymakers must solve problems such as higher electricity costs rather than treating infrastructure itself as the problem. The warning comes as data centers face growing public opposition ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, with Americans increasingly concerned about rising electricity costs and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure. In the memo, Lehane said those disputes are part of broader voter anxiety over affordability, economic uncertainty, and a social contract that many believe has been fractured. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the memo and the midterm elections.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Lobbyist: AI Could Define 2028 White House Race

stories.Headline: Manufacturing’s black art is retiring. AI may be the best chance to keep it
stories.Summary:
As key manufacturing hubs including Singapore continue to age, many veteran engineers are nearing retirement, and new talent is not entering the sector at the same rate. These experienced workers can diagnose problems on the factory floor by ear, smell and instinct, a skill the article calls the black art of manufacturing. That knowledge lives in their heads, and it leaves with them when they retire. Some manufacturers said it can take two to three engineers to replace one seasoned veteran, without a guarantee of the same results.

Factories have digitalised rapidly, with sensors tracking nearly every stage of production, but the article says lots of data does not mean lots of insights. Decisions still depend on the same few experienced people who know what the numbers mean, and some firms treat sensor tracking as a box-ticking exercise. The article says AI trained on production data and engineering drawings could flag a yield dip within minutes, trace it to a temperature drift at an upstream station and recommend a fix. It would act as an assistant to veterans and help new engineers, capturing judgment in a form that can be checked and passed on.

The article says budget for trialling technology is rarely the problem, and the hardest part is change management, because a small process change can ripple down a linear production line. Managers and workers are reluctant to experiment because they run tight schedules and cannot bear the risk of downtime. Manufacturers also treat production data as sacred, so any tool sending data outside the factory would not make it to a trial. Viable AI therefore has to run in-house with security at its core, fit the existing workflow and work alongside floor engineers, who keep the final decision.

The article says deployment is where many companies win or lose, and forward-deployed engineers work on-site to narrow the first deployment to a single line or problem with a measurable outcome. Demonstrating return on investment in numbers the plant manager already tracks is how trust is earned on the floor. The article concludes that AI will not replace the veterans' intuition, but it may give manufacturers a way to capture, explain and pass it on before it retires. It adds that manufacturing may not be the most glamorous sector, but it could be where AI proves its real worth.

Articles.Title: Manufacturing’s black art is retiring. AI may be the best chance to keep it - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Secure vibe coding practices for AI-assisted development
stories.Summary:
Developers who use AI models for coding should treat the tools like a "lazy genie" that may take shortcuts, according to guidance reported by TechGig on November 2, 2026. The article says AI tools can skip safety measures and fail to double-check their work. It warns that developers should not assume AI will keep critical information private or follow cybersecurity best practices. The guidance also says AI may not check the code it generates for possible exploits.

The article says users must spell out privacy specifications, limits on access, and other guardrails such as encryption. It advises asking AI models to reference the OWASP list of top vulnerabilities so flaws are prevented before code is written. It notes that many AI models can create persistent rules or context files, so instructions do not have to be repeated for every task. These can be markdown files or entries in the "Knowledge" section of tools like Lovable agent or the "Memory" section in Replit, and markdown files are useful for safety guidelines because the AI considers them with every prompt. The article also says choosing vibe-coding tools that support audit logs can make it easier to track changes in a project.

The article does not name any person or company as responsible for the guidance, and it gives no direct quotes from officials. It presents the advice as steps developers should take when using AI for coding. The recommendations cover stating security requirements clearly, pointing AI to known vulnerability lists, and using persistent context files. It also suggests audit logs as a way to keep track of changes.

The article gives no details on what happens next, such as new rules or deadlines. It does not say whether the guidance comes from a regulator or a standards body. It does not describe any incident that prompted the advice. The piece is a short report of one minute's reading time, published on TechGig on November 2, 2026.

Articles.Title: Secure vibe coding practices for AI-assisted development

stories.Headline: Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps
stories.Summary:
Meta is seeking to raise between $20 billion and $25 billion in a bond sale on Tuesday, according to CNBC. The sale is expected to be two-thirds in U.S. dollars and one-third in euros, people familiar with the matter said. Final pricing should come Tuesday afternoon, the sources said. Meta declined to comment, and Bloomberg News first reported the plans.

The debt sale comes days after S&P Global Ratings revised Meta's outlook from AA- stable to AA- negative. S&P cited uncertainty about the company's hefty capex spending and negative free cash flow. In its third-quarter earnings report last month, Meta said full-year capex will come in between $135 billion and $145 billion, a $5 billion increase to the low end of its previous guidance. Meta posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion for the latest quarter, joining Alphabet and Amazon in reporting a negative figure.

Meta previously raised $25 billion in an April bond sale. The company said last week that it plans to raise $95 billion to fund its AI initiatives. Of that, Meta intends to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings and an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program. Meta's stock rose 2.7% on Tuesday after dropping in 12 of the prior 14 trading sessions and closing out October with its worst month in four years.

Articles.Title: Meta seeks to raise up to $25 billion in debt sale as AI spending jumps

stories.Headline: Ex-Lawmakers Side With OpenAI In Battle With News Publishers 11/03/2026
stories.Summary:
Two former Republican lawmakers, Rick Santorum of Pennsylvania and Rich Boucher of Virginia, filed a friend-of-the-court brief late last week with U.S. District Judge Sidney H. Stein in New York. They urged the judge to rule that training large language models on news articles and other copyrighted material is fair use. They argued that an AI model relies on works to derive statistical patterns of language rather than to communicate their expression to the public. They said a ruling in favor of fair use is vitally important to the country.

The brief comes in a high-profile lawsuit brought by publishers including The New York Times Co. against OpenAI. The publishers allege OpenAI infringed copyright by using content to train ChatGPT and by reproducing portions of content in outputs generated in response to users' prompts. OpenAI is seeking dismissal of the lawsuit and argues that training a large language model is transformative. The company also says it takes steps to prevent verbatim outputs and that regurgitation of copyrighted content is extremely rare.

Santorum and Boucher wrote that a contrary ruling would impose a de facto licensing regime with grave consequences for AI development. They said the freedom of American scientists, companies and entrepreneurs to train AI is of paramount economic and strategic importance. The publishers responded that the defendants envision a world where they can freely copy entire news articles to generate content that engages users at the expense of publishers. Numerous other outside parties also filed friend-of-the-court briefs on Friday, including digital rights groups, tech industry associations and entertainment businesses such as talent agency William Morris Endeavor.

The digital rights groups and tech industry generally support OpenAI, while entertainment-related businesses oppose the company. William Morris Endeavor contended that its clients are already losing paid work to AI output built on their own copyrighted works. The Computer & Communications Industry Association, NetChoice and TechNet argued that training chatbots on news articles is transformational. Two federal judges have already weighed in, with Judge William Alsup ruling that Anthropic did not infringe copyright by digitizing books it had purchased, while Judge Vince Chhabria said using books to train large language models was transformative but also likely infringed copyright in most cases.

Articles.Title: Ex-Lawmakers Side With OpenAI In Battle With News Publishers 11/03/2026

stories.Headline: Apple beat, then fell: the memory bill is the AI trade's new tell
stories.Summary:
Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results on November 3, 2026, and beat expectations, with revenue of $114.48 billion, up 12% year on year, and earnings per share of $2.10 against $1.99 expected. iPhone revenue was $57.58 billion, up 17%, Mac was $10.79 billion, up 24% and a record, and Services was $31.57 billion, up 10% and an all-time high. Greater China was $17.54 billion, up 21%, but below the $18.5 billion to $18.7 billion consensus, while iPad fell 10% and Wearables and Home fell 8%. Despite the beat, the stock closed 1.83% lower at $338.32 and was last quoted near $329.28 overnight. This was the first earnings report under CEO John Ternus.

The problem was the guidance, not demand: gross margin for the December quarter is guided at 45% to 46%, down from 47.9% actual, with management pointing to higher memory costs and the Siri AI ramp. Management guided December-quarter revenue growth of 7% to 10%, but Services growth of only 8% to 9%, below the roughly 10.7% consensus. Apple's quarterly capex was just $2.24 billion, while quarterly research and development rose 32% to $11.73 billion. Apple does not build AI data centers at the scale of Microsoft, Amazon or Oracle, but it buys the memory in every iPhone, Mac and iPad, and the AI buildout is competing for the same DRAM and NAND supply. The AI boom has redirected memory capacity toward high-bandwidth memory and enterprise storage, tightening consumer memory supply and raising Apple's bill of materials.

On the same day, Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum for about $115 billion in stock, and Oracle filed to raise $20 billion in debt and equity for AI infrastructure. Both were punished: Marvell fell 12.7%, Lumentum 18.6% and Oracle 8.8%. The article says the market is no longer paying for AI ambition alone and is asking who bears the cost, and for Apple the answer is the gross-margin line. On the chart, Apple closed on the lower rail of a six-month rising channel near $338.4, with the upper rail near $355.1. The first support below the channel is $325.8, the October 1 low.

Articles.Title: Apple beat, then fell: the memory bill is the AI trade's new tell

stories.Headline: Google Play policy bans app deception of AI agents
stories.Summary:
Google announced new Play policy rules for AppFunctions on October 29, 2026, and the change was reported on November 2. AppFunctions let apps expose discrete, structured actions that AI agents can invoke. An agent can read a function catalogue, decide to call a function, and pass structured arguments for the app to execute. The updated policy adds an enforcement clause for these functions.

The policy prohibits AppFunctions from deceiving or manipulating AI agents, bypassing security controls, or interfering with other applications. Deceiving an agent includes lying in function metadata or return values, such as describing a read-only function that actually writes, or claiming capabilities an app does not possess. Bypassing security controls means working around user or operating system permissions that an agent should obtain. Interfering with other apps covers eating another app's agent traffic, spamming agents with fake results, or poisoning shared context built from multiple apps.

Google is responsible for the policy, and it extends its existing logic against deceiving human users to AI agents. The company treats AI agents with the same integrity requirements as human users, so apps must not use dark patterns or half-truths when interacting with agents. Google said the policy aims to address bad actors who treat AI agents as a user acquisition channel, similar to how human users are acquired. Developers should audit their function descriptions to ensure accuracy and make return values unembellished.

Articles.Title: Google Play policy bans app deception of AI agents

stories.Headline: ‘Huge step in the regulation of AI in healthcare’ as government accepts independent commission’s AI - Society of Radiographers
stories.Summary:
The government has accepted all 44 recommendations from the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, an independent expert advisory body set up by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency in September 2025. The commission's report followed extensive consultation with NHS unions and professional associations representing staff affected by AI. The Society of Radiographers submitted evidence to the commission so that the views of radiographers were heard. The government announced its response on 3 November 2026.

The accepted proposals include post-market surveillance, which means technologies such as AI image analysis tools, triage algorithms and treatment planning software will be evaluated and audited throughout their entire operational life. The MHRA will issue draft guidance by the end of 2026 on managing changes and updates to AI tools already deployed in clinical settings. In 2027 the MHRA will consult on new standards to qualify and classify AI-enabled medical devices. A programme board will oversee implementation across 10 priority areas.

Jeanette Carter, professional officer for AI and digital technologies at the Society of Radiographers, said the government accepting all 44 recommendations was a huge step for AI in healthcare. She said the society is working to see where it can help contribute to the success of completing the recommendations and will keep members posted. She added that the importance of post-market surveillance has been known for a while, with the Royal College of Radiologists having its own guidance on it. She said there is always a concern with new technology that small deteriorations in accuracy cannot be fully understood without regular review, and that AI is a powerful tool but the human is accountable for reviewing the results.

Articles.Title: ‘Huge step in the regulation of AI in healthcare’ as government accepts independent commission’s AI - Society of Radiographers

stories.Headline: UK regulators warn firms: existing law applies to personal AI agents
stories.Summary:
Four UK regulators said on 30 October that existing law already applies to personal AI agents. The Competition and Markets Authority, the Financial Conduct Authority, the Information Commissioner's Office and Ofcom made the statement through the Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum. They said an agent's autonomy does not reduce a firm's duties. The statement runs to about two pages and offers no new rules, but the regulators promised enforcement and early testing routes.

The regulators said the frameworks that apply include consumer, competition and data protection law, along with payments, financial services, cyber security and online safety. They said product safety and other areas sit beyond these four regulators. They welcomed the technology, which could act for users by buying things and dealing with businesses, but said agents may amplify old risks and add new ones. They named fraud and scams, personal data shared in ways users did not expect, and misleading recommendations. Their questions for developers and deployers cover whether a customer can tell when an agent is acting for them, how authority to act is given, which commercial interests shape its recommendations, and who answers for its decisions.

The regulators said they will not hesitate to use their powers where conduct is reasonably suspected of breaching the law and risks harm. They strongly encouraged firms to come forward early and test products through sandboxes and direct engagement. They conceded there may be more to do and said they are working with government to identify potential gaps in compliance and further regulatory challenges. The statement cites no AI-specific legislation and leans on existing regimes.

For UK businesses, the practical effect is to close off the argument that agents fall into a gap until Parliament acts. Nothing in the statement changes the law, and no case is announced. The first enforcement case will show which regulator moves first and what accountable means in practice. Firms already building agents would be wise to document their answers now, according to the article.

Articles.Title: UK regulators warn firms: existing law applies to personal AI agents

stories.Headline: AI roundup: Lyria lawsuit, Anthropic’s Q3, OpenAI pile-in
stories.Summary:
A shareholder in Alphabet, Google's parent company, has filed a lawsuit against 13 of the company's directors and executives. The filing accuses Alphabet and Google of copying millions of copyrighted sound recordings, musical compositions and lyrics. The suit names Google's Lyria, Mulan and MusicLM models. The article, dated 3 November 2026, says the case promises to be a blockbuster AI-music lawsuit, though it notes it could also end in a quiet settlement.

The filing claims the companies copied millions of copyrighted works. The article does not give other numbers, dates or names for this lawsuit beyond the 13 directors and executives and the three model names. It says the filing is available via MBW. The article does not say what the lawsuit asks for or what it would change.

The shareholder is the party bringing the case, and the article does not name them. The article does not quote the defendants or say how Google or Alphabet responded. It also does not say what the shareholder said beyond the copying accusation. No hearing date or next step for the case is given.

The article places the suit in the wider fight over whether AI training counts as fair use. It says lawsuits involving authors and news organisations, including the New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft, and that music groups have filed briefs in those cases. It says verdicts in those cases, if they reach that point rather than end in settlements, could set a huge precedent for the music industry's own battles. The article gives no further next step for the Lyria lawsuit itself.

Articles.Title: AI roundup: Lyria lawsuit, Anthropic’s Q3, OpenAI pile-in

stories.Headline: Jeff Caudill Appointed to Advisory Board for UCLA Law Strategic AI Program
stories.Summary:
Jeff Caudill, Director of Information Technology and Facilities at Gallagher LLP, has been appointed to the advisory board for the Strategic AI for Legal Professionals Program at UCLA Law Executive Education. The appointment was announced in a citybiz article dated November 3, 2026. The program is designed to help legal professionals understand the legal, ethical, and operational implications of artificial intelligence. Caudill joins a diverse group of legal, technology, and industry leaders who will provide guidance and insight to help shape the program's continued development.

The program features seven modules covering topics including large language models, intellectual property, cybersecurity, data privacy, regulation, and the future of legal practice. It is designed for lawyers in private practice, in-house counsel roles, and government positions. Participants are helped to anticipate emerging changes, evaluate available resources, and develop strategies for integrating AI into their professional practice. The program is offered in partnership with Zschool and uses real-world case studies, current regulatory developments, and practical assignments. Participants earn a certificate of completion at the end of each course.

Caudill said that joining the advisory board will give him a unique opportunity to collaborate with other legal AI professionals. He said that while AI has broad use cases across almost every business vertical, its use in the legal workspace poses unique challenges, and that contributing to how legal professionals learn about AI is important to the future of the profession. Tom Dame, Managing Partner at Gallagher, said it is important that the firm serve clients effectively and responsibly with AI tools, and he called Caudill an invaluable resource in leading the firm's AI initiatives. The article says the new role recognizes Caudill's leadership in this space and his commitment to helping the legal community respond to technological change.

Gallagher LLP has been a trusted partner to businesses and non-profits across the Mid-Atlantic region and nationwide for more than 65 years. The firm represents leading universities, hospitals, financial institutions, real estate developers, and more. UCLA Law Executive Education offers focused online programs and free webinars from eminent legal scholars and industry experts, and participants may earn MCLE credit where applicable. The article does not say what happens next beyond Caudill's role in shaping the program's continued development.

Articles.Title: Jeff Caudill Appointed to Advisory Board for UCLA Law Strategic AI Program

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Says AI Makes Nuclear Weapons 'Look Like Nothing'
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates said artificial intelligence has crossed danger thresholds in biological and cyber capabilities, and he called it the most dangerous thing humans have ever gone near. He made the comments on the Ezra Klein Show in an interview published on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. He said the technology makes nuclear weapons look like nothing, and that the world met the moment with complete silence. The Microsoft co-founder said AI could empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions of people. He also said it could carry out a cyberattack that scrambles all bank accounts and shuts down the electric grid.

Gates pointed to AI's code abilities as his evidence, saying recent models found flaws in code that humans had reviewed for over 20 years. He said a model can spot in minutes where to inject an attack, at a complexity that makes people agree once they see it. He said only nation states once had the resources for such things, and that power now sits with a small group using the latest AI tools. The article also described a Zcash case, in which security engineer Taylor Hornby used Anthropic's Opus 4.8, released the day before, in an audit of the Orchard circuit on May 29. He found a flaw live since Orchard launched in May 2022 and wrote an exploit that minted undetectable counterfeit ZEC in testing, according to Shielded Labs, and an emergency fix followed within days.

Gates said relying on the AI industry to regulate itself is just insane, and he called self-regulation insane while saying there is no supervisory layer today. He said he almost could not believe he was asked whether corporate incentives were enough to keep humanity safe. The interview was published the same day tech CEOs signed a voluntary safety accord at the White House. Anthropic's December 2025 study found AI agents identified $4.6 million of exploitable smart contract vulnerabilities. CertiK put first-half losses at $1.32 billion and said attackers revisiting dormant codebases were likely assisted by automated tooling.

The article said whether attackers have used AI in real-world exploits is not yet established, but it is highly suspected. Blockstream refused to pay a ransom over the Sept. 6 Liquid Network theft and said the world is a different place with the advancements of AI, hinting that AI could have been used in the exploit. Shielded Labs said the Zcash flaw had evaded years of scrutiny by many of the world's best cryptographers. The article did not say what happens next beyond those events.

Articles.Title: Bill Gates Says AI Makes Nuclear Weapons 'Look Like Nothing' - CoinMarketCap

stories.Headline: Court dismisses claims against Lancaster Country Day School in deepfake lawsuit
stories.Summary:
A Lancaster County judge dismissed claims against Lancaster Country Day School and its administrators in a lawsuit filed by parents over AI-generated nude photos, citing legal insufficiency, WGAL reported on Nov. 3, 2026. The lawsuit alleged that the school ignored a tip about a male student creating deepfake nude images of a female classmate. The school argued that administrators were not required to report the tip because the images did not meet the legal definition of child abuse. The two students who created the images were ordered in March to serve probation and community service.

The dismissal ends the claims against the school and its administrators in the parents' lawsuit. The school's argument rested on the position that the tip did not have to be reported because the images fell outside the legal definition of child abuse. The two students who made the images were ordered in March to serve probation and community service. Since the incident, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has signed a bill aimed at protecting children from sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes and hazing.

The judge was responsible for the dismissal, and the school had argued that administrators were not required to report the tip. The two students were ordered in March to serve probation and community service. Shapiro signed the bill after the incident. The bill adds these offenses to the list of incidents that mandated reporters must report to Pennsylvania's child protective services.

The articles do not say what happens next in the lawsuit beyond the dismissal of the claims against the school and its administrators. The articles also do not give a next court date or say whether the parents plan to appeal. The new law signed by Shapiro adds the offenses to what mandated reporters must report to child protective services. The articles do not say when the law takes effect or how it would apply to this case.

Articles.Title: Court dismisses claims against Lancaster Country Day School in deepfake lawsuit

stories.Headline: AI Spending Has Gone From $140 Billion to $740 Billion in 3 Years, and Ackman Is Buying
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman and Ryan Israel, chief executive and chief investment officer of Pershing Square, sent a letter dated November 2, 2026, arguing that Big Tech's capital spending boom is an offensive growth investment with attractive returns. The letter's figures cover combined capital spending at Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Amazon and Alphabet, which rose from about $140 billion in 2023 to about $740 billion in 2026 on company guidance, a calculated 5.3 times. The letter does not break out AI's share of that spending. Pershing owns Microsoft, Meta and Amazon, so the letter argues for Ackman's own holdings.

Capital spending was nearly 12% of the group's revenue in 2023 and an estimated 38% in 2026, per the letter, a shift that pressures free cash flow. Consensus cited by Pershing calls for another 35% increase in 2027, and about $1.5 trillion once other AI builders are included. Pershing estimates one gigawatt of AI data center capacity costs $40 billion to $50 billion and produces $15 billion to $20 billion of annual revenue, which at a 50% incremental margin implies a pre-tax return on invested capital of 15% to 25%. Pershing says revenue could run 15%-plus to 35% above consensus after three years, and if it falls short, the letter argues the companies will cut spending and free cash flow will beat consensus anyway.

By June 30, Pershing had added 552,652 Microsoft shares, a 9.8% increase to 6,206,730, and 535,201 Meta shares, up 20.1%. It cut Amazon by 25.2% to 8,563,857 shares and sold out of Alphabet. The letter does not say Pershing added during October's selloff, and Pershing Square Holdings' net asset value was down 6.9% for 2026 as of October 31. On November 2, Microsoft fell 2.83% to $507.12, Meta slipped 1.34% to $606.73 and Amazon rose 2.2% to $245.63.

The bull case rests on contracted demand, with Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligations growing 73% to $677 billion and AWS backlog reaching $578 billion. The bear case is twofold: Pershing's return math is its own estimate, while Meta is funding its expansion with negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter and a reported bond sale of at least $20 billion. Ackman and Israel host a call at 9:30 a.m. ET on November 3, and the third-quarter 13F is expected in November. It will show whether Pershing kept adding to Meta before its October drop, and a cut there would weaken the letter's case.

Articles.Title: AI Spending Has Gone From $140 Billion to $740 Billion in 3 Years, and Ackman Is Buying - 24/7 Wall St.

stories.Headline: New Mexico student privacy proposal would allow some AI training, exclude existing contracts
stories.Summary:
New Mexico's Public Education Department has proposed a student data privacy rule, 6.11.3 NMAC, and answered questions about it in written responses to Organ Mountain News on Monday. The proposal follows months of questions from parents, school officials and state lawmakers about how children's recorded speech is collected, retained and used, including through the Amira reading assessment in Las Cruces Public Schools. The department said Amira recordings are not biometric voiceprints under the proposal. The rule is open for public comment through Nov. 20, with hearings on Nov. 19 and 20, and would take effect April 1, 2027, if adopted as proposed. The proposal would not categorically ban vendors from using student data to train, develop or improve AI tools that support the contracted educational service, but such activity would need authorization in a contract with PED, a district or a charter school and would have to meet the rule's other restrictions.

It defines a voiceprint as a recording processed into a unique vocal signature capable of identifying a student by voice, and PED said Amira does not do that, though recordings linked to a student's name, account or results may still be protected student information. Schools would have to give parents written notice before collecting biometric information, but affirmative consent would be required only when another law requires it. The rule would not retroactively regulate vendor contracts signed before its effective date, and existing protections such as the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act would continue to apply. PED said the proposal was developed in response to concerns about private companies' handling of student information, drawing on Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act and California's Student Online Personal Information Protection Act, and that New Mexico lacks comparable legislation or rules. The department did not identify Amira as the catalyst and said it will consider public comments and make revisions before adopting a final rule.

In August, Las Cruces Public Schools disabled retention of student voice recordings for the 2026-27 school year and requested deletion of recordings previously collected, and Deputy Superintendent Wendi Miller-Tomlinson told the Board of Education that Amira had confirmed in writing that stored recordings were deleted. The district also made a paper-based assessment available to parents who did not want their children tested digitally. Written comments can be emailed to Rule.Feedback@ped.nm.gov, and the virtual hearing is set for 9 a.m. to noon Nov. 19, with the in-person hearing at the Willie Ortiz Auditorium, 2600 Cerrillos Road in Santa Fe.

Articles.Title: New Mexico student privacy proposal would allow some AI training, exclude existing contracts - Organ Mountain News

stories.Headline: State bill allows consumers to hold AI chatbot providers liable
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers introduced Bill A5607 on Oct. 5, 2026, according to the ABA Journal. The bill targets artificial intelligence chatbots and aims to make them subject to the state’s product liability laws. It would create several content and data privacy requirements for AI chatbot providers. The legislation also characterizes chatbots as products, which means product liability claims would cover them.

Providers found to violate the state’s products liability laws would face $5,000 per violation. The New Jersey attorney general’s office could also take potential action against them. The bill was introduced in the state legislature and has not yet become law. The ABA Journal reported on the bill on Nov. 3, 2026, citing a story from Law.com.

Scott S. Christie, a partner at McCarter & English who focuses on intellectual property and data privacy, spoke to Law.com about the bill. He said the legislation would open the floodgates for lawsuits if it passes. He said that with $5,000 in statutory damages per violation and no need to prove harm, plus a strict liability standard, lawsuits could reach hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of dollars. He also said that if a chatbot provider is violating the statute as to one user, it is probably violating as to all users.

The articles do not say what happens next with the bill, such as whether a committee vote or floor vote is scheduled. They also do not say whether Gov. Phil Murphy supports or opposes the measure. The ABA Journal notes only that the bill was proposed and has not passed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: State bill allows consumers to hold AI chatbot providers liable - ABA Journal

stories.Headline: New York congressman on reelection campaign and AI legislation
stories.Summary:
Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican, spoke with Margaret Brennan on Face the Nation on Sunday, November 2, 2026, about his reelection campaign. Brennan noted that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries had singled out his district as a top target for Democrats. Lawler said he expected to be victorious on Tuesday night. He said that over the last four years he and his staff had closed over 10,000 constituent cases and brought back over $140 million to the district.

Lawler said he had passed over two dozen bills, 17 of which were signed into law. He said his opponent, Cait Conley, had moved into the district from Virginia, while he owns a home there and pays taxes. He said he is the only sitting member of Congress endorsed by a member of the opposing party, naming Jared Golden. He cited the largest tax cut in American history, including lifting the cap on salt, and a housing bill he led.

Brennan asked why Republicans deserve trust when prices have continued to climb. Lawler said inflation rose 21% cumulatively under the prior administration and that war in the Middle East had caused volatility in oil markets. He said growth in the third quarter was 3.4% and that over a million private sector jobs had been created in the past year. He said utilities in New York are up 58% under Kathy Hochul, and that a permitting reform bill would increase domestic energy supply before the end of this Congress.

On artificial intelligence, Brennan said Conley accused Lawler of refusing to legislate AI to protect Elon Musk, whose political action committee had put hundreds of thousands of dollars behind him. Lawler said Conley is paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by two AI companies and would not tell voters what she did to earn those contracts. He said he had no communication with any outside group spending in the race. He said he is leading with Josh Gottheimer on the Stop Rogue AI Act, which would set national standards for rogue agents and bots and require mandatory testing for frontier models.

Articles.Title: New York congressman on reelection campaign and AI legislation - KYMA

stories.Headline: Bill Nygren: We don't know about the AI trade; we don't have conviction on owning those names
stories.Summary:
Bill Nygren, a partner, portfolio manager and U.S. chief investment officer at Harris Oakmark Funds, spoke on CNBC's Power Lunch on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The segment aired at 2:23 PM EST and ran about five minutes. He used the appearance to make the case for value investing. In the interview he said he and his firm do not know about the AI trade and do not have conviction on owning those names.

The articles give no further requirements or changes from the appearance. They list no new rules, no figures beyond the broadcast time and date, and no named companies tied to his comments. The only names given are Nygren, his firm Harris Oakmark Funds, the program Power Lunch and CNBC. The video description repeats his view that the firm lacks conviction on owning AI names.

Nygren is the person responsible for the remarks, speaking as a portfolio manager and U.S. CIO at Harris Oakmark Funds. According to the articles, he said the firm does not know about the AI trade. He also said the firm does not have conviction on owning those names. He framed the discussion as the case for value investing.

The context is a CNBC Power Lunch segment on value investing, posted on the CNBC website. The page also links to other videos, including one with CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz and one with investor Bill Ackman. The articles do not say what happens next or whether the firm will change its holdings. No follow-up, response or next step is reported.

stories.Headline: Report addresses AI use to prepare documents in UK civil proceedings
stories.Summary:
A working group of the UK's Civil Justice Council released the second of two reports on the use and regulation of artificial intelligence for preparing court documents in civil proceedings. The report was published on Nov 3, 2026, and was written by Bernise Carolino. It makes recommendations on litigants-in-person, witness statements and expert evidence. The group had published an interim report on Feb 17, 2026, and considered consultation responses before developing its recommendations.

The report says the Solicitors Regulation Authority, the Bar Standards Board, the Legal Services Board, other professional regulators and legal representatives should regulate AI use in this context. It says a practice direction from the Civil Procedure Rule Committee should guide that regulation, using a functional and risk-based approach. The direction should consolidate and clarify the court's current approach to the accuracy of, the verification of and the responsibility for legal representatives' AI use. It should also offer guidance on existing sanctions for AI misuse and on AI use in specific contexts such as witness statement preparation and disclosure. The report says the Civil Justice Council should urgently address AI use by litigants-in-person, while the rule committee should revise the practice direction as needed.

Sir Colin Birss, the working group's chair, said in a foreword that the group thanks all those who contributed. He said it was greatly assisted by the many responses to the interim report and consultation, and that all responses and the points they raised were considered carefully. For witness statements, the group recommended no new rules for a legal representative preparing and signing a statement. A witness of fact should make a specific declaration that they did not prepare the statement with an AI tool that generated or influenced the substantive content, and the report said this would not prevent the use of any particular AI tool.

For expert witness evidence, the group recommended amending the Civil Procedure Rules by adding a declaration about AI use and revising the AI use guidance for experts. The report says these recommendations aim to help the court and opposing parties scrutinize and test expert evidence. Otherwise, the report opposed introducing declarations regarding AI use. It also did not recommend requiring parties to apply for permission to use AI when preparing materials for submissions in civil proceedings.

Articles.Title: Report addresses AI use to prepare documents in UK civil proceedings - Canadian Lawyer

stories.Headline: A US company argued that lawyers using artificial intelligence should receive lower fees after its trade
stories.Summary:
Flux Drive Inc. sued defendants from another state, accusing them of taking its privately owned technology without permission. A federal district court judge in Colorado dismissed the trade-secrets lawsuit after finding the court did not have legal authority over the Illinois-based defendants. The defendants, represented by the law firm Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, then asked to recover their defence costs. The trial judge reviewed the firm's records and ordered Flux Drive to pay $114,663.11 in legal fees. Flux Drive appealed to the 10th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

Flux Drive argued that the law firm had used artificial intelligence software, that AI tools can complete tasks faster, and that the hours charged were therefore too high. The 10th Circuit rejected this and upheld the award in full. Writing for a unanimous three-judge panel, Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh said AI can make legal research and document writing faster, but the party challenging a bill must provide clear evidence of overcharging. The panel, which also included Circuit Judges Scott Matheson and Richard Federico, said the district court had reviewed the time entries and found them reasonable, and that Flux Drive had failed to point to specific billing entries that were repeated, false or inflated because of the technology.

The ruling sets an early example of how courts may deal with automated tools in the legal profession, and Reuters reported on 2 November that it sets a clear standard for future fee disputes involving technology. Legal analysts say the decision does not give law firms complete freedom to charge for AI-assisted work without question, and courts can still reduce fees if someone shows software did most of a task in minutes while the firm charged for hours of manual work. The decision comes as courts pay closer attention to AI use by law firms, after cases in which lawyers submitted documents with fake legal references generated by AI chatbots. The 10th Circuit has also proposed rule changes requiring lawyers to confirm that a human attorney independently checked all legal authorities cited in appeal filings. The 10th Circuit's formal order leaves the district court's fee decision unchanged, ending the dispute.
