stories.Headline: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race draws significant donations from AI company employees
stories.Summary:
An analysis of Federal Election Commission records, reported by the Alaska Beacon on November 3, 2026, found that Alaska's U.S. Senate race drew more campaign money from employees of AI companies than any other 2026 Senate race. At least 19 employees contributed approximately $119,000 to the campaigns of Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, with most giving close to the legal limit of $3,500 per election, or $7,000 for the primary and general together, and $5,000 a year to a leadership PAC. Many of the donations came from employees of Anthropic, and none of the donors listed an Alaska address, with most living in California. Peltola received at least $56,000, nearly all from Anthropic employees, while Sullivan received about $63,000 for his campaign plus $35,000 through his leadership PAC, True North, for a combined total of about $98,000. Neither campaign responded to requests for comment.

The race also includes Republican Gerald Heikes, who has no campaign and therefore cannot receive donations, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who received no contributions from the AI-company employees examined. The contest became more contentious after a New York Times report that Peltola recruited Daniel J. Sullivan as a spoiler, which her campaign denied to the Times. Once donations to PACs are included, South Dakota Senate campaigns pulled in the most, and the top individual candidate was Republican Mike Rounds of South Dakota with $165,100 to his campaign and PACs. Counting employees of Google, Microsoft, Meta and other big tech firms, Peltola ranked fifth among Senate candidates nationwide and Sullivan 16th, with Peltola supported by close to 150 big tech employees compared with four for Sullivan. Most of the money to both candidates came through joint fundraising committees rather than direct donations.

Brendan Fischer, Director of Strategic Investigations at Campaign Legal Center, said large contributions from a small number of employees in the same industry can suggest donors see a candidate as favorable to their interests, but he cautioned against using employer data as proof of coordinated giving. He said political money often flows toward races where donors believe their contributions can have an impact, and donors wanting to influence the chamber's balance of power may be attracted to Alaska's race since it could determine control of the Senate. Sullivan has advocated expanding data center development in the state and pushed for federal advanced AI data centers on Alaska's military bases, and in April the Air Force sought developers for potential AI data centers on about 4,700 acres across three Alaska installations. Peltola has focused less on data centers and more on affordability and energy costs, according to a Newsweek report, and Sullivan holds approximately $5 million in stock in his family's chemical company, RPM International, whose subsidiaries supply specialized coatings used in data centers, according to The Alaska Current.

An AP-NORC poll from September found that 67% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are worried data centers will impact water supply, and 57% of Democrats and 50% of Republicans believe AI will harm society more than help it in the next 10 years. Krystal Lapp, Interim Executive Director of Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, said the election will have significant impacts on Alaskan land and resource allocation, and that with the boom of AI, politicians and others are inviting people up because of Alaska, adding that the state looks like a cash cow but they are not going to benefit us. In September, the Alaska Beacon reported that the Alaska Department of Natural Resources decided to transfer 30 square miles of land to the state-owned economic development agency AIDEA for a multi-use industrial and energy development district, and AIDEA officials have said there are no existing plans for data centers but that they could potentially be built. Lapp said she is against the executive orders that were put through and against the gutting of the public process, and that by taking away that process they take away that responsibility piece.

Articles.Title: Alaska’s U.S. Senate race draws significant donations from AI company employees

stories.Headline: Mathews Phosa urges lawyers to be wary of using AI in court papers
stories.Summary:
Mathews Phosa, an ANC heavyweight and former Mpumalanga premier, spoke on Tuesday at the Future of Law Conference hosted by LexisNexis in Sandton, Johannesburg. He warned lawyers that using AI to draft court papers irresponsibly could put their careers at risk for lying to court when AI cites case law that does not exist. The conference was looking into the AI phenomenon in the legal and justice sector. Two judgments were delivered recently in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal in which lawyers cited fake case law. Judges reported legal practitioners to the Legal Practice Council for using AI without disclosing it in court and for misleading the court by citing cases that do not exist.

Phosa said the legal fraternity cannot avoid AI because it is already used in the profession. He said technology can now produce legal arguments in seconds, analyse complex contracts and process information on a scale previously unimaginable. He said responsible use of AI is important to lawyers so as not to put their careers at risk. Speaking to Business Day after his presentation, he said a lawyer who quotes case law that does not exist makes a statement knowing it is not true and must be reported to the LPC and charged for unethical conduct. He said there has been an invention of case law that does not exist and that this is dangerous.

Phosa said citing non-existent case law can be problematic, particularly when judgments have to be delivered urgently. He said that in existing South African cases where lawyers used non-existent case law, judges were able to pick up the discrepancies when writing judgments. He asked how one convinces a judge with a lie, saying they will check and the lawyer will be exposed for a lack of professional ethics. He said lawyers carry the responsibility that their whole profession may be on the line if they deviate from responsibility and integrity. He said lawyers must accept that AI is an imperfect tool and that everything it produces needs to be checked.

The government has been grappling with regulating the use of AI, and there is a judicial committee looking into a policy to regulate how judges can use AI. This year, judge Ingrid Opperman delivered a judgment about an acting judge who cited non-existent law or incorrect cases, suggesting AI use was a key factor. Legal bodies such as the LPC and the Black Lawyers Association have also warned about the reckless use of AI. Phosa said regulation needed to look into protecting confidential information, citing the Protection of Personal Information Act and the Cybercrimes Act as important safeguards. He said Africa must not remain a passive recipient of technologies and must generate AI sovereignty, noting that China is producing AI at a speed that cannot be calculated and America is doing the same with six companies.

Articles.Title: Mathews Phosa urges lawyers to be wary of using AI in court papers - Business Day

stories.Headline: Google Tries to Blackmail Schools Into Using Its AI Tools
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Tuesday that it will turn off search engine access for K-12 schools that disable its AI tools, starting as soon as next year. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told The New York Times that search and AI are deeply integrated. He said students at schools that have banned AI will not have access to search and will see a message from their school saying it is not available. Many schools across the country have already bought low-cost Google Chromebooks for classroom instruction.

The change means schools that reject Google's AI services could lose Google search entirely. Google's search algorithm has led the industry for two decades, and its name has become synonymous with research. Lina Khan, the former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said on X that Google had used its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI tools. She noted Google has been found legally liable multiple times for antitrust violations and said the company remains unchastened.

Khan also said that as the public increasingly pushes back against AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who do not fall in line. A January report by the Brookings Institution's Center for Universal Education found that AI can undermine children's foundational development and that the damages it has already caused are daunting. Rebecca Winthrop, one of the report's authors, told NPR that when kids use generative AI that tells them the answer, they are not thinking for themselves. She said they are not learning to parse truth from fiction, to understand what makes a good argument, or to engage with different perspectives.

Articles.Title: Google Tries to Blackmail Schools Into Using Its AI Tools

stories.Headline: New York Lawmakers Crack Down on AI
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Oct. 28 that restricts unsafe AI companion chatbot features for users under 18. The law was sponsored by state Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assemblymember Alex Bores. It prohibits chatbots from encouraging suicide, self-harm, disordered eating or harmful behavior. The law also targets bots that pretend to be human, foster emotional relationships with minors, promote sexual content or discourage children from seeking help from trusted adults. The state attorney general can pursue enforcement against companies that violate the law.

The measure adds to Hochul's broader youth online safety strategy, which includes the SAFE for Kids Act, restrictions on addictive social media feeds and the use of children's personal data, and a statewide policy prohibiting cellphone use during the school day. The governor has also highlighted requirements addressing overnight notifications to minors, AI chatbot crisis referrals and disclosures that users are interacting with artificial intelligence. A separate measure signed this week strengthens security requirements for internet-connected baby monitors. Senator Andrew Gounardes and Assemblymember Jordan Wright have also introduced the RAISE Act 2.0, also known as Senate Bill S10731, a proposal to strengthen oversight of advanced AI developers.

Gonzalez said lawmakers have a responsibility to keep children safe online and that AI companies have profited for too long from rolling out chatbots to underage consumers. She said the bill puts real guardrails on how chatbots talk to children. Matthew and Maria Raine, the parents of Adam Raine, who died by suicide last year after developing a dangerous relationship with an AI chatbot, said the loss of their son did not need to happen. They said he would still be with them today but for a harmful relationship with an unregulated AI chatbot, and they called the new law a significant step forward.

The RAISE Act 2.0 would require major companies to report quarterly on automated AI research and computing resources, and notify regulators within 72 hours of significant increases in risk or research automation. The proposal would also establish independent, state-licensed safety examiners, require risk assessments every 90 days and give regulators authority to restrict certain computing activities when serious risks arise. Companies could face penalties of up to $1 million per day for an initial violation and $3 million per day for subsequent violations. The chatbot law has been signed, while the RAISE Act 2.0 remains under consideration in the Senate Rules Committee and must pass the Legislature and receive the governor's signature before becoming law.

Articles.Title: New York Lawmakers Crack Down on AI - BKReader

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania AI Ad Law Covers Voices and Radio Spots
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed Senate Bill 806, the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, on 22 October. It became Act 99 of 2026 and takes effect 60 days later, on 21 December. The bill’s sponsor, State Senator Nick Pisciottano, told KDKA in Pittsburgh that the point is to protect consumers. He also said the technology will only get better and better, and that Pennsylvania moved fast on this.

The law defines synthetic content to include an audio clip that has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence. An advertiser may not knowingly, recklessly or willfully run an ad that uses synthetic content to create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised without clear and conspicuous disclosure. When a label is needed, it must say the ad contains content that was modified or generated using artificial intelligence. It has to appear the first time the synthetic content is presented, in the same medium, and where technically possible it should be permanent or very hard to strip out. The bill’s definition of clear and conspicuous includes audio delivered at a volume and pace a listener can hear and follow.

There are three exceptions: content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary or criticism, and anything limited to text. Enforcement belongs to the Attorney General or a district attorney, who can seek an injunction, and a court can add a civil fine of up to $3,000 plus legal costs. The law firm Loeb & Loeb noted there is no private right of action, so a listener cannot sue under the act on their own. Libby O’Neill of Loeb & Loeb said an AI-altered real person giving a fake endorsement, which New York and California do not reach, may be covered. She also said an AI spokesperson delivering accurate information may not require disclosure in Pennsylvania.

New York’s law took effect in June and covers synthetic performers, digital humans that look like they are performing, but not audio ads. California’s SB 1050 names the off-camera narrator, but its definition only covers a synthetic performer who is not recognisable as a real person, so a clone of an actual voice falls outside it. Ballard Spahr’s Alan Kaplinsky and John Culhane told advertisers in a 2 November alert to implement appropriate disclosure controls before the December 21 effective date and to check the controls used by their agencies and vendors. The act starts on 21 December, in the middle of holiday ad season, and California’s law follows on 1 January 2027. Neither state has put out guidance on what a spoken tag should sound like, so the first versions will be written by advertisers’ lawyers, and the first test cases will come from state prosecutors rather than listeners.

Articles.Title: Pennsylvania AI Ad Law Covers Voices and Radio Spots - Voice Over Talent Industry News - Voice Over Herald

stories.Headline: AI law firm Crosby bids for Weil Gotshal assets
stories.Summary:
Crosby, an AI-focused law firm, has submitted a bid to acquire part of the assets of Weil, Gotshal & Manges, which is preparing to vote on dissolution. The proposal covers the trademark, brand, and some unspecified internal data of the firm. Crosby is also working to hire some of Weil Gotshal's 1,200 lawyers. The terms of the bid have not been disclosed, and its approval is not guaranteed. Weil Gotshal confirmed to The New York Times that it is preparing to hold a vote on dissolution in the coming days.

According to the reports, the firm began winding down after a likely leadership successor declined the role, several leading lawyers left the company, and a planned merger with Willkie Farr & Gallagher did not take place. Weil Gotshal is described as a 95-year-old firm that once represented Fortune 500 companies in complex restructurings and high-stakes litigation. Crosby operates as a law firm rather than as a developer selling its own artificial intelligence tools to other companies. The startup says it uses AI to provide legal services at a speed that was previously unattainable. The company has raised about $85 million in investment, including $60 million in a Series B round led by Lux and Index in March, with Sequoia, Elad Gil, 01 Advisors, and Bain Capital Ventures also participating.

Crosby says it uses AI to deliver legal services faster and cheaper than traditional firms, and the reports describe the bid as a possible first absorption of a century-old legal institution by an AI-native firm. The articles do not indicate a link between the development of legal AI and Weil Gotshal's problems. If the bid is successful, the firm's brand and part of its assets may pass to Crosby. The deal's structure remains unclear, and a partnership arrangement where Weil Gotshal's human lawyers keep formal ownership while Crosby provides technology and operations is described as most likely. Law firms face strict rules about ownership structures, unauthorized practice of law, and conflicts of interest, and the reports say full AI ownership raises significant regulatory questions.

Traditional firms are also reportedly interested in Weil Gotshal, seeing an opportunity to scoop up talented lawyers at fire-sale prices. Industry observers are already speculating about which firm might be next if Weil Gotshal falls to an AI company. The reports say every mid-tier firm with declining profits and restless partners becomes a potential target, and the precedent could open the floodgates. Whether this particular acquisition succeeds or fails, the reports say the fact that it is on the table marks a point of no return.

Articles.Title: Legal Ethics Roundup: Can AI Be Ethical?, DOJ Lawyers Under Scrutiny, Weil Gotshal Implodes, ‘Rogue Activist Judges,’ Reading Recommendations, Jobs & More - Above the Law

stories.Headline: Tesla's Full Self-Driving didn't promise full autonomy, court rules as 88 owners lose refund bid
stories.Summary:
Eighty-eight Tesla owners in South Korea lost their bid for refunds on Full Self-Driving software. The Seoul Central District Court ruled on Oct. 29 that Tesla had fulfilled its contractual duties, according to the Straits Times. The case began in 2024, when the owners claimed the technology they paid for had not been delivered. The court did not accept the owners' claim that FSD promised Level 5 automation, which would mean driving without any human intervention.

The judges found that delivering the package's remaining features depended on technological progress and regulatory approval. They noted that some capabilities had already been provided, including city-driving features and traffic light and sign recognition for older vehicles using Hardware 3 computers. Customers had also received functions from both basic Autopilot and Enhanced Autopilot. The court found that a full refund was not justified by the wait, because buyers understood that some functions might take a long time to become available.

The ruling concerns Tesla's contractual obligations and does not establish that the software provides fully autonomous driving. The court determined that delays caused by compliance with regulations in South Korea or abroad did not make the automaker liable. Tesla did not immediately respond to the decision. The Straits Times cited a report that 10 owners in China filed a joint lawsuit seeking FSD refunds and damages amounting to triple what they paid for either the software option or the vehicle.

The owners said in the lawsuit that Tesla Korea had been unable to implement the FSD system option in South Korea for more than eight years since it began selling it around March 2017. The ruling acknowledged that customers had received functions from both basic Autopilot and Enhanced Autopilot. The company's first-quarter production and delivery disclosure listed vehicle deliveries, a commonly used measure of its sales. Drivers weighing the gap between what a Tesla promises and what it delivers may want to check which features are active today versus which still depend on future updates and regulatory approval.

Articles.Title: Tesla's Full Self-Driving didn't promise full autonomy, court rules as 88 owners lose refund bid - The Cool Down

stories.Headline: Apollo’s Record AI Lending Begins to Rival Banking Giants
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global's lending reached a record $114 billion in the quarter, a 50% increase over its second quarter lending, according to the Financial Times report on Tuesday, Nov. 3. The private capital group lent to artificial intelligence companies including Anthropic and Nvidia. Apollo has now lent more than $350 billion in the last 12 months, nearly a third more than the prior year. That level is in line with large commercial banks such as HSBC and Citigroup.

Apollo's lending to Nvidia, Anthropic and Elon Musk's SpaceX/xAI involved arranging complicated deals that collateralize large borrowings against valuable chips. Some Apollo rivals have not been as willing to follow this path. Ares Management CEO Michael Arougheti told investors his company has avoided lending against AI chips because he did not know how to underwrite the decline in depreciation curves on that technology. Some large commercial banks also worry about becoming overexposed to individual Big Tech companies after a multitrillion-dollar wave of borrowing, making them hesitant to lend more.

Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok wrote in a note published Oct. 24 that corporate America has invested heavily in artificial intelligence but those efforts have so far not borne much fruit. He said the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Magnificent 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, he added. The note said many corporations were pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

Articles.Title: Apollo’s Record AI Lending Begins to Rival Banking Giants

stories.Headline: Assessment in Schools in the age of AI and digital technologies
stories.Summary:
Generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly integrated into everyday life and education, according to Joe Danso, an EdD researcher writing for Modern Ghana on November 3, 2026. He notes that although the technology is not new and people had used AI unknowingly for years through search engines and navigation systems, the situation changed after ChatGPT was released in 2022. Students now use AI to explain difficult concepts and write assignments, while educators use it to create teaching materials and assist in assessments. Nearly four years after the first model was released, this raises questions about academic integrity, critical thinking and the future of assessment.

Danso argues that assessment should not be just about grades but should reveal what a student understands, where support is needed and whether they can apply knowledge. He gives the example of a chemistry student who memorises a definition and reproduces it in an examination without necessarily understanding how or why a concept occurs, while carrying out an experiment and interpreting results provides stronger evidence of learning. He says using GenAI is not automatically cheating, since prompting AI for ideas differs from submitting a fully AI-generated piece of work as one's own. He calls for a blended approach including oral examinations, group work, presentations and practical demonstrations, and suggests students could be tasked with identifying errors in AI-generated content, verifying information and improving it.

Danso says students should be actively involved in conversations about responsible AI use rather than simply being presented with rules and penalties, and that unequal access to AI and other digital technologies must be addressed so assessment practices do not deepen existing inequalities. He says teaching should remain fundamentally human-centred and the solution is not to ban AI from education, but students should be taught about its limitations and encouraged to use it responsibly, with educators modelling responsible use. He adds that teachers will require additional support and guidance from their institutions and governments to implement effective assessment strategies. He concludes that education must still teach students how to understand an answer, question it and recognise when it is wrong.

Articles.Title: Assessment in Schools in the age of AI and digital technologies - Modern Ghana

stories.Headline: Revenue from the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Powered Chronic Pain Coaching Market is Expected to Surpass $4.61 Billion
stories.Summary:
The Business Research Company published a report on November 3, 2026, saying revenue from AI-powered chronic pain coaching is expected to pass $4.61 billion. The London-based research firm said the market is projected to grow from $1.68 billion in 2025 to $2.06 billion in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of 22.7%. It expects the market to reach $4.61 billion by 2030, with a CAGR of 22.4%. The report describes these platforms as digital tools that use algorithms to tailor coaching to each patient's pain management needs.

The report ties growth to the rising prevalence of diabetes and to sedentary lifestyles that raise obesity and insulin resistance risks. It cited UK Office of Health Improvement and Disparities data showing type 2 diabetes prevalence among English adults aged 17 and older reached 7.0% in March 2024, up from 6.8% a year earlier. It also pointed to wider adoption of digital health technologies and demand for non-drug pain management. North America was the largest market in 2025, which the report attributes to advanced healthcare infrastructure, greater technology adoption and strong investment in digital health innovation.

The report was issued by TBRC Business Research Pvt Ltd, and Oliver Guirdham of The Business Research Company is listed as the contact. Saumya Sahay is named as the expert to speak with, with phone numbers listed for the Americas, Asia and Europe. The company describes itself as providing more than 17,500 market research reports across 27 industries and 60 or more countries. It says it has a team of 350 or more experts across 28 countries and manages over 1.5 million datasets.

The report covers regions including Asia-Pacific, South East Asia, Western and Eastern Europe, South America, the Middle East and Africa. It lists trends for the period to 2030, including adaptive pain management algorithms, continuous patient feedback, wearable devices for pain monitoring and personalized coaching systems. The report also offers market attractiveness scoring, total addressable market analysis and Excel-based forecasting dashboards. A legal disclaimer states that EIN Presswire provides the content as is and accepts no responsibility for its accuracy.

Articles.Title: Revenue from the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Powered Chronic Pain Coaching Market is Expected to Surpass $4.61 Billion

stories.Headline: Judiciary Stuck In AI Rulemaking Rut As Attys, Judges Protest
stories.Summary:
Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence are stalled, according to a Law360 report published on November 3, 2026, by Jeff Overley. The report says the delay involves concerns about burdens placed on litigators. It also cites tension between fast-moving technology and slow policymaking. The report adds that officials are struggling over how to even define the technology at issue.

The article does not give specific dates for any proposed rules or name the officials involved. It does not state what any new rule would require or change. No numbers beyond the publication date are provided. The report describes the situation as a rut rather than a finished policy.

The story is limited to the concerns raised in the report. It says attorneys and judges have protested the stalled progress. It does not include direct statements from named individuals. It also does not say who is formally responsible for moving the rules forward.

The report does not describe what happens next. It gives no timeline for future action. It does not say whether a proposal will be issued or when. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Judiciary Stuck In AI Rulemaking Rut As Attys, Judges Protest - Law360

stories.Headline: Court Vacates Subpoena Ruling, Issues AI Rules In Fracking-Securities Case
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Tyler, Texas, granted a motion for reconsideration on November 2, 2026, and vacated an earlier ruling in a securities case involving the promotion of fracking and COVID-19 virus products. The judge acted after he was told he had erroneously found that a party failed to respond to a motion to quash a third-party subpoena. The case documents include the magistrate judge's October 14 memorandum opinion and order, a motion to dismiss by Boykin, an opposition by Al-Taie, and Al-Taie's second amended complaint. The vacated ruling was the earlier finding that the party had not responded.

The reconsideration ruling means the earlier finding that the party failed to respond no longer stands. Separately, the judge said that going forward all parties must certify whether they used artificial intelligence in drafting filings. The judge also said the court may ignore anything not generated by a human. The articles list the attached documents as Magistrate Judge Love's order on reconsideration, Judge Barker's AI order, and Al-Taie's motion for reconsideration, along with the October 14 memorandum opinion and order, Boykin's motion to dismiss, Al-Taie's opposition, and Al-Taie's second amended complaint.

Magistrate Judge Love issued the order on reconsideration, and Judge Barker issued the AI order, according to the list of attached documents. The articles do not quote either judge directly. The articles say the magistrate judge was told he had erroneously found that a party failed to respond to the motion to quash. The articles do not say who told him this or which party was involved.

The articles describe the case as a securities matter involving promotion of fracking and COVID-19 virus products. The AI rules apply to all parties going forward, and the court may ignore anything not generated by a human. The articles do not say what happens next in the case beyond these rulings. The articles also do not say whether any party has responded to the new certification requirement.

stories.Headline: Wikimedia Urges Court to Separate AI Training From Content Retrieval
stories.Summary:
The Wikimedia Foundation asked a court in an OpenAI copyright case to treat AI model training differently from systems that retrieve and present specific copyrighted works. The foundation filed an amicus brief on Oct. 30 in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation. An amicus brief comes from an organization outside the case that wants to explain how a ruling could affect people or groups beyond the parties. The filing takes neither side in the litigation.

The foundation's argument turns on how an AI system uses copyrighted material. During pretraining, a model learns patterns from a large body of text, and Wikimedia argued that this process typically qualifies as fair use. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, works differently, because a system retrieves particular material and includes it in a response. Wikimedia argued that this kind of use should be subject to licensing requirements. The distinction would separate learning from a broad collection of works from presenting selected content in answers.

The foundation warned of risks on both sides of the question. A ruling that restricts AI training too broadly could curb tools that help volunteers improve Wikipedia, it said. A decision that permits too much use without licensing could lead publishers to limit access to their work. Wikipedia contains more than 67 million articles in over 300 languages. The filing follows the foundation's 2023 response to the U.S. Copyright Office, which called for case-specific reviews of AI fair use.

Articles.Title: Wikimedia Urges Court to Separate AI Training From Content Retrieval - TOKENPOST

stories.Headline: AI training on copyrighted works may violate derivative rights, US court told
stories.Summary:
An amicus curiae brief was filed by Teodor J. Holmberg in the consolidated copyright infringement litigation against OpenAI and Microsoft. The brief was filed before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York on November 2, 2026. It urges the court to recognise the use of copyrighted works as AI training inputs as a separate licensing market. The filing argues that such use may constitute the creation of derivative works under copyright law. The brief makes two alternative arguments under the US Copyright Act.

First, it says preparing copyrighted works for AI training, including through formatting, modification and tokenisation, could amount to creating derivative works under Section 106(2). Holmberg argues that the licensing market for copyrighted material used as AI input must be assessed separately from the market for AI-generated outputs. He contends that converting copyrighted text into tokenised data does not make the use transformative for fair-use purposes. The brief also cites licensing agreements involving OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta, Perplexity, ProRata.ai and Mistral AI as evidence of an emerging commercial market. The filing relies on the Third Circuit's September 29, 2026 ruling in Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v.

ROSS Intelligence Inc. That ruling found that ROSS's unauthorised use of Thomson Reuters' headnotes as AI training data harmed a potential derivative market. The brief distinguishes this from the 2025 decisions in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, which it says wrongly excluded the potential market for AI training inputs from the fair-use analysis. In the alternative, Holmberg argues that if the court finds the use is not covered by existing exclusive rights, it should recognise such use as a distinct property interest supporting state-law and common-law claims.

The filing comes amid competing motions for summary judgment by authors, news organisations and other copyright holders on one side, and OpenAI and Microsoft on the other. The plaintiffs have sought rulings that the companies infringed their copyrights by using protected works to train AI models. The defendants have relied on fair use as a defence. The consolidated litigation, titled In re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, is pending before US District Judge Sidney H. Stein. The amicus brief does not represent a court finding or a determination on the merits of the copyright claims.

Articles.Title: AI training on copyrighted works may violate derivative rights, US court told - ETLegalWorld.com

stories.Headline: Algorithmic kill chains: China’s military AI, Europe’s regulatory mismatch
stories.Summary:
A study from the NATO Defense College examined how China’s People’s Liberation Army is integrating artificial intelligence into its war-fighting doctrine. The authors are Anselm Küsters, scientific director for the Nordic countries and head of the Department of Digitalisation and AI at the Centre for European Policy, and Marius Strubenhoff, an independent expert on foreign and security policy at the same think-tank. They applied large language models to a corpus of over 171,000 Chinese documents spanning 2000 to 2025. The study is titled Decoding the Dragon: A Language-Based Analysis of China’s Vision of AI Warfare.

The study found that surveillance-related terms dominated the corpus by a wide margin. Computer vision accounted for 49.4 per cent of the subfield distribution, robotics for 12.5 per cent and natural language processing for 6.2 per cent, while AI safety was under two per cent. References to meaningful human control in the People’s Daily peaked in 2021, when UN deliberations on lethal autonomous weapons were most intense, and declined sharply afterward. The number of military AI publications grew from 52 papers in 2016 to 181 in 2024.

The authors write that near-term PLA investments appear geared toward battlespace transparency that supports information dominance and precision strikes. They say the dominance of surveillance applications suggests near-term crisis instability will stem from information asymmetries rather than rogue autonomous weapons. They conclude that positive state narratives and the decline in meaningful human control rhetoric after 2021 signal growing Chinese confidence and waning commitment to international norms. They are careful not to overstate China’s current capabilities, noting it is not quite on the verge of autonomous military dominance.

Europe’s EU AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national-security purposes from its scope. The Dual-Use Export Control Regulation is export-centric and reactive and does not yet cover foundation models, reinforcement-learning environments or synthetic datasets. The GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive are strong on individual rights but not designed to counter adversarial exploitation of European data streams by a foreign military. European Parliament resolutions in 2018 and 2021 urging a ban on lethal autonomous weapons without meaningful human control remain legally non-binding.

The study addresses its recommendations to member states rather than to the EU as an institution. It calls for investment in adversarial robustness research, counter-ISR technologies and human-machine teaming architectures. It says effective arms control requires technical measures that are intrusive and analogous to Chemical Weapons Convention inspection protocols, and it calls for treaty obligations targeting autonomous target selection and non-reconstructible black box military AI systems. The article describes possible EU measures including a dedicated Defence AI Instrument, amending Annex I of the Dual-Use Regulation, a Strategic Data Spaces regime and a European strategic autonomy framework requiring unanimous member-state agreement.

Articles.Title: Algorithmic kill chains: China’s military AI, Europe’s regulatory mismatch - EU Perspectives

stories.Headline: Law firms paying more for AI skills, creating opportunities for law graduates
stories.Summary:
Robert Half's 2027 Salary Guide, reported by the National Jurist on November 2, 2026, found that law firms are paying more for artificial intelligence skills. Jamy Sullivan, executive director of the legal practice at Robert Half, said 77% of law firms are increasing pay for relevant AI expertise. She said law firms are clearly signaling they will pay more for AI expertise going into 2027. The findings point to opportunities for candidates who can bring specialized skills to an employer.

The guide gives several figures. Within legal overall, 67% are paying more for relevant AI skills, compared with 77% for law firms specifically. Sullivan said 74% of legal employers are offering higher-than-planned salaries to attract new hires, compared with 57% nationally across the professional fields surveyed. Nationally, 72% of employers are increasing pay for candidates with AI expertise, and 64% say starting salary offers are more competitive than three years ago. Starting pay for attorneys with two to three years of experience is projected to rise 3.6% in 2027, attorneys with four to nine years of experience are expected to see a 3.9% increase, and in-house counsel with four to nine years of experience are projected to see a 3.4% gain, all above the 2.2% average growth expected across legal positions.

Sullivan said professional growth deserves attention alongside compensation and flexibility. She asked whether there is a mentorship program and how people get access to career development and ongoing professional development. She said that is something younger generations weigh when looking at job opportunities and the overall employment experience. The article says students comparing first-job offers should look beyond the headline salary and ask about mentorship, training, work schedules and benefits.

San Francisco, Denver and Seattle lead the surveyed cities in the share of employers offering higher-than-planned starting salaries, at 66%, 65% and 64%. Dallas follows at 61%, Minneapolis at 60% and Boston at 59%, while the shares are 57% in Atlanta, 54% in Washington, D.C., 52% in Los Angeles, 50% in Houston, 48% in New York and 47% in Chicago. The article says these are findings across professional fields, not rankings of legal salaries or the highest-paying cities for new lawyers. It also says the findings do not guarantee a higher offer for every graduate.

Articles.Title: Law firms paying more for AI skills, creating opportunities for law graduates - National Jurist

stories.Headline: San Antonio teachers are using AI. Schools are figuring out the rules. - San Antonio Express-News
stories.Summary:
Brent Ritchey, an eighth grade U.S. history teacher at Briscoe Middle School in San Antonio, began using chatbots in 2022 after OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public. He fed the program Texas learning standards for the American Revolution and asked it to plan a lesson. Four years and 40 models of ChatGPT later, he uses education-focused AI tools in his classroom. His students have interviewed Abraham Lincoln, created documents about 18th century events using slang, and received feedback on writing assignments.

Northside Independent School District, where Ritchey works, has approved 10 AI tools for educators. In the next few weeks, the district plans to roll out ChatGPT for Teachers, a private platform for educators to create and share lessons across schools and districts, according to Director of Academic Technology Carrie Squyres. North East ISD allows employees to use tools including Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot. San Antonio ISD rolled out the AI platform Coursemojo last year to teach reading at some schools, and Somerset ISD launched Subject.AI over the summer to help high schoolers catch up in classes where they had fallen behind.

Ritchey said teachers cannot be replaced by AI but can accept that students will use it and should be taught to use it properly. Torie Marquez, North East ISD's executive director of technology services, said that when something is adopted at such a large scale, people have to shift their thinking about whether it is a trend or longer term, and she believes AI is here to stay. Jessica Saenz, a Madison High School English teacher, called learning the tools tedious but said she was impressed the feedback touched on each part of the rubric, and that we gain the ability to do more in less time. Patti Holub, chief technology officer at Education Service Center Region 20, said training teachers takes time, money and staff, and the center launched four online AI courses in October.

Northside ISD's employee handbook prohibits feeding identifiable student information into AI when developing special education plans and using AI tools to determine student grades, stating that AI is a tool and not a replacement for human judgement. The guidance does not outline enforcement beyond saying the district will continue to monitor use and misuse of AI applications. Deepti Tagare, a UTSA professor who studies AI in schools, said educators should not use AI in grading, identifying cheating or predicting how students will perform academically. Squyres said she cannot ensure that all of Northside's 95,000 students learn to leverage AI under the current policy that lets teachers decide how much they use it, and she warned against creating inequity across classrooms.

Articles.Title: San Antonio teachers are using AI. Schools are figuring out the rules. - San Antonio Express-News

stories.Headline: Forbes Names Sonal N. Mehta to Its Inaugural List of America's Top Lawyers for AI
stories.Summary:
Forbes named WilmerHale partner Sonal N. Mehta to its inaugural list of America's Top Lawyers for AI, the firm announced on November 3, 2026. The publication described the list as recognizing the top artificial intelligence practitioners in the country. Only fifty lawyers nationwide were selected for the recognition. The honor followed Mehta's selection in September to Forbes' 2026 list of America's Top Lawyers.

Forbes chose honorees through a rigorous, multi-stage editorial process. Candidates were evaluated on factors including reputation, industry honors, influence on the AI legal landscape, advocacy performance, client and peer feedback, thought leadership and involvement in significant matters. Mehta is a trial lawyer who represents many of the world's leading technology companies in high-stakes disputes. Her clients range from Silicon Valley's largest companies to cutting-edge startups, and she serves as both lead counsel in the courtroom and trusted adviser in the boardroom.

Mehta litigates complex cases across antitrust, commercial, class action, false advertising, intellectual property, privacy and government-facing matters. She also leads WilmerHale's Palo Alto office as Partner-in-Charge and serves as Vice Chair of the firm's Litigation/Controversy Department. The firm said the recognition comes as artificial intelligence reshapes how companies innovate and compete. The full list is available on Forbes.com.

Articles.Title: Forbes Names Sonal N. Mehta to Its Inaugural List of America's Top Lawyers for AI

stories.Headline: Korea Display Industry Association, KOSA Join Forces to Expand AI Adoption in Manufacturing
stories.Summary:
The Korea Display Industry Association signed a memorandum of understanding with the Korea Software Industry Association on November 3, 2026, at the KDIA building in Korea. The agreement is meant to speed up the adoption of artificial intelligence across display manufacturing operations. Lee Seung-woo, vice chairman of KDIA, and Seo Sung-il, vice chairman of KOSA, posed after signing the cooperation agreement. KDIA announced the partnership on November 3.

The partnership covers five areas, which are matching technologies and expanding networks between AI and software companies and display manufacturers, training specialists in AI and software for the display industry, advancing technologies that combine display and AI, jointly organizing seminars and conferences, and sharing domestic and international industry trends and information. The two associations aim to connect manufacturing companies' operational needs with relevant AI and software solutions. They want to help small and midsize materials, components and equipment suppliers adopt technologies suited to their production processes and business conditions. They also plan to identify AI implementation projects for individual companies and train specialists to carry them out.

Lee Seung-woo of KDIA said manufacturing AX was an important means of improving productivity and manufacturing competitiveness in the display industry. He added that the association would expand cooperation between AI and software companies and display manufacturers. The two associations previously co-hosted the "AX Connect Day: Display & Manufacturing" event in October. That event showcased AI adoption cases and solutions from display materials, components and equipment companies and facilitated business matchmaking between manufacturers and AI providers.

Articles.Title: Korea Display Industry Association, KOSA Join Forces to Expand AI Adoption in Manufacturing - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: AI: Data Centers on the Ballot in 15 Governor Races. AI-RTZ #1259 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
On Election Day in the US, AI data centers became a top issue in governor races for the first time in this AI tech wave. The Information analyzed candidate platforms and public statements and found that of the 36 states electing a governor, 21 have at least one major-party nominee backing a data center moratorium. In five states both nominees back a pause: Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas. In three more, Maine, New Mexico and New York, a pause backer is likely to win based on recent polls. In seven others, Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Vermont, the race is close between a pause backer and a candidate who does not back one.

Those 15 states hold more than a third of the US population and some of the biggest AI data center projects. OpenAI's Stargate with Oracle has large sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico, and SoftBank's SB Energy plans an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Three sitting governors have already paused new large-scale data centers: Kathy Hochul in New York, Greg Abbott in Texas and Tina Kotek in Oregon. The pauses vary in length from 45 days to three years and in scope, with New York's applying to facilities above 50 megawatts. Every statewide pause so far has relied on halting new environmental permits, and Abbott has also frozen new grid hookups in Texas while Kotek stopped deals on state land in Oregon.

Of the 46 top nominees not calling for a moratorium, 38 back at least one other restriction, most commonly ratepayer protection. Hawaii is the only state where neither candidate is campaigning on data center limits, and the split is not cleanly partisan, with Republican candidates backing moratoriums in Maryland and Iowa. Abbott said developers had dug their own grave, and his challenger Gina Hinojosa called his pause an election-year stunt. New Hampshire's incumbent said she would need the state budget next July, while her opponent promised an executive order on day one. Google's head of data center energy said the bottleneck on Earth is permits and grid studies, not power, and that space data centers could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Earth.

At the start of this year only about 40 localities had bans on data centers, and by August there were over 500, driven by power bills, water use, noise and blight. A Pew Research Center poll in August found six in ten US adults would be uncomfortable with a new data center in their area, and a University of Pennsylvania poll found more than 60 percent now oppose new data centers nearby, up from 49 percent in March. Anthropic named moratoriums and other restrictions as a business risk in its IPO filing, citing New York and Texas, and SB Energy and Nscale named the same risks in their own filings. Google lost about $500 billion of market value in a day, and OpenAI has raised less than half of its $30 billion target.

Articles.Title: AI: Data Centers on the Ballot in 15 Governor Races. AI-RTZ #1259 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: U.S. Midterms to Decide Fate of $2.5 Trillion in AI Data Center Investment as Governor Races Emerge as Wild Card
stories.Summary:
With three days to go before the U.S. midterm elections, Wall Street is focusing on governor's races rather than Congress, because authority over data center permitting and power and water regulation sits at the state level. Market research firm Cleanview estimates that 10 governor's races will affect data center investment plans totaling 67.4 GW and $2.5 trillion. Texas holds roughly 25% of U.S. data center capacity expected to come online by 2030. Jefferies warned that if the Democratic candidate for Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa, wins, her pledge to halt new construction could put 13.3 GW of announced projects at risk. Incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott is pushing to strengthen power and water reviews.

Georgia and Ohio are also seen as key states, with community opposition over grid strain and water use intensifying in both. In Ohio, the Senate race is a separate variable: cryptocurrency groups have poured more than $50 million into efforts to defeat Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown, a crypto skeptic, in his matchup against Republican incumbent Jon Husted. If Brown returns to the Senate and Democrats win a majority, oversight of the crypto industry by financial regulators could tighten. Some companies are reportedly holding off on issuing billions of dollars in high-yield bonds while they wait for policy clarity. If data center construction is delayed, financing schedules and plans to recoup investments could be thrown off together.

RBC Capital Markets said in a report that governors are on the front lines of AI and data center regulation. JPMorgan noted that President Donald Trump has said he would veto legislation restricting the expansion of the AI industry, and that it is realistically difficult for Democrats to win enough seats to override a veto, so federal gridlock offsets policy risk. Kevin Shea, a senior equity analyst at BNY Wealth, said policy uncertainty around data centers will not reverse the AI investment flow itself but could disrupt project timelines and costs. Analysts say projects that have yet to secure new permits and power supply contracts face the greatest risk of schedule delays and cost increases from tighter regulation. The direction of the investment environment is likely to be decided not in Washington but in state capitals.

Articles.Title: U.S. Midterms to Decide Fate of $2.5 Trillion in AI Data Center Investment as Governor Races Emerge as Wild Card - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: More Democratic Governors Could Shake $2.5 Trillion AI Buildout
stories.Summary:
U.S. midterm elections began on Nov. 3, with voters filling 35 Senate seats, all 435 House seats, and governorships and state legislative seats in 36 states. Washington's political establishment broadly expected Democrats to win the House by a wide margin, with the Senate seen as a close contest. Attention also focused on governorships, where Democrats were seen as having a chance to win a majority for the first time since 2010. Wall Street estimates that AI infrastructure investment exposed to Democratic governors alone exceeds 3,300 trillion won, or about $2.5 trillion.

Democrats were expected to win 230 to 240 of the 435 House seats, where the current split is 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies. Governorships currently stand at 26 Republicans and 24 Democrats, and Democrats were seen as likely to add two to four. The 100-seat Senate is divided among 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats and two independents who lean Democratic, and 35 seats were being contested. Even a 50-50 split would let Vice President JD Vance cast tie-breaking votes as Senate president. The dominant issue was severe inflation, with U.S. gasoline at $4.13 a gallon on Nov. 3, and a Financial Times poll with Focaldata from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1 found 68% of respondents dissatisfied with Trump's handling of prices.

Trump said in a podcast interview released by the New York Post on Nov. 1 that he would probably become "Mr. Veto" if Democrats won congressional majorities, and predicted they would come to him to cut a deal after bills were repeatedly rejected. The Justice Department, led by Todd Blanche, said on Nov. 3 it had deployed about 1,000 election monitors and observers across all 50 states, triple the scale of the 2022 midterms. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin warned on X that people who vote illegally would be tracked down and prosecuted, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement wrote that it would find, track, arrest and prosecute them. Democratic governors in Washington, North Carolina and Colorado mobilized National Guard members for election monitoring.

Financial markets focused on gubernatorial races and data center regulation, because community opposition to data center construction is emerging across the United States. The outcomes in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, where large-scale AI infrastructure projects are planned, could have a decisive impact on the industry, and Texas accounts for about 25% of U.S. data center capacity expected to be operating by 2030. If Democrats capture both chambers, Trump could slide into an early lame-duck period, and Britain's Telegraph reported on Nov. 2 that parts of the White House and the Republican Party were worried Democrats would pursue impeachment. Britain's Times reported that officials including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and the White House counsel's office spent months drawing up ways for the president to advance his agenda without congressional approval, and Reuters reported that Miller and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought had been reviewing such steps since April.

Articles.Title: More Democratic Governors Could Shake $2.5 Trillion AI Buildout - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI-powered law firm Crosby launches ad campaign in NYC subway
stories.Summary:
Crosby Legal, an artificial intelligence law firm, launched an advertising campaign in the New York City subway, according to a report published on November 2, 2026 by The Ticker, a student news site at Baruch College. The ads carry the phrase "In Memoriam: The Billable Hour." The campaign targets billable hours, which the article describes as the core revenue driver of established big law firms. The firm is trying to disrupt how corporate legal work is bought and sold.

Crosby charges per document instead of traditional hourly rates. It focuses on automating high-volume commercial contracts such as nondisclosure agreements, master services agreements and data processing addenda. The article says Crosby has already signed tech clients including Cursor, Ramp and Clay. The firm says clients get predictable legal budgets and faster turnaround times on standard transaction paperwork.

The article says New York State ethics guidelines strictly prohibit nonlawyers from owning law firms or sharing legal fees with licensed attorneys. To comply, Crosby operates as a managed services organization that handles software development and business operations, while partnering with a licensed law firm entity that delivers actual legal services. Software agents create automated redlines, score risk factors and conduct counterparty analysis on incoming agreements. Ultimate legal liability remains with human attorneys, who must actively supervise automated workflows to protect client privilege, verify document accuracy and avoid unauthorized practice violations.

The article says the subway ads are an unusual way to sell legal services to corporate executives, but the location relies on Manhattan's geography. Thousands of startup founders, corporate officers and legal workers see the campaigns daily as they commute between Midtown financial centers and Wall Street. The article says similar campaigns by enterprise software and financial technology providers have shown that urban transit ads can drive customer acquisition. It says traditional law firms face pressure to reduce fees, introduce new pricing models or increase their use of automation as corporate legal departments seek faster results and predictable costs.
