stories.Headline: Why AI Is Redefining Fiduciary Best Practices
stories.Summary:
Don Trone, CEO and co-founder of the Behavioral Governance Institute, published an opinion article on November 3, 2026, in 401(k) Specialist arguing that fiduciary best practices are no longer sufficient on their own. He wrote that the practices built over the past 25 years brought structure and accountability to investment stewardship, but that Artificial Intelligence has exposed their limits. He said a process can be complete while the reasoning behind it stays weak, and that a committee can follow its policy and vote unanimously while missing a flawed assumption. He described Augmented Intelligence, guided by Behavioral Governance, as a stronger model because it supports the human judgment that decides whether a process serves others' best interests.

Trone laid out a framework built on four linked dimensions, which he listed as Knowledge, Judgment, Reasoning and Execution. He said the aim is to connect what professionals know, how they decide, and how those decisions show up in actions and outcomes. He pointed to observable "Signals," such as a board member asking for contrary evidence before a vote or a chair inviting dissenting views, as evidence of decision quality. He also described a Special Purpose Avatar, built on what he called a 72 Cell, 288 Signal Meta-Framework, that can question assumptions and raise alternative viewpoints before consensus hardens. He noted that generative AI can produce inaccurate statements, miss context and reinforce biases, so responsible use requires curated sources, verification and human oversight.

Trone said fiduciaries remain accountable for accepting or rejecting what the system recommends. He argued that the real question is not whether AI beats human judgment, but whether a disciplined partnership of the two produces better decisions than either can alone. He said professionals need enough technical understanding to question the system, enough ethical discipline to resist convenient answers, and enough leadership to act when evidence challenges consensus. He added that organizations should check whether this combination improves the quality of inquiry, the handling of uncertainty and follow-through after decisions.

Trone has been called the "Father of Fiduciary" and was the principal founder of fi360. He wrote that traditional best practices laid an important foundation for prudent stewardship, and that Augmented Intelligence offers a chance to build beyond it. He said the most effective fiduciaries of the future will not just show they followed a prudent process, but will be able to show why their decisions deserve confidence. The article is an opinion piece and describes no regulatory or legal change.

Articles.Title: Why AI Is Redefining Fiduciary Best Practices

stories.Headline: China to explore AI applications in financial regulation, services: report - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China will explore using artificial intelligence in financial regulation and services, according to a report submitted to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, the country's top legislature. The report was submitted by the State Council and was under deliberation at the session, Xinhua reported on November 3, 2026. It set out five priorities for the next stage of financial development. These include keeping an appropriately accommodative monetary policy, strengthening financial regulation and improving financial services to the real economy.

The report said China will use various policy tools to ensure ample liquidity and will keep evaluating and improving its monetary policy framework. On regulation, the country will crack down on illegal financial activities, explore AI applications in financial management and services, and strengthen protection of financial consumers. It will also increase support for infrastructure networks, technological innovation and small businesses. The report called for expanding the international use of the yuan, attracting more foreign financial institutions and long-term capital, and further developing an independently controlled cross-border yuan payment system.

On risk prevention, the report highlighted the use of monetary policy tools to support the capital market and continued implementation of the property sector's white-list mechanism. It said China has stepped up financial support for the real economy. From October 2025 to September 2026, new aggregate financing to the real economy totaled 33 trillion yuan, about 4.9 trillion U.S. dollars. A total of 88 companies went public on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, with nearly 90 percent of them being high-tech firms.

Articles.Title: China to explore AI applications in financial regulation, services: report - Xinhua

stories.Headline: California’s ‘No Robo Bosses Act’: New Restrictions on Employers’ Use of AI
stories.Summary:
On September 30, 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 947 into law, known as the No Robo Bosses Act. The law adds Part 5.5.5 to the California Labor Code and governs automated decision systems in the workplace. It takes effect on July 1, 2027. The signing followed Newsom's 2025 veto of a broader predecessor bill.

The law bars employers from relying solely on an automated decision system to make disciplinary or termination decisions. If an employer primarily relies on such a tool, a human must corroborate the decision using the data behind the output or other supporting information. Employers must give affected employees a written postuse notice when informing them of the decision. The notice must be plain language, stand alone, and state that the employer primarily relied on the system, that a human reviewed and corroborated the output, contact information for questions, and that retaliation is prohibited. Employees may also request a meaningful, objective description of their own data used by the system.

The labor commissioner may investigate, order temporary relief, issue citations, and file civil actions, with a $500 civil penalty per violation. Public prosecutors, including the California attorney general and local district attorneys, may also bring civil actions seeking injunctive relief, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees. The law does not create a standalone private right of action, but claims may be brought under the Private Attorneys General Act. Employers covered by a collective bargaining agreement are exempt if the agreement explicitly waives the requirements, provides for wages and working conditions, and protects against algorithmic discrimination.

The law is one of several AI measures Newsom signed, including restrictions on AI-driven workplace monitoring. California has also adopted AI regulations through the Fair Employment and Housing Act and privacy mandates such as the California Consumer Privacy Act. Other states, including Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, and Texas, and New York City, have laws restricting automated tools for significant employment decisions. With the effective date approaching, employers may want to inventory covered tools, prepare notice templates, set up processes for employee data requests, and train managers.

Articles.Title: California’s ‘No Robo Bosses Act’: New Restrictions on Employers’ Use of AI - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Google Legend Starts AI Firm at 58, Targeting $50 Billion Value
stories.Summary:
Jeff Dean, the former Google chief scientist who led work on the Gemini artificial intelligence models, founded a startup called Discovery Loop in August with three Google researchers. The company is seeking funding at a target valuation of $50 billion, about 67 trillion won, foreign media reported on Nov. 2. Dean had spent 27 years at Google, joining in 1999 as its 30th employee, and he also led development of the Tensor Processing Unit, Google's custom chip. He left the company in August, and Google shares fell 4% on Aug. 5, the day news of his exit emerged.

Discovery Loop is building an automated system in which AI proposes research hypotheses, runs thousands of experiments at the same time and then adjusts the hypotheses based on the results. The goal is to automate machine-learning research itself, leading to recursive self-improvement, in which AI builds better AI. The industry was stirred again last month by news that Chen Guangyu, a prodigy born in 2009 who worked on the Kimi K3 model at China's Moonshot AI, had joined the firm. Dean, 58, declined an interview request at an AI event held on Oct. 28 at Stanford University in Palo Alto, California.

Dean said he was at a stage of focusing on building the organization. In a lecture at the event, he explained that the reason for automating machine learning is to achieve faster scientific discovery. He said that if a system has solved 5,000 problems through AI innovation, the 5,001st should be something it can learn to solve on its own from the problems that came before. He said the company has built the agents and the harness it uses for its own development and automation, and that about 20 automatic improvement loops are running now.

Dean left Google, a large corporation, to found the venture as a public-benefit organization because he wants to concentrate on research goals. Inside Google, his departure had a bigger impact than the step back from frontline management by Demis Hassabis, the DeepMind chief known as the father of AlphaGo. The global tech industry is watching Dean's next move, and Silicon Valley paid particular attention to the startup because of his long record at Google. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported funding effort.

Articles.Title: Google Legend Starts AI Firm at 58, Targeting $50 Billion Value - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: 261 teachers of Air Force schools cyber-trained to protect students from online exploitation, AI misuse
stories.Summary:
261 teachers from 42 Air Force schools have completed a certification course as cyber crime intervention officers, the defence ministry said on Monday. The training is meant to help them protect students from online grooming and exploitation, misuse of artificial intelligence, gaming-related harms and financial frauds. It also enables the teachers to preserve digital evidence and act as first responders. The programme was run through the Information Sharing and Analysis Centre Foundation, or ISAC.

The initiative is called ScrollControl, a child digital safety programme. Under it, Air Force schools can form cyber clubs, certify students on cyber safety, hold awareness sessions for parents and staff, and use an age-appropriate content rating platform for families. Schools can also be recognised as cyber-safe schools. The Indian Air Force Educational and Cultural Society, under Air Headquarters, onboarded the schools onto the programme. The defence ministry said the training and certification include empanelment on the National Security Database and 24x7 victim support through cyber lawyers, cyber psychologists and forensic experts.

The ministry said the effort is led by the Indian Air Force Educational and Cultural Society to build cyber safety capability within the Air Force schools community. It said the programme comes as children are widely exposed to unregulated digital spaces, with affordable high-speed internet, smart devices and social media access. The initiative coincides with national cyber security awareness month. CBSE has directed affiliated schools to include cyber safety best practices through the monthly observance of Cyber Jagrookta Diwas, and the ministry said ScrollControl helps Air Force schools meet that requirement with trained in-house capability.

Articles.Title: 261 teachers of Air Force schools cyber-trained to protect students from online exploitation, AI misuse - The Times of India

stories.Headline: AI giants are offering billions in bonds, competing with European governments for investor capital
stories.Summary:
Four of the biggest US technology companies, Amazon, Alphabet, which owns Google, Meta and Oracle, have sold about $250 billion in dollar bonds since the start of 2025, according to a tally of US regulatory filings by AI Industry Reviews. They have sold a further €37 billion, or $41 billion, in euro bonds. Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, recently joined with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars. More than $1 trillion, or €900 billion, is pouring into the artificial intelligence build-out.

Goldman Sachs expects total new AI hyperscaler bond sales to reach $420 billion next year, with about €60 billion issued in euros according to the Dutch bank ING. France, Germany and Italy have seen sovereign bond yields rise sharply in recent months, straining public finances. France's public debt stands at 119% of gross domestic product and its deficit is still above 5%, and yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5% over the past six months. France's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at BNP Paribas, called the phenomenon bond abundance and told DW the hyperscalers' presence in the euro bond market is already high enough to create competition within the corporate sector and between companies and governments for fixed income funds. Economists at the European Central Bank said in August that the euro bond market was adapting well but warned the AI giants could make it harder for other companies and sectors to access finance. They questioned whether the bloc's markets can smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment. Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, co-author of a study for the OECD published in January, told DW that in the United States AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, while the opposite appears to hold in several European countries.

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies, finding that interest costs as a share of sales among Stoxx 600 firms have risen by nearly half since 2022 and cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period. European firms could face pressure to cut investment in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments. Cities and regions, whose borrowing funds schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects. The article says AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, but that US Big Tech's appetite for capital could add further pressure next year because of the additional billions in new bonds planned.

Articles.Title: AI giants are offering billions in bonds, competing with European governments for investor capital

stories.Headline: Three questions that will define AI's political power
stories.Summary:
The 2026 midterms will be the first test of how voters feel about the AI race, according to Axios. The article says the results will show whether campaigning on AI regulation, or aligning with tech figures like Elon Musk, helps or hurts candidates ahead of 2028. It also says candidates can no longer afford half-baked AI agendas. The piece lays out three questions about AI politics and names the races it is watching on Election Day.

Some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue rather than backing candidates based on their AI positions. Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation group, launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over AI positions in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California, and backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who called AI the most important issue and tied it to jobs and affordability. Democratic group Tomorrow Together ran ads against Republicans' AI records in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Competing groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their ads largely avoided AI itself.

Musk was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million, and his spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration made him both a powerful backer and a target for Democratic attacks. In Texas' 10th District, Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk. In Kansas' 1st District, Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned on her DOGE experience and criticized Musk's influence in her challenge to Republican Rep. Tracey Mann. Other races watched include Ohio's Senate contest, where Republican Jon Husted benefited from Musk's America PAC spending against Democrat Sherrod Brown, and the Texas Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.

A few candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could shape whether the next Congress has a louder bloc pushing back on industry efforts to limit regulation. In Michigan, El-Sayed wants a cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on super intelligence, and he has attacked Republican Mike Rogers, who benefited from Musk-affiliated spending. In Colorado's 8th district, Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill, and in California's 11th district, Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry. In Minnesota's 2nd district, Democrat Matt Little would add a voice to the push to ban data center construction and non-disclosure agreements nationally. The article says competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

Articles.Title: Three questions that will define AI's political power

stories.Headline: New York passes law restricting children’s use of AI chatbots
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on October 28, 2026, that restricts how AI chatbots interact with children. The bill, S9051B/A10379C, adds Article 48 to the state's General Business Law and was approved by state lawmakers earlier in the year. It bars operators of AI companions from giving minors certain features, including presenting the chatbot as human, claiming a personal relationship with the user, encouraging self-harm or isolation, and generating sexually explicit content. The law takes effect on June 1, 2027, according to one report, while another says January 2027.

The law defines a covered AI companion as a generative AI system with a neutral language interface, through writing or sound, that gives ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs. It lists 12 categories of unsafe features, which also include flattery or sycophancy, emotional appeals, and using information about a user's mental or physical health from an earlier session. Operators must use age assurance methods under Article 45, and self-declaration can only be relied on when a user says they are a minor. Operators must offer more than one method, including one that does not rely on government ID and lets the user stay anonymous, and collected age information must be deleted right after use. Some services are exempt, including certain internal and customer-service chatbots.

Enforcement rests with the New York Attorney General, who can seek an injunction, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties of up to twenty-five thousand dollars per violation, and who must keep a website for public complaints. Affected users can also bring private civil actions. Hochul wrote on social media that as a mother and grandmother she believes kids deserve to be kids, without dangerous AI chatbots putting their safety and mental health at risk, and said Big Tech was on notice. Her office cited Common Sense Media research that 72% of teenagers have used an AI companion and 52% use one regularly.

The law follows earlier state rules. Article 47, which took effect in November 2025, requires AI companions to tell users they are not human at the start of an interaction and at least every three hours, and to have protocols for signs of suicidal ideation or self-harm. Article 45, the SAFE for Kids Act, restricts algorithmically personalised feeds and nighttime notifications for users under 18 without parental consent. Reports linked the push to lawsuits, including a settlement by Google and Character.ai in January over the death of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer in 2024, and a suit by the family of 16-year-old Adam Raine against OpenAI in August 2025. With the signing, providers face a firm compliance date and the law moves from debate to implementation.

Articles.Title: How New York’s proposed law restricts AI chatbot interaction with children - The Indian Express

stories.Headline: NYC Local Law 144: AI Is No Defense, $1,500 Fines [2026]
stories.Summary:
New York City published a joint enforcement policy on artificial intelligence in late 2026, and the message is that software is no excuse for breaking the law. The policy came from three city agencies: the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, the Commission on Human Rights, and the Taxi and Limousine Commission. It builds on NYC Local Law 144 of 2021, which covers automated employment decision tools used to screen candidates or employees in the city. That law has been in force since January 1, 2023, and the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection began enforcing it on July 5, 2023. The new policy does not change the statute; it states that the city is willing to treat vendor software as the employer's own conduct.

Local Law 144 is a transparency and testing law and does not ban automated screening. Employers must complete a bias audit no more than one year before using a tool, post a summary of the most recent audit results and the tool's distribution date on their website before use, and tell New York City candidates and employees that a tool will be used and which qualifications or characteristics it will assess. That notice must come at least 10 business days before use. Candidates can request an alternative selection process or an accommodation, and employers must post the type and source of the data the tool uses along with the data-retention policy. The statute provides a civil penalty of up to $500 for a first violation and $500 to $1,500 for each subsequent violation, and the New York State Comptroller describes the enforcement power as penalties of $500 to $1,500 per day.

Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su said New Yorkers do not lose their rights when a decision is made or facilitated by technology, and that a company that breaks the law is responsible for what its technology does. The agencies' interagency enforcement letter states that an entity cannot avoid responsibility for violations because of reliance on an algorithm, AI, or other technology, and that legal responsibility exists regardless of whether a human being or a machine carried out the actions. In December 2025 the New York State Comptroller audited the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection's handling of the law and concluded that enforcement was weak, pointing to problems in complaint intake and compliance reviews. The department's on-record view, as described by the Comptroller, is that stakeholder education combined with complaint-based enforcement works best.

The city's position arrives alongside federal developments. In Mobley v. Workday, a federal court granted conditional certification on May 16, 2025, allowing a nationwide collective action under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act to proceed, and the court rejected the argument that the company was merely a software provider. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission filed an amicus brief supporting the theory that an AI vendor could be directly liable under Title VII, the ADA, or the ADEA. The commission removed its published AI-hiring guidance in January 2025 and voted 2-1 on June 4, 2026 to adopt a new National Enforcement Plan for fiscal years 2025 through 2029, which de-emphasizes disparate impact and does not name AI hiring as a standalone priority.

Articles.Title: NYC Local Law 144: AI Is No Defense, $1,500 Fines [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: Global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on innovative regulatory tools
stories.Summary:
The article, published by China Daily on November 3, 2026, argues that global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on new regulatory tools. It says human intelligence still exceeds machine intelligence, since the human brain is 10 to 100 times more complex than today's most advanced AI models. It adds that this gap is narrowing fast and that humanity may soon face a technological singularity, a point where AI surpasses human capabilities. The piece was presented as part of the discussion around the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai.

The article points to research on digitally reconstructed brains, including Google's digital fruit fly brain, which copies the exact neuronal wiring of a real fruit fly. In trials, these digital flies played gobang, simulated car driving, transcribed text such as "Hello, world" and even simulated slicing doner kebabs. The article also cites optogenetics, recognized by the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, which allows precise control of neural circuits such as those governing sleep and wake cycles. It says a neural circuit's function is plastic, defined and reshaped by its training and operational environment.

The article says responsibility for governing AI rests entirely with humanity, because all artificial systems are built, trained and nurtured by people. It cites OpenAI's release of AI-derived solutions to long-standing unsolved mathematical puzzles, but says these results were not autonomous. It notes that human-defined research priorities, investor funding and teams of mathematicians and computer scientists made them possible. It also invokes philosopher John Searle's Chinese Room Argument to show that AI systems lack full autonomy and cannot progress without human support.

The article says medical AI deployment must be bound by multi-layered guardrails, including ethics committee approval, regulatory authorization and patient consent. It adds that interdisciplinary collaboration among data scientists, clinicians, pharmacists and nursing staff is needed. It suggests traditional physical supervision can be modernized, just as physical fences are gradually replaced by GPS-powered virtual fences. It concludes that both the promises and perils of AI stem from human choices, and that multilateral cooperation on next-generation regulatory tools is urgently needed.

Articles.Title: Global AI governance requires multilateral cooperation on innovative regulatory tools - China Daily Global Edition

stories.Headline: Google’s New Rules Hand Schools Hard Choices About AI and Search - Education Week
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026, that it will turn off its Gemini chatbot and Google Search for K-12 student accounts unless a school district administrator chooses to turn on one or both. The change means traditional searches without AI summaries will not be an option for students. Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said during a November 2 virtual meeting that Search and AI are deeply integrated. Google said in its statement that it is updating Search for schools to make it better for learning. District administrators will get two levels of control, and settings can differ by grade.

A district could ban AI for one group, limit another to Guided Learning, and give older students the full search experience with AI summaries. Any group barred from AI would also lose Search. Phillips said the changes will start early next year. Guided Learning began rolling out in Google Classroom on November 3 for schools that already enabled Gemini. Google said its goal is to give school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products as they see fit, and that schools have told the company they want control.

Yvette Renteria, chief program officer at Common Sense Media, said getting rid of Google Search eliminates the chance to embrace critical thinking in the classroom. She said having Google Search without AI search is the best option, and that Google is not providing it. Sen. Richard Blumenthal said Google is once again prioritizing profits over people. Former FTC Chair Lina Khan wrote on X that Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. In August, Google opened a Gemini tab in Google Classroom for students of all ages in districts that already allowed its AI tools.

Since then, New York City banned student-facing AI through 8th grade, and Los Angeles Unified imposed a one-year moratorium on generative AI on its devices. Sens. Blumenthal and Josh Hawley gave Google until November 2 to answer nine questions, including why AI became the default on school devices. Google's statement did not mention the senators' letter or address the nine questions. Google said it will pilot the Guided Learning version of Search in select schools this month.

Articles.Title: Google’s New Rules Hand Schools Hard Choices About AI and Search - Education Week

stories.Headline: Foreign AI election interference claims under Online Safety Act probe, ministry tells Parliament
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's Communications Ministry told Parliament on November 4 that the government will use existing communications and cyber safety laws to counter an alleged foreign-linked artificial intelligence influence campaign targeting Malaysian voters. The ministry said this in a written parliamentary reply the day before to Pasir Mas MP Tuan Haji Ahmad Fadhli Shaari, who asked what steps the government would take to investigate foreign election meddling through generative AI platforms, including Claude. The ministry confirmed that the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission is treating the allegations seriously and has sought detailed technical clarification and supporting evidence from Anthropic, the US-based creator of Claude. The controversy began with a September threat intelligence report from Anthropic, which said a commercial actor had used Claude to develop core parts of a covert political influence campaign. Enforcement action will be pursued under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998, alongside the Online Safety Act 2025 and related statutes under the commission's purview.

The agency will coordinate with federal security bodies, criminal investigators, and social media platform providers where necessary. At the same time, the Digital Ministry is drafting a standalone AI Governance Bill to codify corporate accountability, risk mitigation requirements, and developer liabilities across the artificial intelligence life cycle. The reply gave no firm timeline for introducing the bill in Parliament. Anthropic attributed the activity to BBS Bilisim Teknolojileri, a technology firm based in Istanbul, saying the operation tried to build synthetic persona networks, automated bot accounts, and bespoke propaganda websites.

The operation reportedly harvested demographic census records and voter data to profile electorates across all 222 federal parliamentary constituencies. The Turkish company denied involvement on September 11, and Anthropic said it had shut down the offending accounts and that the campaign showed no evidence of gaining meaningful organic traction among genuine users. After the disclosures, Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said urged authorities to mount a comprehensive and independent investigation. The ministry did not disclose whether Anthropic has responded to the commission's queries, whether police have registered a formal criminal investigation, or how existing domestic statutes can effectively hold offshore technology operators and foreign-based software firms accountable beyond Malaysian borders.

Articles.Title: Foreign AI election interference claims under Online Safety Act probe, ministry tells Parliament - Yahoo

stories.Headline: Inaccurate information, algorithmic bias undermine justice - Kaduna Attorney-General warns young lawyers
stories.Summary:
James Atung Kanyip, the Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Kaduna State, spoke at the Votive Mass and Opening of the New Legal Year of the National Association of Catholic Lawyers, Catholic Diocese of Kaduna. The event was held at Holy Family Catholic Church in Barnawa, Kaduna, on a theme of AI and legal automation and the opportunities and risks they pose for Catholic lawyers. Kanyip, who is also a member of the association, encouraged lawyers to embrace artificial intelligence and legal automation to improve legal practice and access to justice. He made the call while also urging caution about the risks of the technology.

Kanyip said AI could help lawyers with legal research, document organisation, routine drafting and information management. He said this could reduce delays and costs and let practitioners spend more time on complex legal matters and their clients. He warned that inaccurate information, algorithmic bias and breaches of client confidentiality could undermine justice if the technology is used without proper safeguards. He stressed that lawyers must verify AI-generated information and remain professionally accountable for their work.

Kanyip further emphasised that technological advancement must uphold human dignity, fairness and the common good. He reaffirmed the Kaduna State Government's commitment to strengthening justice institutions and improving access to justice. The articles do not say what specific measures or rules, if any, will follow from his remarks. They also give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Inaccurate information, algorithmic bias undermine justice - Kaduna Attorney-General warns young lawyers - Daily Post Nigeria

stories.Headline: NJ's Proposed Liability for AI Chatbots May ‘Open the Floodgates,' Attorneys Say
stories.Summary:
New Jersey lawmakers advanced a bill in October that would let people sue the providers of artificial intelligence chatbots under the state's products liability law. The bill moved quickly through an assembly committee, according to a report by Nicholas Malfitano published by Law.com on November 2, 2026. The article says the proposal would make chatbots subject to products liability rules. Defense attorneys warned that the change could "open the floodgates" to claims.

The articles give few other details about what the bill requires or changes. They do not list a bill number, a vote count, or the names of the committee or its members. The only date given is the Law.com publication date of November 2, 2026, and the only time frame is that the bill advanced in October. The article also does not say when the full assembly might vote or what penalties the bill would set.

A plaintiff attorney described the bill as a key consumer protection measure, according to the article. Defense attorneys said it could "open the floodgates" to claims, the report states. The articles do not name any of the attorneys or say which firms or sides they represent. They also do not give any other statements from lawmakers or the bill's sponsors.

The context is that the bill is still legislation under consideration in Trenton, not law. A related Law.com article from October 30, 2026, by Michael J. Epstein, says the legislation would establish new liability rules for companies that develop and operate generative AI systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the committee's action. They do not report a scheduled vote, a fiscal analysis, or a position from the governor.

Articles.Title: NJ's Proposed Liability for AI Chatbots May ‘Open the Floodgates,' Attorneys Say - Law.com

stories.Headline: ROSS Intelligence asked US appeals court to revisit AI case over Westlaw
stories.Summary:
ROSS Intelligence asked a US appeals court on November 3, 2026, to rehear a copyright case that Thomson Reuters brought against it over Westlaw headnotes. ROSS argued that the panel asked the wrong question about its fair-use defense. It said AI models train on existing material, much of it copyrighted, to produce output that looks nothing like the training material, much as authors read books to develop their own style. It warned that if feeding copyrighted materials into training is infringement whether or not the outputs resemble the work, AI development will come to an abrupt halt.

The request asks the appeals court to revisit the panel's decision in the Thomson Reuters copyright case over Westlaw headnotes. ROSS frames its fair-use defense around how AI models learn from training material rather than reproduce it. The articles give no further dates, numbers or names beyond Thomson Reuters, Westlaw and ROSS Intelligence. The filing is dated November 3, 2026, at 20:51 GMT.

ROSS Intelligence is the party making the request, and it said the panel asked the wrong question on fair use. It compared AI training to authors reading books to develop their own writing style. It argued that AI models train on existing material, much of it copyrighted, to generate output that looks nothing like the training material. It said that treating such training as infringement would bring AI development to an abrupt halt.

The articles do not describe the wider context or say what happens next beyond the request for a rehearing. No ruling on the request is reported. The case concerns Thomson Reuters' copyright claims over Westlaw headnotes. The filing is listed as an official statement with a court document attached.

Articles.Title: ROSS Intelligence asked US appeals court to revisit AI case over Westlaw - MLex

stories.Headline: ‘This Is Evil’: Critics Hammer Google Plan to Shut Off Search Access for Schools That Reject Its AI
stories.Summary:
Google, owned by Alphabet, plans to cut off access to its search engine for US schools that fully disable its artificial intelligence tools, according to a New York Times report published on Tuesday. The change is set to begin early next year. Schools that ban the AI will lose Search as well, even though Search is the most widely used internet search tool in the world. Google has become deeply embedded in US classrooms, many of which use its Classroom platform and give students low-cost Chromebooks. Under the policy, schools that fully turn off Google's AI will also lose Search, and students there will see a message from their school saying it is not available.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, said Search and AI are deeply integrated. The Times reported that school leaders who want students to keep using Search within Google's system will have to accept the company's AI. Many US schools have been banning AI for young students over concerns that it harms critical thinking and enables cheating. Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission under President Joe Biden, accused Google of using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. She said the move shows the danger of letting an unregulated monopolist control an essential service, and she noted that multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose city banned AI in elementary and middle schools earlier this year, said no corporation should dictate how children are taught. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont called the threat extortion and tied it to President Donald Trump's claim that AI leaders could regulate themselves. Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus wrote, "This is evil," and author Kashana Cauley said schools should not be held hostage by district-wide Chromebook deals. Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, told the Times that the policy is a clear example of the tech industry forcing AI on people who have said they do not want it, and he expects it to fuel backlash against the industry. The article does not say what action, if any, regulators or lawmakers will take next.

Articles.Title: ‘This Is Evil’: Critics Hammer Google Plan to Shut Off Search Access for Schools That Reject Its AI - Common Dreams

stories.Headline: NJ lawmakers want safeguards for police use of AI, facial recognition software
stories.Summary:
Two bills in the New Jersey Legislature would require the attorney general’s office to study how police departments use facial recognition software and artificial intelligence and to recommend statewide policies for their use. The Assembly’s Public Safety and Preparedness Committee cleared both bills on Oct. 19. Democratic Assembly members Al Abdelaziz, Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Ellen Park sponsored the facial recognition bill, A-759. Assembly members Chris Tully, Annette Quijano and Balvir Singh introduced the artificial intelligence measure, A-3076.

A-759 would require the attorney general to report on what kinds of facial recognition technology are available to police and how accurate they are. A-3076 sets similar study requirements for artificial intelligence and also calls for a statewide policy requiring officers to review AI-generated police reports for accuracy and completeness. State Sen. Benjie Wimberly, a Passaic County Democrat, is expected to introduce identical bills in the upper chamber. California adopted a law, effective Jan. 1, 2026, requiring disclaimers on police reports created with AI help, officer certification that the reports were checked, retention of the first AI draft and an audit trail. Utah passed a law in 2025 requiring every agency to create an AI policy, add disclaimers and have officers certify their review.

Assemblyman Joe Danielson, a Somerset County Democrat who chairs the committee, said lawmakers need to explore how to help public safety departments use the tool while maintaining privacy, security and public trust. Singh, a Burlington County Democrat, said many departments in his district already use AI to write reports without statewide guidance, and that the technology can add details and change phrasing in ways that alter an officer’s account. Tully, a Bergen County Democrat, said AI tools are being marketed aggressively to police as time savers, and that there must always be a human in the loop. Wimberly said lawmakers should not wait for something to go wrong before establishing safeguards.

Jason Williams, a justice studies professor at Montclair State University, said facial recognition is not foolproof and false matches can send officers after innocent people. He said AI-generated reports can omit context, misstate sequences and make uncertain claims sound settled, and that officer review is necessary but may not be sufficient. He said he would rather see accountability measures, clear restrictions, independent audits, disclosure to defendants and community involvement than studies. The bills’ sponsors said the attorney general reports are a first step toward creating the right laws and regulations.

Articles.Title: NJ lawmakers want safeguards for police use of AI, facial recognition software - The Jersey Vindicator

stories.Headline: AI-related demand tests U.S. factories' paces
stories.Summary:
American factories kept expanding in October, according to two new manufacturing surveys, as surging demand for AI-related equipment strained supply chains and pushed prices up. The Institute for Supply Management's manufacturing index rose 1 point to 55.5 last month, the 10th straight month of expanding activity after a yearslong slump. Production accelerated at the fastest pace since November 2021. S&P Global's manufacturing gauge dipped slightly by 1 percentage point to 54.9, but the firm says the sector is on its best run since early 2022, and hiring accelerated to its fastest pace in more than five years.

Both surveys show strains from heavy demand for AI-related equipment, along with higher energy costs and war-related shipping disruptions. S&P Global said manufacturers' selling prices rose at the sharpest rate in four years. ISM's prices index slipped by 2.7 percentage points to 75.2% last month but still signaled widespread increases in raw material costs. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global, said in a release that demand often exceeds supply, so producers have been increasingly able to pass higher costs on to customers, notably for energy-related inputs.

One manufacturer told ISM that any commodity consumed by AI and data centers is in a crunch, both for supply and pricing. A machinery manufacturer described extraordinary demand for semiconductors and defense equipment, saying lead times and prices are increasing and some carry COVID-19 era delays, with four weeks now 50 weeks, and that the company is hand to mouth. A chemical products manufacturer said costs had risen more than 6% this year and that uncertain economic policy had made it impossible to make sound long-term decisions. The manufacturing resurgence is a bright spot for the U.S. economy, but surging AI-related demand is testing factories' ability to keep up as prices continue to surge.

Articles.Title: AI-related demand tests U.S. factories' paces

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a legal complaint on Wednesday alleging that an artificial intelligence company lets users create sexually explicit pictures and videos of minors, or “nudify” them. The suit was filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County against A2E, an AI image platform, and its owner, Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm. The 26-page suit claims the company’s practices are “unconscionable,” “deceptive,” and “unfair” under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Uthmeier said his office is also investigating possible criminal offenses.

The suit’s first allegation is that the product lets “predators” “nudify non-consenting Floridians,” including children, and lets users alter images of adults to look like children. The suit cites a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than 100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year-old stepson. The complaint says the software warns users that nonconsensual sexual use is “strictly prohibited” but that the defendant tries to shift all responsibility for compliance to users. Uthmeier also announced that the Office of Statewide Prosecution charged Jerry Jesus Reyes, a 26-year-old from Kissimmee, with 100 felony counts after a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children.

The counts include one allegation of transmission of child pornography, 86 allegations of unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual performance by a child, and 13 allegations of unlawful possession of materials depicting sexual activity with animals. Uthmeier said at a news conference in Orlando that creating the vehicle does not exempt a company from liability, and that the software is the “manufacturing hub” churning out the content. He said the state wants to make the company pay and shut it down. He called the Reyes case “disgusting, disturbing, depraved” and “inhumane.”

A2E did not respond to a request for comment from the Phoenix. Uthmeier says a 2025 Florida law requiring social media companies to delete deepfakes, or AI-generated sexual depictions of people made without consent, is in play in the case. He faces his first election in less than a week, after being appointed to his post last year by Governor Ron DeSantis. Since his August primary election, he has hosted 26 news conferences.

Articles.Title: Florida Attorney General: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids - Kiowa County Press

stories.Headline: AI company accused of generating child porn claims it’s been ‘cooperating with law enforcement’ in Florida
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against A2E, an AI software that generates images, accusing it of producing sexually explicit pictures of children in violation of state law. The suit was filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County. The defendant named in the case is Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm that owns A2E. Uthmeier announced the suit at a news conference in Orlando earlier this week. The 26-page suit alleges that A2E committed unconscionable, deceptive and unfair practices under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

The first allegation is that the product lets predators nudify non-consenting Floridians, including children, and allows users to alter images of adults to feature child-like appearances. The suit cites a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than 100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year-old stepson. In 2025, Florida lawmakers approved a measure requiring social media companies to delete deepfakes, which are AI-generated sexual depictions of people created without their consent. A2E said it learned about the news and is consulting with its legal team. The company said it has always treated child sexual abuse material very seriously since the very beginning.

It also said it has been cooperating with law enforcement to detect and prevent all kinds of CSAM, contrary to the attorney general's claim. Uthmeier said that creating the vehicle does not give exemption from liability, and that the software is the manufacturing hub churning out the child porn content. He said the state wants to make them pay and shut them down. Uthmeier's suit claims the Tampa predator was arrested thanks to the efforts of law enforcement and that the defendant never reported the abusive and criminal images. The articles do not say what happens next in the case beyond the filing and the company's statement that it is consulting its legal team.

Articles.Title: AI company accused of generating child porn claims it’s been ‘cooperating with law enforcement’ in Florida - Orlando Weekly

stories.Headline: Sources: the US DOJ has inquired about the impact of Nvidia's Hugging Face deal on AI competition, as antitrust enforcers continue to probe Nvidia's conduct (Reuters)
stories.Summary:
The two articles supplied give almost no detail about the inquiry itself, so this account is limited to what they show. According to a headline carried by Techmeme and credited to Reuters, sources say the US Department of Justice has asked about how Nvidia's deal with Hugging Face affects competition in artificial intelligence. The same headline says antitrust enforcers are still probing Nvidia's conduct more broadly. The Techmeme page is dated October 28, 2026, and the text of the Reuters report was not included.

Because the articles do not describe the deal or the questions put to anyone, there are no figures, dates or terms attached to the inquiry to report. The headline does not say what Nvidia agreed to with Hugging Face, how much was involved, or whether any approval or remedy is being sought. It also does not say which officials made the inquiry, when it began, or who was contacted. Nothing in the material indicates that the inquiry requires any change by either company at this stage.

On responsibility, the only attribution is to unnamed sources cited by Reuters, who say the Justice Department has been asking about the deal's competitive impact. Neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face is quoted in the supplied material, and the Justice Department's own position is not given. The Techmeme page is mostly a roundup of unrelated technology news, chiefly Apple's launch of a touchscreen MacBook Pro, so it adds nothing further on this story. The inquiry is described only as part of continuing scrutiny of Nvidia.

The second article offers some background on Hugging Face, though nothing about the inquiry. Cheddar published a video interview on October 26, 2026, in which Irene Solaiman, the company's Chief Policy Officer and SVP of Strategy, discusses open-source AI, model sharing, safety and the fight for transparency. Its headline describes Hugging Face as changing who gets to build artificial intelligence. Neither article says what happens next, so how the Justice Department's questions might develop, or whether they could lead to formal action, is not addressed in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Delaware DOJ launches probe of OpenAI following Hugging Face hack - Spotlight Delaware

stories.Headline: UAlbany researcher calls for transparency and digital literacy as AI spreads in politics - WRGB
stories.Summary:
A researcher at the University at Albany examined how voters react when they believe artificial intelligence is used in political campaign messages. Seulki Lee-Geiller, of the university's Center for Technology in Government, published the study on Sept. 24 in the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties. The study is titled "AI as a partisan cue: the relational dynamics of AI-assisted campaign messaging in election integrity perceptions." Lee-Geiller ran an online survey experiment with 3,055 U.S. participants in June and July 2024, ahead of that year's presidential election. Participants were randomly split into four groups and shown a hypothetical campaign letter from a presidential candidate.

The letter's content was the same for everyone, but the groups got different information about how it was made. One group saw no mention of AI, one was told AI helped draft the letter, and two others were told AI was used by either the participant's preferred party or the opposing party. Participants then rated election integrity measures such as fairness, authenticity, freedom from fraud and whether voters' interests were represented. Lee-Geiller said simply knowing AI was used did not significantly change views on fairness or authenticity, but people were more likely to think AI was being used to target messages to specific audiences. Bigger differences appeared when party affiliation was added.

On a five-point scale, the average authenticity rating was 3.71 when AI use was attributed to a participant's preferred party, compared with 3.37 when it was attributed to an opposing party. Lee-Geiller said transparency, consistent standards and digital literacy can help people make more informed judgments about AI-assisted messages, regardless of who is using the technology. The study is described as exploratory and focused on short-term reactions to hypothetical campaign materials rather than real-world election conditions. Lee-Geiller said additional research could look at how perceptions evolve with repeated exposure to AI-assisted messaging during actual campaigns.

Articles.Title: UAlbany researcher calls for transparency and digital literacy as AI spreads in politics - WRGB

stories.Headline: Meet NKY schools’ AI integration specialist. He’s the only one in the state.
stories.Summary:
Clint Litzinger became the AI integration specialist for the Northern Kentucky Cooperative for Educational Services, a role created about 18 months ago by 23 Northern Kentucky school districts. The cooperative includes all 13 districts in Boone, Kenton and Campbell counties and is one of Kentucky’s eight regional cooperatives. NKCES staff and its governing board of superintendents began discussing the position about two years ago, according to Chief Academic Officer Robb Smith. Litzinger spent a decade as a middle school science teacher before becoming a technology lead at Bracken County School District, one of the cooperative’s member districts. He began experimenting with AI using ChatGPT when it first came out in 2022.

The cooperative’s purpose is to support school districts by letting them share resources, training and purchasing power. Smith said it has become common for cooperatives or districts to hire instructional technology staff over the past decade, but NKCES wanted to take the next step. He said they wanted someone strong with instructional technology who was also a futurist and innovator. Executive Director Amy Razor said they were really looking for a unicorn, and then Litzinger’s application came across their desk. Litzinger said he applied because he had always been fascinated by technology.

Litzinger’s job is not to prescribe AI tools or their use in Northern Kentucky districts, but to explore those options alongside NKCES partners. He leads professional development workshops for educators and said he saw AI as the next revolution of education. Smith described a moment in society when everyone suddenly became interested in the possibilities of artificial intelligence and education. Razor said finding somebody who likes serving a region takes a special gift, because every district has a different need. Litzinger’s phone has rarely stopped ringing since he began the role.

Articles.Title: Meet NKY schools’ AI integration specialist. He’s the only one in the state.

stories.Headline: 'AI Made the Decision' Is Not a Defense: What NYC Employers Need to Know About the City’s AI Enforcement Position
stories.Summary:
New York City has said that employers remain responsible for following anti-discrimination and worker-protection laws when they use automated systems in employment decisions. The city's position was set out in a Law.com article by Keith Gutstein, published on November 2, 2026. The article says employers cannot avoid liability by claiming that an algorithm or AI system made the decision. It reports that the city has reaffirmed this enforcement stance as artificial intelligence becomes more common in employment decisions.

The article says employers are still liable for unlawful results even when an automated system contributes to them. It says audits and human review can help but do not replace legal compliance. The piece is described as an 8 minute read and was published at 7:00 AM. It frames the issue as a basic question of who bears legal responsibility when an algorithm contributes to an unlawful result.

The article attributes the position to New York City rather than to a named official, and it does not name any individual who made a statement. It says the city has reaffirmed that employers remain responsible for complying with applicable laws. The article presents audits and human review as helpful measures, not as substitutes for meeting legal duties. It does not give any further details of what employers are required to do.

The article does not say what happens next or describe any specific enforcement action, penalty or deadline. It does not give any dates for future steps or name any agency involved. It does not say whether guidance or rules will follow. The article does not provide any further context beyond the city's stated position.

Articles.Title: 'AI Made the Decision' Is Not a Defense: What NYC Employers Need to Know About the City’s AI Enforcement Position - Law.com

stories.Headline: Highland Park reups contract with location-data platform Placer.ai
stories.Summary:
The City of Highland Park approved a contract renewal with the data analytics company Placer.ai on Oct. 26. The City Council voted to extend a partnership that began in 2023. The new agreement runs from Dec. 1 through Nov. 30, 2029, a three-year term. The previous three-year contract was $72,000 annually, and the new agreement is $82,145.

Placer.ai is a proprietary market and location intelligence platform. The City says the service has helped with marketing campaigns, business and economic development, event planning and attracting new developments. The platform identifies locations of new businesses, tracks foot traffic in the business district and recognizes how streets and other safeties are used. Its data is reportedly stripped of identifying information, and the insights the service offers remain the same under the new deal.

City Communications Manager Amanda Bennett said the City has seen many positive applications from the insights gained from the data. She cited the benefits of data visualizations and analytics available for both City applications and local businesses. Bennett called the unique reports a high value component for businesses and said the platform gives the City accurate comparative statistics it could not get elsewhere. She said the City trusts Placer.ai more than generative AI because it analyzes analytical data, and a City staff member helps interpret reports for business owners.

The City relied on Placer.ai event data to inform its marketing campaign with iHeartMedia and to optimize marketing by converting engagement rates into visits. Local businesses can request unique reports and business district level analysis from the City's Office of Business Development. Before 2023, the City reportedly relied on rough head counts to measure event attendance. The City has measured the platform's success through real world applications, feedback from staff and the public, and regular evaluation of its software subscriptions.

Articles.Title: Highland Park reups contract with location-data platform Placer.ai

stories.Headline: AI agents surge on protected transactions, Arkose says
stories.Summary:
Arkose Labs published its Q3 2026 State of Agentic AI Trust Report on 3 November 2026, finding that personal AI agents are increasingly carrying out online transactions for consumers. The report is based on production data gathered between July and September. It found that 97.7% of legitimate AI agent sessions included no verified identity disclosure. More than 65% of Arkose Labs customers encountered AI agents on protected transactions such as logins, registrations and checkouts, across banking, gaming, technology and travel sites.

Sessions from Meta's Muse, described as a personal AI agent built for consumer use, rose more than 30-fold in September, while other agents remained broadly flat. Arkose Labs classified 77.4% of AI agent sessions as legitimate, compared with 7.9% of known bot sessions. It also found that 70.5% of registration sessions were identified as fake-account attempts. The report groups agents into three categories: self-disclosing good agents, non-disclosing good agents and malicious agents, and it describes Muse as a non-disclosing good agent because it appears on networks as a Chrome browser.

Kevin Gosschalk, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Arkose Labs, said the findings reflected a wider concern among security leaders. He recalled that at a recent banking industry summit, the CISO of one of the world's largest banks said a technology had arrived ahead of the controls for the first time in his career. Gosschalk said the report makes clear how difficult it has become for companies to distinguish legitimate, revenue-driving agents from malicious ones. Mitchell Davies, Lead Researcher in the Arkose Cyber Threat Intelligence Research team, said the presence of automation alone is no longer the deciding factor, and that the real question is what the agent came to do and what its intent is.

The report says businesses face a new problem as consumer-facing AI agents become more common in routine digital activity, and the challenge is no longer only identifying automation but deciding whether an automated session reflects a legitimate customer action or a malicious attempt at fraud. It notes that the automated flows used by AI agents overlap with those commonly targeted by attackers. Arkose Labs said Instinct was designed in a way that made 96.8% of its sessions appear medium or high risk, yet neither Instinct nor Muse had a single session linked to an attack. Davies said each company must decide how to handle agents accordingly, taking its industry and risk posture into consideration, and that a bank will have different controls in place than a retailer.

Articles.Title: AI agents surge on protected transactions, Arkose says - TechDay US

stories.Headline: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers led by Lu Wang has published a paper introducing AskStream, a benchmark for streaming video understanding. The work has ten other authors, including Zhuoran Jin, Longxiang Wang, Junhong Chen, Yupu Hao, Yao Xu, Daojian Zeng, Yubo Chen, Kang Liu, Guang Liu and Jun Zhao. The paper was posted on arXiv on 3 November 2026 and runs to 42 pages with 9 figures. It falls under computer vision and pattern recognition and also computation and language. The paper argues that proactive models should have a third action beyond waiting or answering, namely asking for missing information.

AskStream is described as the first multi-turn benchmark spanning uncertainty from both the video and the user. It has four task categories and eight subtasks, with 438 videos and 2,714 manually annotated frame-level time windows across three types: wait, ask and answer. Even the strongest model reaches only 52.18% on the proposed Ask-F1 metric in both multiple-choice and open-ended settings. The authors say existing proactive paradigms assume the information needed to answer a query is complete, so models can only wait or answer. They note that in the real world information is often incomplete because of uncertainty from the video or the user.

They argue this uncertainty can make a model wait forever or produce highly hallucinatory responses. They therefore propose redefining proactive interaction to include asking, so models can actively seek the missing information before answering. The paper states that the results highlight substantial limitations in proactive information seeking under uncertainty. It provides links to a project page, code and the dataset. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the release of these resources.

Articles.Title: AskStream: When and What to Ask Proactively under Uncertainty in Streaming Video Understanding

stories.Headline: Culver City's AI boom attracting Silicon Valley firms and making 2-year-old restaurant Hollywood's latest power lunch spot
stories.Summary:
Over the past year, more than a half-dozen AI startups have moved into Culver City, a 1.2-square-mile city, as part of tech's push into the entertainment industry. Sean Parker, a co-founder of Napster and former Facebook president, opened an office in the Hayden Tract last month as part of the expansion of his San Francisco-based Cantina Labs, which he founded in 2023. Parker also took part in an $80 million rescue of the AI image firm Stability AI. Luma Labs, a $4 billion Palo Alto-based startup co-founded by Amit Jain, opened a 7,000-square-foot facility called the Dream Lab in Culver City last year. Other AI startups that set up shop in Culver City this year include TrueShort, PhantomX and Native Foreign.

The Laurel Grill, which opened two years ago, has become the de facto power lunch spot for the area's studio and AI executives. It sits atop the Culver Steps, overlooking the Culver Studios and the Culver Hotel, and was opened by Dean McKillen and Phil Howard, the owners of Laurel Hardware and Ysabel. A bartender at the spot said it is frequently packed with Amazon, Apple and Sony execs. George Strompolos, who set up his startup Promise AI in a building in the shadow of the Sony water tower, said every time he meets with an Amazon exec it is at the Laurel Grill. Council member and former mayor Dan O'Brien likened the place to Culver City's version of The Ivy.

Strompolos launched Promise AI alongside former YouTube exec Jamie Byrne and filmmaker Dave Clark, with backing from Peter Chernin's North Road and Andreessen Horowitz. He previously ran the digital media and entertainment company Fullscreen from offices in Culver Studios but sold that company to AT&T's Otter Media. O'Brien said the commercial real estate market "bottomed out last year" and that the city has been telling the AI crowd they are welcome. However, another city insider said the feeling is not totally unanimous among council members, who are balancing a welcome for the AI crowd with sensitivity to a creative community that is wary of the technology.

Most people credit Mike Gioia and Todd Terrazas, who founded the four-year-old conference AI on the Lot, for spearheading the AI push into Culver City. The conference has taken over Amazon MGM's Culver Studios for the past two years, and the company also has its own office space between the studio gate and the Culver Theater, which Amazon took over in 2022. Last month during LA Tech Week, the group held an AI job fair on the Culver Steps and routinely offers its office space to AI filmmakers. Earlier this year, the Thunderbird School of Global Management at Arizona State University held its LA chapter meetup at Laurel Grill.

Articles.Title: Culver City's AI boom attracting Silicon Valley firms and making 2-year-old restaurant Hollywood's latest power lunch spot - Page Six

stories.Headline: China Regulator Warns AI Investment Boom Crowds Out Traditional Industries
stories.Summary:
Xiao Yuanqi, a vice minister of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, warned on Tuesday that excessive global investment in AI is crowding traditional industries out of financing and driving up their borrowing costs. He made the remarks at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Hong Kong on Nov. 3. He said massive capital inflows into technology companies are pushing up leverage levels and could fuel excessive expansion. The article also cites estimates that AI adds 0.5 to 1 percentage point to US growth and 0.1 to 0.3 percentage points to Europe's.

The warning concerns the effect of heavy AI investment on borrowing costs and credit risks for traditional industries. The article says past tech bubbles have not always caused downturns, because productivity gains often support long-term growth. It gives no further details on any specific measures or policy changes. The figures it provides are the estimated growth contributions for the US and Europe.

Xiao is responsible for raising the issue, in his role as a vice minister of the National Financial Regulatory Administration. According to the article, he warned that the capital flowing into tech companies is raising leverage and could lead to excessive expansion. The article does not say what he proposed as a response. It also does not give further comments from him beyond these points.

The context is a global boom in AI investment and concern about its side effects for other sectors. The article notes that past tech bubbles have not always ended in downturns, since productivity gains can support growth over time. It does not say what happens next or what steps, if any, the regulator will take. It also does not give a timeline for any action.

Articles.Title: China Regulator Warns AI Investment Boom Crowds Out Traditional Industries - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: Bills could control how ‘surveillance pricing’ impacts what you pay for products
stories.Summary:
Michigan lawmakers have introduced bills to restrict surveillance pricing, the practice of companies using consumers' personal data to set individual prices. The legislation is led by Reps. Steve Frisbie, R-Battle Creek, and Rylee Linting, R-Grosse Ile, and was introduced earlier this year. The bills passed the House and are now pending in the Senate Economic and Community Development Committee. The practice draws on data such as online browsing history, location and shopping patterns to set prices for individual customers.

The Federal Trade Commission has also looked into the practice. In a January 2025 report, the agency said third-party pricing services can use consumers' location, demographics, browsing habits and shopping history to tailor prices and promotions. The FTC said the findings raised questions about how companies use personal data to determine what consumers pay and called for further investigation. In August, the agency sought public comment on a proposed enforcement policy statement saying undisclosed uses of personal data to set prices could violate federal law against unfair or deceptive practices.

Kyle Zawacki, legislative director of the ACLU of Michigan, said surveillance pricing is when tracking cookies and information collected by websites and social media are used to charge people more because they need something. He said the worry is that consumers may not know how their information is used or whether it affects the prices they pay. He said it is a problem if people are charged more because of who they are, the color of their skin or their zip code. The ACLU has been advocating for a legislative solution and argues the issue is not how companies gather information but how they use it to manipulate consumers' economic choices.

The Michigan Retailers Association has warned Congress not to lump together all variable pricing. The association contends that proposed limitations should clearly differentiate surveillance pricing from other methods, including discounts, seasonal sales and price changes based on supply, demand or inventory. It has urged policymakers to consider how proposed restrictions could affect retailers. The state Attorney General's Office administers Michigan's Consumer Protection Act, which bans unfair or deceptive business practices and lets the attorney general investigate and file lawsuits.

Articles.Title: Bills could control how ‘surveillance pricing’ impacts what you pay for products - The Manchester Mirror

stories.Headline: AI Cloud Stocks Fall as Big Tech Capex Comes in Light: Fastly Sinks 6%, Oracle and Nebius Drop 3%
stories.Summary:
On October 28, Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases for its first quarter of fiscal 2027, below the Wall Street consensus of $50.7 billion and short of its own $50 billion target. Alphabet reported $51.36 billion in capital expenditures against a consensus of $55.09 billion. The next day, AI cloud stocks fell, with Fastly down 6% at $25.43, while Oracle at $140.57 and Nebius at $177.56 each dropped 3%. Alphabet stock fell 11% to $287.67, and Microsoft slipped 1% to $523.30.

Microsoft chief financial officer Amy Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries expected in the quarter were delayed. She said she expects capital spending of more than $50 billion next quarter and about $170 billion for the calendar year, and she maintained that customer demand continues to exceed available supply. On October 28, Oracle stock had rallied 11% to close at $144.54 after its investor day, where it forecast $30 billion in free cash flow by fiscal 2029. Oracle capped new financing through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, split evenly between equity and debt, and reaffirmed a $225 billion revenue target for fiscal 2030 along with $664 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Those Oracle targets followed negative free cash flow of $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, and the funding cap helped ease debt concerns. Fastly is up 150% this year after six straight quarters of earnings beats, and on August 5 it lifted its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $732 million to $746 million. Nebius is up 112% this year, and three customers made up 24%, 21% and 14% of its revenue in the second quarter of 2026. CoreWeave stock was at $64, up 0.1% and essentially flat, and it is down 11% year to date.

The next test for Microsoft is whether its delayed third-party capacity arrives in the second half of its fiscal year, as Hood expects. A smooth transition could restart the revenue ramp for Nebius and CoreWeave, while another slip could stretch their revenue schedules further. Upcoming spending updates from other cloud giants could either confirm that worry or ease it. For Oracle, the open question is whether it stays within its new funding cap while it keeps building data centers, and Fastly's growth rests more on AI traffic and security demand than on hyperscaler budgets.

stories.Headline: UBS says AI investment boom remains intact despite growing scrutiny of spending
stories.Summary:
UBS published a report on Monday, November 2, 2026, saying the AI investment boom remains intact despite growing investor concerns about infrastructure costs, financing risks and whether technology companies can turn spending into profits. The Swiss bank said strong third-quarter results had reinforced confidence in demand for AI infrastructure. It raised its estimates for global AI capital expenditure to $1 trillion in 2026 and $1.4 trillion in 2027, and added a forecast of $1.5 trillion for 2028. UBS pointed to accelerating cloud growth at Alphabet, Microsoft and Oracle, with cloud revenue growth of 103%, 48% and 62% respectively in their latest reported quarters.

The report said higher investment has unsettled markets, with Alphabet and Meta shares falling sharply after investors focused on rising capital expenditure and negative free cash flow. UBS warned that financing pressures among specialist cloud infrastructure providers, known as neoclouds, could lead to project delays, repricing and industry consolidation, though it expects limited disruption because these companies account for only about 8% of its capital expenditure estimate. It also cited risks from AI replacing existing revenue streams, pointing to slower search revenue growth at Alphabet as its AI Mode currently generates less revenue. For investors in the US and UK, UBS said the AI theme remained attractive but recommended greater selectivity, diversification across the AI value chain and exposure to financially strong companies with pricing power and reasonable valuations. It favours foundries, computing and power infrastructure, and also recommends diversifying into industrials, healthcare and financials.

TechCrunch reported on October 30, 2026, that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft had outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion, and it expects to spend up to $205 billion this year. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months and expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter and is guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. Microsoft recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected, which it blamed on delays in capacity from third-party providers.

According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. TechCrunch said the anxiety spilled across the market on Friday, with the Nasdaq falling 2.9% and chip stocks also dropping. It said the muddied waters could complicate Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO, after the AI company filed to go public earlier that week, and that the Financial Times reported Blackstone had warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO. UBS expects greater volatility as investors shift their focus from AI spending commitments towards monetisation and returns.
