stories.Headline: Alphabet Stock Rises as Google Seeks Fresh Billions for AI Investments
stories.Summary:
Alphabet shares rose 1.5% on Monday morning, November 2, 2026, as the Google parent opened a seven-tranche euro bond offering, according to GuruFocus. The sale is the company's second euro-denominated debt issuance this year. The offering covers maturities ranging from two to 19 years. Initial pricing guidance for the shortest fixed-rate notes was about 60 basis points above mid-swaps, while the longest-dated bonds carried a spread of roughly 205 to 210 basis points.

The structure gives Alphabet access to investors with different maturity preferences and spreads its borrowing across several periods. Mid-swaps serve as a benchmark for pricing euro-denominated bonds, and the spread is the extra yield above that benchmark, which helps set the issuer's borrowing cost. Final pricing may differ from the initial guidance. The article does not say how much money Alphabet aims to raise.

The move follows a sharp sell-off after Alphabet's quarterly results. On Thursday, October 29, 2026, the shares fell 12.64% on the Nasdaq to close at $283.82, wiping out about $482 billion in market value, the worst one-day fall since the company began trading in 2004, The Hindu reported. In Friday pre-market trading the stock slipped a further 0.42% to $282.64. Revenue grew 25% year on year to $127.6 billion in the quarter ended September 30, while net profit fell to $26.5 billion from $35 billion a year earlier, largely due to losses on equity investments.

Capital expenditure was $51.4 billion in the September quarter, mostly on data centres, servers and networking equipment, against $42.3 billion in cash from operations, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi said infrastructure spending was a major reason, along with inventory for Google's Tensor Processing Units and a $5.2-billion payment tied to a European Commission fine. Alphabet kept its 2026 capital expenditure guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending would rise significantly in 2027. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said growing queries through AI Mode were affecting advertising revenue because Google earns less from them than from traditional Search, and chief executive Sundar Pichai said query growth was the highest in five years.

stories.Headline: Larridin Raises $30 Million in Series A to Prove AI’s Impact Across the Human and Agent Workforce
stories.Summary:
Larridin, Inc., an AI value measurement platform based in South San Francisco, announced on November 2, 2026 that it raised $30 million in Series A funding. Pelion Ventures led the round, with existing investors Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures taking part. New investors included GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Alumni Ventures and Cougar Capital. The financing brought Larridin's total funding to $47 million.

The company said it has measured more than 2 billion AI sessions and tracked more than 82,000 workflows end to end. Across its customers, Larridin reports a 47% average increase in measurable team output and a median $2.4 million in AI spend optimized within the first year. Larridin said it will use the funding to speed up product development and expand its teams. It also announced a quarterly Engineering AI Impact Report, drawing on data from more than 1,000 engineers.

Russ Fradin, the CEO of Larridin, said enterprise AI has moved from an innovation budget to financial accountability. He said the investors share the company's conviction that firms must prove tangible business value from rising AI spend. Jeff Kearl, a General Partner at Pelion Ventures, said Larridin gives leaders transparency into AI and ties each dollar spent to measurable outcomes. Alex Rampell, a General Partner at a16z, said the company's growth and customer partnerships show it has built an indispensable platform.

Larridin's customer data shows why traditional adoption metrics fall short, according to the company. At one customer, 92% of engineers were active AI users, yet a single engineer accounted for roughly 65% of the team's AI spend in one week. At another, Larridin found a 66x difference in cost per shipped engineering change between two comparable AI tools. The report also found that AI-assisted pull requests rose from 35% in April to 62% in September, while median wait times for initial human code reviews grew by 50% over the same period.

stories.Headline: South Korea to double spending on AI and chips in 2027 - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said in his annual budget speech to parliament on Monday, November 2, 2026, that the country will double spending on AI and semiconductors in 2027 to a record high. He told lawmakers that 21.3 trillion won, about US$16 billion, would go to chipmaking and artificial intelligence, covering areas from data centres to robotics. He said the figure was nearly double this year's amount and that the government would make bold investments in AI and future growth engines to boost the economy's growth potential. He also pledged to use the technology to turn the military into what he called a smart, elite force.

The 2027 budget plan totals 821 trillion won, a 12.8 percent increase on-year and the largest budget proposal on record. The defence budget would rise around eight percent from this year to 73.3 trillion won, with the aim of securing nuclear-powered submarines and KF-21 fighter jets. Lee said Seoul aims to rapidly transform the military into a smart, elite force through integrated manned and unmanned systems based on AI, robots and drones. The government will also invest 4.7 trillion won in frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for the country's own AI model, which he called a national strategic asset, and 2.1 trillion won in electricity, water supply and industrial complex infrastructure.

Lee is the one responsible for the plan, and he now needs parliament to pass the budget proposal, which the articles say is likely given his party's majority. In June, Lee announced a public-private partnership centred on three mega-projects, aiming to expand chip production hubs nationwide, establish robotics research and development centres, and build gigawatt-scale AI data centres. The government at the time unveiled plans for nearly $1.2 trillion in investment, equivalent to more than two-thirds of South Korea's GDP, and Samsung and SK hynix also announced plans in June to invest more than 4,755 trillion won in the country, a record level of corporate investment. In September, Seoul announced plans for a 162.3 trillion won Future Fund next year, aimed at channelling record tax revenues from the chip boom into long-term growth.

The context is that South Korea is a tech powerhouse, home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, two of the world's three biggest makers of memory chips, which are in huge demand thanks to the AI boom. South Korean chipmakers have seen profits and share prices skyrocket as frenzied demand for AI infrastructure squeezes the global supply of memory chips, and the boom has spurred chip engineers and other workers to seek higher payouts in tense negotiations at companies including Samsung and SK hynix. North Korea has recently tested a slew of weapons, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which it said used AI technology. Last year, Seoul announced an agreement with Washington to build nuclear-powered submarines, with Pyongyang slamming the submarine programme as a dangerous attempt at confrontation.

stories.Headline: AI Glasses Can Replace Your Prescription Glasses, But Should They?
stories.Summary:
AI smart glasses can now be fitted with prescription lenses, and Ray-Ban lets customers order Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed by uploading a prescription. The lenses are possible because most AI glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra technology built in, and from a distance a pair of Ray-Ban Meta looks like any other glasses. The articles say the prescription itself is not the hard part of the decision. Instead, buyers are told to weigh weight, battery life and privacy before swapping their everyday glasses for AI eyewear. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams, while smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams, which is fine for a few hours but becomes a burden over a full day.

AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies, so all-day wear requires constant recharging, and once the battery drains the glasses work only as regular glasses with no AI features. The Courts of England and Wales have banned Meta glasses from courtrooms, and New York followed suit in July. Many schools around the world have also banned students from wearing AI glasses during class, and many companies have barred them from their premises. Meta has been facing scrutiny after outsourced workers were able to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses, and the company says content is sometimes reviewed by humans to improve the product experience. The articles also note that even with the camera off, audio features can be a problem, since a real-time translation feature could upload confidential conversations to a third-party server.

A German nonprofit has filed a criminal complaint over Meta smart glasses privacy. Some users have stopped wearing AI glasses in public because of the backlash, fearing they could be labeled stalkers or weirdos. Taken together, the technical limitations make AI glasses more of a second option than a replacement for everyday glasses, and privacy is described as the real deal-breaker. The articles say buying AI glasses with prescription lenses is entirely possible, but clear limits remain before they can fully replace everyday eyeglasses. For the market to grow in earnest, the industry still faces the task of making hardware lighter, improving power efficiency and securing trust in how captured photo and audio data is handled.

stories.Headline: Maryland Election Officials Reporting Few AI Deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Maryland election officials have received five complaints under a new state law targeting AI-generated election disinformation, and they found only one violation, a campaign advertisement that gave voters the wrong Election Day date. The law was enacted in June. The State Board of Elections reviews complaints and works with the attorney general's office to seek removal of inaccurate information and issue corrections, according to board spokesperson Lexy Rhoden. She said the board's authority is limited to false information about the time, place or manner of an election, its results or voting rights, and complaints outside that scope go to the state prosecutor's office. The state prosecutor's office declined to comment on ongoing investigations or describe its review process, citing office policy.

Violations of the law can carry penalties of up to five years in prison or a $5,000 fine. Donald Tobin, an election law professor at the University of Maryland's Carey School of Law, said the law requires a deepfake to be created with intent to harm someone, and he expects legal challenges to test how courts apply that requirement. He said lawmakers had to balance regulating harmful uses of AI with constitutional protections for political speech. Candace Turitto, director of the University of Maryland's Applied Political Analytics Program, said the penalties might not discourage some campaigns, since a campaign could benefit from media coverage or from persuading voters who do not know the information is false. She described a candidate deciding the benefit outweighs a $5,000 fine and possible legal action that might not come until after an election.

In one incident, former Republican gubernatorial candidate Ed Hale posted an AI-generated photo depicting his then-primary opponent, Dan Cox, embracing Gov. Wes Moore, and a spokesperson for Moore said the post was reported to the State Board of Elections. Moore's lawyers also reported an advertisement that they alleged used his likeness to falsely suggest he opposes November's redistricting ballot measure, and the board has not answered repeated questions about the status of that complaint. In Anne Arundel County, Chick and Ruth's Delly, a restaurant owned by District 7 Democratic candidate Spencer Jones, posted an AI-altered version of the Capital Gazette's front page that called Jones the incumbent and included a line the newspaper's story did not contain. Jones said an ad agency that manages the restaurant's social media ran a photo of the real front page through AI to improve its clarity, and the AI hallucinated the additions. He apologized, removed the post and issued a corrected version the next day.

Of the nine local election directors The Baltimore Sun contacted, four responded, and none said they had reported an instance of AI-generated election disinformation this election season. Gary Holmes, Cecil County's election director, said he has seen AI-generated social media content promoting campaigns but nothing he considered election disinformation that warranted reporting. Ruie Marie Lavoie, Baltimore County's election director, said she was surprised her office had not encountered such disinformation, though it has dealt with other false claims on social media, including one saying voters had to pay postage to return mail-in ballots. Erin Perrone, Carroll County's election director, urged voters to get information about election dates, polling places and voting hours directly from local election offices. Caroline County Election Director Allison Murphy said voters can report suspected election misinformation to the State Board of Elections, whose website includes a form for reporting suspected false information about elections, results and voting rights, whether or not it was created with AI.

stories.Headline: Palantir's U.S. Revenue Soars 119% as Commercial Revenue Surpasses Government Revenue for the First Time. Here's Why Its Growth Is Still Surging, Even as Other AI Stocks Falter
stories.Summary:
Palantir Technologies reported third-quarter results on Nov. 2, 2026, that beat Wall Street's expectations. Revenue of $2.3 billion rose 96% year over year, the company's highest-ever growth rate, and climbed 20% quarter over quarter. Earnings per share of $0.44 surged 144%, while analysts had expected revenue of $2.2 billion and EPS of $0.41. The U.S. commercial segment, which includes the Artificial Intelligence Platform, led the way.

U.S. commercial revenue rose 148% year over year and 29% quarter over quarter to $984 million, passing U.S. government revenue for the first time. U.S. government revenue grew 96% year over year and 18% sequentially to $953 million. Total contract value closed in the quarter was $2.92 billion, up 6% year over year, and the U.S. commercial segment closed $1.46 billion of that, up 11%. Net dollar retention was 165%, meaning existing customers spent 65% more than a year earlier.

CEO Alex Karp argues that businesses should not casually hand their data to others, particularly those selling AI solutions. He says doing so gives away proprietary knowledge, workflows and strategic advantage, which he calls a business's alpha. Palantir uses boot camps to show businesses how to get real-world AI results and a solid return on investment, and customers keep coming back once they see the evidence. The article says this is why Palantir's growth continues even as AI rivals stumble.

U.S. commercial remaining deal value rose 79% year over year and 4% quarter over quarter to $6.52 billion. The company's Rule of 40 score rose to 158%, and operating cash flow and adjusted free cash flow were $1.2 billion each, at roughly a 53% margin. Cash and equivalents totaled $10.56 billion, and management raised full-year revenue guidance to roughly 91% growth from 82%. The article notes Palantir trades at 125 times earnings and says the stock won't suit every investor.

stories.Headline: Meta’s AI grab meets resistance, presenting an opportunity for news media publishers,264280
stories.Summary:
Meta updated its terms to let web scrapers and bots crawl any domain associated with Facebook and Instagram business accounts and feed that content into its products, including its AI systems. The terms have no opt-out and reach reporting on a publisher's own servers, not just content uploaded or shared on Meta's platforms. Under pressure, Meta removed the word "train" from its Oct. 16 revision but left "develop" in place. Attorney Matt Topic told Nieman Lab that "develop" is broad enough to include "train."

Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Tennessee Republican who chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology and the Law, said the update could harm businesses and creators who depend on Meta's platforms, and she argued the terms give Meta sweeping authority to scrape content. California Democrat Adam Schiff wrote to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg insisting the company withdraw the terms as written. The Norwegian Media Businesses' Association, a coalition of major Norwegian publishers including public broadcaster NRK, filed the first lawsuit against Meta over the terms, and a Norwegian court blocked them from taking effect on Nov. 20 until it could assess their legality. Lene Eltvik Vindfeld, the association's board chair, said the court agreed Meta holds a dominant position in the relevant market and that the new terms are unreasonable. The European Publishers Council signed a joint letter to the European Commission arguing the terms violate the Digital Markets Act, and EPC director Angela Mills Wade said publishers must retain control over additional uses of their content, including for AI, and the ability to negotiate licenses and payment.

Meta moved implementation from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20 to consult with publishers and advertisers. Meta vice president of communications Andy Stone said the company is committed to getting this right, that it would not make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders, and that it could delay implementation beyond Nov. 20 if needed. Meta insists the update applies only to its ads and business products and that it is not changing how it uses web crawlers. After Stone's tweet on Oct. 28, Blackburn pushed back, saying a vague promise to consult is not nearly enough and that Meta must commit to meaningful changes protecting the intellectual property rights of American creators.

Until then, the existing terms remain in place. The article says robots.txt files carry no legal weight, and that tools at the CDN level verify which crawler is hitting a site and block ones a publisher does not approve, though a block can sit in a contested legal zone, so counsel should review an access policy first. It says Google already pays roughly 100 publishers for AI-sourced answers, and that publishers should treat machine access as a priced product through licensing agreements and metered access for unlicensed bot crawlers. It adds that with a Norwegian court freezing the rollout, European publishers pressing for binding safeguards and two U.S. senators demanding the terms be withdrawn, publishers should use the extra time from the delays.

stories.Headline: AI is disrupting the art of campaigning
stories.Summary:
At least 220 campaign ads in the current US election cycle have used AI-generated content, according to the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising. More than $137m has been spent airing these ads. Two examples involve James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan. One ad shows Talarico wearing a dress and singing about transgender children, while another shows El-Sayed laughing at cards reading “Death to America” and “Celebrate 9/11”.

A recent survey by the American Association of Political Consultants found that 83% of campaign strategists and political consultants regularly use AI for their work. El-Sayed paid $170,000 to Daisychain, a company offering an AI-powered platform that holds personalised conversations with voters over text messages. The progressive group Swing Left has volunteers record voice memos of conversations with voters, and AI software analyses hundreds of these recordings to help campaigns tailor their messages. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful Democratic House candidate in California, had three staffers use AI to code replacements for virtually all the campaign’s paid software.

Yasmin Radjy, Swing Left’s executive director, said AI gives campaigns a much better ability to understand the idiosyncrasies of a voter. Eric Wilson of the Centre for Campaign Innovation argued that the core of a campaign, connecting with voters, is still a people business, and that AI lets campaigns do more of that than the boring, busy work. He also said concerns about AI attack ads are overblown, likening them to political parody. The AAPC found that at least 38% of voters had received election information from an AI search summary.

A study by the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, a think-tank in London, found that leading chatbots gave wrong, incomplete or outdated answers to over a quarter of basic questions about the midterms. VisionHeight, a cyber-security firm, recently uncovered dozens of apparently AI-generated websites masquerading as local newspapers, designed to trick chatbots into pumping out favourable coverage of certain congressional candidates. A Russian disinformation network is thought to be behind videos in which a supposed former student falsely accuses Talarico of sex crimes. Of the $137m spent on AI ads, 88% has come from Republican campaigns and aligned groups.

stories.Headline: Study reveals widespread abuse involving non-consensual AI-generated intimate images.aspx
stories.Summary:
A study published in the International Journal of Human, Computer Interaction found that about one in 15 adults has experienced AI-generated image-based abuse. The survey covered more than 7,200 adults in the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia. It found that 7% had experienced at least one form of this abuse since turning 18, including having an intimate image of themselves created or altered with AI without consent, having such an image shared without consent, or being threatened with its sharing. Almost 87% of victim-survivors reported at least one impact on their lives, including effects on health and wellbeing, relationships, work or finances.

Lead author Professor Nicola Henry from RMIT University conducted the research with support from Google. She said the findings show how widely this abuse affects people across the community, not just celebrities and public figures, and that the true scale may be greater because some people never learn that images of them were created or shared. Higher rates were reported by people under 35, people from racial and ethnic minority backgrounds, men, and people with disability. Men reported the abuse at 10.2% compared with 3.8% for women, though women reported more negative reactions and impacts, including fear for their safety and effects on mental and physical health.

Henry said the findings strengthen the case for greater responsibility on technology companies to prevent this abuse before it occurs. She pointed to Australia's proposed digital duty of care as an opportunity to shift the focus from responding after abuse happens to requiring online services to prevent foreseeable harm. She added that regulation and new laws are not enough, and that better education, accessible support for victim-survivors, and safety built into AI tools from the outset are also needed. Co-author Dr Rebecca Umbach, a staff user experience researcher at Google, said understanding who experiences this abuse, how it occurs and its impacts is essential for designing more effective prevention and responses.

The findings build on two earlier studies using the same international dataset. One found that 3.2% of respondents reported creating, sharing or threatening to share AI-generated sexual images without consent, with the most common motivation among those who shared being for fun or as a joke. Another found that almost one in five adults had deliberately viewed AI-generated sexual images of real people, excluding those who did so solely to report or remove the material. The research program was funded by Google, and the international team is continuing its work to better understand and prevent AI-generated image-based abuse.

stories.Headline: Context engine vital for reliable agentic AI architectures
stories.Summary:
A context engine is vital for reliable agentic AI architectures, according to an InfoQ article reported by TechGig on November 3, 2026. The article says this engine systematically selects, injects, compresses, and expires information before it reaches the model. It argues that context engineering, which builds the system managing context, matters more than prompt engineering for agentic AI. Agentic systems need separate management of context, memory, and knowledge, each serving a different purpose.

Context is the immediate, active, and temporary information an agent uses at any moment. Memory provides persistence so agents retain information beyond a single interaction, and knowledge acts as the system's official textbook holding core business logic and policies. The context lifecycle has four stages: selection, injection, compression, and expiration and refresh. Selection identifies high-value data points, injection formats information for the model, compression summarizes data to respect token limits, and expiration retires stale assumptions. Token economics means optimizing attention real estate within LLM limits to avoid high costs, latency, and degraded performance.

The context engine is the orchestrator responsible for selecting, filtering, ranking, structuring, compressing, safeguarding, and delivering information to the LLM. The article says this is a shift from simple prompt engineering to systems engineering. It states that hallucinations in large language models often come from unmanaged or impoverished context windows, not broken models, and that proactive context management can suppress inaccurate associations. Effective architectures must balance historical memory, such as prior interactions and user preferences, with real-time input, such as current tasks and live telemetry. Knowledge curation should distill raw data into structured knowledge graphs or condensed summaries.

The article says overloading context windows can cause the Lost in the Middle phenomenon, where models fail to retrieve facts buried in massive inputs. It says tiered memory architectures, including working memory, short-term session cache, and long-term asynchronous persistence, are necessary to manage agent knowledge. These architectures help avoid anti-patterns like context stuffing and stale data loops. The article presents this as part of a series on agentic AI architecture.

stories.Headline: Armed with AI, hackers target endpoint security blind spots, raising stakes for CISOs
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike reported that a China-linked group it tracks as VAPOR PANDA used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17, 2026. The targets included government agencies and businesses in at least 14 countries, and researchers confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine of them. At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers directed AI agents to check running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to see whether CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor was installed. ARTEX runs multiple AI agents that carry out intrusion tasks under human direction, and CrowdStrike found the group used it against several organizations at once, with operators stepping in at key decision points. The findings followed an October 21 report from Microsoft on a separate campaign in which another China-linked group, Storm-0940, used ARTEX to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases and abusing compromised ConnectWise application credentials.

The attacks relied on weaknesses security teams have faced for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated, and at a US pharmaceutical company an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with broad administrative permissions. CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model, and although the framework's developer withdrew the original open-source project in October after reports of misuse, copies and modified versions remain available. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said in October research that financially motivated attackers had also used ARTEX in data-theft extortion operations.

Akshat Tyagi of HFS Research said the techniques are familiar but the ability to run them in parallel is not, and that AI lets smaller teams pursue targets without adding personnel. Jonathan Ong of Omdia said AI can greatly cut the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, though sophisticated exploitation still needs technical expertise, and he warned that concerns about AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defenses. Tyagi said CISOs should make sure monitoring covers their whole environment rather than assuming current deployments are complete, and Amit Kumar Jena of Kanerika recommended continuously measuring endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, alerting when machines stop reporting, enforcing SAML signature validation and limiting cloud privileges. Keith Prabhu of Confidis pointed to gaps between security systems and urged better asset visibility and detection across systems, and Tyagi also recommended rotating credentials regularly and watching unusual account activity.

Ong said frameworks like ARTEX could become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era, referring to a commercial penetration-testing tool widely abused by criminals and state-backed groups. Tyagi expects such tools to be adopted more widely by financially motivated criminals over the next 12 months, and Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response over buying more AI tools or expanding teams. The observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions, and Tyagi said fully autonomous attacks have not arrived, though that does not reduce their speed. For defenders, the challenge is spotting suspicious activity early enough to stop automated intrusion attempts from growing into broader compromises.

stories.Headline: AI Executive Appointments in November 2026
stories.Summary:
Dan Driscoll joined OpenAI as Senior Counsellor for National Security Modernisation, a move reported on November 3, 2026. He had been Secretary of the US Army, a position that ended in September 2026. OpenAI said he will work with senior leadership and external partners on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security. He will focus particularly on working with US allies to advance responsible use of the technology. Nuala Larkin became Eptura's first Chief AI Officer, the company announced.

She had been Eptura's SVP of Global Customer Support, CX Operations and Hardware. In the new role she will lead the companywide AI strategy, aiming to simplify work, raise productivity and improve employee and customer experiences. Eptura describes itself as an AI-native platform trusted by more than 11,000 organisations in 115 countries, including 50% of the Fortune 500. Barret Zoph joined Google DeepMind as VP of Research. He was a research scientist at Google Brain from June 2016 to August 2022, then served at OpenAI as VP of Research, Post-Training from September 2022 to October 2024.

He co-founded Thinking Machines Lab as CTO from October 2024 to January 2026, returned to OpenAI as VP and GM of B2B from January 2026 to August 2026, and has been an angel investor in AI companies since August 2022. Sam Altman, OpenAI's CEO, said AI should give people more power over their lives and people should have a say in how it is developed. He said the US has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI, and he welcomed Driscoll to strengthen American leadership. Driscoll said he spent much of his career in public service, first as a Soldier and most recently as Secretary of the Army and Acting Director of ATF. He said national security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years, and that he is joining OpenAI to help the US and its allies put the technology to work responsibly.

Larkin said AI adoption does not happen when people are given new tools, but when AI becomes part of how teams work daily. She said Eptura's focus is finding where AI removes friction, proving what works and making those approaches repeatable. Zoph wrote on X that he started his AI career in the Google Brain Residency class and is excited to rejoin. He said he will work on RL and Post-Training, and that Google has all the ingredients to continue to be incredibly successful in the AI space.

A separate article reported that Americans vote in the midterms on November 3, judging the races mainly on affordability, with the Iran war and rapid AI growth also shaping choices. A Gallup survey of 1,200 adults, conducted by telephone between 1 and 19 October, found half of registered voters described the economy and healthcare as extremely important, and 47 per cent rated the Iran situation as extremely important. Gallup included the Iran conflict and AI data centre construction in its midterm list for the first time. A Fox News poll found nearly nine in ten voters expect AI to change how they live in the next few years, with 53 per cent saying the change would be significant.

stories.Headline: Nvidia to Showcase Latest AI Infrastructure at AI Day Seoul 2026 Starting Nov. 9
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Nov. 2 that it will hold Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul from Nov. 9 to 10. The event will showcase the latest technologies in agentic AI, physical AI and AI infrastructure. Developers, startups, partners and researchers will gather to share technology trends and industrial applications. A total of 2,000 participants are expected to attend. The event will open on Nov. 9 with a keynote plenary session featuring senior Nvidia executives.

Deepu Talla, Nvidia's vice president of robotics and edge AI, will discuss Nvidia Isaac, Nvidia Cosmos foundation models and the future of AI factories. Jonathan Cohen, Nvidia's vice president of applied research, will address agentic AI. Jung Koo-hyung, manager of Nvidia's solutions architect team, and Jesse Clayton, senior product marketing manager for AI infrastructure, will introduce the AI factory blueprint and the Nvidia DSX ecosystem. A total of 20 partner companies will deliver presentations, including Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, LG Electronics, Naver Cloud, Doosan Robotics, Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Dell Technologies, Deloitte, Hancom, MegazoneCloud, MSI and SK Telecom. SK hynix will demonstrate how CUDA-X and PhysicsNeMo can accelerate semiconductor device and process simulations.

Samsung Electronics will share methods for using PhysicsNeMo-based physical AI to simulate liquid and gas flows and AI agents to automate semiconductor design exploration. LG Electronics will showcase a closed-loop learning system based on Nvidia Isaac GR00T and examples of its use in actual factories. Attendees will be able to take five Nvidia certification exams free of charge during the event, including those covering AI model and application development. On Nov. 10, paid hands-on training sessions and invitation-only events will take place. Three courses will cover large-scale AI inference deployment and optimization, simulation, training, validation and deployment of robotics workflows, and the development of secure agents based on large language models.

stories.Headline: Setting guidelines for using AI in the classroom
stories.Summary:
Before the start of this school year, New York City officials banned generative AI for public preschools through eighth grade, and Los Angeles educators banned access to generative AI platforms on school devices for all grade levels. In recent polls, 75% of parents reported supporting pausing AI in schools, while 73% of respondents said children already use AI for schoolwork. Alphabet, Google's parent company, has offered discounted Chromebooks to schools since at least 2011, and Gemini is included in Google's Chrome web browser. Because Google does not allow its AI summaries or chatbot to be turned off, Fairfax County Public Schools developed its own plug-in to block Google AI search results.

The article calls for clear guidelines rather than temporary pauses, since AI is embedded in many online platforms. It says state lawmakers must define academic standards and adopt appropriate guardrails for responsible use of AI in classrooms. The Heritage Foundation developed model legislation for AI in schools that prioritizes human-centered learning and oversight, transparency, safety and data security. The model says schools should not be required to adopt AI into lesson plans, but for those that do, educators should help students tell the difference between getting help with homework questions and plagiarism.

The authors say state lawmakers should respect parent rights and require schools to obtain parent consent for AI use, and educators should offer alternatives when families opt out. They say AI vendors should not gather student data for targeted advertising or sell or rent this information, and educators must follow state and federal privacy laws such as the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. They say teachers should prohibit AI companions that mimic personal relationships, since romantic conversations or simulated friendships have no academic use and interfere with children's social skills and healthy development. Florida recently adopted rules for AI in schools that are consistent with many of these provisions.

The article says state officials recognize that teachers and students can use AI effectively, and that banning AI will not eliminate the use of large language models but will cause the activity to go unmonitored. It warns that if AI use goes underground, the potential for cheating increases, with potentially disastrous consequences for student learning. It says lawmakers should use lessons already available in research and in the media on effective and ineffective uses of technology to advance policy ideas dedicated to protecting student privacy and promoting student learning. It says state officials should adopt thoughtfully designed boundaries for student and teacher use of AI, including restrictions on non-academic uses, so teachers can blend AI into instructional guidance and help prepare students for the future.

stories.Headline: China's AI trade has crashed. Now Beijing is trying to stop the stock market slide.
stories.Summary:
China's AI stock trade fell sharply, and Beijing responded with support measures for the market. On Monday, the central bank announced a new round of swap operations to support stocks. It said 31 securities firms and fund managers had applied for more than 100 billion Chinese yuan, or $15 billion, in liquidity support. Authorities also lowered financing costs for share buybacks and encouraged major technology companies to repurchase shares.

The downturn followed a rally driven by Beijing's September 2024 stimulus push and later by investor enthusiasm for Chinese AI and semiconductor companies. By late October, the STAR 50 index, which includes major semiconductor companies, had fallen roughly 40% from its midyear peak, erasing about $480 billion in market value, according to Reuters' calculations. The broader CSI 300 index fell 8.5% in October, its steepest monthly decline in more than a decade. The selloff added to pressure from a prolonged property downturn, weak consumer spending, and sluggish economic growth. After rising Monday on expectations of government support, Chinese stocks came under renewed pressure Tuesday, with the CSI 300 closing little changed, the Shanghai Composite falling 1%, and the tech-heavy STAR 50 sliding 4%.

Analysts at 22V Research, Michael Hirson and Houze Song, wrote in a note on Monday that the measures appeared intended to put a floor under markets rather than to engineer another rally like the September 2024 push. They said the liquidity support could help break a cycle in which investment firms are forced to sell holdings to meet investor withdrawals. They also pointed to weak domestic growth, waning optimism about US AI capital spending, and disappointment with the pace of domestic technological progress. They wrote that they were skeptical the authorities would attempt to engineer a broad-based rebound in equities, which they said would require more powerful tools than have been signaled so far.

A separate discussion on the Value Options Podcast covered the wider AI spending boom. Tim Travis said big technology companies had long financed spending from operating cash flow but were now turning to debt and equity as capital expenditures reached hundreds of billions of dollars. He cited long-term Meta bonds at around 7%, Oracle bonds at 9%, and Corweave financing at 15%, and said Meta could raise close to $100 billion or more in equity across this year and next. Tobias Carlisle said the technology could be real and grow for decades while stock prices still fall, comparing it to the early 2000s. He said a crash in this case would mean the biggest names coming down, since those names make up the entire market at the moment.

stories.Headline: China’s robot makers have mastered the moves. Now comes the race for AI brains
stories.Summary:
Chinese robot makers are shifting from building humanoid robots that can run, dance and perform backflips to developing the artificial intelligence that could make them useful across more jobs. This field, called embodied AI, focuses on software that lets robots understand their surroundings, learn unfamiliar tasks and adapt without being programmed for every job. Chinese embodied AI companies raised 93.5 billion yuan, or US$14.1 billion, across 322 deals in the first half of 2026, five times the amount a year earlier, according to the data research firm ITjuzi. Funding is increasingly reaching specialist developers of robot intelligence alongside manufacturers, as competition drives down hardware prices.

American startups including Physical Intelligence, Skild AI and Generalist are developing software to teach robots different skills without extensive retraining. Generalist has said its GEN-1.5 model completed around 60 per cent of simple tasks after viewing a demonstration lasting between three and 12 seconds. China's X Square has published research showing robots acquiring handling skills from a single human video without retraining the model for each task. Specialist Chinese startups including X Square, Galaxea and Spirit AI have each reached valuations of roughly US$3 billion, going by company disclosures. UBTech advertised a chief scientist position with compensation of up to 124 million yuan, and Unitree has about 30 researchers developing AI that predicts how objects behave.

Dermot McGrath of the Shanghai consultancy ZenGen Labs said robot makers have concluded that the margin won't come from the hardware but from the brain. Spirit AI co-founder Gao Yang said the brain is the weakest link in the complete robotics stack, and X Square co-founder and chief operating officer Yang Qian said the aim is for robots to shift from being driven by code to being driven by common sense. Spirit AI has hired around 1,000 people to record everyday and industrial activities, while ACE Robotics uses wearable sensors to capture workers' movements and grip forces. Ant Group's robotics unit Robbyant said it trained a model using 160,000 hours of material, including 50,000 hours of human-guided robot movements, and DexForce said it can prepare some industrial tasks for deployment within six to eight hours.

Chinese firms face shortages of advanced Nvidia chips due to US export controls and a squeeze on initial public offering funding amid regulatory concerns over inflated valuations and overcrowding. Zhu Mingxuan of JoyIn Technology said the chip shortage will become a serious problem for China's embodied AI industry as robots become more powerful. Battery maker CATL said Spirit AI robots connect flexible wires during battery-pack testing at its Zhongzhou plant, reporting insertion success above 99 per cent, and Robbyant said its robots handle orders in two Shanghai pharmacies. Unitree founder Wang Xingxing said the company had tested OpenAI's GPT-6 on robots with encouraging results, and that GPT-7, if released next year, could bring robotics its own ChatGPT moment. Consultant Georg Stieler said that if the question is when a customer can count on such systems, he would add years, not months.

stories.Headline: What's next for the proposed AI data center?
stories.Summary:
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology proposed a consent-based framework for sharing data to train artificial intelligence models, according to a TechGig report published on November 1, 2026. The framework is called the Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture, or DEPA, for AI training. It aims to help startups, businesses and academic institutions access large-scale, India-specific datasets. It also seeks to protect citizens' privacy and ensure compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The framework builds on India's existing DEPA system, which supports consent-based data sharing through efforts such as Account Aggregator. It sets out technical pillars including Confidential Clean Rooms, Differential Privacy, Electronic Contracts and Zero-Trust Security. Training Data Providers would register anonymised and encrypted datasets on a data exchange platform, and Training Data Consumers could request a dataset for specific uses. An electronic contract system would check requests against data-sharing policies before granting access, and training would happen in a secure environment so raw data stays inaccessible to consumers.

The framework proposes that trained models undergo independent checks for bias, fairness, security, safety and explainability. Only models that pass these checks would receive approval for pilot deployment and scaling. Oversight would continue after deployment through continuous monitoring, periodic reviews and traceability of model outputs back to the data and contracts used in training. The framework defines key stakeholders as Training Data Providers, Training Data Consumers, and Data Collectives or Data Collabs.

The new framework follows draft guidelines from the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India on responsible use of AI in telecom networks and service delivery. TRAI sought stakeholder inputs on those guidelines by November 27. TRAI's draft guidelines are rooted in the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines, which the Centre had previously released to foster innovation and safe development of AI offerings while mitigating risks. The TechGig article does not say what happens next for the DEPA framework beyond these steps.

stories.Headline: North Korea’s hackers supercharge crypto heists with AI skills
stories.Summary:
North Korea’s hacking group TraderTraitor carried out the recent US$6.3 billion Binance crypto heist, according to the FBI. The group is a state-sponsored unit of elite hackers, possibly only about a dozen members, and it was previously named in a 2022 joint warning from the FBI, CISA and the US Treasury. Blockchain investigation firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis also attributed recent crypto thefts to TraderTraitor. The group is believed to be responsible for 89 per cent of reported crypto hack losses in 2026, according to Chainalysis.

The Binance hack took about 20 minutes, and the stolen cryptocurrency was worth nearly 20 per cent of North Korea’s estimated annual economic output. About US$2.8 billion was frozen afterwards, leaving net outflows of US$3.6 billion. Binance said an initial investigation found a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer as the point of breach. The group’s previous largest hack was 2025’s US$1.5 billion Bybit heist. In 2024, UN experts said North Korea’s cyber thefts and illicit financial activities could be funding about 40 per cent of its weapons of mass destruction programmes.

Park Seong-su, a staff threat researcher at cybersecurity firm Zscaler, said the group looks for a big haul and targets crypto-related businesses, learning their infrastructure and tampering with it or with fund transfer processes to carry out large-scale theft. He said new AI tools have significantly lowered the barriers to such skills and greatly increased the speed of these operations. Nick Carlsen, senior investigator at TRM Labs, said the group’s novel techniques suggest it is making ample use of AI, and that its core method is the human part, combining hacking skills with social engineering. Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies, said crypto hacking has evolved beyond a criminal means of making up for foreign currency shortages for the Kim Jong Un regime. Adam Farrar, a former director on the US National Security Council covering Korea, said there now seems to be enough cash to support conventional forces, including new naval vessels and drone technology.

North Korea has for decades picked its best and brightest students to join hacking teams, training them at specialised institutions like Moranbong College in Pyongyang, according to defectors and experts. The country is isolated from the global financial system due to sanctions over Kim’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes, and its hackers have become one of its most important sources of revenue. Crypto exchanges are beefing up security, especially for employees with key access, to protect against TraderTraitor’s methods. Some closer observers of North Korea say the US has diminished capacity to actively engage on the Korean Peninsula as it devotes resources to conflicts in the Middle East and efforts to counter China and Russia, and Lim said North Korea is exploiting this period as a golden opportunity to accelerate the development of its military capabilities.

stories.Headline: Analysis-October dive for AI-related shares tests broader US stock market's resilience
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, US artificial intelligence and technology stocks fell sharply after disappointing results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel, according to a Reuters analysis published on November 2. On the last trading day of the month, the tech sector dropped 4.2%, including a nearly 29% tumble for Intel, and the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. For the whole of October, the S&P 500 tech sector slid 6.8%, its biggest monthly drop since March 2025. Investors were worried about the large financing needed for heavy spending on AI and began to question whether the returns would be strong enough to justify it.

Even so, the wider market held up much better than tech and AI shares. Nine of the S&P 500's 11 sectors gained in October, and the benchmark index ended the month down less than 1%. More than 70% of S&P 500 companies rose over the month, and indexes for small and mid-cap stocks also climbed. The S&P 500 is up more than 10% so far in 2026. Tech alone makes up a 38% weight in the S&P 500, and Oxford Economics estimates that about one-third of recent US economic growth comes from AI, including direct investment in AI infrastructure and some effect from stock market gains on consumer spending.

Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide, said one month of tech weakness alongside strength elsewhere is possible, but another month of steep drops would be hard mathematically and even harder psychologically. Angelo Kourkafas, senior global investment strategist at Edward Jones, said corporate and consumer fundamentals remain healthy, so investors want to keep equity exposure but reduce their AI concentration and add to areas offering different sources of return. He added that if big tech companies start pulling back on capital spending, which has supported growth and earnings across the economy, that could drive a broader move away from risk. Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at Empower, said the economy looks good because of AI rather than the consumer, so a meaningful pullback in AI would change market dynamics.

The S&P 500 closed below its 100-day moving average on Friday for the first time since April. Matthew Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak, said that when the index has broken below that trendline in any material way in the past two years, a much further drop followed in the weeks after. He said in a note that if the major averages begin to fall more convincingly, investors will likely stop rotating into other sectors and start moving into cash. The articles also note that investors would see a main warning sign if the large AI companies significantly cut their spending plans.

stories.Headline: Morgan Stanley issues a fresh warning about AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Morgan Stanley issued a fresh warning about AI stocks in a note reported on November 3, 2026. The firm's chief U.S. equity strategist, Mike Wilson, said he expects semiconductor stocks to fall another 10% to 15% before bottoming around mid-November. He projected the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index could drop to 9,500 points. The warning followed a steep selloff in chip shares, with the Semiconductor ETF falling 28.1% from its June peak of $656 to $471.51.

The articles tie the decline to heavy spending on AI infrastructure without clear returns. Amazon reported negative trailing 12-month free cash flow of $42.4 billion, and Alphabet posted about $9 billion in negative quarterly free cash flow. Morgan Stanley expects hyperscaler AI spending to reach $1.58 trillion by 2027. Nvidia has 91.7% of its projected 2027 revenue tied to AI infrastructure demand, and five companies including Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and Intel make up roughly 39% of the SOXX portfolio. The articles also cite S&P Global data showing the share of companies abandoning most AI initiatives rose from 17% to 42% in a year, and Gartner finding that 72% of CIOs are breaking even or losing money on AI deployments.

Wilson linked the expected decline to tightening financial conditions and a structural dependency, because chip earnings rely on spending commitments from a small number of large technology companies. He noted the correction has been grinding on for months. In a separate note, Morgan Stanley said it remained optimistic about Bloom Energy despite a paused data center project, keeping an Overweight rating and a $310 price target. RBC Capital reiterated an Outperform rating and a $335 price target on Bloom Energy.

Crusoe paused a 1.8-gigawatt data center campus in Cheyenne, Wyoming, at its customer's request, and the project had planned to use 900 megawatts of Bloom Energy fuel cells plus grid power. Morgan Stanley said the pause represented about $2.65 billion in revenue potential for Bloom, allocated from a 1-gigawatt master supply agreement signed with AEP in December 2024, and said contractual protections should help safeguard earnings. Bloom shares fell nearly 10% before recovering, and the stock was up 137.34% for the year. The articles say the historical pattern of stocks rallying after midterm elections is not guaranteed, citing geopolitical conflict in Iran and local pushback against AI data centers as risks.

stories.Headline: Finding peace, one click at a time: AI-made virtual sanctuaries draw young South Koreans
stories.Summary:
A 26-year-old South Korean job seeker surnamed Park created an online Buddhist temple called Sansa using vibe coding, an AI-assisted programming method that builds software from natural-language instructions, according to news reports on Nov 1. The site opened on Oct 29 and drew more than 100,000 visitors a day, with total visits surpassing 600,000. Visitors enter a temple set in a dense forest, with a large Buddha statue in the centre of the main prayer hall. Each visitor gets an avatar of a young Buddhist monk with a randomly assigned name such as Leisurely Cloud or Soft Moonlight.

Using their avatars, visitors can wander the temple, greet others by pressing their palms together, kneel on cushions to perform 108 bows, turn prayer beads and listen to chants. The site has no chat or messaging features, so visitors share the same prayer hall without interacting. The idea grew out of Park's own job-hunting struggles, when he wanted to unwind at a temple but lacked the time and energy to go. Park told a local news outlet that temples appeal to people his age because they welcome everyone, even non-Buddhists. He said seeing so many people respond made him realise many others were just as tired as he was.

Park said maybe all they really needed was a quiet place to take a break without having to say anything. The temple's success inspired similar AI-powered platforms modelled after Catholic and Protestant churches. Chanmi offers a virtual Catholic church with pews, votive candles and rosaries, where visitors can listen to hymns while Angelus bells ring three times a day, at 6am, noon and 6pm. Goyottul recreates a Protestant church where visitors can share prayer requests and listen to sermons.

Sung Hae-young, a professor of religious studies at Seoul National University, said Buddhism resonates with young people struggling with uncertainty because it acknowledges that life is full of suffering and offers ways to overcome it through their own understanding. Sung said that straightforward approach is what makes it appealing. Sung also said people want a sense of peace and sacredness like at a place of worship, but do not necessarily want to be tied to a religious community or feel pressured to believe unquestioningly. Sung said anonymous online spaces offer exactly that.

stories.Headline: Embodied AI's Next Frontier: Integrating Intelligence with Real-World Systems
stories.Summary:
Envision announced on Nov 2, 2026, that it had completed the world's first commercial deployment of an integrated 800-volt direct current power system in a large-scale AI data center. The system is now powering live computing workloads at the company's Galaxy AI data center campus in Ulanqab, China. The campus began operations in August 2026. The announcement was issued through PR Newswire and carried by The Manila Times.

The system combines solid-state transformers, battery energy storage and equipment that adjusts direct-current voltage for computing hardware. It delivers power end to end, from a 10 kV medium-voltage AC input to an 800V DC bus and on to the server rack. The architecture is meant to simplify data center power systems, improve conversion and watt-to-bit efficiency, and cut cabling and copper needs. The campus has a planned capacity of 3GW and is designed to support up to one million AI accelerators running in parallel at full build-out. More than 80% of its power is planned to come from direct renewable electricity connections.

Kevin Huang, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of Energy Storage and AIDC Power Systems, said AI data centers need power systems that coordinate renewable energy, energy storage and the grid to meet computing demand. He said the integrated 800V DC system is now powering live computing workloads and shows an end-to-end architecture linking renewable supply with computing demand. He described this as a critical step in turning power-compute coordination from a strategic vision into an operational reality. The company's Dubhe Controller, supported by its Dubhe Energy Foundation Model, coordinates the transformers and batteries in real time to match supply with demand and manage sudden load swings.

The deployment comes as the industry moves toward 800V DC infrastructure for next-generation AI data centers, and Envision says its system is operating commercially ahead of wider adoption. The system provides a reference for that transition. Envision aims to scale the approach through its Mission Gobi initiative, which targets 5GW of green AI data center capacity in desert regions worldwide by 2030. A separate Straits Times item published on Nov 4, 2026, carried the headline about embodied AI's next frontier and stated that the issuer is solely responsible for its content, without giving further details.

stories.Headline: Anthropic on deal spree for AI computing power
stories.Summary:
Anthropic faced a shortage of computing power for its artificial intelligence ambitions late last year. The company then signed dozens of contracts to secure resources for its growing ambitions. These deals were with former cryptocurrency miners, data center start-ups, and chipmakers. Anthropic also partnered with tech giants, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and SpaceX, to secure computing power.

To speed up construction, Anthropic hired data center experts and bought data center equipment. The company explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers. It also considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power. Dario Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, described the needed computing power as a "cone of uncertainty" at The New York Times's DealBook Summit in December. stories.Headline: AI success takes more than a promising pilot project
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks CIO Jessie Xia said organisations are launching AI projects faster than ever, but governance is lagging behind. She said the nature of AI lets it move faster than earlier technologies, and that about 88 percent of AI adoption is happening faster than a governance structure can keep up. She explained that AI is more distributed than other technologies, with security, data, legal and risk teams all involved in decisions, and many organisations lack clear decision-making arrangements. Xia said many organisations put policies on paper but need to build them into architecture and process controls, with traceability and clear accountabilities.

Xia said moving from a trial to production is a challenge even with good governance, and the typical obstacles are security, data quality and integration with existing systems. She said a business department may build something quickly but then struggle to reach production, and a Thoughtworks survey found about a third of respondents reported data quality and integration as issues. She said a pilot can work in controlled settings, but integrating with other systems in large organisations requires looking at how new applications fit the current infrastructure. She also said ROI and ownership economics need careful consideration, and Thoughtworks has a Chief AI Officer on its leadership team to coordinate software development, governance, infrastructure and security.

Xia said AI literacy will become increasingly important, but critical thinking and judgement will become more valuable as people's roles change. She said people will need to challenge what AI is doing, check for biased responses and define how AI and humans should interact. She said Australian organisations are doing well but most show qualified maturity on AI governance, with 55 percent embedding dedicated technology leads in business units, 48 percent establishing formal AI governance and operating models, and 38 percent standardising software and digital transformation across business units. Her advice was to establish clear accountability before scaling, put identity, data access, monitoring and traceability into systems and automate them where possible, and measure value while investing in workforce capability.

Separately, Siemens CEO Roland Busch and Naver CEO Choi Soo-yeon spoke at APK 2026 in Seoul on Saturday, urging companies to move beyond AI pilot projects toward measurable productivity gains. Choi said businesses must first organise information scattered across paper records, employee computers and departmental systems into formats AI can use, and ensure it is accurate, up to date and accessible. She said generating reports with AI does not automatically raise productivity, and companies should measure whether it reduces waiting times, improves efficiency or removes repetitive tasks. Busch said adoption has to come from the top, and cited a Japanese automaker that deployed Siemens technology across 10,000 machines with a payback period of less than three months.

Choi highlighted Naver's experience running more than 200 delivery robots at its 1784 headquarters for over four years, showing the challenges of reliable AI services in spaces shared with people. In an audience poll, 41 percent of respondents named data sharing and interoperability as the biggest barrier to scaling industrial AI across regions. Busch called for clear data-sharing policies and specialised expertise, noting customer data could train industrial AI models without leaving company premises. Busch warned that repetitive, rules-based jobs would face displacement and called for reforms in education and workforce training, while Choi said Naver keeps hiring each year but would need new business models to offset rising AI costs.

stories.Headline: KAIST develops technology to cut AI training time by up to 70%
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on Monday that a research team led by Professor Lee Jae-gil of the School of Computing had developed CluSTER, a fine-tuning technology for large language models. The team included Kim Hyun-jin, a doctoral student in the School of Computing, as first author. The work was presented in October at EMNLP 2026, a leading international conference on natural language processing. The technology selects training data efficiently and distributes it across multiple GPUs. Fine-tuning a large language model for specialized fields such as medicine or coding requires extra training on domain-specific data.

CluSTER analyzes how each data sample affects AI training and groups samples that produce similar learning outcomes. It then selects only the necessary samples from each group and spreads them so that multiple GPUs each handle distinct learning information. The team tested the approach on models with about 7 billion and 13 billion parameters, using three coding and medical datasets. Using only about 31 percent of the full training data, the team cut training time by up to 69.6 percent while maintaining nearly the same AI performance, so training that would take 10 hours took about 3 hours. Lee said that to improve AI training efficiency it is important not only to use more GPUs but also to make smart choices about what data to train on.

He said the research is meaningful because it can reduce the training burden of large-scale AI models by making better use of existing GPU resources. The technology is expected to ease the burden on companies and research institutions that build customer service AI, medical support AI or coding assistance AI using their own proprietary data. Performance was mainly verified in a four-GPU environment, and the technology also outperformed conventional methods in an eight-GPU setup. Further validation across diverse corporate datasets and training environments will be needed before it can be applied in real-world industrial settings. Work also remains to refine the software so it can integrate smoothly with existing AI training systems.

stories.Headline: Straive and Anthropic Partner to Advance Responsible Enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
Straive, a global data and AI operationalization company, announced a partnership with Anthropic on November 3, 2026, according to a Business Wire release carried by AiThority. The partnership aims to combine Anthropic's AI capabilities with Straive's governance and operational expertise. The goal is to help global enterprises build, deploy and run AI responsibly across business workflows. Straive supports organizations in financial services, healthcare and life sciences, manufacturing and supply chain, media and entertainment, education and research, and publishing.

The partnership is meant to help organizations use AI in industry-specific settings while keeping the oversight and operational controls their teams need. Straive will focus on connecting AI capabilities to real workflows, defining where people remain involved in decisions, and supporting solutions as business needs change. Straive brings together data readiness, domain expertise, solution design, governance, human oversight and continuous improvement through its Build AI, Run AI capabilities. The article gives no financial terms or timeline for the partnership.

Naveen Gattu, Chief Growth Officer at Straive, said responsible AI has to be built into how a solution is designed, deployed and used every day. He said the partnership brings together Anthropic's focus on safe AI with Straive's domain expertise and operational approach. Sean Manning, VP and Global Head of Partnerships at Straive, said enterprises need a clear path from AI capability to responsible use in their operations. He said working with Anthropic aims to help customers address the data, workflow and governance requirements that matter when AI moves into production.

Separately, Tencent Cloud announced a strategic partnership with OmniOps, a Saudi AI infrastructure technology company, at the 2026 Tencent Global Digital Ecosystem Summit, according to a PR Newswire report carried by The Manila Times on November 2, 2026. OmniOps will contribute its inference technology, local deployment capabilities and market expertise to support enterprise AI platforms and model inference workloads across Saudi Arabia. stories.Headline: Oaktree’s Howard Marks Says AI Stumbles Boosted Skepticism
stories.Summary:
Howard Marks, co-chair of Oaktree Capital Management, said in an interview with Bloomberg TV that recent stumbles in artificial intelligence related markets have somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility around the sector. He said people are now saying hold on and being more thoughtful and skeptical, which he called very healthy. Marks had written in a note last year that he was on bubble watch. His comments came as investors showed less tolerance for tech companies whose core businesses are cooling beneath an unprecedented AI spending spree, and recent results from Alphabet and Amazon fueled concerns that AI is eroding the businesses financing those investments.

Marks said that over the last couple of years there had been great excitement about buying into or lending to AI, making it a crowded trade. He said that if you think you are in the later innings and everybody is excited, it has been done a lot, and that standards have come down and prices have gone up, so you have to be cautious. He gained attention in January 2000 for a memo called bubble.com, in which he warned of dot-com mania ahead of the bust. Referring to the massive amounts of AI funding companies have sought, he said firms are in an AI arms race raising trillions of dollars, and that a trillion is a dollar a second for 31,000 years, which nobody can think about. He said the question investors should ask is whether there can be enough business and profit to produce an attractive return, and that the answer is who knows, so that has to be taken into account.

In a separate Bloomberg TV interview, Jody Jonsson, vice chair at Capital Group, said there is a disconnect between what AI companies expect and the pace at which enterprises can adopt the technology. She said this is showing a little in market reactions, with the idea that it may not be happening as fast as everyone thought or that the return on investment is not clear. She said markets are getting very concerned about the scale of capital raising and whether there is enough appetite in equity and fixed income for all the issuance coming to fund it. Jonsson said the debt picture is complicated because much of the financing sits off balance sheet in unconsolidated vehicles, concentrated among a handful of companies that do business with one another, and that the more they lend their credit to others, the more fragile the system becomes.

stories.Headline: Apple is all in on AI — its own and everyone else’s
stories.Summary:
Apple held its quarterly earnings call on November 3, 2026, and reported its best-ever fiscal year for revenue and earnings per share. iPhone revenue rose 17.5% from a year earlier to a September quarter record of $57.6 billion, while Mac revenue climbed 24% to $10.8 billion, its highest level in four years. Shares still fell in premarket trading on Tuesday after Apple warned that rising memory costs would squeeze profit margins in the holiday quarter. AI and Apple Intelligence were mentioned a record 45 times on the call, according to the financial research platform AlphaSense, more than on the call after Apple unveiled the technology and plans for a revamped Siri in June 2024.

Apple's approach combines on-device processing, its own servers, and outside AI technology, and Siri AI uses models developed with Google's Gemini technology. Apple reportedly plans to let users choose among outside AI providers for features such as writing tools and image generation. Apple spent $2.2 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, compared with Amazon's $77.3 billion and Alphabet's $51.4 billion, and its operating expenses rose 21% to $19.2 billion as it increased research and development spending, including on AI. Siri AI launched in beta for US English users in September and expanded to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.

CFO Kevan Parekh cited a wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time and said AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch to get the latest capabilities. CEO John Ternus, on his first earnings call in the role, said he sees tremendous opportunity in AI and that Mac is having an AI moment of its own. Ternus said features relying on server-side models, including Siri AI and intelligent photo editing, will have usage limits, and customers who need more capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future. He compared this to iCloud tiers, which began largely as storage but have gained more capabilities and features.

Apple has more than 2.5 billion active devices, and it positions itself as the interface through which consumers use AI, including competitors' technology. The Wall Street Journal reported that Apple was on pace to bring in more than $1 billion in App Store fees from generative AI apps in 2026, according to the analytics firm AppMagic, though OpenAI has begun directing potential subscribers to pay through its website instead. Gap is running AI entirely on Mac Mini computers for loss prevention across hundreds of stores, and Christie's is running local models on Mac Studio computers to improve workflows including pricing estimates. Earlier this year, then-CEO Tim Cook said customer recognition of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio's capabilities for AI and agentic tools was happening faster than Apple had predicted, leading to higher-than-expected demand.

stories.Headline: EAC ministers approve AI module for university students
stories.Summary:
Ministers from the East African Community approved a foundational artificial intelligence module for university students across the region. The decision was made at the 21st Sectoral Council on Education, Science and Technology, Culture and Sports, held from October 27 to 31, 2026, at the newly completed Inter-University Council for East Africa headquarters in Kampala, Uganda. The ministers directed partner states to consider integrating the module into university degree programmes. They tasked the Inter-University Council for East Africa with developing a regional implementation framework to guide the rollout.

The module is meant to give undergraduates basic AI knowledge, practical applications and responsible use, regardless of their field of study. The Council also directed the development of AI certification benchmarks for Kiswahili. It adopted the EAC Artificial Intelligence Strategy, the EAC Digital Transformation Strategy and the EAC Biotechnology Strategy, which were developed by the EAC Secretariat with the East African Science and Technology Commission. The ministers approved the establishment of a Regional Artificial Intelligence Network of Universities and endorsed three regional AI instruments for teacher education covering curriculum and competencies, institutional policy and codes of conduct. They also approved the EAC Technical and Vocational Education and Training Qualifications Framework and called for faster alignment of Mutual Recognition Agreements for engineers, architects, accountants and veterinarians with Annex VII of the Common Market Protocol.

EAC Deputy Secretary General Andrea Ariik Malueth, who is in charge of Infrastructure, Productive, Social and Political Sectors, said education systems needed to prepare young people for a rapidly changing labour market through stronger foundational learning and improved teacher development. He urged ministers to ensure decisions had clear responsibilities, realistic timelines and the resources needed for implementation, and warned that limited financial and institutional capacity could slow the programmes. Uganda's minister of state for Education and Sports for Primary Education, Phyllis Chemutai, who chaired the ministerial session, said the region must work collectively to remove unnecessary barriers to the recognition of qualifications while safeguarding professional standards and the quality of services. She said Uganda would review its laws, regulations and policies to support implementation of the agreements.

The Council noted that some public and private universities had not fully implemented an earlier directive requiring students from partner states to pay tuition fees under the same regime as national students, in the host country's local currency. The Inter-University Council for East Africa, working with national higher education regulators, will conduct a regional assessment and present its findings to the 23rd Sectoral Council. Kenya confirmed it will host the sixth East African Community Arts and Culture Festival, known as JAMAFEST, in Nairobi in February 2027, with a theme on AI and digital technology in preserving cultural heritage and promoting tourism. The meeting also considered a framework for regional participation in Pamoja AFCON 2027, which Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will jointly host, and the Secretariat was directed to bring technical experts together to review the draft concept by November 2026. The meeting acknowledged support from Germany, the European Union and the World Bank through initiatives such as the EAC AI Alliance.
