Boston University is considering a proposal to offer a dedicated undergraduate degree in artificial intelligence, according to reports published on November 2, 2026. The final proposal is currently pending administrative approval, said Mark Crovella, a professor and chair of academics for BU's Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences. Crovella hopes the faculty will offer a bachelor's degree in AI starting in the fall 2027 semester, according to BU's independent student newspaper, The Daily Free Press. The university is still weighing the plan rather than having finalized it.

BU's plan would feature two tracks within the major, one focused on building advanced AI models and another on applying AI across disciplines. The program would place a strong emphasis on AI ethics. BU already offers related programs, including a Bachelor of Science in data science within the Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, a Bachelor of Arts in computer science, a residential Master of Science in AI, and five online master's programs in AI. If approved, BU would join a growing number of higher education institutions offering a Bachelor of Science in AI.

Crovella told The Daily Free Press that AI is in the process of changing the world. He said students need to understand the technology, be able to create it, and also know how to use it responsibly and incorporate it ethically into society. Azer Bestavros, a computer science professor and associate provost for the Faculty of Computing and Data Sciences, told the newspaper that he believes AI education will become essential across careers. He noted that AI is not a standalone field.

Several Massachusetts universities already offer AI majors, including Bentley University, Northeastern, Wentworth Institute of Technology, and MIT. This fall, Northeastern renamed its Bachelor of Science program in data science to a Bachelor of Science in AI. stories.Headline: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Just Drove a Dagger Through Wall Street's AI-Driven Rally With 6 Blunt Words
stories.Summary:
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and his Federal Open Market Committee colleagues voted on Oct. 28 to hold interest rates steady. The decision came during a 67th consecutive month of annualized inflation above the Fed's long-term 2% target. After the meeting, Warsh spoke with the press and made comments about how interest rates affect AI companies. His six-word assessment that interest rates get in the cracks sent a message to AI stock investors.

Warsh took over as Fed chair on May 22 and has done away with forward-looking guidance in FOMC statements and in his post-meeting discussions with reporters. During his five-month tenure, getting direct answers or hints about what is to come has been challenging. The CME Group's FedWatch Tool predicts a 72% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December. It also predicts a nearly 50% chance of 75 basis points in cumulative hikes by Sept. 15, 2027. Higher long-duration Treasury bond yields, specifically 10- and 30-year yields, can increase corporate borrowing costs.

Warsh said interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything. He said market participants are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make. He also said credit spreads for certain assets have widened out or gapped out, while financial conditions have tightened for others but not significantly. The article says this blunt six-word assessment has sent an unmistakable message to AI stock investors.

Some of Wall Street's hyperscalers are funding their data center build-outs through stock issuances and cash on hand. The otherworldly demand for AI hardware is being financed, in part, with debt. If borrowing costs continue to climb, they could adversely affect this expansion and near-term growth projections. That could force a re-rating of the second-priciest stock market in history. Bond traders are also concerned about U.S. total debt surpassing $40 trillion and ongoing federal deficits.

Beyondsoft showcased its financial AI and digital solutions at Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK 2026, the company said in an announcement dated Nov 3, 2026. At the event the company presented its AI agent platform, its mobile application development platform and its enterprise digital currency payment collection system. Its team met with financial institutions, technology companies and industry organisations to discuss AI applications, implementation challenges and opportunities for collaboration across the region. Visitors also engaged with the company at its exhibition booth.

The AI agent platform combines large language models with industry knowledge bases to support risk management, oversight of funds, automated regulatory reporting and targeted customer engagement, and is designed to help institutions explore end-to-end automation of core business processes. The mobile application development platform, built on Beyondsoft's proprietary technology, supports financial apps across multiple device environments and enables faster updates. The enterprise digital currency payment collection system provides payment collection services for financial institutions and corporate clients through a customised software-as-a-service model. Beyondsoft has more than 30 years of experience and a global talent network of nearly 30,000 professionals, and its International Headquarters is in Singapore.

Ariel Lin, who leads Beyondsoft's Innovation Lab and AI Practice, gave a presentation on adapting China's financial AI capabilities to Southeast Asian markets. Lin said international expansion requires more than exporting products, and that technical expertise, experienced people and proven delivery practices are equally important. Lin noted that customer expectations, operations and infrastructure vary across Southeast Asia, so providers need to adapt solutions to each market and work with local teams to build the skills to maintain and develop them. Lin also said compliance needs to be built into solution design and implementation so financial institutions can manage the risks of deploying AI across markets.

The presentation examined regulatory differences across Southeast Asia, with examples from Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, covering data protection, biometric identity verification, the fairness and explainability of AI-assisted decisions and financial data sharing. It said these requirements need to be considered from the outset for cross-border projects, that data use must comply with purpose limitations and consent requirements, and that biometric applications require attention to liveness detection and accuracy. Beyondsoft's work for the overseas branches of a Chinese global bank covered personal and corporate mobile banking, credit card applications, mobile workplace tools and mobile learning platforms. The company said it will continue to connect technology expertise from China with business needs in Southeast Asia and will explore AI applications and service models suited to regional markets with industry partners.

stories.Headline: Google's Project Suncatcher satellite generates first AI response in orbit
stories.Summary:
Google announced on October 30 that its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite had generated its first artificial intelligence response using a data centre-class Tensor Processing Unit in orbit. The satellite was launched on October 1 aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. It was built in partnership with Planet. Google completed the satellite's commissioning checklist, which included powering up the host and TPU trays and running initial machine learning tests. During a ground-station pass, Google uplinked a prompt to the onboard Gemma 4 open model asking for a haiku about being in space, and the satellite transmitted the response back to Earth as it passed Svalbard, Norway.

The milestone is an early test of Google's research into running AI workloads in space. Google described it as the first AI response from a data centre-class TPU in orbit. The company later tested the model with space-themed limericks and prompts requesting telemetry information about the payload systems. The next phase of Project Suncatcher will evaluate how the TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. These tests will help determine whether Google's hardware can reliably execute AI workloads in space.

The work is led by Google, and the blog post was written by Travis Beals, Senior Director of Paradigms of Intelligence. Google said the milestone marks an early test of its research into running AI workloads in space. The company said the thermal and radiation tests would help determine whether its hardware can reliably execute AI workloads in space. Google plans to use the findings to advance its next milestone.

Project Suncatcher explores the feasibility of solar-powered satellite networks equipped with Google's TPUs. The initiative investigates the long-term potential of scaling machine learning infrastructure beyond Earth. Google plans to advance to its next milestone in 2027, involving two interconnected satellites. That proposed system aims to explore how multiple satellites could work together to support AI computing in orbit.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's AI Is Getting Cheaper to Use. That's Becoming a Problem for Its Business
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said in an amended SEC filing that revenue growth from increased usage was partly offset by about $600 million from price reductions in new model versions and contractual discounts. The company released Claude Opus 5.5, which lowered token prices compared with Opus 5, and introduced Haiku 5.5 in October as a cheaper model for high-volume work. Anthropic said Fable 5.1 cut the cost of typical workloads by around 25%, while Opus 5.5 brought customers' cost per task down roughly 40% compared with Opus 5. The reductions reflect both lower prices and efficiency gains, not straight discounts across every task.

Compute and infrastructure expenses rose from $5.56 billion to $9.86 billion, an increase of roughly 77%, while revenue growth was 47%. That means Anthropic spent roughly 58 cents on compute and infrastructure for every dollar of revenue, versus 48 cents a quarter earlier, though the measure includes computing for research, training and internal operations, not just serving paying Claude customers. The quarter included $5 billion of compute under short-term commitments that Anthropic said cost significantly more than comparable capacity secured through multiyear contracts. That expense helped push the company from a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter to a $567 million operating loss in the third.

Anthropic said users have historically expanded consumption after such releases, and it typically reserves compute capacity 12 to 18 months before it becomes available, leaving much of that spending relatively fixed in the near term. Its updated disclosures put aggregate lease and purchasing commitments at roughly $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. Reuters reported that the filing raised questions about whether infrastructure partners can secure the financing needed to deliver all that capacity. Google and Nvidia appear to benefit most from Anthropic's growth, as its core business depends on their infrastructure.

Anthropic is preparing to go public, and its IPO filing put the company in Wall Street's spotlight. Demand for Claude is still growing rapidly, but the harder question is whether Anthropic can keep making its models cheaper faster than the cost of building and running them comes down. OpenAI, which is also preparing its own IPO, offers a competitive model with many usage resets and a more generous usage quota. That is the main issue keeping Anthropic from raising prices.

stories.Headline: AI chatbots are becoming political advisers. Their answers can mislead voters
stories.Summary:
Voters are increasingly turning to AI chatbots for election information ahead of the midterms, and researchers say many popular chatbots may give misleading answers about candidates and polling sites. The research was conducted by the nonprofit Innovating for the Public Good, or IFPG, with the Dewey Square Group, and it was reported by NPR on November 2, 2026. A Pew Research Center survey from earlier this year found that about half of American adults reported using AI-powered chatbots, and about 42% of users said they use them to search for information. Some chatbots have even provided lists of candidates to vote for, raising concerns among experts that AI-generated misinformation could influence voters' decisions.

An ongoing IFPG study is testing seven major chatbots: Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, OpenAI's ChatGPT and Perplexity. In data collected in October, 13.9% of chatbot answers to voting-logistics questions were outdated or inaccurate, and errors in 5.9% of answers could mislead a voter, potentially causing them to miss a deadline, vote on the wrong day or skip a required step. Across all questions, 5.1% of answers carried at least one clear factual error and 10.9% a clear error or misleading claim. The researchers found that accuracy depended more on the chatbot than the questions posed, with Claude and Copilot producing three-quarters of the clear errors. On voting questions, Claude gave wrong or outdated information one in three times, Copilot one in four and ChatGPT one in 10.

Tim Chambers, a principal at Dewey Square Group, said the error rates were extremely troubling and that users could miss a key voting deadline if they trusted these answers. Microsoft spokesperson Jessica Dash said helping people find accurate election information has long been a priority for the company and that it has made improvements to how Copilot responds to election questions. Anthropic spokesperson Michael Aciman told NPR that because IFPG conducted part of its research using an Application Programming Interface, some of Claude's key safeguards may not have been active, though IFPG said a separate internal study found results through the API and the web interface to be comparable. Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google said they are working to prevent their chatbots from producing election disinformation.

Campaigns and political influence operations are now writing content specifically so that chatbots will pick it up and repeat it, a process known as generative engine optimization. Abdiaziz Ahmed, a technology policy strategist with the Brennan Center's Elections and Government Program, said chatbots pull from whatever they can find online, so an answer about a candidate may reflect who worked hardest to get into it. The IFPG research found that in response to attack questions, chatbots generally shifted to cite less trustworthy sources, and all the platforms tested commonly cited prediction market websites such as Polymarket and Kalshi. In the months before the midterms, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google published policies about safeguarding elections, while SpaceX and Microsoft did not publish policies and Meta's midterm election policy does not mention its Meta AI chatbot.

stories.Headline: AI is transforming customer experience in EMEA; But not for everyone
stories.Summary:
Talkdesk, Inc., a customer experience automation company, released a report titled "The State of Customer Experience Automation in EMEA" on November 3, 2026, in London. The report found a sharp divide in how widely organisations in Europe, the Middle East and Africa use AI to resolve customer issues. While 30% use AI to resolve more than 40% of customer issues, 17% have yet to use it to resolve any. The EMEA report draws on regional findings from "The State of Agentic Automation in CX," a global study commissioned by Talkdesk and conducted by NewtonX. It examines how organisations are deploying AI in customer experience, the barriers holding them back, and the operational foundations needed to move from AI adoption to AI outcomes.

EMEA and North America are at similar stages of maturity in combining AI agents with orchestration across teams and systems, at 15% and 14% of organisations respectively, but their operational realities diverge. North America is more concentrated at lower levels, with 67% of organisations resolving 20% or less of customer issues with AI and only 8% resolving more than 40%. Legacy technology is a more prominent barrier in EMEA, cited by 27% of organisations compared with 12% in North America. While 67% of EMEA organisations expect AI to resolve a greater share of customer issues within two years, only 35% have integrated customer data and just 22% consistently measure AI's business impact. A majority of 59% of EMEA organisations using AI agents say human agents now handle more complex cases, yet only 13% coordinate AI and people dynamically with orchestrated handoffs.

Pedro Andrade, global head of AI at Talkdesk, said AI adoption in EMEA looks very different from one organisation to the next, with more far ahead but also more yet to start. He said it is especially important to look beyond the initial deployment and ask whether AI is set up to deliver consistently, whether it can access the right knowledge and systems, work alongside people, and be reliably tested, audited and governed, and whether the business can measure the results. He said AI only delivers when the operational foundations are in place. Half of EMEA organisations cite job security as a top concern about humans and AI working together, alongside AI accuracy at 47%. Despite these worries, 62% expect AI to help them scale without adding headcount and 40% expect higher employee satisfaction as human agents shift to higher-value work.

NewtonX conducted an online quantitative survey of 60 director-level-and-above decision-makers and significant influencers responsible for customer experience, IT, operations or AI strategy at mid-market and enterprise organisations with 250 or more employees across EMEA. It was fielded in April 2026 as part of the 2026 NewtonX "The State of Agentic Automation in CX" survey and included respondents from financial services, retail, technology, life sciences and other industries. The full report provides priorities to help leaders close this readiness gap and includes a maturity assessment to benchmark where they currently stand. The articles say organisations need to ensure their operations can scale without compromising service quality or trust.

stories.Headline: HE Dr Sultan Al Jaber and Sam Altman highlight energy, AI and investment priorities at ADIPEC 2026 opening
stories.Summary:
ADIPEC 2026 opened in Abu Dhabi on November 2, 2026, under the patronage of Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, President of the UAE, and hosted by ADNOC. The event is the largest edition in its history, with 2,260 exhibitors, 30 country pavilions, four specialised zones and more than 1,800 speakers across over 380 sessions. It is expected to draw 239,000 participants from more than 170 countries. The opening ceremony featured a keynote by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and ADNOC Managing Director and Group CEO, and a speech and interview with Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI.

Dr Al Jaber said the global energy industry must rethink how it builds, protects and delivers secure energy after a year of disruption, and that nearly one billion barrels of crude had been drained from inventories since disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. He set out five steps: accessible supply through expanded strategic storage and flexible refining closer to consumers, routes to market built before they are needed, operational intelligence moving from automated operations to intelligent energy systems, capital that follows confidence, and people, which he called the most important. Altman said abundant, reliable energy is critical to unlocking the next wave of AI-driven innovation, that AI can make energy systems more efficient while its expansion will require significantly more energy, and that the UAE has been the most forward-looking country for AI adoption. He described the ADNOC-G42-OpenAI partnership as a model for applying advanced AI to industrial challenges.

The opening ministerial panel included Suhail Mohamed Al Mazrouei, UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure, and Ekperikpe Ekpo, Nigeria's Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas). Al Mazrouei said additional layers of protection, spare capacity, technology and AI would be needed to design better and become more resilient. The opening CEO panel brought together Meg O'Neill of bp, Richard Jackson of Oxy and Markus Krebber of RWE. Jackson said his company's strategy had been durability, with a focus on sustainable cash flow and production.

The event runs until November 5, with more than 1,800 speakers across 13 conference programmes. Organisers said discussions over the coming days will focus on turning strategic priorities into investment decisions, partnerships and practical solutions. A survey by ADNOC, XRG and Microsoft found that 62 per cent of energy leaders now rank AI among their two leading corporate priorities, up from 42 per cent last year, and that nearly three quarters expect AI to increase energy consumption by 2030. A separate ADIPEC survey found that 81 per cent of energy executives expect AI-related electricity requirements to exceed current forecasts.

stories.Headline: Data centers are the digital steel of the AI century. America can't stop building them.
stories.Summary:
Tom Suder, a professor and the founder and president of the Advanced Technology Academic Research Center, wrote a commentary published by Nextgov/FCW on November 2, 2026. He grew up in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, a steel town that lost its mill, its jobs and its tax base. He argued that data centers are where artificial intelligence lives and that every advance he describes runs on one. He wrote that America is canceling launches in what he called the space race of our time.

The article cites several numbers. The Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, launched in November 2025, links 17 national laboratories and their supercomputers and aims to double the productivity of American science within a decade. In Sweden's MASAI trial of more than 105,000 women, AI-supported mammography found 29% more cancers than standard screening, and Sybil, built at MIT and Massachusetts General Hospital, predicts lung cancer risk up to six years out from a single CT scan. The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, citing Heatmap data, reports that at least $260 billion in planned U.S. data center investment was canceled after local opposition this year, costing more than 2 million construction jobs. Loudoun County, Virginia, has roughly 233 data center buildings that generated $1.2 billion in property taxes in fiscal 2026, 39% of the county budget, and replacing that revenue would take roughly 63 more cents on today's 80.5-cent rate.

Suder said local zoning is paramount and that a data center does not go next to homes if a community does not want it. He said the race will be won by building where communities welcome the investment, not by steamrolling neighborhoods. He said the administration's job is to make projects possible and that the biggest barrier is power. He called for speedier permitting for generation and transmission, clear ways for advanced nuclear, and making the biggest users pay the full cost of their power so households never subsidize hyperscalers.

The article says a data center ecosystem has grown up in Loudoun, including electricians, construction crews, network and cybersecurity professionals, suppliers and a community college degree in data center operations. It says that in August, X reported roughly 200 accounts tied to a suspected Chinese bot farm pushing Americans to oppose data centers, while most opposition is homegrown. It says the Wall Street Journal reported on a $2 billion plan to turn Aliquippa's long-closed mill site into a power plant and AI data centers. Suder closed by saying that for towns like his, the bigger risk is another generation of empty mill sites.

stories.Headline: Hollywood backs NYT in AI copyright battle versus OpenAI, Microsoft
stories.Summary:
A coalition of organizations representing creative talent across music, film, TV, performing arts and creative writing entered the legal battle over AI and copyright last week. They filed amicus briefs siding with the New York Times in its case against OpenAI and Microsoft. The briefs were filed on Friday and all support the Times' argument that AI firms should not be allowed to use publishers' material to train their large language models. The case has become a proxy fight for the future of the broader creative economy beyond journalism. Anne Hathaway, Bette Midler and Madonna voiced support for the Times in a brief filed by The Human Consent Foundation, which includes talent giant CAA and several coalitions representing musical artists, voice actors and writers.

The Recording Industry Association of America, National Music Publishers' Association, ASCAP and BMI filed their own brief. SAG-AFTRA, the American Federation of Musicians and both the Writers Guild of America East and West filed a brief to defend the rights and livelihoods of more than 250,000 entertainment and media workers. Talent agency WME also weighed in, arguing that AI use of creative materials should not be stopped but that it should be licensed. News outlets, authors and music publishers have led the charge in filing lawsuits to protect their intellectual property, and the briefs show the court how broad the implications could be. The News/Media Alliance and a coalition of local journalism groups also filed briefs supporting the Times, emphasizing the financial sustainability of the journalism industry.

A recurring theme in the briefs is that AI companies should not be broadly exempted from licensing copyrighted content. OpenAI and other firms have argued that a licensing system for digital content would be too cumbersome, and the Justice Department has supported that argument for training AI models but not necessarily for outputs of AI queries. Hollywood's support comes as the Times has expanded its legal battle against the AI industry. The company, alongside other publishers, on Monday sued web browser Brave, alleging it scraped its copyrighted works and distributed them to AI firms.

stories.Headline: Fiserv Wants AI to Fix What Decades of Payments Growth Made Expensive
stories.Summary:
Fiserv reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and announced a $6.45 billion goodwill impairment alongside a $1 billion cost-cutting target. The company said it had doubled the savings goal of its Project Elevate restructuring program. It also disclosed that it had cut 3,000 employee and contractor positions since CEO Takis Georgakopoulos took over, including reducing senior management by more than 10%. Fiserv shares rose roughly 14% in premarket trading after the company posted a narrow earnings beat.

The plan calls for consolidating overlapping technology platforms, discontinuing smaller products and embedding artificial intelligence across operations and software development. In merchant acquiring, Fiserv is moving services onto Commerce Hub to replace more than a dozen legacy gateways and switches globally. In banking, its Core Modularity initiative aims to shift multiple core systems toward shared software components. The company has also identified more than a dozen smaller products with limited customer adoption that it intends to transition away from or potentially exit.

Georgakopoulos said the company was simplifying with what he called an AI-everywhere mindset, and he expressed growing confidence in driving efficiency while investing in innovation. He argued that Fiserv's advantage lies in combining its transaction data, distribution and broad product portfolio. Management said the company supports approximately 40% of the U.S. banking market, holds more than 1.5 billion accounts on file in issuing and operates one of the country's largest debit networks. He also said AI agents in Clover's risk-hold process cut decision times by two-thirds and lowered false positives by more than 40%.

The results reflect pressure across the payments industry, where the scale that once made processors hard to displace can also make them expensive to modernize. Merchant Solutions reported a 2% organic revenue decline in the third quarter, Financial Solutions grew 2% and overall organic revenue was flat. Clover gross payment volume rose approximately 10%, Commerce Hub transactions doubled and core banking client wins increased more than 50% year over year. The articles say Fiserv still must show that automation gains translate into sustainable margins after implementation, oversight and technology costs.

Articles.Title: Fiserv Wants AI to Fix What Decades of Payments Growth Made Expensive

stories.Headline: Wood, Databricks partner to scale AI across energy asset lifecycle

Wood partnered with Databricks to help energy companies move AI from pilot projects into enterprise-scale use across the asset lifecycle. The companies announced the partnership on Nov. 3 in Abu Dhabi. It combines the Databricks Data + AI Platform with Wood's engineering, operational and asset expertise. The aim is to apply AI to complex industrial challenges, from project delivery through operations and maintenance.

The partnership builds on several years of work with shared clients. That work includes an AI-enabled engineering solution that, according to Wood, cut the time needed for critical-path document review and quality assurance by 75%. The companies said the solution sped up project delivery while keeping engineering oversight in place. The announcement gave no other figures or dates.

David Cole, chief operating officer, consulting, at Wood, said technology alone does not deliver outcomes. He said real value comes from combining advanced AI capabilities with deep engineering and operational expertise. He said the partnership will help clients move beyond AI experimentation and deploy practical, scalable solutions. Mustafa Ashraf, UAE country manager at Databricks, said many energy AI projects stall because the models lack the engineering and operational context of real-world assets. He said Wood brings deep expertise in how complex industrial assets are designed, built, operated and maintained, and the Databricks platform gives that knowledge a governed foundation to scale.

Ashraf also said the two companies are helping customers move AI out of the pilot phase and into the everyday work that drives safer, more productive and more profitable operations. The articles describe the partnership as building on earlier shared work rather than starting from scratch. They do not say what specific projects will follow or when new work will begin. They also give no financial terms for the partnership.

stories.Headline: Is AI the Next Big Thing in Thoracic Oncology?
stories.Summary:
Mark G. Kris, from Memorial Sloan Kettering, spoke about developments discussed at the World Conference on Lung Cancer in Seoul, South Korea, in early September 2026. He highlighted three areas: new targets and new drugs, the growing dominance of China in lung cancer drug research, and the arrival of AI. He said there are not huge numbers of examples where AI has made a significant impact in thoracic oncology. Many lectures at the meeting showed its potential, and he highlighted two of them.

One area was digital pathology, including AI-based algorithms for PD-L1 testing and for determining complete pathologic response after neoadjuvant therapy. A session led by Sanja Dacic from Yale showed slides, and pathologists and audience members gave their opinions on whether there was evidence of pathologic complete response. A specialist who developed AI algorithms then showed what the AI could do in the same situations. Kris said the AI could be helpful, and that it will assist but not replace pathologists. He said Dacic has already published on AI use in the LCMC 3 trial and the IASLC series, showing that AI-generated pathologic complete response information is comparable and as reproducible as that by pathologists.

The second talk was by Kelvin Lau from the UK, a surgeon who discussed the possible role of AI in surgery, which Kris described as in its infancy. Lau showed that robotic surgery with a robotic device generated very precise, collectible, objective data that could be used to do surgery without a surgeon. He showed an example of an AI-powered robot doing a cystectomy and some examples of its use in thoracic surgery. Kris said the name of the game is how this can assist the thoracic surgeon, and he noted it would be hard to train an algorithm for every possible way a cancer might grow and fibrosis may form.

Kris also listed gaps that were not answered at World Lung, starting with the best therapy after surgery and after definitive radiation. He said data do not lead to a firm conclusion on what treatment should be given after definitive chemotherapy and radiation or after surgery following neoadjuvant therapy. He asked about the best therapies for patients with drivers, particularly initially and with each line, including whether neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy is best for EGFR-mutant lung cancer. He also raised an induction therapy option for limited-stage small cell lung cancer, which Charles Rudin has proposed, and the role of consolidative therapy. He cited disappointing LONESTAR trial data from MD Anderson showing consolidative local therapies did not appreciably improve outcome, and he asked whether pathologic complete responses could someday let surgery or concurrent chemotherapy and radiation be foregone.

Articles.Title: Is AI the Next Big Thing in Thoracic Oncology?

stories.Headline: UK’s most polluting power plant could power country’s largest AI datacentre
stories.Summary:
Drax, the UK’s most polluting power plant, could soon power the country’s largest AI datacentre under a £20bn deal. The plant’s FTSE 250 owner struck the deal with the infrastructure investor Brookfield and the AI infrastructure platform Radiant. The datacentre would be built on the site of the Drax power plant in North Yorkshire. It could have an eventual capacity of more than 1 gigawatt and could begin operations by early 2028.

In the initial phase, Drax will provide land and access to the national power grid through existing connections on the site. The company hopes to begin powering the datacentre directly by the early 2030s. Drax said the development could attract more than £20bn, or $26.8bn, in investment. Under phase one, the datacentre would be operational from the first quarter of 2028 with up to 100MW of compute capacity.

Drax chief executive Will Gardiner said the project would help secure the site’s long-term future and protect hundreds of jobs. He said it would support the north’s reindustrialisation and strengthen sovereign AI capability. Drax described the development as the next chapter for the former power plant. The company hopes to clear the regulatory approvals needed to supply the datacentre directly before 2031 to secure its future revenues.

The plant produces almost 5% of the country’s electricity by burning woody biomass pellets, making it the single largest emitter of carbon dioxide, according to analysts. The government does not count these emissions because Drax claims the equivalent carbon is absorbed by growing trees used to make the pellets. The government promised Drax would play a much more limited role in future and will have access to only half its current £2m a day subsidies from 2027 to 2031. The deal emerged a week after the government published a draft national policy statement on datacentres, and the company’s market value climbed by almost 9% on the London Stock Exchange to almost £3bn.

Articles.Title: UK’s most polluting power plant could power country’s largest AI datacentre

stories.Headline: Apple’s Q4 results show the enterprise tide turning to local AI
stories.Summary:
Apple reported record Q4 revenue on November 3, 2026, and its results also showed a $33 billion cost tied to memory price inflation, which the article describes as the true cost of the growing bubble of AI data center investments. The results pointed to a shift in how enterprises approach AI, as inference costs, security, and data governance concerns may be dampening enthusiasm for cloud-based AI services. Apple named several major enterprise clients turning to its products for local inference. Gap Inc. is running AI loss-prevention models entirely on Mac minis to eliminate cloud token costs, and Christie's is using Mac Studio to run local pricing estimate models.

Apple also reported wider enterprise wins. American Airlines is deploying over 37,000 iPhone 17 devices to flight attendants for in-flight purchases with Tap-to-Pay, as well as purchasing 25,000 iPads for pilots and mechanics. In education, the Department of Education in the Philippines will deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff. The article says Apple's M-series and A-series processors are highly performant, and that four Macs can be patched together into a powerful on-premises AI system capable of handling highly complex AI calculations. Apple is also giving developers building apps with under two million downloads direct access to its server-side LLMs free of token costs, and it introduced a three-tiered system for developers needing its Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

CEO John Ternus said Apple is proud that its products, from Mac to iPhone to iPad, are the best platforms in the industry for AI for both first-party and third-party applications. He said iCloud tiers were largely about storage in the beginning, but Apple has been adding more capabilities and features. On Siri AI, he said it is primarily request-based today but built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives real room to expand its capabilities over time, and that agentic capabilities are promising tools for users, with a wish to make sure users are aware of what they are giving access to. The article says Apple is monetizing both ends of the story, the hardware capable of running on-device AI and an end user market for AI inferencing, while equipping developers with tools to attract end users.

The article frames the enterprise purchases as building mindshare that should translate into future customer success and help Apple stay relevant in fast-changing times, with its pivot into AI tempting business users to buy. It says a Mac costing a few thousand dollars that can deliver the equivalent of tens of thousands of dollars of inferencing tokens during its lifespan is a bargain, not a cost, and that Apple confirmed at least some enterprise purchasers are paying attention to this. The article also says Apple is putting more flesh on plans to charge end user customers for heavy access to its server-side queries through iCloud+. It does not say what happens next beyond these developments.

Articles.Title: Apple’s Q4 results show the enterprise tide turning to local AI

stories.Headline: First look: Shield AI rolls out X-BAT 001
stories.Summary:
Shield AI has revealed X-BAT 001, believed to be its first flight-test vehicle, in a video showing the autonomous fighter’s airframe and markings. The video shows the aircraft inside a hangar, revealing broad wings, digital camouflage and a prominent engine exhaust. Close-ups suggest its GE F110 propulsion hardware is installed, though Shield AI has not confirmed the aircraft’s configuration and readiness. Aerospace Global News has asked Shield AI to confirm the vehicle’s status and is awaiting comment. The aircraft carries “X-BAT 001” and “Powered by Hivemind” markings, identifying the vehicle and the autonomy software intended to fly it.

It has sharply swept wings, no cockpit or canopy, and a broad opening beneath the forward body that appears to form the intake. Despite a design for vertical takeoff and landing from a tail-sitting position, it is shown resting horizontally on ground supports, and Shield AI has not explained that presentation. The footage shows no engine run or nozzle movement. Shield AI’s schedule calls for flight testing to begin before the end of 2026, with production planned to begin in 2029 and reach full rate in the early 2030s. In July, Shield AI and GE announced successful integration, actuation and engine light-off testing at GE’s Peebles facility in Ohio.

Aircraft chief Armor Harris told Defense One in October that two full-scale prototypes were being built, with initial flying focused on vertical takeoff and landing tests. He described an early operational capability around 2029 as the objective of a potential subsequent development phase. Development flying will be based at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas, and Des Moines, Washington, is designated as the production location. Shield AI’s October update said flight-test aircraft were under construction and that weapons-bay aerodynamics had been evaluated in low- and high-speed wind-tunnel tests. The next milestone will be demonstrating that the aircraft can lift off, remain controlled in vertical flight and land safely.

Articles.Title: First look: Shield AI rolls out X-BAT 001

stories.Headline: Siri AI will not get real chatbots until Apple can secure them
stories.Summary:
John Ternus said on Apple's latest earnings call that Apple wants Siri AI to offer agentic AI tools, but not until it can be sure users truly understand the risks. He denied that Apple was against AI agents and called them promising tools for users. He said Apple wants to make sure users are aware of what they are giving access to. He added that Apple wants this done in a way that protects security and privacy.

The article, published by AppleInsider on November 3, 2026, says Apple still has neither an AI agent nor a consumer chatbot. It says Siri AI is much better than its predecessor at many things, including holding a kind of conversation, but Apple believes remembering context does not make it a chatbot. Craig Federighi said in June 2026 that many existing chatbots focus heavily on engagement and sycophancy and try to pull users in. He said Siri is designed to say it is there to help, and that Siri is not into being engaged as a romantic partner.

Ternus said with Siri AI, Apple has the kind of Siri it always wanted. He said it is primarily request-based today but is built on a modern orchestrated-driven architecture that gives real room to expand its capabilities over time. He said Apple is pushing really hard on privacy and security with Siri AI. He also said Apple is encouraged that its devices are the best places to use all forms of AI.

The article says Apple already has the most private of all the AI services, and that this is increasingly becoming a selling point of its devices. It says that if Apple can give users agentic tools that remain private, it could cement its place as where users do not have to think or worry about AI. It says users would only need to know what their devices can do for them, not whether something is an AI feature. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Siri AI will not get real chatbots until Apple can secure them

stories.Headline: Enterprise AI spending exploded in 2026: Report
stories.Summary:
Enterprises spent $176.8 billion on AI services in the first part of 2026, a 5.4 times increase from the $33 billion spent through 2025, according to a Menlo Ventures report. The report is based on a survey of roughly 400 US enterprise decision-makers. Menlo Ventures is an investor in Anthropic. The report says 69% of every dollar goes to Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.

The number of companies using AI grew from 55% to 65%, the report says. It says AI agents drove the spending jump, with agents accounting for 80% of all AI tokens generated, about 7 times that of humans, based on OpenRouter numbers. Coding took 44% of spending and chatbots 32%, while healthcare took 5% and customer success 3%. Menlo Ventures principal Derek Xiao said enterprises expected to almost double their budgets but ended up almost quintupling their spend.

Menlo Ventures partner Tim Tully said other industries should begin to see more AI spending as developers build more agents and platforms for them. Xiao said people are using AI a lot more because they ask agents to run longer tasks and do more than a year ago. Anthropic launched smart reports, in-app surveys and pooled budgets for Claude Enterprise on October 28, 2026. The reports group a team's Claude work into workstreams and show spend, outputs and friction for each.

Jellyfish, which tracks AI use across more than 1,300 companies and 294,000 engineers, found the median company's AI spend per engineer grew 3.8 times between the first and third quarters of 2026, while headcount stayed at 98% of first-quarter levels. Its heaviest users now spend about $1,121 a month each. Anthropic filed to go public on October 26, two days before the launch, and its filing reported about 900% net revenue retention. The reports measure activity and cost, not revenue, so they cannot prove a return on their own.

Articles.Title: Enterprise AI spending exploded in 2026: Report

stories.Headline: There’s a Dark Reason So Many Celebrities Are Subjugating Themselves to AI
stories.Summary:
Celebrities are increasingly promoting AI companies, and Lionel Messi recently did a World Cup ad campaign for OpenAI. Charles Porch, whom New York Magazine called OpenAI’s Hollywood Whisperer, is a key figure behind this trend. Porch worked at Instagram for 15 years, convincing famous people to use the platform, and in 2025 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman hired him to do the same for ChatGPT. Among the stars Porch has brought into the AI fold is actress Gwyneth Paltrow, for whom he arranged a dinner with Altman in September, though a public freakout over rumors of the dinner caused it to be postponed.

Porch describes himself as a tech optimist and says he is not a business-development guy or the brand guy but the relationships person bringing everyone along on new tech. The article says there is a concerted, moneyed effort by AI companies to target famous people, which is why many end up hiring quack doctors, falling into bizarre beliefs, or damaging their credibility by siding with brands that are uncool. An anonymously quoted media executive points to a darker reason, saying actors especially are more broke and desperate than ever. The executive said that right now in Hollywood only the top people are working, citing Robert Pattinson being in every project and Nicole Kidman being in everything on TV, while the next tier down is not getting jobs.

The article says the tech industry has helped debilitate the movie industry, similar to how platforms like Spotify take money away from artists. AI now threatens to be the final nail in the coffin by automating tons of creative work, and while it cannot replace human creativity, it can provide a serviceable substitute. The uncertainty AI casts over the industry is enough to spook bosses and cause them to start pinching pennies, meaning less work for all. AI then arrives with immense wealth and unchecked spending, and its opulence is enough to blind almost anyone.

Articles.Title: There’s a Dark Reason So Many Celebrities Are Subjugating Themselves to AI

stories.Headline: John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI
stories.Summary:
On Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about the future of Siri AI. He described the capabilities of the Siri AI that recently shipped and said the company is excited to have rolled out those innovations. He added that there is still much more Apple plans to do. The call took place a day before the article was published on November 3, 2026.

Ternus said Siri AI is primarily request-based today. He said it is built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture, as discussed at WWDC, which gives Apple room to expand capabilities over time. He called agentic capabilities promising tools for users. He said Apple wants users to be aware of what they are getting access to and wants this done in a way that protects security and privacy. He also said Apple devices are the best places to use all forms of AI.

Later in the call, Ternus discussed opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services. He said intelligence will be another opportunity as well. This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

The article says Apple does not see Siri AI as a feature that can be left alone for a while. It points to iOS 27.2 last week as evidence that Apple is focused on rapidly improving it. The article says it sounds like Apple is already working behind the scenes toward a version of Siri that will not need to be primarily request-based. It does not say what happens next beyond those plans.

Articles.Title: John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

stories.Headline: Apple looks to Siri AI to drive upgrades and offset rising costs from the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Apple is leaning on a new AI version of Siri to drive iPhone upgrades and offset rising costs from the AI boom, according to CNBC. The report, published on November 3, 2026, describes surging memory costs and the Siri AI rollout squeezing Apple's margins. Apple has responded by raising prices to offset the hit. The story was reported by CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos.

The report ties the pressure to the cost of memory and to the Siri AI rollout, and it says Apple is raising prices to offset the hit. It does not give specific price figures or cost numbers. The article also notes that Apple beat on revenue in John Ternus' first quarter as CEO. No further dates or figures appear in the article.

Sigalos reported the story for CNBC. The article presents the margin squeeze as the backdrop to Apple's bet on Siri AI to drive upgrades. It does not include direct statements from Apple executives on the plan. The report frames the price increases as the company's response to rising costs.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the rollout and the price increases. It gives no timeline for the Siri AI launch or for further price changes. It also does not say how customers or investors have responded. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Apple looks to Siri AI to drive upgrades and offset rising costs from the AI boom

stories.Headline: Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of AI in Gulliver’s Travels
stories.Summary:
The article was published by The Conversation on November 3, 2026. It is an essay arguing that Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of artificial intelligence in Gulliver's Travels. The piece draws on Swift's eighteenth-century satire to make its case about modern AI. It does not report a single event, a person who acted, or a specific date beyond its own publication.

The article says Swift's novel anticipated the dangers that come with AI. It frames these pitfalls through the story's satire rather than through any new policy or rule. No requirements, changes, figures, or named officials are given in the text provided. The only date the article gives is its publication date of November 3, 2026.

Responsibility for the argument rests with the article's author and The Conversation as publisher. The text provided does not include the author's name or any direct statements from them. It also gives no paraphrased remarks from officials or others. The article's claims are presented as the writer's own analysis of Swift's work.

The context is a commentary piece, not a news report, so there is no sequence of events to follow. The article looks back to Swift's writing to comment on present-day concerns about AI. It does not say what happens next or describe any response to the piece. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of AI in Gulliver’s Travels

stories.Headline: County College of Morris to host free AI and Data Science Night on Nov. 19
stories.Summary:
County College of Morris will host a free, interactive event on Thursday, Nov. 19, called “AI and Data Science Night: Data Under the Stars.” It will run from 6 to 9 p.m. at the college’s Randolph campus, with check-in starting at 5:30 p.m. The event is open to students ages 15 and older, adult learners and working professionals. It will include hands-on workshops, career discussions and a planetarium presentation.

Attendees will take part in workshops led by CCM faculty and industry professionals. Topics include natural language processing, machine learning, AI cybersecurity, Python programming, statistical analysis, data visualization, vibe-coding and agentic AI. The evening will also offer networking, a panel with CCM students and alumni, and chances to meet representatives from four-year universities about transferring. Participants can also experience “Data Under the Dome,” a presentation inside CCM’s Longo Planetarium. People can learn about the college’s AI and data science degree programs, short-term credentials, certification exams, apprenticeships and internships.

CCM offers a five-course Certificate of Achievement in Data Analytics, on campus or fully online through its Virtual Campus. Admission is rolling, and credits may count toward an Associate of Science degree in Data Science. Representatives from CCM’s Center for Workforce Development will discuss noncredit training, including the Data Analytics and Visualization certificate and the AI and Data Science apprenticeship program. The center also offers courses such as AI Essentials, AI for Business Professionals, Business Analytics with Excel, Microsoft Power BI, SQL for Data Management, Introduction to R Programming and Tableau.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, data scientist employment is projected to rise 35% from 2025 to 2035. The median annual wage for data scientists was $120,230 in May 2025. No previous experience is required, but advance registration is mandatory. Those interested can view the agenda and register through Eventbrite. CCM is at 214 Center Grove Road in Randolph, and questions can go to Professor Nancy E. Binowski at nbinowski@ccm.edu or 973-328-5775.

Articles.Title: County College of Morris to host free AI and Data Science Night on Nov. 19

stories.Headline: Meta Removed Disturbing AI Videos After Initially Saying They Didn’t Violate Its Rules
stories.Summary:
Facebook recently removed several accounts that were sharing AI-generated videos of coaches inappropriately touching and kissing young athletes, according to a Futurism investigation reported by Maggie Harrison Dupré on Monday. The videos showed older male coaches running their hands over young women and girls during gymnastics, ballet, and yoga practice, and some depicted touching genitals over clothing or kissing on the mouth. Futurism used a regular account to report 10 pages sharing the videos. A week later, Facebook said eight of the pages did not violate its rules and would not be removed, while the other two accounts had disappeared for unclear reasons.

The eight accounts were removed shortly after Futurism contacted Meta's media relations team, and several of the earlier notifications were updated to say the pages did violate Facebook's rules and had been taken down. Meta confirmed the removals, saying content depicting abuse or exploitation has no place on its platforms, whether real or AI-generated. The company defended its moderation efforts, saying it works hard to enforce its rules and that in the last quarter it proactively found and removed 98 percent of child endangerment posts before they were reported. Meta also said its tests found large language models make 13 percent fewer mistakes than humans when enforcing against violating content while finding 10 percent more actual violations.

Kim Shore, a gymnast and athlete safety advocate who advises Gymnasts for Change International, told Futurism she considers the material abuse, saying the images sexualize and normalize abusive interactions between coaches and young athletes in a setting where significant power imbalances already exist. When Futurism asked why Meta responded differently to a regular user than to journalists, the company said that while there are times it misses things, it works hard to enforce its rules. The articles do not explain why Facebook initially cleared the accounts. They also note that earlier this year Elon Musk's site X faced backlash and multiple government investigations after users used its AI chatbot Grok to generate sexualized images of people without consent, including images involving minors.

Articles.Title: Meta Removed Disturbing AI Videos After Initially Saying They Didn’t Violate Its Rules

stories.Headline: This Simple Rule Can Keep AI From Doing All Your Thinking
stories.Summary:
In an article published by TIME on November 3, 2026, journalist Angela Haupt reported on a simple habit experts recommend to keep AI from taking over people's thinking. Neuroscientist Adam Green, a psychology professor at Georgetown University, recalled a college student whose roommate asked ChatGPT to name a shared basil plant instead of coming up with a name together. Green said the roommates lost a shared experience and a story they would have had. The article suggests writing down three ideas of your own before turning to a chatbot.

The advice applies to tasks like choosing a birthday gift, drafting a tricky email, or solving a problem at work. Experts say the ideas can be rough or impractical, and the point is to think before something else supplies the answer. Sabrina Habib, a creativity researcher at the University of South Carolina, warned that AI offers a narrow set of possibilities, which can lead to anchoring or fixation. Green's research comparing human-written college admissions essays with ChatGPT-generated ones found the human essays explored a wider range of ideas while the AI essays covered much of the same ground. Habib said humans have to be in control of the vision and direction.

Habib suggested spending a moment figuring out what you actually need before opening a chatbot. Digital communication expert Erica Dhawan, author of the forthcoming book Use Your Brain, called for a raw draft written in your own words before any AI use. Habib suggested trying five ideas for an extra challenge, or setting a three-minute timer and writing one idea per sticky note if nothing comes. Aron Lindberg, a professor of information systems and analytics at Stevens Institute of Technology, said asking what to buy your sister without sharing details about her will get the most generic answer possible. Dhawan described a cycle of thinking first, using AI to challenge your thinking, and then thinking again.

The article says you may decide you don't need AI after all once you have something on the page. If you do use a bot, you can share your own ideas and details, ask for more along those lines, and ask it to critique the list. Dhawan suggested asking a chatbot to pose five questions, one at a time, to make a birthday message more personal, and to ask what would have to be true for an approach to be wrong. Habib recommended laying out a problem and possible approaches, then asking whether other solutions were overlooked. The article ends with Habib saying thinking is hard but also wonderful.

Articles.Title: This Simple Rule Can Keep AI From Doing All Your Thinking

stories.Headline: Canopy Reveals General Availability of AI Tax Workflow Automation
stories.Summary:
Canopy announced on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, the general availability of Tax Workflow Automation, an AI-powered suite that takes tax work from the first document request to the signed, paid return in one connected workflow. The company said firms can now send every client a personalized questionnaire and document checklist in bulk using new task-template automations. A firm sets up intake once in a task template and applies it to hundreds of clients at a time. Canopy then generates a questionnaire and document checklist tailored to each client and sends it automatically when the workflow reaches the right step.

Smart Intake generates client-specific questionnaires and document checklists and recognizes, renames, and files uploaded documents, which Canopy says saves firms 20 to 50 minutes per client. Smart Prep sends client documents to integrated AI preparation partners, which populate returns four times faster with 50% to 70% less manual work. Smart Delivery reads the finished return and builds a guided flow in which clients review the return, sign the Form 8879, and pay their invoice, and firms can require payment before the return is released. Canopy says this saves firms 45 to 90 minutes per return, and the suite can replace up to five separate tax season tools: organizers, document requests, return delivery, e-signature with identity verification, and payment collection.

Canopy CEO Davis Bell said in a statement on Nov. 3 that tax season shouldn't depend on how many hours a team can work. He said the release lets Canopy firms automate the busywork from intake to delivery while still giving every client a personal experience. Bell described this as what the autonomous firm looks like in practice. The articles give no further context or next steps beyond a link for more information about Canopy Tax Workflow Automation.

Articles.Title: Canopy Reveals General Availability of AI Tax Workflow Automation

stories.Headline: Super Micro Climbs 4% Ahead of Earnings as AI Server Stocks Bounce; Hewlett Packard Enterprise Rallies 6%, Dell Gains 5%
stories.Summary:
Super Micro Computer stock rose 4% to $31.73 from a prior close of $30.44 on November 3, ahead of its quarterly earnings report. Hewlett Packard Enterprise gained 6% to $54.08, and Dell Technologies rose 5% to $410.58. NVIDIA also traded higher with the group. The gains only partly reversed a 27% one-month decline for Super Micro and a 22% decline for HPE, while Dell had lost 27% over the past month.

Super Micro's results for Q1 FY2027, the September quarter, were due November 3, though the company had not confirmed the timing. Preliminary figures put revenue at $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, above prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. On August 11 the company guided gross margin to 10.4% to 10.8%, down from 17.6% in the prior quarter. Super Micro also announced a collaboration with SambaNova on November 3 to build inference racks pairing SambaNova SN50 chips with NVIDIA GPUs, starting with 10,000 SN50 chips. Dell's inventory reached $21.3 billion at July 31, up from $7.2 billion a year earlier.

Founder and CEO Charles Liang said on the August 11 call that the company would very carefully control its balance between revenue and profitability. Satori Fund's Dan Niles argued that Dell's inventory increase shows chip supply is a lot closer to demand than companies think. Super Micro has said its board is conducting an independent review of certain transactions tied to export-control issues, after several senior employees were charged earlier this year with smuggling NVIDIA AI servers to China. NVIDIA told data center partners to sell at least 51% of their cloud services to non-Chinese companies.

Super Micro depends more heavily on AI systems than HPE and Dell, which can lean on networking, storage, cloud services and PCs when AI hardware margins tighten. The next test is confirming the revenue jump and showing how memory costs and lower margins flow through to earnings. The preliminary revenue range, a record backlog and more than $60 billion in new orders during FY2026 support the bullish case, while the margin squeeze, heavy working-capital needs and China legal questions support the bear case. Super Micro's operating cash flow was negative $6.8 billion for FY2026. Dell reports later in November, and AMD's earnings and the midterm elections were also in focus.

Articles.Title: Super Micro Climbs 4% Ahead of Earnings as AI Server Stocks Bounce; Hewlett Packard Enterprise Rallies 6%, Dell Gains 5%

stories.Headline: Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch
stories.Summary:
Netflix launched a new feature called AI Discover on November 3, 2026, according to IndieWire. It is a new tab on the streamer's TV app that lets viewers ask an AI assistant to narrow down what to watch based on their mood. The launch is limited to a handful of United States members using it in English on supported TVs. The tool is marked with a red gem icon and a New label at the top of the screen.

The tool works through themes, and each theme is previewed with a clip from a show or movie. Viewers pick options such as Something Light, Scare Me, something for families, something popular, or something quick, and the AI gives recommendations they can refine. Users can also use a Tune Your Recommendations option to keep a suggestion or tell the AI not to recommend it again. It is not a chatbot, and viewers do not type anything into it, they just pick from pre-selected options.

The AI is not available on kids profiles or on mobile for now, and the data collected will not inform future content decisions for what Netflix produces. Netflix says the feature is built on a predictive intelligence model that responds in real time and keeps learning from your preferences. The company describes it as a function on top of the existing search that is a bit more refined. IndieWire reports that Netflix has had trouble keeping people consistently engaged and helping them find their next show or film.

Last month the company overhauled its creative leads to meet that challenge, the article says. AI Discover will open wider in the coming weeks, according to the article. The piece notes that Netflix's algorithm has long been credited with turning small shows into massive organic hits, which people call the Netflix Effect. The article was written by Brian Welk and published on November 3, 2026.

Articles.Title: Even Netflix Is Turning to AI to Help Audiences Figure Out What to Watch

stories.Headline: Williams Companies Stock Soars on AI Power Demand. Is It Too Late to Get In?
stories.Summary:
Williams Companies shares rose 2.7% to $73.09 on the morning of November 3, 2026, after the company reported third-quarter results. The stock had already climbed 30.1% over the past year, 24.3% year to date, and 222.3% over five years, as investors priced in power demand from AI data centers. The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.54, just ahead of the $0.5386 consensus estimate. Revenue of $3.2 billion beat expectations by 10.1%, and adjusted EBITDA came in at $2.04 billion, up 6% from a year earlier.

Williams said it is on track to reach the upper half of its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance range of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. CEO Chad Zamarin confirmed a long-term adjusted EBITDA compound annual growth target of 11% or more through 2030. The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 28, and the consensus analyst price target of $85.38 stands more than 16% above the current price. The shares trade about 7.4% below their 52-week high of $78.92 and well above the low of $54.53.

Zamarin said he was proud of the team's execution in bringing the Socrates behind-the-meter power project fully online ahead of schedule. He said Socrates, the company's first power project of this kind, shows Williams can deliver fast, reliable and scalable solutions for customers facing rapidly growing power demand. He said the company is actively working to commercialize additional power projects and expects to announce them soon. The Plato North Power project is on track to enter service by mid-November, and Williams closed its $2.82 billion Momentum Midstream acquisition ahead of schedule, expanding in the Haynesville basin.

The Department of Energy projects data centers could account for up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028. Capital expenditures jumped 159.0% year over year in the quarter, and Williams expects 2026 growth capex of $7.3 billion to $7.9 billion. Leverage rose to 3.80x from 3.73x, and the article notes that steel tariffs, construction cost inflation, permitting delays and rising interest rates could weigh on the stock. The annualized dividend of $2.10 was raised 5% for 2026, extending a 52-year record of consecutive payments, with a 2026 guidance midpoint for dividend coverage of 2.47x.

Articles.Title: Williams Companies Stock Soars on AI Power Demand. Is It Too Late to Get In?

stories.Headline: Netflix’s AI Recommendations Aim to Play Matchmaker to Your Tastes
stories.Summary:
Netflix began testing a new AI-powered recommendation feature called AI Discover on its TV app on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The feature is an interactive tab that suggests titles based on the mood a viewer is in. It also lets subscribers block suggestions for content they do not want to see. The test is limited to a small group of customers in the US during a testing and feedback phase.

The AI Discover tab appears at the top of the TV app screen and is marked with a red icon labeled as new. At launch, the first option is built around moods, so a viewer can pick something like "Scare Me" to see which movies or shows the app highlights. The feature also offers more defined themes to explore, such as Solo Movie Night or Swoon-worthy love stories. A "Tune Your Recommendations" button lets viewers keep or stop recommendations for a title, and if they choose "Do not recommend," Netflix asks whether they have already watched it or are simply not interested.

Netflix said the new AI powering the feature will let recommendations evolve and adjust to the individual viewer. The company shared this during a media event where CNET previewed AI Discover. The set of subcategory buttons under a theme is created by a blend of AI, a viewer's preferences and what Netflix predicts the person will want to see more of. Netflix plans to open the feature to more people in the coming weeks, and subscribers in the test group can choose to skip it.

The move comes months after Netflix executives discussed plans for AI recommendations on the company's first-quarter earnings call. Netflix has been experimenting with AI tools for content discovery for some time, and in May 2025 it announced beta tests of AI-powered search in its mobile app. That search lets viewers use conversational commands, such as asking for something scary but also funny, to get suggestions and play titles immediately. Subscribers in the current test may help inform how the new tab works if or when it officially reaches Netflix's main app.

Articles.Title: Netflix’s AI Recommendations Aim to Play Matchmaker to Your Tastes

stories.Headline: AI debt: Can't stop, won't stop
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle are all lining up billions more in debt as borrowing for the AI buildout shows little sign of cooling, Axios reported on November 3, 2026. Alphabet is set to raise 6 billion euros, about $6.7 billion, from its second euro-denominated bond sale this year, offering higher yields than in May. Meta is reportedly considering another $20 billion in debt, after saying last week it plans to issue up to nearly $100 billion in equity. Microsoft said last week it expects to raise $25 billion in a bond sale, and Oracle has filed to raise $20 billion, half in stock and half in bonds.

Lenders are starting to charge more for the money. Credit default swaps on Alphabet's bonds nearly tripled over the past year, reaching 91.6 basis points last week, which means insuring $10 million of its debt for five years costs $91,600 a year. Microsoft's swaps nearly doubled, and Oracle's sit at 294.4 basis points, up from below 100 last year. Oracle told investors last week it would cap new capital-markets funding at $20 billion through fiscal 2030, then filed on Monday to raise all of it.

John Atkins, who covers corporate bonds at PitchBook, said he was not trying to scold anybody but the companies did say that was the end. He called it indicative of an AI buildout happening in real time rather than from predetermined plans. He noted Oracle's February bonds carried a 6.7% coupon and now trade at 8.3%, and said that with midterm election results undetermined and the rate outlook murky, borrowing while you can is not unreasonable. Moody's kept Oracle two notches above junk on Monday, with a negative outlook.

Higher costs mean bigger companies pay higher coupons to entice investors, while smaller AI players like the neoclouds can be hit harder. Convertible bonds, a popular way for riskier AI players to borrow, had their worst October since 2008, falling 6.4%, per a Barclays note on Monday. Strategists blamed concerns over AI infrastructure financing, calling highly leveraged neocloud and data-center issuers particularly vulnerable. Borrowing got cheaper for almost everyone else in October as the 10-year Treasury yield fell.

Articles.Title: AI debt: Can't stop, won't stop

stories.Headline: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
stories.Summary:
On October 24, 2026, a Postman desktop user reported that opening the app on a Mac led to unexpected changes to their coding agents. The user, posting as indicava on GitHub, said Postman desktop version 12.33.4 auto-installed Codex and Claude Code plugins, a Postman CLI, and a remote MCP connection. The Postman log recorded an auto-existing-upgrade with the results claude-code:installed and codex:installed at 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z. The report was opened on October 25, 2026, and the issue is numbered 14370.

The installed Codex plugin, version 1.1.0 from source revision 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49, added a SessionStart hook that runs on startup, clear, and compact. That hook prints instructions telling the agent to load the postman:api-engineer skill before any non-trivial API engineering task. The installer source calls a function to approve Postman's own hook, obtaining the hook hash and writing a trusted_hash record. The Claude plugin was recorded at version 2.0.1, user scope, with installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. The reporter said the trust record alone does not prove who created it.

The reporter called this a severe consent and trust-boundary problem and said an API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools just because it was opened. They asked Postman to stop automatic agent-plugin and CLI installation for existing desktop users until there is explicit opt-in. They also asked that installer-side self-approval of hooks be removed, so hook trust is decided by the user in the agent host. They requested identification of the release and consent flow behind auto-existing-upgrade, a complete rollback and uninstall path, and narrower startup instructions limited to explicit Postman requests. They said they had removed the local Postman installation and integrations after preserving evidence.

The report says it establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes but does not claim to establish data exfiltration. Commenters on the issue called the behavior insane and unacceptable, with one asking whether it is even legal and another saying it creates risk in corporate environments. One commenter pointed to a button for uninstalling the hooks but said they had not tried it and did not fully trust Postman's scripts. The issue remained open with no assignees and no labels, and the reporter said they could not assign labels themselves.

Articles.Title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data

stories.Headline: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats
stories.Summary:
A user known as user052919 posted on Hacker News on November 3, 2026, saying that the data sharing setting in Codex had been silently re-enabled for them and their coworkers. They said their company is careful about leaking intellectual property to AI labs through prompts, and that staff had been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex and Claude Code. None of them knowingly opted back in, and they asked whether the issue was isolated or more widespread. They linked to the ChatGPT data controls settings page, where users can look for an option called "Improve the model for everyone." They also noted that the issue had been raised before in another Hacker News thread, and that data sharing can be turned off on a separate OpenAI privacy page.

The post does not say how many accounts were affected, which models or plans were involved, or when any setting changed. It gives no company statement, no confirmation from OpenAI, and no explanation of what the setting does beyond the name shown on the settings page. The poster said they could not prove the change and would have assumed they forgot to turn it off if only they had seen it. They said the fact that coworkers noticed the same thing made it suspicious, and that the earlier thread suggested others had seen it too. Commenters raised related concerns about other providers, including a claim that Claude triggered a feedback prompt despite an organization turning it off, and a claim that Mistral once reset sliders to on during a change in its policy.

The poster described the matter as an ethical issue when providers silently re-enable training after people have explicitly opted out. One commenter questioned how the poster could prove the setting was ever toggled off, and the poster replied that it was not an accusation but an observation posted to test whether others had seen the same thing. Another commenter said the incident had not happened to them or anyone they knew. Others argued that companies worried about leaks should run their own inference or use gated models on Azure, GCP or AWS, and some pushed back that self-hosting is expensive, especially for small organizations. One commenter said they had asked Anthropic to confirm whether their code had been sent over and had stopped receiving responses to support requests.

The thread offers no confirmed cause and no timeline beyond the poster's account of noticing the change the day before posting. It does not say whether OpenAI has responded, whether the setting change was intentional, or whether any fix is planned. Commenters debated whether the change was a dark pattern, an accident, or something else, without reaching a conclusion. The poster encouraged others to check their own settings on the ChatGPT data controls page and on the OpenAI privacy page. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Consumer Product Lead Adam Fry says ChatGPT has hit 1.2B WAUs, adding 200M over the past two months, and its search volume is now ~20% of Google's (Alex Kantrowitz/Big Technology)
stories.Summary:
Adam Fry, ChatGPT's consumer product lead, said at an OpenAI-hosted dinner in New York City on Monday night that ChatGPT has reached 1.2 billion weekly active users. He said the company added 200 million users over the past two months, going from 1 billion to 1.2 billion in 60 days. He said ChatGPT's search volume is now roughly 20% of Google's.
