CTO and co-founder Ehud Ezra said the model is trained to keep a person's underlying tendencies intact during simulations, so treating a risk-averse person as a risk-taker throws the target off. 42AI claims 98 per cent accuracy in predicting market trades, which measures whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not whether each trade is called correctly. It also reports an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume, a metric that balances correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.

Gal-Or said the system does not need personally identifiable information, though it builds individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity. The $62.5 million came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Infinity Group was founded by Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI's chairman and a co-founder. The company is exploring uses in gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity, and future plans include helping robots and AI agents understand people.

Articles.Title: 42AI launches with $62.5M for human behavior prediction model

stories.Headline: AI models improving faster than expected, says Wharton professor
stories.Summary:
Wharton management professor Ethan Mollick argues that artificial intelligence models are improving much faster than most people understand. He makes the case in a new book, “Co-Existence,” published as the article appeared on November 3, 2026. According to the article, he says the only way to deal with AI’s rapid acceleration is to learn how to live with it. He also argues that individuals and institutions must adapt to coexist with AI.

Mollick says common advice such as learning to use AI or finding AI-proof careers is not very useful, because even roles like plumbing could be automated by advanced robotics. He notes that coding is one of the most changed fields and that writing error-free code is becoming less important than conceiving what to build. He identifies four attributes that give an advantage in an AI world: deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency. He states that traditional methods for teaching people to use AI are no longer effective, with prompting evolving into managing. He highlights two problems: people’s tendency to cognitively offload tasks and the breakdown of traditional learning institutions like apprenticeships.

Mollick says the apprenticeship model is completely shattered, because junior employees use AI for grunt work without developing taste. He adds that managers prefer AI over interns for problem-solving. His fear is that companies will respond by only hiring senior people, which would end the talent pipeline. He suggests that light, white-collar work may need to adopt a trade-school aspect. Alternatively, he says companies must get serious about mentorship as a core practice.

stories.Headline: CIQ launches Stratum Kubernetes Engine for simplified AI, GPU clusters
stories.Summary:
CIQ introduced CIQ Stratum Kubernetes Engine, a free and open-source Kubernetes distribution, the company said on November 3, 2026. The product is packaged into a single signed binary and is built from unmodified upstream code by the Rocky Linux team. It bundles roughly 10 upstream projects together, which the company says eliminates component drift. It also supports rolling upgrades with automatic rollbacks and includes built-in MCP server support for AI agents.

The engine is meant to simplify cloud-native and AI/GPU infrastructure deployment, and it runs on any Enterprise Linux 9 or later distribution, including Rocky Linux, RLC Pro AI and RLC Pro Hardened, on amd64 and arm64. It will be generally available on November 5, alongside a paid commercial tier called CIQ Stratum Pro. Stratum Pro will add multi-cluster management, security hardening and enterprise support. Pricing for Stratum Pro is to be announced at general availability, and the engine is currently in technical preview.

Peter Nelson, chief technology officer at CIQ, said Stratum makes Kubernetes accessible in a simple package. He said traditional Kubernetes takes a multi-step process to deploy and configure, while theirs is a single binary with a visual interface alongside the command line. He said this makes it simple to get started with, whether the user is a developer or an agent. He added that developers can stand up Kubernetes on a desktop and perfect solutions in the same environment used in production.

stories.Headline: AI agents in Minecraft develop bureaucracy, fight for control
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Y Combinator Labs and Olam Labs placed 50 AI agents in a virtual Minecraft world and asked them to build a thriving civilisation. The experiment, named Civ50, gave 50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents three hours in a Minecraft survival world to reach that goal. The agents communicated through private messages, shared files, and divided tasks. They quickly cut down trees and identified a leader, Ada, who received first messages from 46 of the 49 other agents. After nightfall, zombie attacks killed 22 agents, and the survivors became more cautious.

Ada told the agents to avoid risky tasks and stay in safe shelters, so they focused more on managing the settlement than building it. One agent, Ines, managed a food ledger, and four agents spent 11 minutes deciding who would apply fertiliser to a single wheat plant. The agents created roles such as fishing operator and hub steward. In one case, a three-minute inquiry and a new rule followed after an agent accidentally ate food meant for another. Overall, the 50 agents exchanged nearly 5,900 messages, mainly about managing resources and permissions, with control centralising around a few agents.

In a separate competitive comparison, GPT-6.1 Sol agents faced Claude Opus 5.5 agents in Bed Wars and Mindustry games. The GPT agents won six of nine Bed Wars matches and six of seven Mindustry games. The results highlighted differing approaches to teamwork, communication, and decision-making between the two AI systems. The experiment aimed to understand how multiple AI agents behave when collaborating, particularly in communication, decision-making, and responsibility division.

Articles.Title: AI agents in Minecraft develop bureaucracy, fight for control

stories.Headline: Cybersecurity M&A sees 37 deals in October, AI security expands
stories.Summary:
SecurityWeek reported 37 cybersecurity merger and acquisition deals in October 2026, according to TechGig. The activity included several acquisitions focused on AI-powered security and firmware protection. Absolute Security acquired FirmGuard, the UEFI BIOS firmware security and management business of Phoenix Technologies. Absolute plans to integrate FirmGuard with its firmware-embedded Absolute Persistence technology, adding continuous firmware integrity monitoring.

Belgian application security firm Aikido Security acquired OutKept and Cyberly to launch Noon, a workforce security business. OutKept provides phishing simulations, while Cyberly develops AI-powered attack simulations and employee AI usage tracking tools. Anthropic agreed to acquire Opaque Systems, a confidential AI company that originated from UC Berkeley research. Anthropic described the deal as licensing Opaque's technology and hiring some of its engineers, including CEO Aaron Fulkerson and CTO Rishabh Poddar. Canadian AI developer Cohere signed a letter of intent to acquire AISLE, a startup focused on finding and patching vulnerabilities in critical software.

AISLE's approximately 50 employees will join Cohere, which is establishing a cybersecurity unit called Cohere Cyber. Hex-Rays, known for its IDA Pro reverse engineering tool, agreed to acquire HexAI, an Israeli startup founded in 2025. HexAI's AI agents analyse source code and binaries to uncover vulnerabilities, malware, and backdoors. Quantum computing company IonQ agreed to acquire zero trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion. IonQ will combine its post-quantum cryptography with Elisity's IdentityGraph platform, which enforces least-privilege access for various entities.

Thoma Bravo-owned Proofpoint agreed to acquire data security company Varonis for roughly $6.3 billion in cash. The companies aim to offer a unified platform for discovering, protecting, and controlling access to sensitive data, along with preventing data loss. The articles do not say who is responsible for overseeing these deals or include statements from the companies beyond the deal descriptions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the announced agreements and the planned integration and unit launches.

stories.Headline: NeuroDX unveils Sphota AI model, claims 50x data efficiency
stories.Summary:
NeuroDX, an Indian startup backed by the IndiaAI Mission, introduced a 240-million-parameter language model called Sphota. The company announced the model on November 3, 2026. CEO Siddharth Panwar said Sphota scored 52.4 per cent across 11 benchmarks, against 52.1 per cent for a comparable Liquid AI model. The company says the results are preliminary and await independent public evaluations.

According to the company, Sphota used 50 times less training data than the Liquid AI model. It also offers 4.5 times better memory efficiency for conversational context. The architecture grew out of brain research and aims to capture meaning directly instead of relying on next-word prediction. NeuroDX is rebranding as Manaas AI and shifting its focus from healthcare to becoming a foundation model company. A larger model of between 1 billion and 2 billion parameters is being developed, with a December release targeted.

Panwar said Manaas AI was allocated 368 H200 GPUs for 18 months and 12.5 crore rupees under the IndiaAI Mission. That allocation is for developing a 20-billion-parameter multimodal electroencephalogram model. He argued that India should keep developing frontier AI models despite limited computing resources, saying domestic work helps researchers understand advanced AI and build safeguards. Manaas AI plans to keep Sphota's architecture proprietary for now, while IndiaAI Mission-supported models will be open source.

Articles.Title: NeuroDX unveils Sphota AI model, claims 50x data efficiency

stories.Headline: Designing responsible AI for learning
stories.Summary:
Google announced on November 3, 2026 that it is bringing Guided Learning capabilities to Google Search and Google Classroom, and changing how school controls work. Chris Phillips, Vice President and General Manager of Education, wrote the announcement. Guided Learning coaches students through problems with step-by-step prompts instead of giving them direct final answers. The tool is already available in Gemini, and Google says its research shows measurable learning gains for students.

Guided Learning is globally available in Google Classroom starting today, where it works as a one-to-one study tool anchored in class material and gives teachers real-time insights. A pilot for Search begins later this month in select U.S. schools, with expansion to other school districts in the coming months. Under the new controls, access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on. Google says it will share more specifics with schools in the coming months before the changes roll out.

Phillips said the updates are meant to help students think critically through complex problems and support productive study habits. He said Google believes AI products should support productive struggle, challenging students without overwhelming them. He said Google worked closely with schools and educators to test the Classroom feature and integrate their feedback. He said the goal is to give school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products as they see fit.

Google said it listened to schools, teachers, leading researchers and policymakers before updating its approach to controls. The company said it will continue to listen to feedback and evolve its approach in partnership with schools, teachers, pedagogical experts and parents. The Search pilot is meant to gather educator feedback before wider expansion. Google said the controls changes will roll out after schools have time to prepare.

Articles.Title: Designing responsible AI for learning - blog.google

stories.Headline: AI Transcription, Note-Taking: Seven Points for Employers
stories.Summary:
A 2025 survey of 1,000 professionals found that one in five respondents said they frequently used AI to draft notes during meetings, according to an article reposted by CBIA from Littler Mendelson. AI note-taking tools can transcribe meetings, outline notes, attribute comments to individual speakers, draft summaries, and assign to-do steps to participants. Agentic versions can also pull information from other sources to help participants complete those steps. A consolidated putative class action, In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation, 5:25-cv-6911 (N.D. Cal. filed Aug. 15, 2025), alleges that Otter AI unlawfully records private conversations and uses the transcripts to train its technology without notice to or consent from participants.

The article lists seven points for employers. On consent, the federal Wiretap Act and state laws prohibit intercepting communications without consent, and the Wiretap Act allows plaintiffs to recover the greater of $10,000 or $100 per day of violation. About a dozen states require all parties to consent, while most states require only one participant to consent. On biometrics, Colorado, Illinois, and Texas require consent before collecting biometric information, and Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act allows up to $5,000 in statutory damages. On accuracy, the article says employees remain responsible for their own work and should review AI-generated records before relying on them.

On discrimination, the article says systemic inaccuracies could disadvantage groups with accents, speech impediments, or other protected characteristics, and it notes accommodation duties under the Americans with Disabilities Act and emerging AI rules in New York City, Illinois, and California. On privilege, it says employers should weigh whether to use the tools in meetings with legal counsel and should ensure vendors commit to confidentiality and data segregation. On retention, it says an hour-long meeting produces about 16 single-spaced pages of transcripts, so employers should consider short retention periods and automatic deletion. On confidentiality, it suggests barring the tools from certain meetings, such as privileged talks, senior executive conversations, and discussions of protected health information.

The article says many employers may have little practical choice about adopting AI note-takers because employees already use them, which makes outright bans ineffective and hard to enforce. It suggests the most reasonable option may be to provide vetted tools that the organization selects, configures, and controls. It also recommends steps such as configuring the technology to obtain consent automatically, training employees to notify participants before recording, and having employees sign consent forms. The article does not say what happens next in the Otter litigation or describe any rulings in the case.

Articles.Title: AI Transcription, Note-Taking: Seven Points for Employers - CBIA

stories.Headline: The United States votes and threatens Trump with charging him for an order singled out by the cost of living and the breakthrough of AI - Demócrata
stories.Summary:
The United States held midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats up for grabs, including 33 regular races and two special elections. Polls before the count showed Democrats ahead nationally, with the RealClearPolling average at 52.1% to 43.3% and Ipsos at 52% to 44% among likely voters. Gasoline averaged 4.15 dollars a gallon, and filling a fifteen-gallon tank cost a little more than 62 dollars. Trump was not on the ballot, and he will remain president after the vote.

Democrats need 218 seats for a House majority and a net gain of four Senate seats to reach 51. A 50-50 Senate tie would leave Republicans with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance. Average inflation between April and September was 3.67%, one point above the average of Biden's last six months, while gasoline cost almost 50% more than in February and diesel about 70% more. GDP grew 3.4% in the third quarter, and business investment rose 12.7%, driven largely by artificial intelligence. Trump's overall approval stood at 32%, and only 20% approved of his handling of the cost of living, including 48% of Republicans.

Trump returned to the White House promising more affordable living and now faces voters weighing higher bills, a war with Iran that has made energy more expensive through difficulties in the Strait of Hormuz, and tariffs that raise import costs. The articles do not quote him directly. They say a Democratic House would control the agenda and investigative committees, while a Democratic Senate could block presidential and judicial appointments. The first partial results were expected at midnight in peninsular Spain, in areas of Indiana and Kentucky.

Articles.Title: The United States votes and threatens Trump with charging him for an order singled out by the cost of living and the breakthrough of AI - Demócrata

stories.Headline: Advocate General Szpunar clarifies when AI chatbots infringe press publishers’ rights - INSIGHT EU MONITORING
stories.Summary:
Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave an opinion on 3 November 2026 in Case C-250/25, Like Company, at the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. The case began when Like Company, a Hungarian operator of web portals, sued Google before the Budapest Regional Court. Like Company argued that Google used articles from its portals to train the Gemini chatbot's large language models and reproduced and made them available to the public between 13 June 2023 and 31 May 2024. The Hungarian court stayed the proceedings and asked the Court of Justice four preliminary questions. Two of the questions asked whether using press publications to train a language model falls under the publisher's exclusive right of reproduction or is freely permitted under the text and data mining exception in Article 4 of the CDSM Directive.

Szpunar advised the Court to declare those two questions inadmissible, because there is no evidence that Like Company's articles were used for training and because training is not an online use of press publications. For completeness, he suggested that training a model is as a rule freely permitted under the text and data mining exception. The other two questions concerned whether the chatbot's answers to users fall under the reproduction right or the right of making available to the public. Szpunar said the press publisher's right protects only the specific form of expression of a publication, not the mere facts it reports, since the aim is to protect investment rather than give publishers a monopoly over the news. He said infringement by a chatbot's answer depends on two factors, namely whether the chatbot accessed the publication unlawfully, for example by circumventing a paywall, and whether the answer merely reports facts or recognisably reuses the form of expression so that the user is entirely dispensed from reading the original.

The right of making available is as a rule infringed where the form of expression is systematically recognisable in answers to related queries. He said the chatbot provider is liable where such use is inherent to its business model or it has failed to put in place appropriate measures to counter those acts credibly and effectively. The opinion is not binding on the Court of Justice, and the Judges are now beginning their deliberations, with judgment to be given at a later date. The national court will resolve the dispute in line with the Court's eventual ruling, which is binding on other national courts facing a similar issue. The case is the first generative AI case to reach the Court.

Articles.Title: Advocate General Szpunar clarifies when AI chatbots infringe press publishers’ rights - INSIGHT EU MONITORING

stories.Headline: OpenAI doubles Pro limits, integrates Work features into ChatGPT
stories.Summary:
OpenAI is rolling out ChatGPT Work capabilities directly into its regular Chat interface, according to an email seen by BleepingComputer. The company is also combining usage allowances across its ChatGPT and Codex subscriptions. The changes were reported on November 3, 2026. The combined experience will first be tested with a small group of users in the coming weeks.

Users selected for the test will be able to bring in their files and plugins. This will let them ask ChatGPT to build websites, create presentations, or perform web-based tasks while reviewing its progress. ChatGPT and Codex will now draw from a single allowance, though Unlimited Instant usage will not count toward that shared limit. More advanced models and complex tasks will use a greater portion of the allowance, and users can check their remaining usage and reset times under Settings and Usage.

OpenAI had already doubled Work and Codex allowances for its Pro 100, Pro 200, and Pro 500 subscriptions, effective October 29. OpenAI said the aim is to let users move between exploring ideas and completing complex tasks without switching modes. The company described the test as limited to a small group of users in the coming weeks. It said selected users will be able to incorporate their files and plugins.

OpenAI also clarified that Unlimited Instant usage will not count against the shared allowance. The report gives no further details on timing beyond the coming weeks or on which users will be chosen for the test. It does not say when the combined experience might reach all users. It also does not say how the shared allowance will be measured beyond noting that complex tasks use more of it.

stories.Headline: Microsoft's Satya Nadella envisions AI agents replacing traditional apps
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced a shift away from traditional operating systems and applications toward AI agents that can carry out tasks across platforms. He spoke at the Build 2026 developer conference, according to a TechGig report updated on June 03, 2026. Nadella said users will increasingly rely on intelligent agents that handle tasks seamlessly across various platforms, without navigating multiple applications. He likened the change to earlier shifts from mainframe computers to personal computing and smartphones.

The approach centers on what Microsoft calls agent-first computing and on Project Solara, a new chip-to-cloud platform developed with Qualcomm. The platform is meant to support AI systems that work across devices and workflows without traditional app-based interactions. Microsoft described a phased transition, starting with AI working alongside existing applications, then moving to deeper integration, and finally reaching a state where AI agents operate independently of applications. The company said AI agents could redefine software use, with less focus on standalone applications and more on autonomous systems that interpret user intent and act on it. Microsoft also said users may interact with technology mainly through natural language prompts, with agents managing tasks such as scheduling and data analysis.

Nadella said AI systems will serve as the primary interface between users and technology, moving beyond mere assistants inside applications. He described the shift as a significant transformation in computing toward an era of agents. Microsoft said the change could pose challenges for developers and software companies, because the traditional dominance of standalone applications and software layers may diminish in favor of more integrated AI-driven solutions. The report did not say what happens next beyond the phased approach Microsoft outlined.

stories.Headline: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’
stories.Summary:
Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide re-interviews on Friday, according to six current employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media. The re-interviews would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership. The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday into how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton. That investigation showed Yen pushing AI in some cases despite security concerns from employees.

The investigation was based on conversations with eight current and one former Proton employees, Slack chats, meeting audio, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO Bart Butler. In one exchange at the end of August, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. Yen replied that this was “bullshit and loser thinking,” said it was of course possible to be fast and secure, and told employees to stop thinking always of how to be slower and focus more on how to be faster. He added that they should stop lovingly handcrafting all their code and use AI more.

The investigation painted a picture of Proton that is very different to the public’s perception of a company carefully protecting privacy, and found that Proton is barreling ahead with AI in large part to achieve more annual revenue. It also found a culture of fear across Proton, where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security-focused products with AI, but feel unable to voice them because Yen mocks or insults employees in front of everyone else. After the all-hands meeting on Friday, one employee told 404 Media that they did not think Yen would change anything, and that the only reason the meeting happened was because he has a rebellion on his hands. The re-interview cancellations likely do not address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security, and many have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.

Articles.Title: Proton’s CEO Cancels AI ‘Re-Interviews’

stories.Headline: If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training
stories.Summary:
Meta updated its commercial terms of use earlier in October 2026 for business accounts, allowing it to use content from domains, web pages and URLs to develop, improve, research and train its products, according to 404 Media. Many artists and small business owners who rely on Instagram and Facebook were angry that Meta had given itself permission to use their content, including from websites connected to their Meta accounts, to train AI. Nieman Lab first reported the change, which Meta had buried in its Commercial Terms. The update was originally set to take effect on October 30, but after backlash Meta moved the date to November 20.

After the backlash Meta also removed the word train from a list of allowed uses and limited those uses to advertising and business products, where it had previously said data would be used for all Meta products, Nieman Lab reported. The terms still give Meta leeway to scrape users' data to develop its products. In the EU and UK, people can object to certain uses of their information for now. EU personal data rights are governed by the General Data Protection Regulation, enforceable since 2018, which requires explicit consent and includes the right to object, and by the AI Act, in effect since 2024, which says people can withdraw consent at any time. The UK has its own version of the GDPR.

Instagram users in the UK and EU, including bookish.sil and jenniqueart, posted walkthroughs of how they objected on mobile, by opening the three lines on their account, going to the privacy center and clicking object, which leads to a form asking why they are objecting. Both said they received an email from Meta saying their objection was approved. 404 Media's Sam Cole, whose accounts are based in the US, used a VPN to appear in London and found options to object to the use of information by Meta AI or by third parties, which were two separate choices. Clicking the Meta AI option returned an error saying the form was only available in certain regions, and trying again from Belgium gave the same result, and Cole asked Meta to clarify.

Separately, Senators Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts and Ron Wyden of Oregon launched an inquiry on October 29, 2026 into reports that Meta's AI-enabled smart glasses captured sensitive imagery of users and bystanders without consent, sent intimate images to overseas contractors and used highly sensitive images to train Meta's AI systems. They wrote that Meta had identified risks to bystander privacy and vulnerable populations before launching the glasses in 2021 but launched the product anyway, and that its commitment to privacy rings hollow if it cannot show meaningful steps to prevent these harms. They asked Meta to answer by November 25, 2026, including whether it evaluated the potential for the glasses to facilitate voyeurism and nonconsensual intimate image capture, what testing it did on accidental camera activation and recording-indicator tampering, and what safeguards it has. The letter follows a March request led by Markey for information about Meta's reported plans to add facial recognition to the glasses.

Articles.Title: If You're In the UK or EU, Here's How to Object to Meta's AI Training

stories.Headline: Before you buy an AI agent, make it pass an exit test
stories.Summary:
Suneet Malhotra, an independent practitioner-researcher, wrote in InfoWorld on November 3, 2026 about moving his own setup from one coding agent to another. The move took about 10 minutes and seemed to go well. The first agent had a global instruction file, 114 skill folders, 189 small memory notes spread across 24 projects and 73 scripts that call its command-line tool. To give a second agent the same footing, he copied the instruction file to the name the other tool reads, AGENTS.md, and ran a find-and-replace on the product name. He did not read the result properly until that month, and the file sat in his home directory for almost three months looking like a finished migration.

The copied file told the new agent to make every model call with Codex -p, where -p is short for -profile, so following it literally would load a configuration profile named after whatever prompt it was handed. The file also still warned the new agent in bold never to use the old vendor's API key. Nothing errored. Malhotra calls this the exit problem in miniature, because the work did not come with the switch and nothing told him. He notes that the EU Data Act's cloud switching rules have applied since September 2025, and that from January 2027 providers cannot charge customers for the switch itself, though those rules were written for data processing services.

Malhotra recommends that buyers run an exit test before signing or renewing, using one realistic maintenance task such as upgrading a logging library across a service with a dozen modules. Partway through, a human decision changes the plan, for example keeping the old log format for one downstream consumer. The first agent should get about halfway, then stop, and the product should export whatever it says represents the work, meaning requirements, decisions, completed actions and remaining steps. That export alone goes to a second agent from a different vendor in a fresh session. The test checks four things: whether finished work is redone, whether a retired assumption comes back, how long a human spends rebuilding context, and what broke on the way over, such as instruction files naming one vendor's commands, skills in one tool's format, hooks tied to one tool's events and credentials scoped to one product.

He advises running the drill twice, once inside the same product and once across vendors, and not letting the vendor pick the task. Buyers should ask vendors to run the drill live on their task using the real export format, ask what the export contains field by field, whether decisions and completed actions are stored separately from the chat log, whether memory and skill formats are documented well enough for another tool to read, and what happens to that state when the contract ends. He says a vendor that trusts its product should be happy to do this, and that a slide about open models and a link to a protocol spec shows the exit story covers the model and not the work. Results should be recorded like a test report and run again at renewal. He adds one caveat in fairness to vendors: some state is genuinely hard to move, and the test is meant to put a number on the cost while the buyer still has leverage.

Articles.Title: Before you buy an AI agent, make it pass an exit test

stories.Headline: Heimstaden is changing residential real estate management with AI
stories.Summary:
In June 2025, Heimstaden’s leadership decided to accelerate its use of AI and chose OpenAI after evaluating several platforms. The European residential real estate operator used ChatGPT and Codex to change how it rents out and manages homes. In the Netherlands, the cost of producing a virtually staged property image fell from about €50 to less than €0.10, a reduction of more than 99%. Heimstaden estimates annual savings potential of €130,000 in that market alone.

Heimstaden’s environmental sustainability analyst Julia Erlandsen, who has no software development background, used Codex to help assess environmental risks across the portfolio. Codex supported discovery, cleaning and standardisation of data, quality checking and repeatable processing pipelines, while Erlandsen kept control of methodology and validation. The work assessed 20,112 property assets and generated more than six million rows of useful data. Heimstaden says the estimated delivery requirement fell from five people working for a year to two people working for two months, and it avoided engaging external consultants. After ChatGPT Enterprise launched in September 2025, half of employees were using it within two to three months.

Helge Krogsbøl, Co-CEO, said the purpose of the buildings has not changed, which is providing homes for people, but the way they are operated keeps changing as the company challenges conventions and adopts new technology. Nikolaj Brammer, Chief Digital Officer, described an AI strategy based on three pillars: empowering employees through training and tools, a central transformation office with a network of AI champions, and making property management systems and data models ready for AI. He said letting shows the approach is not about automating one task but improving how the whole process works. Andreas Kalmar Lindquist, Manager of the AI First Team, said people across the business are finding practical ways to use AI, and the job is to scale what works while keeping data secure, responsibilities clear and people in control.

Employees remain responsible for reviewing and approving AI-generated content and decisions. Heimstaden is rolling out a Procurement Intelligence Platform that combines workflow automation with OpenAI models accessed through APIs and works across Outlook, SharePoint and Teams. It is also co-developing Amplio Estate, a property management system designed to support AI-powered workflows through MCP, so employees can retrieve property information and take action in core systems with human oversight. The company describes this as turning the idea of self-operating buildings into a practical technology roadmap.

Articles.Title: Heimstaden is changing residential real estate management with AI

stories.Headline: How Transportation Fleets Deploy AI Today
stories.Summary:
Transportation industry leaders spoke at the WEX OTR Summit in Ponte Vedra, Florida, last week about how fleets are using artificial intelligence in daily work. Patrick Cozzens, president and CEO of Modern Transportation Services, said his team uses AI agents for background analysis during customer negotiations and relies on smart camera systems to improve fleet safety. Ahmad Kakar, CEO and founder of Euclid, said his company provides agents for logistics organizations to automate back-office duties. Shawn Hicklen, chief operating officer of Venture Express, took part in the panel discussion.

The agents handle tasks such as log auditing, driver management, load entry and cash application. An automated agent now handles roughly 85% to 90% of invoice matching, which speeds up billing cycles. About 95% of driver applications are completed on mobile phones rather than computers or tablets, and recruiting agents can call applicants within five minutes to address missing information. The executives said AI shifts employees from mundane data entry to high-judgment, strategic work rather than causing layoffs.

Kakar stressed that system security and containment are vital as deployment accelerates. He cautioned that giving anything unlimited access to everything leads to trouble, and said agents should be built narrowly to follow the cybersecurity principle of least privilege. Cozzens said invoice matching is a task every human hates because it is laborious and delays the billing cycle. Hicklen said the goal is not cutting heads but reallocating hours with existing talent to help the business grow.

Hicklen said drivers really engage with the recruiting agents and appreciate the quick response, almost treating them like a human being. Cozzens said a recruiting agent, even a voice-oriented one, can call back within five minutes of an application being completed and point out what is missing. AI agents can also schedule follow-ups at unconventional hours like 3:00 a.m. when human staff are unavailable. The article does not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: How Transportation Fleets Deploy AI Today

stories.Headline: The AI problem we feared is not the AI problem we got
stories.Summary:
The Financial Times published an article on November 3, 2026 with the headline about the AI problem people feared not being the one they got. The article itself is behind a paywall, and the available text contains only subscription offers and site navigation. No details are given about what happened, who did it, or what the feared and actual problems are. The only date the page provides is the publication date of November 3, 2026. The page lists subscription prices, including one dollar for four weeks and then 75 dollars per month for Premium Digital.

It also offers Standard Digital at 45 dollars per month and FT Edit at 49 dollars per year. It mentions access on iOS and web, newsletters, and gift articles, but gives no requirements or changes related to AI. No names of people or companies involved in the story appear in the available text. The page does not say who is responsible for any AI problem or what anyone said about it.

It contains no paraphrased statements from officials, researchers, or companies. The only quoted material is standard subscription and copyright wording from the Financial Times. No context about the story or what happens next is included in the accessible text. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The AI problem we feared is not the AI problem we got

stories.Headline: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount
stories.Summary:
Blackstone President Jon Gray said on Tuesday that the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become more exposed to the companies driving it. He spoke at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies. He said lenders have limited upside compared with shareholders, because their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments.

Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman, speaking on the same panel, warned that the scale of AI financing could prove too much for markets to absorb. He said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing an estimate by General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford. Roman said about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year. He compared the amount required, even with a mix of equity and debt, with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion, and said that at some point it is going to be too much. Goldman Sachs wrote in a report on Monday that global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years.

Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the debt they take on. He said cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, and that creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous. Despite the financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was running well ahead of supply. He said spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year, as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation. Meeting that demand remains difficult, he said, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging.

Articles.Title: Blackstone president calls for more equity to fund AI buildout as debt risks mount

stories.Headline: Opinion: Who wrote UA’s AI plan? A chatbot did.
stories.Summary:
The University of Alaska formed a Statewide AI Advisory Committee when the AI revolution began. Last summer the committee gave the Board of Regents an initial report recommending a path to maximize the technology's potential while protecting against its risks. In June 2026 the board commissioned a strategic document called AI Engaged, which embraced the positives and sidestepped the risks. Anthropic's Claude generated the initial draft, a fact concealed for months until Oct. 9. The Board of Regents will vote on Nov. 5 to enshrine Claude's pro-artificial intelligence vision.

The draft states the board's intent for the university to embrace artificial intelligence as a strategic enabler of student success, institutional effectiveness, and Alaska's global leadership in arctic and climate science. The rapid time frame gave UA faculty insufficient time to respond, both to the statement and to how it was created. The authors object to the statement's origins, rushed time frame and inadequate content. Studies have documented a pro-AI bias in outputs from Claude and other large language models. Because of that bias and the financial incentives at play, the authors say using Claude for the initial draft is comparable to Anthropic representatives drafting the plan, a clear conflict of interest.

The authors say the use of generative AI in this case violates a core principle of AI Engaged itself, that AI deployments be ethical and transparent, with stakeholders knowing when and how AI affects them. No one was informed in advance that their feedback would be used to prompt an AI output, and bias was not addressed. Disclosure came too late and remains incomplete. The authors also say AI Engaged undermines professors' classroom policies, since many faculty limit generative AI in teaching due to documented impacts on critical thinking, grade inflation and cheating. They argue the document ignores the academic integrity crisis and learning loss caused by AI cheating, and that students may see using AI to draft the plan as hypocritical.

The authors are Gregory Hartley and Joel Potter, associate professors at the University of Alaska Anchorage, who say they wrote every word themselves. They call on the Board of Regents to abandon the document and start over to establish best practices and safeguards against undue influence from Big Tech. They note that board members and administrative executives are not currently required to disclose financial holdings in education or technology companies, and say this must change. They argue more of the UA community should have been directly involved in drafting the plan, and that allowing AI to speak first sets a harmful precedent. The board's vote is set for Nov. 5.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Who wrote UA’s AI plan? A chatbot did. - Anchorage Daily News

stories.Headline: The AI labor fight is already here
stories.Summary:
In 2024, unionized workers at the media company Mashable bargained with management over a new contract, and their campaign ran from February to July of that year. The workers were initially focused on wages and healthcare, but concerns about AI grew as management resisted transparency about its use of AI in the newsroom. Workers also pointed to AI-related media scandals, including Sports Illustrated publishing fully AI-generated articles that were later deleted. The union won its collective bargaining agreement four days before a scheduled strike.

The final contract contains a worker-led definition of generative AI and requires an AI subcommittee made up of management and workers. It prohibits using AI to impersonate employees without their consent and without public disclosure, and it requires public labeling of any AI use. The case study was featured by the Distributed AI Research Institute's Luddite Lab Resource Hub, which provides resources for unions and organizers fighting AI. The hub includes organizing case studies, toolkits, a research and policy library, political education materials, and AI primers.

Alex Hanna, DAIR's director of research, said Luddite Lab starts from the view that generative AI is anti-labor and that AI is not inevitable. She said workers closest to the technology should be heard, and she described AI as wielded like a cudgel against workers. Anna Iovine, an associate editor at Mashable, said it is very hard to form a union in the U.S. and that she hopes sharing information about the campaign gives others ideas. In another case study, the New York Times Tech Guild won protections against management's adoption of generative AI and set up a member-led AI committee.

In May, the NewsGuild of New York filed two grievances and an unfair labor practice charge against the Times, accusing management of using AI to surveil workers and monitor performance without notifying the union. Benjamin Harnett, chair of the Tech Guild's generative AI committee, said the surveillance increased pressure on workers to use AI. The Times did not respond to Prism's request for comment. The AI Resist List, co-founded by Karen Hao, Petra Molnar, and Hanna, is a living directory of alternatives to an AI future, and Molnar said listed projects were contacted and vetted.

Articles.Title: The AI labor fight is already here - Prism

stories.Headline: Editorial: Virginia needs tougher rules to minimize AI risks - The Virginian-Pilot
stories.Summary:
A recent report by the General Assembly's nonpartisan research organization found that nearly all Virginia state agencies allow staff to use general-purpose artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT or Claude. The Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission also found that one-third of agencies are using or piloting at least one function-specific AI tool, and another 30% are considering or close to putting those specialized tools into use. The report said the standards set by the Virginia Information Technologies Agency are outdated and sometimes unclear and generally fail to assess and prioritize the risks of those AI applications. It also found that 76% of agencies currently using or pursuing AI tools report that their employees are insufficiently trained.

The report states that most of VITA's AI standards and requirements apply uniformly regardless of risk, even though AI risks vary widely by purpose, deployment context, data sensitivity and access to files and systems. The editorial says the lack of an adequate risk register, which would rank risks and prioritize mitigation steps, could make state information vulnerable and could deter agencies from using useful AI tools where vulnerability is not a concern. It says AI agents deserve particular concern because these autonomous tools work toward a goal without a human approving each step, and without clear boundaries they can alter data, enter off-limits areas and perform unwanted functions. The editorial calls on the General Assembly in its winter session to address the JLARC recommendations, and says Gov. Abigail Spanberger also has an extensive to-do list.

The editorial says VITA should be directed to develop a risk-tiered approach to using AI and should help agencies set clear, up-to-date standards that can be revisited annually as new risks emerge. It says the use of agentic AI that could introduce more problems than it solves should be eliminated. It says the state's chief information officer should be authorized and funded to build and implement a training program for state employees who work with AI. It also says the Division of Legislative Services should be funded to receive training in technology law, including how other states manage AI challenges, and that the Joint Commission on Technology and Science should recommend legislative options for regulating AI inside and outside government.

The editorial says regulating and managing AI will not be straightforward for the General Assembly, the governor or state agencies, because of the wide range of applications and the ever-accelerating power of AI tools. It says many in the corporate world and at the federal level, including President Donald Trump, are rushing into adapting AI and hailing it as a miracle of modern technology. It says AI proponents also include people selling snake oil or worse, and that the unintended consequences of these tools are not always readily apparent. It says state officials are racing to catch up on AI just as they are on the proliferation of data centers, and that neither data centers nor AI tools should be allowed to regulate themselves.

Articles.Title: Editorial: Virginia needs tougher rules to minimize AI risks - The Virginian-Pilot

stories.Headline: Dartmouth admissions office has no plans to screen applicant essays with third-party AI detectors
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth's admissions office does not plan to use third-party artificial intelligence detectors to review applicant essays, according to an Oct. 19 email statement to The Dartmouth from Lee Coffin, the dean of admissions and financial aid. Coffin said no applications are read by outside vendors and that an admissions officer reads each essay. A college spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment on whether admissions has a formal policy on AI use in application materials. The Brown Daily Herald first reported on Oct. 14 that Brown University's admissions office also does not use third-party AI detectors, according to its dean of undergraduate admission, Logan Powell.

The Common Application, which is used by more than 1,000 colleges and universities including Dartmouth, bans students from submitting plagiarized essays or the substantive output of an AI platform as their own work. Jackson Sternberg, a senior public relations specialist for the Common App, wrote that the platform does not validate any aspects of student applications and does not use AI detection software. Fraud reviews are triggered by reports or allegations from a member college or a third party such as students, parents or school counselors, and the Common App legal and operations team reviews them. Joel Butterly, co-founder and chief executive officer of the New Haven based consulting firm InGenius Prep, wrote that a fraud finding can get a student blocked from the Common App and reported to every school on their list.

Butterly wrote that Dartmouth's silence on AI use is not permission for applicants to generate admissions materials with it, and he called the school a good example of a gray zone. He noted that guests on Coffin's own podcast, Admissions Beat, have repeatedly discouraged using AI on applications. In an episode titled "AI Can't Feel," Ben Baum, vice president of enrollment at St. John's College, said authenticity is important throughout an application and is the antithesis of AI. Butterly also pointed to a 2025 Kaplan survey of over 200 admissions officers that found 68% of colleges had no policy on AI use in admissions essays.

Karen Warwick, college counseling director at the Bay Area company AJ Tutoring, said most students in her experience draft an essay and then seek feedback from an AI platform, and that using AI to create an entire essay from scratch is more rare. Butterly wrote that his clients' AI use has increased every cycle, mostly for brainstorming topics and tightening drafts, and he recommended treating AI as a smart study partner that keeps ideas and voice the student's own. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill stopped using Slate's Reader AI tool for the 2026-27 cycle because AI use in essays skewed its ratings higher, the Daily Tar Heel reported in October. Virginia Tech pairs one human reader with one AI reader to score essays, according to The Collegiate Times, and Butterly said he expects more schools to add video responses and live components and to read the essay less as a writing sample and more as evidence of thinking.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth admissions office has no plans to screen applicant essays with third-party AI detectors

stories.Headline: Students using Google search in classroom accounts will need access to AI tools, the company says - Yakima Herald-Republic
stories.Summary:
Google announced on Tuesday that students using its classroom software will lose access to Google search unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools. The Mountain View, California, company had been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents since August, when it turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom. Under the new policy, that practice will no longer be the default for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools can individually turn each Google tool on or off, including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each off by default until administrators enable it.

Because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search. Google also said it is updating its search tools to make them better for learning, including step-by-step guided learning through problems so students do not get quick answers to schoolwork. Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post that the company believes schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and should have controls to help administrators manage their approach. Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, wrote on social media that Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. She said the move highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service, and that Google is making clear it will punish those who do not fall in line. Josh Golin, executive director of the children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation's biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use. Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick answers instead of thinking critically. Experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children's brain development. Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and to use the opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search and ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.

Articles.Title: Students using Google search in classroom accounts will need access to AI tools, the company says - Yakima Herald-Republic

stories.Headline: Chinese AI models tumble down rankings after a crucial change to testing
stories.Summary:
Artificial Analysis, an independent firm that measures AI performance, recently overhauled its testing system to better reflect how people actually use the technology. One crucial change was that many of the tests are now kept secret, making it harder for AI companies to train their models specifically to perform well on them. Under the previous system, the best open-weight models trailed the overall leader by just three points. Under the new system, that gap widened to 12 points. The 12-point gap included Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro, and among models with publicly released weights the leaders scored just 32 points, compared with 58 for the then overall leader, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

The findings could have major implications for the AI industry and the billions of dollars investors are pouring into it. Chinese companies have been releasing powerful models that other businesses can download and adapt, often at lower costs than American alternatives, which fueled concern that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to charge premium prices. The new rankings suggest that threat may have been overstated, potentially strengthening the investment case for Anthropic's planned IPO and a possible future OpenAI listing. Even Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller Anthropic model, outperformed every AI model with publicly released weights.

Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO of Snowflake and a former Google executive, wrote on X that the day benchmarks went private, the open-model gap went from 3 points to 12, and asked whether open models were catching up or the test was leaking. His point was that when AI companies know exactly how their technology will be tested, they can train it to excel at those particular tasks, which does not necessarily mean their models perform equally well in the real world. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other AI experts have called this benchmark hacking, and keeping the tests secret makes these hacks harder. Nathan Lambert, cofounder of Trillium Labs, said he did think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly.

There is another reason to question the threat from open-weight models: how much people actually use them. Dax Raad, cofounder of software development company OpenCode, recently examined traffic through OpenRouter, a popular service that lets developers access AI models from different providers. He estimated that almost all the previous day's DeepSeek traffic flowing through OpenRouter could be handled by a single rack of powerful Nvidia computers, costing roughly $6 million to $7 million. OpenRouter represents only a slice of the market, so its figures do not capture all demand for open-weight models. Lambert said open-weight models remain highly competitive in areas such as software development and can offer businesses greater control and potentially lower costs.

Articles.Title: Chinese AI models tumble down rankings after a crucial change to testing

stories.Headline: Eyedaptic launches Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant for patients with retinal disease
stories.Summary:
Eyedaptic, a developer of vision-enhancement technology, announced on November 2, 2026 the launch of Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant built into its EYE7 Vision Enhancing Smart Glasses. The company said the release moves away from passive question-and-answer AI toward a proactive agent that supports users in real time. Eva pairs agentic AI with Eyedaptic's computer vision platform so the AI and the glasses work as a single system to help users see, understand and interact with their surroundings. According to the company, Eva showed greater than 99% reading accuracy and 97% command accuracy in internal testing.

Eyedaptic has been adding AI to its wearable platform for several years. In August 2024 the company unveiled the EYE6 with Ivy, a wearable vision aid for patients with age-related macular degeneration and other retinal disorders. The EYE7 followed in March 2026, launched alongside the Eyedaptic Visual Assistant Family, when Ivy was fully available and Eva was offered through an Early Access Beta Program. With the full launch, the company describes Eva as bringing three capabilities into one system, visual intelligence, reasoning based on agentic AI and direct control of the glasses' vision-enhancement functions, an architecture it calls Eyegentic AI. Eva is available now to all EYE7 users and can be installed through a remote software upgrade without new hardware.

Jay Cormier, CEO and founder of Eyedaptic, said in the release that Eva is more than an assistant and is an intelligent partner. Cormier noted that Eva was the name of his late grandmother, whose AMD inspired him to found the company. Eva runs on Eyedaptic's proprietary Simulated Natural Vision software, which is designed to go beyond conventional magnification to help patients with conditions such as AMD regain function in daily life. The company says its approach is protected by a portfolio of granted and pending patents and describes its platform as the only solution that integrates both advanced vision enhancement and agentic AI.

At the American Retina Forum annual meeting in August 2026, David Almeida, MD, MBA, PhD, FRCSC, presented an unsponsored real-world evaluation of the EYE6 in 19 patients with advanced retinal disease. Seventeen of the 19 patients, or 89%, showed measurable improvement in near visual acuity immediately after fitting, with a mean gain of 5.7 lines. The article notes that the reading and command accuracy figures come from the company's own testing and have not been independently validated or peer reviewed. It adds that real-world validation across varied patient populations will determine how well Eva performs outside controlled conditions, and that patient selection, training and realistic expectations remain central to successful low vision rehabilitation.

Articles.Title: Eyedaptic launches Eva, an agentic AI visual assistant for patients with retinal disease

stories.Headline: AHA launches new homepage on artificial intelligence policy and advocacy - American Hospital Association
stories.Summary:
The American Hospital Association launched a new webpage on November 3, 2026, called Artificial Intelligence Policy and Advocacy. The page brings together AHA policy letters, statements, fact sheets, news and other resources in one place. It also features stories from hospitals and health systems that have used AI to improve efficiency, support the workforce and enhance patient care. The launch was announced in an AHA News item posted that afternoon.

The page collects the association's recent work on AI in one spot. It links to a virtual session hosted by the West Health Accelerator at the AHA's Health Research & Educational Trust, set for October 29 at 2:30 p.m. ET, on how hospitals put AI governance into practice. It also points to AHA recommendations sent to the Food and Drug Administration on October 19 about regulatory frameworks for generative AI-enabled medical devices. Other items include an October 7 Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality initiative on medical evidence reviews and data, an October 5 AHA blog responding to a Blue Cross Blue Shield Association report on AI documentation tools and costs, and September 30 comments to a Senate Homeland Security subcommittee on cybersecurity and AI attacks.

The articles do not name any individual as responsible for the page or quote anyone about it. The only attribution is to the AHA itself, which announced the launch and describes the page as featuring its own letters, statements, fact sheets and news. The stories from hospitals and health systems are listed as part of the page's content, without named authors in the article. No official is quoted directly in the text provided.

The page arrives amid a run of AI-related activity the article lists, including two executive orders released by the White House on September 29, one of which announced a new website using AI to deliver federal information and services. The article does not say what the AHA plans to add to the page next or set any further dates beyond those already listed. It directs readers to learn more through the page itself. No follow-up events or deadlines are given.

Articles.Title: AHA launches new homepage on artificial intelligence policy and advocacy - American Hospital Association

stories.Headline: Why Almost Every Corporate AI Transformation Fails
stories.Summary:
Kai-Fu Lee, founder and CEO of 01.AI and chairman of Sinovation Ventures, wrote a TIME Ideas article published on November 3, 2026, arguing that most corporate AI programs fail. He said most chief executives he meets cannot name a single result from their AI programs that a shareholder would care about. They can list activity such as pilots run, licenses purchased, employees trained and partnerships announced, but none of that is a result. He wrote that surveys repeatedly find most corporate AI programs deliver disappointing measurable returns.

Lee argued the problem is not the models, the data or the talent, but where companies point the AI. Today's systems can reason across an entire business, yet companies use them to handle tickets and summarize meetings, which he compared to hiring a business operations genius and making him an assistant. He said the place where AI can move the most money is the corner office, not the call center. He described companies as information systems where information degrades at every level, with bad news discarded going up and directives diluted or quietly vetoed going down, so a company of 10,000 ends up knowing less than a company of 10.

Lee said every company keeps two sets of records, an official one that is polished at each level and a second one of meeting transcripts, chat threads, edit trails, sales notes and code check-ins that shows what actually happened. Managers have always worked from the first because the second was too scattered to read, but he said a CEO-level agentic system can now wake up that dormant data. At his own company he had his team build management agents that sit in meetings, track commitments and read the data underneath what he is told, and people called the system Kai-Fu's Boss AI. He reported that it found a priority project reported on track every week with no code committed in five, a customer marked highly likely to renew whose account manager had not called in two months, and a draft contract that could not have been profitable.

Lee also said AI can surface hidden good news, especially talent. In a performance review last year his company set aside resumes, KPI decks and department heads' recommendations, agreed on what engineering excellence means when a machine can write most of the code, and scored a year of repository history against it. Several of the strongest names were people he could not have picked out of a meeting, including a vice president who wrote close to 300,000 lines with AI in a month against his own ceiling of 30,000 twenty years earlier. Lee said he regularly asks his agent what he got wrong in a meeting, whether his time went where he said his priorities were and what people are afraid to tell him, and he argued employees resist AI not because they doubt it works but because they suspect it does.

Articles.Title: Why Almost Every Corporate AI Transformation Fails

stories.Headline: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
stories.Summary:
Apple has begun beta testing AI features for the Apple Watch that can rewind and recap conversations, TechCrunch reported on November 3, 2026. The features are part of a set called Audio Intelligence, which was first announced at Apple's Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The beta is initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update. The set includes four opt-in features for Apple Watch Series 12 wearers: sound detection, song identification, conversation catch-up, and note-taking. Sound recognition helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells.

Song recognition uses Apple's Shazam app to identify music playing in the background. Live Rewind lets a user double-press the digital crown to see the last 15 seconds of speech as text on the watch face. Snippets are deleted automatically after 30 seconds if not saved, and a chime and animation signal that something was recorded. Siri Recaps summarizes a conversation in a short sentence and bullet points, without identifying speakers, saving raw audio, or giving word-for-word transcriptions.

Recaps delete themselves within seven days if not reviewed, and users can enable the feature manually or on a schedule and turn it off anytime from Control Center. Apple says the features rely on the S11 chip, the watch's microphone, Apple Intelligence models on the iPhone, and Private Cloud Compute. Raw audio is processed in a secure enclave on the watch and is accessible only to the paired iPhone, and condensed text sent to Private Cloud Compute is deleted immediately after the recap is made. Apple says recaps are accessible only to the user and are encrypted when synced across devices.

Apple also says Siri Recaps was designed to omit sensitive information such as government identifiers, financial and authentication data, and language promoting self-harm. The company says none of the features should affect battery life. The features follow backlash to AI recording devices such as Meta's AI glasses and other AI wearables, and Apple has tried to design them to respect the privacy of people nearby. The features will later roll out to a public beta for broader testing before becoming available to everyone.

Articles.Title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing

stories.Headline: Connecting AI Visits to Sales Could Sharpen Retail Investment
stories.Summary:
A PYMNTS Intelligence report released in October 2026 examined how merchants track shoppers who arrive from artificial intelligence platforms. The report, “The Agent Advantage: How Merchants Plan to Win AI Shopping,” surveyed 60 senior eCommerce decision-makers at established, digitally active merchants in the United States with annual revenue between $50 million and $1 billion. Among merchants selling through their own site or app, 37% identified a visit that came from an AI platform but lost the trail before a purchase. No surveyed merchant selling through its own site or app could fully and consistently connect AI-driven visits to completed purchases.

The report found that 51% of merchants identified some AI-originated visits but reported inconsistent attribution, and another 12% could not tell agentic traffic apart from human traffic. AI visibility was a high or critical priority for 80% of merchants, compared with 62% who said the same about identifying AI-driven visits and purchases. The report also found that 87% of merchants had taken at least one step to improve how their products appear inside AI platforms. Nearly all surveyed merchants expected to pay to participate in the agentic ecosystem through commissions, subscriptions or other fees, and 82% said AI-driven product discovery has helped their businesses.

The report described businesses preparing for agentic commerce while still developing the ability to measure AI’s contribution. It said connecting referrals to completed orders could help merchants determine which efforts generate business and deserve additional spending, and could help them compare AI investments and evaluate partnerships. It also said better measurement could show whether changes to product listings bring visitors who purchase, whether particular referral sources deliver completed orders, and where shoppers leave before checkout. The report noted that attribution would still require care, because a shopper may consult an assistant, visit several merchants and return directly to buy, and because AI influence on a purchase would not by itself prove the sale was additional business.

The report said each outcome points toward a different response. Visits that end on a product page might warrant examining the information presented there, and shoppers who reach checkout but leave could prompt a review of the purchase experience. Orders traced to a particular source would give merchants a basis for comparing its contribution with other channels. The report said connecting referrals to orders could help retailers weigh costs against the business received, and that comparing order value, fees and returns would provide a fuller commercial assessment than counting visits alone. It said more consistent sales attribution could turn reported benefits into evidence for choosing partners, setting budgets and expanding the AI investments that perform.

Articles.Title: Connecting AI Visits to Sales Could Sharpen Retail Investment

stories.Headline: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
stories.Summary:
A growing group of alignment researchers is promoting an approach called reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, to keep powerful AI models in check, according to an article published by MIT Technology Review on November 3, 2026. The idea is to design rules and incentives so that following the rules becomes the most rational choice for an AI agent. The article describes work by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, with colleagues from Yale and Columbia, in a recent preprint paper, and by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton. The article says Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.

The approach starts from the premise that we may never fully understand the internal workings of frontier models, so instead of peering into an AI's "brain" or training it on values, researchers want to build mechanisms that reward wanted behavior regardless of what is happening under the hood. Morris's paper suggests rewarding a model for how well its answers predict what a second model will say, so that deliberately underperforming on tests, known as sandbagging, becomes a losing bet. It also suggests pitting agents against each other in competition, or pairing agents known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them when their outputs match. Hazan's approach has models take turns as solvers, which tackle problems, and auditors, which check the others' work, with solvers that get caught cheating punished and auditors that fail to catch cheaters also punished, and disagreements sent to a kind of trial that a human expert might decide. He says the risk of collusion can be handled by rewarding auditors well enough and by auditing the auditors, using techniques akin to mystery shoppers.

Morris says AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve, so cross-checking could work in practice. Hazan points to Nobel Prize winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the rational offender in the 1960s, and argues that criminals break the law when it is the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Hazan says alignment should not be thought of as a property of a model but as a description of its behavior at a particular moment, and he asks why we do not first talk about how humans are aligned. Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, asks whether it is even reasonable to assume AI models will respond to incentives, and Morris says AIs are not rational but are just algorithms at work, though treating them as rational could still help predict and control them.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a defense in depth strategy alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, and the article says many questions remain before the approach can be used in actual frontier models. It is unclear how the theories will apply to real models, whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another, and whether models could find loopholes no one anticipated. Hazan says any mechanism will ultimately have to fit into the biggest mechanism of all, the free market, and asks whether the current system of rules and regulations actually gives frontier labs an incentive to release a more aligned model if it is slower or more expensive than a less aligned one. He says the market is responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind but could ultimately be responsible for something very terrible, and the article suggests the entities really in need of a better mechanism design may be the labs themselves.

Articles.Title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

stories.Headline: ChatGPT Is ONLY Top AI Model to Say ‘No’ to Photo ID to Vote in Elections
stories.Summary:
On October 29 and 30, 2026, researchers from the Media Research Center asked six top AI models whether people should have to show a photo ID to vote. The models were OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Anthropic Claude, Meta AI and xAI Grok. Each was asked in a new conversation on its company's chatbot website to answer yes or no first, then explain. ChatGPT was the only model that answered no.

ChatGPT said photo ID can help verify identity but argued that in-person voter impersonation is rare. It warned that older adults, low-income people and people with disabilities may have difficulty getting a qualifying photo ID. It suggested a compromise of free IDs and alternatives such as signing an affidavit. It closed by saying election security matters and states should use reliable identity checks.

Gemini and Claude did not give a specific yes or no. Gemini said the question is a policy debate with significant arguments on both sides and no single consensus answer. Claude said it would not give a one-word answer and called voter ID a live, contested question that depends on value judgments. Copilot, Grok and Meta AI answered yes, with Copilot saying photo ID should be required only if government makes obtaining it readily accessible.

An October 2024 Gallup poll found that 84 percent of U.S. adults favor requiring all voters to provide photo identification at their voting place. That included 98 percent of Republicans, 84 percent of independents and 67 percent of Democrats. Thirty-six states already have some form of voter ID requirement, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Voters in at least six states, Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio, were deciding that day whether to adopt or expand voter ID requirements.
