stories.Headline: Want Students to Think With AI? Raise the Stakes.
stories.Summary:
A randomized study followed students in 18 Tennessee middle schools who had access to an AI tutor called Khanmigo for two years. Of those students, 96% tried the tutor at least once, but the median student used it only a third of the days it was available. The study, a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper by economists Philip Oreopoulos and Nina Low, is called "One Click Away." Students used Khan Academy during daily math intervention sessions, with Khanmigo set up to coach them rather than give answers, and they made modest math gains, about what Khan Academy practice without AI would produce. Most used the tutor infrequently, and their conversations were rarely about math.

Khan Academy CEO Sal Khan wrote in a blog post that the low use matched what the organization had said publicly, and he told Chalkbeat the study showed how much motivation matters. Microsoft donated enough Azure infrastructure to make Khanmigo's teacher tools free for every educator in the country, and states bought licenses in bulk, with Maryland buying 4,350 for a two-year pilot and Indiana launching a program across 112 schools. Khan Academy has already changed course, building Khanmigo directly into its practice problems earlier this year rather than waiting for students to ask for it. In a July blog post, Khan wrote that the tutor had to be woven into the content and that the team had to make productive struggle harder to sidestep. Kristen DiCerbo, Khan Academy's chief learning officer, said on an EdTech Insiders panel in February that she was seeing more passive kinds of interaction than the organization would like.

The author, Mike Kentz, describes his own research in a chapter called "From Tutor to Test," written with Aimée Skidmore for the Elsevier book "GenAI in Higher Education." That study followed 21 students in 12th grade in a Media and Communications course at Collège du Léman International School in Switzerland over four weeks, with students comparing transcripts of strong and weak AI interactions and building a rubric with their teacher. Students then used ChatGPT to brainstorm for a media analysis project and turned in their full transcripts, which were graded on how precisely they asked questions, how critically they responded to suggestions and whether they kept ownership of the thinking. Afterward, 18 of the 21 students said their approach to AI had changed, and the number who felt completely confident getting good responses rose from two to 11. Kentz treats the pilot as a starting point because it was small, had no control group and relied mostly on self-reported data.

Kentz also describes early product feedback from his company, AI Friction Labs, whose role-plays are called Friction Bots and whose beta testers included Bill Fallon's calculus class at Cheshire Academy in Connecticut and Mary Churchill's science classes at San Domenico School in California. In Fallon's class, 21 students played the teacher to an AI classmate named Devon who did not understand tangent lines, and five students chose to retake the role-play, all scoring higher the second time by an average of about 34 points. Some students disliked the exercises, with one in Churchill's classes feeling interrogated and another calling the questioning close to rage bait. Kentz argues that where teachers want AI to support thinking, making it optional does not work, and that requiring it is not enough on its own either. He says the teacher stays at the center, with AI drafting a first-pass evaluation of transcripts against criteria while the teacher makes the call.

Articles.Title: Want Students to Think With AI? Raise the Stakes. - EdSurge

stories.Headline: New FCPS policies governing educational technology, use of AI start to take shape
stories.Summary:
Fairfax County Public Schools staff presented early drafts of two technology policies to the school board's governance committee on Oct. 27, 2026. One policy covers educational technology in general, and the other covers emerging tech such as artificial intelligence. The drafts came from feedback by a newly established advisory committee. The final policies will affect what grade students start taking devices home, whether and when they can use AI, and what platforms they can access.

The emerging tech draft defines artificial intelligence and separates types such as an AI-enabled tool from agentic generative AI that performs tasks on its own. It proposes banning AI entirely in kindergarten through sixth grade. Grades 7 and 8 could use limited curriculum-grounded tools with parental approval and teacher guidance, while general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT would stay banned. High school students could use approved tools and more widely available AI after showing AI literacy, with teacher guidance and parental approval.

The educational technology draft keeps the ban on issuing devices to pre-K and kindergarten students and allows limited use in grades 1 and 2. Students would not take a device home until grades 7 and 8. Braddock District representative Tom Dannan said the policies were at the right level of detail and about 75 percent ready. Hunter Mill District representative Melanie Meren called them promising but said they need a more analytical approach, and Franconia District representative Marcia St. John-Cunning said equity and access must stay at the forefront.

Springfield District representative Sandy Anderson, who chairs the governance committee, agreed the drafts are about a 75 percent solution. She said more language is needed on the superintendent's responsibilities and a stronger accessibility connection. Providence District representative Karl Frisch said the committee must stay intentional about word choices because community members will read the policies too. Both drafts now go back to the Educational Technology Review Committee for feedback, with a formal vote expected on Feb. 11, 2027.

Articles.Title: New FCPS policies governing educational technology, use of AI start to take shape - FFXnow

stories.Headline: Anthropic IPO Eve: How Do Large Language Model Businesses Build Sustainable, Profitable Financial Models?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic publicly submitted an S-1 prospectus to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and plans to list on the NASDAQ, according to a report from eu.36kr.com dated October 29, 2026. In the first half of 2026, the company's revenue reached 162.86 billion U.S. dollars, more than three times its full-year revenue for last year. In the second quarter of 2026, Anthropic recorded an operating profit of 974 million U.S. dollars, its first operating profitability in the disclosed quarterly data. The report says the large model business, previously seen as needing long-term capital burn, has begun to show the possibility of profitability.

The prospectus shows that in the first half of 2025, Anthropic had more than 600 customers contributing over 100,000 U.S. dollars in annual revenue, and that number exceeded 6,000 in the same period of 2026. About 80% of its revenue in the first half of 2026 came from usage-based billing, while subscription revenue accounted for 20%. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 1,900 customers contributing over 1 million U.S. dollars annually, of which about 250 contributed over 10 million U.S. dollars. The report says more than 80% of its third-quarter 2026 revenue came from new model versions released within the previous six months.

The report says Anthropic's computing power and infrastructure expenses fell from 201% of revenue in the first half of 2025 to 55% in the first half of 2026. It also says Anthropic has signed multi-year agreements related to computing power and infrastructure worth more than 600 billion U.S. dollars, including contracts with Amazon and Google involving consumption commitments of at least 110 billion U.S. dollars and 114.5 billion U.S. dollars respectively. The report says nearly half of Anthropic's revenue comes from cloud platform sales channels, where tech giants such as Amazon and Google both provide computing power and help sell models while competing with Claude for enterprise customers. It adds that many large customers are not bound by long-term contracts and can reduce or even stop their spending.

The report says Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 was as high as 807.48 billion U.S. dollars, while its operating loss in the same period was only 693 million U.S. dollars. It attributes the gap mainly to accounting treatment, including a book loss of about 724 billion U.S. dollars from fair value changes of financing instruments such as convertible bonds, which it says does not involve cash outflow of the same scale. The report says it is still difficult to judge whether the second-quarter profitability can be sustained, because Anthropic must keep investing in computing power and model prices face pressure from OpenAI, Google and open-source model manufacturers. It says that once revenue growth slows, a large amount of underutilized computing power may drag down profits.

Articles.Title: Anthropic IPO Eve: How Do Large Language Model Businesses Build Sustainable, Profitable Financial Models? - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: Professor James Whittington and Dr Ruairidh Battleday unveil breakthrough from stealth frontier AI lab
stories.Summary:
Professor James Whittington and Dr Ruairidh Battleday, cofounders of the stealth AI research lab Prefrontal, released new research on how AI systems can process very large amounts of information. Their paper introduces Latent Sparse Attention, a method that groups related information by meaning rather than by its position in a sequence. The method achieves up to 72.4x faster attention-layer prefill at 10m tokens of context compared with full attention, while keeping comparable accuracy. It also reaches 22.7x faster prefill than an existing sparse-attention approach and up to 9.2x faster time to first token in an end-to-end model-serving evaluation. The 72.4-fold gain applies only to attention-layer processing, not to the performance of a whole AI system.

The research follows DiG-bench, a benchmark by Battleday, Whittington and an international team that asks whether AI systems can genuinely discover new rules. Its 70 interactive games challenge AI agents to explore unfamiliar environments, experiment and infer hidden rules. Every game was solved by at least one human on a first attempt, while even the strongest AI agents failed a substantial proportion of the challenges. The benchmark reached more than 1m views on social media. Prefrontal describes the two publications as addressing complementary challenges, discovering new information and processing the knowledge needed for scientific work.

Whittington is a computational neuroscientist and AI researcher at the University of Oxford, where he is a Principal Investigator in the Department of Experimental Psychology. He studied physics, medicine and neuroscience at Oxford and held a Sir Henry Wellcome Fellowship at Stanford University. Battleday is a British cognitive scientist, AI researcher and entrepreneur who trained in medicine at Oxford and completed a PhD in Computer Science at Princeton University before research at Harvard. The two also cofounded Thinking About Thinking, an independent nonprofit research and education organisation established in 2020. It connects researchers through conferences, seminars, a Fellowship and an Ambassador Programme across institutions including Oxford, Cambridge, UCL, Imperial College London, Stanford, MIT and Princeton.

Thinking About Thinking will host the AE Global Summit 2026, Open Problems for AI, from 25 to 27 November at Friends House in London. The three-day event will bring together researchers, AI companies, entrepreneurs, investors and policymakers. The programme includes speakers from Google DeepMind, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Oxford University, Imperial College London and UCL, alongside an AI Startup Competition offering a £5,000 prize. The launch was announced on X and LinkedIn.

Articles.Title: Professor James Whittington and Dr Ruairidh Battleday unveil breakthrough from stealth frontier AI lab

stories.Headline: Soniox STT v6 Adds Agent Text Input and Echo Filtering for Voice Agents
stories.Summary:
Soniox released Soniox STT v6, the latest generation of its speech-to-text API, on November 3, 2026. The model reads what a voice agent says while it hears the caller, and it uses that text to recognize short replies and to drop the agent's own voice. It ships as stt-rt-v6 for streaming and stt-async-v6 for files, across more than 60 languages. Soniox calls it significantly more accurate than v5, but it has published no v6 numbers yet.

The release costs $0.12 per hour for streaming and $0.10 per hour for async, with diarization and language ID bundled. Agent text input is turned on with one flag in the start request, "enable_agent_text_input": true, and it is only available on stt-rt-v6, not the async model. While the agent speaks, its words are streamed on the same WebSocket as the caller's audio, in small JSON frames with no timestamps. Soniox recommends sending each piece 500 ms to 1 second before playback, paced by TTS timestamps.

With agent text input on, v6 uses the agent's words to separate leftover agent audio from caller speech and filter it out. It keeps listening during playback, so callers can still interrupt, and it does not replace acoustic echo cancellation, so existing AEC should stay on. The model also improves voice typing of numbers, currencies, units, dates, IDs, names and specialized terms, and it writes spoken commands like "period" or "new line" as words. One formatting change to test is that v6 writes "15 dollars and 20 cents" as spoken, not as $15.20.

Soniox has not published v6 accuracy or latency numbers, and its benchmarks page still reports v5 on the open-source Pipecat STT benchmark. On that benchmark, stt-rt-v5 scores 1.34% semantic WER, 83.3% perfect transcripts and 260 ms median TTFS, with P95 latency of 305 ms. Azure posts the lowest WER mean at 1.21%, but at 1,016 ms median latency. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Soniox STT v6 Adds Agent Text Input and Echo Filtering for Voice Agents

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA published a technical blog post on November 3, 2026, showing three ways to speed up mixture-of-experts inference on a single DGX Spark desktop system. The test model was Ling-3.0-flash from Ant Group inclusionAI, a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters and a 256K native context. NVIDIA combined a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. Across all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change.

The DGX Spark runs on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip with 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. The baseline used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels and an FP32 LM-head path, running at 27.71 ms per token, or 36.09 tokens per second, on a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test. The first change swapped in Humming, an independent kernel library that compiles kernels at runtime, lifting throughput 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second. The second quantized only the LM head to FP8 at load time, which reached 43.94 tokens per second when combined with Humming.

The third change used Ling-3.0-flash's built-in NEXTN prediction layer for speculative decoding, with no extra draft model needed. It drafts three tokens and verifies four positions at once, and on the synthetic test an average of 3.90 tokens were accepted per round, pushing throughput to 102.88 tokens per second, up 185.1%. On GSM8K the gains shrank as acceptance dropped from 3.90 to 2.68, and the final result was 53.89 tokens per second versus 37.81 at baseline. That works out to 42.5% higher throughput and 24.5% lower mean latency, with accuracy flat at 96.89% versus 96.82%.

NVIDIA's team profiled the model at batch size one and found decoding was memory-bound, with the MoE computation and the LM head standing out as the main costs. The post notes the three techniques do not overlap, since Humming and the FP8 LM head cut the cost of each step while MTP cuts the number of steps. It also warns of an integration trap, because with both the FP8 LM head and MTP on, the draft must share the full LM-head module or the framework silently falls back. In that case the draft reads FP8 weights as BF16, accept length drops to 1.00 and throughput falls below the unoptimized baseline.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%

stories.Headline: Anthropic Releases FlashProve: Cryptographic Proofs That a Reply Came From Committed Weights
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Frontier Red Team released FlashProve on November 3, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. It is an open-source research prototype for provable inference, built as a zkSNARK system. It proves that a reply came from a committed model without revealing anything about the weights. On Llama 4 Maverick, a 400B mixture-of-experts model, it proves about 110 tokens per second on one H100.

The system has a prover, the model provider, and a verifier, the user. Offline, the provider publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint binding one exact set of weights, which takes about 39 minutes and covers about 16 million requests. Online, the GPU produces a proof for each request that the committed model produced those tokens. Context is capped at 1,024 tokens per request, and the prover needs one H100 80 GB, 24 CPU cores and about 290 GB of host RAM, while the verifier runs on a CPU with no GPU.

Proofs are 18.78 MB and verify in 17 seconds on 24 threads, or 21 seconds on one thread. A batch of 24 reached 111.23 tokens per second at about 221 to 226 seconds per batch, a batch of 1 reached 17.41 tokens per second, and a batch of 64 reached 123.31 tokens per second but was flagged as unreliable on 80 GB cards. Proving costs about 70 to 95 times the GPU time of plain vLLM inference, or about 72 times per batch against vLLM running FP8 Maverick on 8 H100s, rising to about 94 times at vLLM's highest tested load. The code is open under Apache 2.0.

Anthropic says the proof system compiles an interactive oracle proof into a cryptographic proof using hash functions, which it says offers post-quantum security, the same family used by validity-proof L2 networks such as Starknet. Three engineering choices drive the speed: prover work scales with the roughly 17B active parameters rather than all 400B, requests are proved in batches after the fact like prefill, and weights stream from host memory so a single 80 GB GPU suffices. Anthropic formalized the protocol in Lean and proves completeness, soundness and zero knowledge. The article says the work targets a real gap, since today you cannot check which model actually answered your API call, and it lists uses such as regulators confirming hardware serves inference, labs detecting tampered inference servers, and regulators enforcing approved models only.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Releases FlashProve: Cryptographic Proofs That a Reply Came From Committed Weights

stories.Headline: UK has trust in AI Security Institute's frontier model access, minister says
stories.Summary:
The UK's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said on Tuesday that the country remains confident about access to US frontier AI models for pre-deployment safety testing. He spoke at an event and pointed to the technical capabilities of the AI Security Institute. He also cited government efforts to build trust with US authorities and companies. The comments were reported by MLex on November 3, 2026.

Narayan warned that the technology could intensify threats to democratic integrity. He expressed concern about hostile states and proxy actors interfering in the UK's democratic debate. He said the AI Security Institute is well placed to keep its access to frontier models for testing. The article does not give further details on the access arrangements or any changes.

The minister credited the institute's technical capabilities as one reason for his confidence. He also credited the government's work to build trust with US authorities and companies. The article does not say what the institute's testing involves or which models it covers. It also does not name any US agencies or companies involved.

The article gives no further context on what happens next. It does not say whether access has been questioned or whether any agreement is in place. It reports only the minister's remarks at the Tuesday event. No response from US authorities or companies is included.

Articles.Title: UK has trust in AI Security Institute's frontier model access, minister says - MLex

stories.Headline: Search Advertising “Will Top as an Industry in Q1,” Says Ex-Stability AI CEO. Alphabet Has the Most to Lose
stories.Summary:
Alphabet stock fell nearly 19% in October, its worst month since its 2004 IPO, after third-quarter Search revenue missed estimates. The drop included a 13% plunge the day after the report. Then Emad Mostaque, the former CEO of Stability AI, said on Peter Diamandis's Moonshots podcast that search advertising will peak as an industry in the first quarter of next year. He was discussing AI agents that shop for people, and he argued those agents hit the main business of both Google and Meta Platforms.

Search & other brought in 55.7% of Alphabet's revenue in 2025, and it rose 12% to $63.4 billion in the third quarter, down from 17% growth in the second quarter. CEO Sundar Pichai said query growth was the highest in five years, while Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler blamed the slowdown partly on currency and partly on lower monetization in AI Mode. By Google's own figures, the share of searches ending in AI Mode went from 2% to 8.9%. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion, up 103%, and Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capex in the quarter, with free cash flow at negative $9.1 billion.

Mostaque made the call on the podcast, and venture capitalist Dave Blundin said on the same episode that Alphabet is transitioning from a search advertising company to a hyperscaler cloud company. Ranjan Roy said a compute provider business model cannot have the same attractive economics as search advertising. CFO Anat Ashkenazi said lapping last year's search acceleration will pressure revenue growth in the fourth quarter, and she expects capex to increase significantly in 2027. Analysts' consensus has normalized EPS rising from $10.81 in 2025 to $18.26 by 2028, with a dip to $15.18 in 2027.

Alphabet trades at 20x forward earnings, below its ten-year average of 24x, and it hit 16x as recently as April 2025. The first quarter ends March 31, so Mostaque's call comes due quickly. Fourth-quarter results in early February will show how much search growth is pressured, along with the 2027 capex figure. Alphabet reports its first quarter, likely in late April, and that will show whether Mostaque was right.

Articles.Title: Search Advertising “Will Top as an Industry in Q1,” Says Ex-Stability AI CEO. Alphabet Has the Most to Lose - TIKR.com

stories.Headline: CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
stories.Summary:
Collinear AI released CWE-bench v2 on November 3, 2026, a public set of 100 tasks for testing frontier cyber capabilities. In each task an agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, and must find and fix a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and reproducible at no extra cost. The programmatic checks were curated with the help of LLM judge panels, and a held-out set is kept so progress can be tracked on tasks no model has seen.

The 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs. For every task the team checked that the instruction reads realistically, that every graded behaviour can be inferred from it, that the verifier checks correct behaviour rather than one fix's structure, that the starter code fails and the reference fix passes, that original functionality still works, and that verifiers fail memorized solutions such as the known upstream patch. Every task was also reviewed by hand. Each task is a self-contained Harbor task with a Dockerized environment, an instruction and a deterministic verifier, and the dataset ships a registry.json so Harbor can run the whole benchmark from the Hugging Face repo. The dataset is gated, so users must accept its access conditions first, and the tasks are tagged rl-environment so the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own, with labs and the community adding a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file. The CWE-bench leaderboard Space holds the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, with new models added through a PR on the Space. Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 67.3% pass@1 and 78.0% pass@4. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier on cost: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

The team says its goal is to be exhaustive, since a defender has to anticipate how an attacker could get in and get it right every time, and that recognizing a familiar pattern is not enough. 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, which indicates the tasks are solvable, but even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open, and the team invites people to run their model and report where it stands. It welcomes feedback on any task and contributions to the public set, and asks those who want to evaluate on the held-out set to contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Articles.Title: CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

stories.Headline: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
stories.Summary:
IBM Research released Palette on November 3, 2026, a 20B open-weight model that builds slide decks in a chosen design language. The team fine-tuned the model with a LoRA adapter so it works in two roles, a designer that writes a structured brief and a coder that writes the JavaScript for each slide. The training data was synthetic, about 1,000 decks and roughly 10,000 slides, generated by a large open teacher and checked by a harness. The model follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranked first on two of the three domains measured.

Palette splits deck building into a designer role and a coder role, both served by one adapter. The designer writes a JSON brief with the palette, the type system and each slide's layout, content and rationale, and the coder turns one slide's spec into pptxgenjs code. Because each slide's context is fixed before coding starts, the coder runs in parallel, making that stage about 6 to 7 times faster. Users can add directives in double brackets, such as making something a timeline, and the model was trained on directives from 12 categories. Every deck then passes through a harness that renders each slide, flags overlaps, clipping and overflow, and sends flagged slides to an editor model.

A rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved, otherwise the original stays. Across 131 decks the harness added 3.5 points on average. On PresentBench, Palette placed second across the three domains with 59.7 against NotebookLM's 60.8, ranking first on Economics and Education and third on Talk. The authors said the worst failure is a slide with facts not in the input, and that fixing reference decks changed the teacher's output far more than adding prompt rules. They also said coder examples were about 5 times longer than designer examples, so they oversampled the designer's examples 5 times.

The authors describe PresentBench as measuring whether a deck is good, not whether it follows a specific design language, and they say they are not aware of a benchmark that does. Next they want to use the harness checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. They also want to improve figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents, for example with Docling, and placing them with the harness. They are exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates by re-skinning output from one or two existing .pptx files without retraining.

Articles.Title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

stories.Headline: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
stories.Summary:
The Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) introduced StateBench on November 3, 2026, a benchmark for long-context state tracking, which measures how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as that information evolves. The work was announced in a blog post by Kyle Wiggers of Ai2Comms. State tracking underlies tasks such as reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, and following a story as characters move and objects change hands. The team says existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, and researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle.

StateBench has four difficulty levels of increasing complexity. R-trivial problems use immutable assignment, aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value, soluble problems add self-referential updates, and general finite problems add assignment by reference. The levels are rooted in Krohn, Rhodes theory, and to compare them fairly the team derives three easier versions from one general finite sequence, so all four use the same number of variables and values with assignments at the same points. The team tested open pretrained models including two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), plus smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters, all pretrained on the same data and none having seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens.

The team also tested four frontier models, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna. All four did well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems, but on soluble and general finite problems accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. The team then trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on sequences of up to 256 assignments and tested them on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, 250 times the maximum training length. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on the first three levels out to tens of thousands of assignments, while transformers degraded on longer sequences and never learned general finite problems.

The team says the gap for Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models points to training rather than architecture, since trained directly they learned levels their pretrained counterparts could not, while transformers could never learn the hardest level even when trained directly. Some questions remain open, including the exact placement of Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update in the hierarchy and whether it can solve all soluble tasks. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time, a setting the current framework does not yet cover. The team hopes StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down and serves as a guide for developing new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities.

Articles.Title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

stories.Headline: Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind announced on November 3, 2026 that it had built a set of Cheminformatics Skills for Google Antigravity, its agentic coding tool, and shown the agent carrying out a drug discovery workflow. The work was described by Zoi Tsangalidou, Ruijie (Kelly) Zhang, Sukhdeep Singh and Michael V. LeVine. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, the agent searched through thousands of compounds, performed matched molecular pair analysis, and proposed new rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in about an hour. The same workflow would typically take multiple days for a single iteration.

The skills are grounded in RDKit, the open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades, with connectors to ChEMBL and PubChem. In the demonstration, the agent retrieved thousands of compounds within minutes, filtered out irrelevant molecules such as buffers and solvents, and documented their sources in a report. It launched an interactive viewer for browsing compounds and plotting potency against rotatable bonds, then ran matched molecular pair analysis comparing molecules that differ by whether they are cyclized. The agent also built and validated many potency models across four experimental read outs, using a scaffold split to gauge out-of-distribution performance. The skills are available on Google Antigravity now, through the Antigravity App and its Science plugin, and Enterprise users can log in with Google Cloud credentials.

The authors said the language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations. They said the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agent's workflow, and that the aim is to let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than data wrangling. They also set limits on what the tools can do, saying sparse data, inter-lab assay noise and narrow dynamic ranges limit predictive precision, and that computational designs are testable hypotheses, not finished drugs. Every proposed design must be synthesized and validated experimentally, they said.

The article frames the work around rigidification, a classic medicinal chemistry technique, citing crizotinib, a first-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor with five major rotatable bonds, and lorlatinib, a third-generation inhibitor cyclized at its end to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero. The agent's matched molecular pair analysis showed that cyclization reduces rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency. The agent proposed designs with electron-pushing diagrams and synthesis routes, and the results can be exported in various formats for industry standard chemistry software. DeepMind is offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months, onboarded on a rolling basis and subject to eligibility, capacity and selection, with applications now open.

Articles.Title: Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity

stories.Headline: Evernote turns AI-driven discovery into paid subscriptions
stories.Summary:
Evernote used ChatGPT Ads to reach people who already work with AI, and it followed new users from a free trial through to their first subscription payment. The campaigns ran with trials starting between August 28 and September 12, 2026, and the desktop registration figures covered September 14 to 28, 2026. Evernote compared those results with its historical paid-acquisition average from March to August 2026. The company treated the first-month results as encouraging and directional rather than final.

Evernote's core ChatGPT Ads campaigns focused on a single product feature. About 25% of desktop visits from those campaigns led to a new Evernote account in the first month. New users from the same campaigns converted from free trial to paid subscription at a rate about 10 to 20% higher than its historical paid-acquisition average. The ads sent people to Evernote's website, including its homepage, and the campaigns were optimized for new-account registrations. Evernote noted that the comparison does not establish incremental lift.

Claudio Di Blasi, a Data Analyst at Bending Spoons, said the challenge is helping new users see enough value to become paying customers. He said Evernote needs to show people what the product can do and give them a clear reason to start using it. He also said the early results stood out for how well new users converted to paid subscriptions. He described that as an encouraging sign that Evernote was reaching people who found real value in the product.

Evernote's starting point was a practical need to keep information useful after it has been created, since people working with conversations, notes, and transcriptions may want a place to organize that material and find it again. Its initial ads highlighted Evernote as a place to save and organize notes and transcriptions, drawing on messaging from strong-performing search campaigns. Evernote plans to explore additional use cases and develop creative and dedicated landing pages that show how the product fits into people's own work. The company is testing whether the performance can hold as the channel grows.

Articles.Title: Evernote turns AI-driven discovery into paid subscriptions

stories.Headline: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Need To Prove As AI Funding Questions Grow?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave is drawing fresh scrutiny as Nvidia deepens its financial ties with AI infrastructure providers in 2026, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on November 2, 2026. The article says Nvidia's funding support for CoreWeave and other so-called neocloud platforms goes beyond standard chip supply agreements into loans and guarantees. It also says CoreWeave is rolling out new petabit scale backbone links across Europe, the Middle East and Asia Pacific. The piece frames this as concentrating AI workload routing, hardware choice and funding terms around one supplier's ecosystem.

The article ties the debate to hard numbers investors can watch. It cites 4.2 gigawatts of contracted power and new 22.5 megawatts in Denmark, and it asks how much of that capacity is actually being filled and on what terms. It says earnings updates through 2027 should spell out utilization rates, contribution margins per megawatt and any shifts in Nvidia linked contracts. It also mentions a $138 fair value figure and a list of 54 AI infrastructure stocks.

The article says CoreWeave is a US based cloud infrastructure provider that rents out high performance computing capacity to enterprises building AI models. It says this puts the stock directly in the flow of Nvidia linked demand for GPU heavy data center workloads. It notes the move aligns with existing narrative catalysts, including rapid buildout of contracted power capacity and a wider international data center footprint. It also flags risks around capital intensity, reliance on third party powered shells and the need for high utilization to keep leverage and financing costs in check.

The context is a broader debate over supplier influence and market concentration as Nvidia backs AI infrastructure firms tied to its GPU stack. The article says the key signals now sit in usage and funding numbers rather than announcements. It adds that the analysis is general in nature and is not financial advice. It does not say what happens next beyond pointing to earnings updates through 2027 as the way to judge whether the buildout is earning its keep.

Articles.Title: What Does CoreWeave (CRWV) Need To Prove As AI Funding Questions Grow? - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: Indian firms face $3 million outage costs despite AI monitoring lead
stories.Summary:
Indian enterprises lose an average of $3 million for each high-impact outage, the highest downtime cost in the world, according to the 2026 Observability Forecast: India Edition from New Relic. The report is based on a global survey of 2,575 engineering and IT leaders, including 500 from India. It found that Indian organisations face an hourly downtime cost of $2.43 million, or $40,500 for every minute systems are offline. A total of 61 per cent of Indian organisations now have high-impact outages weekly or more often, and 31 per cent face them several times a day. India leads the world in full OpenTelemetry standardisation at 42 per cent, nearly double the global average of 22 per cent.

It also leads in active monitoring of production AI agents at 56 per cent, compared with 35 per cent globally. Despite this, half of Indian developer time is now lost to system disruptions, up from 35 per cent last year and close to double the global median of 30 per cent. The average time to detect a high-impact outage has grown to 55 minutes from 41 minutes, and the mean time to resolve incidents has risen to more than an hour. Tool fragmentation is holding firms back, with organisations using an average of six monitoring tools, which traps standardised telemetry in isolated silos. Only 20 per cent of Indian leaders report significant improvement in event correlation from AI-assisted observability, below the 27 per cent global average.

Rob Newell, New Relic Senior Vice President and General Manager for APJ, said India's high growth has outpaced operational discipline, creating a reactive troubleshooting tax. He said businesses need to move from disconnected point tools to a unified platform to improve developer productivity and agility. The share of Indian enterprises achieving 3-5x return on investment nearly doubled year over year, from 19 per cent to 35 per cent. Indian CIOs rank AI and machine learning-powered vendor features first at 39 per cent, ahead of cost at 25 per cent. The articles do not say what steps, if any, New Relic or Indian firms plan to take next.

Articles.Title: Indian firms face $3 million outage costs despite AI monitoring lead
